original_evidence.body_text:
\# Does Copper Plating Tarnish\? Corrosion and Durability of Pogo Pin Contacts

Yes\, copper plating can tarnish\, oxidize\, and eventually corrode when exposed to air\, moisture\, salts\, or other aggressive substances\. Unprotected copper may gradually turn brown\, black\, or green as its surface reacts with the surrounding environment\.

But in magnetic Pogo Pin connectors\, copper plating has an important protective application that many people overlook\.

At SUNMON Electronics\, selected magnetic connector designs use N52 neodymium\-iron\-boron \(NdFeB\) magnets protected by a Nickel–Copper–Nickel \(Ni–Cu–Ni\) coating\.

The coating consists of three successive layers\:

Inner Nickel \(Ni\) → Copper \(Cu\) → Outer Nickel \(Ni\)

The first nickel layer provides an adherent metallic foundation\, the intermediate copper layer contributes to coating continuity and surface leveling\, and the final nickel layer helps protect the copper and corrosion\-sensitive magnet underneath\.

This three\-layer structure is particularly important because N52 neodymium magnets are powerful but brittle and susceptible to corrosion if their protective coatings fail\.

In this guide\, we’ll explain why copper plating tarnishes\, what causes plated metal to rust\, why copper is covered with nickel\, and how engineers can protect magnetic Pogo Pin connectors from corrosion\, wear\, and impact damage\.

\#\# 1\. Does Copper Plating Tarnish\?

Copper is highly conductive and widely used in electronics\, but it reacts with substances in its environment\.

When exposed to oxygen\, moisture\, sulfur compounds\, or other pollutants\, copper gradually develops surface corrosion products\.

This process is commonly called copper tarnishing or copper oxidation\.

The appearance depends on the chemical reactions taking place\.

Surface Appearance \| Possible Cause \| What It Means 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Reddish\-brown \| Formation of copper\(I\) oxide \(Cu₂O\) \| Early oxidation or surface patina 
Dark brown or black \| Copper oxides and other corrosion products \| Progressive tarnishing 
Green or blue\-green \| Copper carbonates\, sulfates\, chlorides\, or other compounds \| Environmental corrosion products 
Rough or powdery deposits \| More extensive corrosion or contamination \| Requires further inspection 
Red\-orange rust near coating defects \| Corrosion of exposed iron\-containing substrate \| Potential substrate corrosion 

Copper tarnishing should not automatically be described as iron rust\.

Rust refers specifically to corrosion products associated with iron and iron\-containing materials\. Copper develops its own oxide and salt compounds\.

For example\, copper exposed to oxygen may form copper oxides\, while long\-term atmospheric exposure involving moisture\, carbon dioxide\, sulfur compounds\, or chlorides can produce different colored surface deposits\.

Green corrosion products may include basic copper carbonates\, but they may also consist of copper sulfates or chlorides\, depending on environmental conditions\.

The Canadian Conservation Institute’s guidance on recognizing active corrosion provides useful examples of how copper corrosion differs from the corrosion of other metals\.

\#\#\# Why This Matters in Magnetic Pogo Pin Connectors

In SUNMON’s Ni–Cu–Ni\-coated neodymium magnets\, the copper layer is normally not exposed to air\.

Instead\, it is protected beneath the final nickel layer\.

This is an important distinction\.

The purpose of the coating system is not simply to prevent the copper from changing color\. It is to keep moisture and corrosive substances away from the underlying NdFeB magnet\.

If the outer nickel layer remains continuous and the entire coating is properly manufactured\, it reduces exposure of the intermediate copper and the magnet substrate\.

However\, scratches\, pinholes\, poor adhesion\, and mechanical damage can compromise that protection\.

\#\# 2\. Why Does Copper Plating Rust or Corrode\? Four Main Causes

Copper\-plated components may develop discoloration\, corrosion\, or even red rust\, depending on the substrate and the exposure conditions\.

Understanding the cause is essential because surface copper oxidation and corrosion of the underlying metal require different solutions\.

\#\#\# 2\.1 Damaged Plating or High Coating Porosity

One common cause of corrosion is an incomplete protective coating\.

If a copper coating is too thin\, has excessive porosity\, or contains scratches that penetrate through the layer\, the underlying substrate may become exposed\.

Typical coating defects include\:

\- Pinholes formed during electroplating\.
\- Inadequate coating thickness\.
\- Scratches caused by handling or assembly\.
\- Poor coating coverage around sharp edges\.
\- Cracks caused by mechanical impact\.
\- Localized adhesion failures\.

When moisture reaches the substrate through these defects\, corrosion may begin\.

For a copper coating deposited over iron or steel\, the exposed substrate may form a galvanic couple with the surrounding copper when an electrolyte is present\.

Because copper is generally more noble than iron\, the exposed iron can become the anodic region and corrode preferentially\.

This effect can become particularly severe when a small area of exposed substrate is surrounded by a relatively large coated surface\.

The phenomenon is described in scientific research on the porosity and corrosion resistance of deposited metal coatings\.

What happens in an N52 magnet\?

SUNMON’s magnetic connectors use NdFeB magnets rather than ordinary steel as the magnetic material\.

Nevertheless\, the same general engineering concern applies\: a defect in a more corrosion\-resistant coating can expose a much more reactive substrate\.

When moisture reaches vulnerable phases within the NdFeB material\, localized corrosion may accelerate\.

This is why coating continuity\, edge coverage\, and surface quality are critical in magnetic connector manufacturing\.

\#\#\# 2\.2 Corrosion of the Base Metal Beneath the Plating

Another important failure mechanism occurs when corrosion begins beneath a coating\.

For copper\-plated steel\, moisture entering through a damaged area can cause the iron substrate to rust\.

Iron corrosion products generally occupy more volume than the metal consumed during the reaction\.

As corrosion progresses\, the expanding products can exert stress beneath the coating\.

This may cause\:

\- Blistering\.
\- Localized swelling\.
\- Coating delamination\.
\- Cracking or peeling\.
\- Further moisture penetration\.
\- Accelerated substrate deterioration\.

The same broad failure pattern can occur in coated neodymium magnets\, although the exact corrosion chemistry differs from ordinary steel\.

NdFeB corrosion products may accumulate beneath defective coatings\, creating internal stress and damaging the protective layers\.

Once corrosion penetrates beneath the coating\, the problem can spread beyond the original defect\.

As K\&J Magnetics explains in its investigation of magnet corrosion\, neodymium magnets can lose magnetic performance as corrosion damages the underlying material\.

For precision magnetic connectors\, coating blistering should therefore be treated as a potential sign of substrate damage\, not merely a cosmetic defect\.

\#\#\# 2\.3 Oxidation of the Copper Layer Itself

Even when the substrate remains protected\, an exposed copper layer can still tarnish\.

Copper reacts with substances such as oxygen\, water vapor\, and atmospheric contaminants\.

Depending on environmental conditions\, it may form\:

Copper\(I\) oxide \(Cu₂O\)\: Often associated with a reddish or brown surface appearance\.

Copper\(II\) oxide \(CuO\)\: Typically dark or black\.

Basic copper carbonates\: May contribute to green patina under suitable atmospheric conditions\.

Copper sulfates or chlorides\: May form in environments containing sulfur compounds or chlorides\.

The chemical composition of a green copper patina cannot be reliably identified from color alone\.

The Smithsonian Museum Conservation Institute references research demonstrating how atmospheric pollutants and coastal exposure influence copper corrosion products\.

For precision components\, copper oxidation matters because it can affect surface appearance\, coating integrity\, and\, when copper is used as a contact surface\, electrical contact behavior\.

However\, a stable surface patina and active localized corrosion are not the same thing\.

The severity of the problem depends on the actual material condition and application requirements\.

\#\#\# 2\.4 Environmental Corrosion\: Humidity\, Salt\, and Pollution

The surrounding environment strongly influences corrosion\.

High humidity\, condensation\, dissolved salts\, industrial pollutants\, and aggressive cleaning chemicals can all increase the risk of coating deterioration\.

Particularly demanding environments include\:

Coastal environments\: Airborne chlorides and moisture can promote localized corrosion\.

Wearable electronics\: Sweat contains salts and other compounds that may affect exposed metal surfaces\.

Outdoor docking stations\: Rain\, condensation\, temperature fluctuations\, and contamination can challenge coating integrity\.

Industrial equipment\: Chemical vapors\, cleaning agents\, and airborne particles may damage protective surfaces\.

A coating that works well in a dry indoor environment may perform differently in a device frequently exposed to sweat or saltwater\.

For this reason\, plating selection should always consider actual operating conditions rather than appearance alone\.

\#\#\# Summary\: Why Copper\-Plated Components Corrode

Corrosion Cause \| Failure Mechanism \| Potential Consequence 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Thin or porous plating \| Moisture reaches the substrate through defects \| Localized substrate corrosion 
Scratches or impact damage \| Protective barrier is broken \| Exposed copper or base metal 
Base\-metal corrosion \| Corrosion products accumulate beneath coating \| Blistering\, peeling\, cracking 
Copper oxidation \| Copper reacts with its surroundings \| Brown\, black\, or green discoloration 
Humidity and salt exposure \| Electrochemical corrosion accelerates \| Reduced coating durability 

These failure mechanisms explain why copper plating alone is not always a sufficient final protective finish\.

For corrosion\-sensitive components such as sintered NdFeB magnets\, a carefully designed multilayer coating provides a more suitable protection strategy\.

\#\# 3\. Why Is Nickel Plated Over Copper to Prevent Oxidation\?

Nickel plating over copper provides an additional protective surface that reduces direct exposure of the copper layer to air\, moisture\, and corrosive contaminants\.

This is one of the key reasons a Ni–Cu–Ni coating is used on many neodymium magnets\.

The protective benefit comes from the complete coating structure\, rather than the copper layer alone\.

\#\#\# 3\.1 Nickel Provides a More Protective Exterior

Copper can oxidize relatively easily when exposed\.

Nickel also reacts with its environment\, but it can form a relatively stable surface film that helps limit further corrosion under suitable conditions\.

When a properly deposited nickel layer covers copper\, the nickel becomes the exposed surface\.

This reduces direct contact between copper and the surrounding atmosphere\.

Consequently\, copper tarnishing is less likely as long as the protective nickel remains intact\.

\#\#\# 3\.2 Nickel Reduces Moisture Access to the Copper Layer

A continuous nickel coating provides a physical barrier between the environment and the intermediate copper\.

In a properly manufactured multilayer system\, the coating structure helps limit pathways through which moisture can reach the substrate\.

However\, the effectiveness depends on\:

\- Nickel coating thickness\.
\- Coating density and porosity\.
\- Surface preparation\.
\- Adhesion between layers\.
\- Coverage around edges and corners\.
\- Absence of damage during assembly\.
\- Actual environmental exposure\.

A nickel coating with through\-pores or cracks cannot provide the same protection as an intact\, properly qualified coating\.

\#\#\# 3\.3 Multiple Layers Can Improve Coating Continuity

One potential advantage of using three deposited layers instead of a single metal layer is that defects in one layer may not align directly with defects in the next\.

A well\-designed multilayer structure can therefore reduce continuous corrosion pathways\.

The intermediate copper layer also provides a relatively ductile metallic deposit that can contribute to leveling and coating integrity\.

A peer\-reviewed study published in Applied Surface Science in August 2026\, Electroplated Ni\/Cu\/Ni Coatings on Sintered Nd\-Fe\-B Magnets\, investigated the role of individual coating layers\.

The researchers reported that coating\-layer structure and deposition conditions influenced porosity and corrosion resistance\, with the outer nickel layer playing a particularly important protective role\.

The results support the use of a carefully controlled multilayer structure rather than relying on exposed copper alone\.

\#\#\# 3\.4 Does Nickel Plating Completely Prevent Copper Oxidation\?

Not under all conditions\.

Nickel plating significantly improves protection when properly applied\, but it is not an absolute guarantee against corrosion\.

If the outer nickel is scratched\, worn through\, poorly adhered\, or contains connected pores\, the underlying copper may become exposed\.

In saltwater or other aggressive environments\, this exposure can lead to localized corrosion and eventually damage the magnet substrate\.

Therefore\, the engineering objective is to minimize the pathways through which corrosive substances can reach vulnerable layers\, not to claim that the coating can never corrode\.

\#\# 4\. How Does SUNMON’s Ni–Cu–Ni Plating Protect N52 Neodymium Magnets\?

SUNMON uses N52 NdFeB magnets with Ni–Cu–Ni plating in selected magnetic Pogo Pin connector products\.

The protective structure consists of three successive electroplated layers\.

\#\#\# Layer 1\: Inner Nickel — Adhesion Foundation

The first nickel layer is deposited onto the prepared magnet surface\.

Its main functions are to establish an adherent metallic coating\, provide initial protection\, and support the subsequent copper layer\.

The magnet must undergo appropriate surface preparation to achieve reliable adhesion\.

Poor cleaning or activation may result in weak bonding\, defects\, or early coating separation\.

\#\#\# Layer 2\: Copper — Intermediate Protective Layer

The copper layer is deposited over the first nickel coating\.

Copper is more ductile than the sintered NdFeB magnet\.

As an intermediate layer\, it can contribute to surface leveling\, coating continuity\, and the overall corrosion\-resistance performance of the multilayer system\.

However\, copper is not intended to remain exposed as the final outer coating\.

\#\#\# Layer 3\: Outer Nickel — Final Protective Surface

The final nickel layer covers the copper\.

It acts as the main exposed protective metal coating and reduces contact between the intermediate copper layer and environmental contaminants\.

It also contributes to surface durability during normal handling and assembly\.

The protective structure can be summarized as follows\:

Layer \| Material \| Primary Role 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Base material \| N52 NdFeB magnet \| Magnetic attraction and alignment 
First coating \| Nickel \| Adhesion foundation and initial protection 
Intermediate coating \| Copper \| Leveling\, ductility\, and multilayer continuity 
Outer coating \| Nickel \| Exterior corrosion protection and surface durability 

\#\#\# Why Not Use Copper Plating Alone\?

An exposed copper coating may tarnish and develop corrosion products over time\.

A single copper layer can also be vulnerable to scratches\, pinholes\, and inadequate coverage\.

By applying an outer nickel layer\, the coating system gains an additional barrier against environmental exposure\.

For corrosion\-sensitive N52 magnets\, this is generally more appropriate than leaving copper exposed\.

It is important to distinguish the protective roles of the different layers and verify their performance through coating inspection and application\-specific testing\.

\#\# 5\. Does Copper Plating Wear Off\?

Yes\. Copper plating can wear off due to repeated friction\, abrasion\, poor adhesion\, or mechanical impact\.

All metallic coatings have finite thickness\.

Whether wear causes a problem depends on the contact conditions and whether the coating is intended to be a functional sliding surface\.

\#\#\# Abrasive Wear

If a copper\-plated part repeatedly rubs against another surface\, material may gradually be removed\.

Abrasive particles\, sharp edges\, or high contact pressure can accelerate this process\.

\#\#\# Mechanical Impact

Strong impacts can crack or deform a coating and may damage the substrate underneath\.

This is particularly important for brittle neodymium magnets\.

\#\#\# Poor Adhesion

Improper surface preparation or plating conditions may result in weak adhesion\.

Under mechanical stress\, the coating can peel\, blister\, or separate\.

\#\#\# Corrosion\-Assisted Wear

When a coating is already damaged\, moisture may enter exposed areas\.

Corrosion can then weaken the remaining protective layers and cause further deterioration\.

For Ni–Cu–Ni\-coated magnets\, the intermediate copper layer is normally protected by the outer nickel\.

Therefore\, engineers should evaluate the durability of the entire coating system\, not copper abrasion alone\.

\#\# 6\. How Durable Is Copper Plating\, and How Long Does It Last\?

Copper plating does not have a universal service life\.

Its durability depends on the substrate\, coating thickness\, adhesion\, surface exposure\, and the conditions in which the product operates\.

For a Ni–Cu–Ni\-coated N52 magnet\, additional factors include magnet geometry\, housing protection\, magnetic force\, and repeated mechanical loading\.

\#\#\# Factors Affecting Coating Life

Factor \| Influence on Durability 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Plating thickness \| Affects coating continuity and tolerance to wear 
Adhesion \| Poor adhesion increases peeling risk 
Porosity \| Connected pores can allow moisture penetration 
Humidity \| Can accelerate corrosion 
Salt exposure \| Increases the risk of localized electrochemical attack 
Magnet collision \| May crack plating or fracture the substrate 
Edge geometry \| Sharp corners may be more vulnerable to damage 
Housing protection \| Helps reduce exposure and impact 
Mating frequency \| Influences long\-term mechanical loading 

\#\#\# How Long Does Copper Plating Last on a Magnet\?

A well\-manufactured and protected multilayer coating may remain functional for many years under suitable conditions\.

However\, there is no reliable universal lifetime that applies to every Ni–Cu–Ni\-coated magnet\.

For example\, a magnetic charging connector used occasionally in a dry indoor environment may have very different corrosion and wear risks from a connector installed on a marine device\.

Service life should therefore be evaluated according to the intended environment and qualification requirements\.

A connector rated for 10\,000 mating cycles does not automatically have a guaranteed ten\-year corrosion life\.

Mating durability and corrosion resistance are separate performance characteristics\.

\#\# 7\. Will Copper Plating Corrode in Brine Water\?

Yes\. Exposed copper plating can corrode in brine water\, especially when the environment contains high concentrations of dissolved salts\.

Brine water generally contains salts such as sodium chloride\.

These salts increase the conductivity of the water and can promote electrochemical corrosion\.

\#\#\# How Saltwater Attacks Damaged Coatings

If a nickel\-plated magnet has a crack or pinhole\, chloride\-containing water may penetrate the protective layers\.

Once it reaches a vulnerable surface\, localized corrosion can begin\.

If the NdFeB substrate is exposed\, corrosion may spread beneath the coating\.

This can lead to blistering\, peeling\, or structural deterioration\.

\#\#\# Does Ni–Cu–Ni Plating Make a Magnet Waterproof\?

No\.

Ni–Cu–Ni is primarily a corrosion\-protection coating\.

It should not automatically be considered a waterproof encapsulation system\.

A coated magnet may resist humidity and moderate environmental exposure while still being unsuitable for continuous saltwater immersion\.

K\&J Magnetics provides practical examples in its saltwater corrosion investigation of neodymium magnet coatings\.

The results demonstrate that corrosion behavior varies with coating type\, surface damage\, and exposure conditions\.

\#\#\# What About Outdoor Magnetic Connectors\?

For magnetic connectors exposed to rain\, sweat\, condensation\, or coastal conditions\, engineers should consider additional protective measures\.

These may include recessed magnets\, protective housings\, sealing materials\, encapsulation\, and corrosion\-resistant coating specifications\.

For outdoor applications\, see SUNMON’s guide to Waterproof Magnetic Connectors\: IP65 vs\. IP67 vs\. IP68\.

A corrosion\-resistant magnet coating alone does not establish an IP waterproof rating\.

Ingress protection must be evaluated at the assembly or device level\.

\#\# 8\. Why Do Strong N52 Magnets Break Easily\?

Corrosion protection is only one part of magnetic connector reliability\.

Another important concern is the mechanical brittleness of N52 neodymium magnets\.

N52 magnets provide strong magnetic attraction relative to their size\, making them useful for compact electronic connectors\.

However\, sintered NdFeB is a brittle material\.

It cannot absorb large impacts in the same manner as a ductile metal\.

\#\#\# High Magnetic Strength Does Not Mean High Mechanical Toughness

A magnet may provide excellent magnetic retention while remaining susceptible to cracking\.

When two strong magnets approach each other\, their magnetic attraction accelerates the mating components\.

If the magnets collide directly\, the resulting impact can damage the material\.

Potential failures include\:

\- Chipped edges\.
\- Surface cracks\.
\- Fractures beneath the coating\.
\- Coating delamination\.
\- Loose magnetic fragments\.
\- Corrosion developing around damaged areas\.

\#\#\# Why SUNMON Considers Magnet\-to\-Magnet Clearance

For magnetic connector designs where strong attraction could create damaging impacts\, SUNMON considers structural methods to prevent the magnets from colliding directly\.

One approach is to recess the magnets within the connector housing\.

Mechanical shoulders or housing stops establish the final mating position\, leaving a controlled distance between the opposing magnet surfaces\.

This clearance helps reduce direct impact loading on the brittle magnets\.

\#\#\# Why the Clearance Must Be Carefully Controlled

A larger distance between magnets generally reduces attractive force\.

Therefore\, the designer must balance magnetic retention against impact protection\.

Too little protection may increase the risk of magnet damage\.

Too much separation may reduce retention force and docking stability\.

The optimal geometry depends on magnet dimensions\, magnetic polarity\, housing configuration\, assembly tolerances\, and the required holding force\.

There is no universal magnet clearance suitable for every connector\.

The selected design must also allow the electrical Pogo Pins to compress to their specified working height\.

The magnet clearance and electrical contact compression are different design requirements\.

For a more detailed engineering discussion\, see SUNMON’s Magnetic Pogo Pin Connector Design Guide\.

\#\# 9\. How to Protect Copper Plating and Ni–Cu–Ni\-Coated Magnets

Reliable corrosion protection requires a combination of coating quality\, suitable component design\, and environmental control\.

\#\#\# 9\.1 Use an Appropriate Multilayer Coating

For many standard magnetic connector applications\, a properly manufactured Ni–Cu–Ni coating provides a practical protective structure\.

The coating should be selected and validated according to the actual operating environment\.

\#\#\# 9\.2 Control Plating Thickness and Porosity

Ensure that the coating specification defines the required thickness\, surface quality\, and inspection criteria\.

Critical edges\, holes\, and corners should receive adequate attention\.

\#\#\# 9\.3 Prevent Scratches and Direct Magnet Collisions

Use appropriate assembly handling\, protective housings\, recessed magnets\, and mechanical stops where needed\.

Avoid allowing strong magnets to snap together uncontrollably\.

\#\#\# 9\.4 Reduce Exposure to Moisture and Salt

Where possible\, prevent direct contact between the magnet and water\, sweat\, cleaning chemicals\, or other corrosive substances\.

Applications involving outdoor exposure should consider additional sealing\.

\#\#\# 9\.5 Inspect Coating Integrity

Examine plated magnets for scratches\, discoloration\, blistering\, peeling\, and other visible defects\.

Any sign of coating separation may require further evaluation\.

\#\#\# 9\.6 Validate Environmental Performance

Perform suitable environmental and mechanical tests based on the actual application\.

Relevant testing may include salt spray exposure\, humidity evaluation\, impact testing\, coating inspection\, and repeated connector mating\.

For high\-reliability products\, the entire connector assembly should be evaluated rather than relying only on magnet coating data\.

\#\# 10\. Magnet Plating vs\. Pogo Pin Contact Plating

In a magnetic connector\, the magnet and Pogo Pin contacts perform different functions\.

The magnets provide attraction and alignment\.

The Pogo Pins transmit electrical power or signals\.

Their plating specifications should therefore be evaluated separately\.

\#\#\# Ni–Cu–Ni Plating for N52 Magnets

The purpose of this coating is primarily to protect the corrosion\-sensitive NdFeB material\.

The nickel and copper layers work together as a multilayer protective structure\.

\#\#\# Nickel and Gold Plating for Pogo Pin Contacts

Pogo Pin contacts commonly use a nickel underlayer with gold plating on the contact surface\.

Nickel helps limit copper migration into the gold coating and supports the plating structure\.

Gold provides oxidation resistance and helps maintain stable electrical contact performance\.

For further details\, read SUNMON’s Nickel Plating for Electronic Connectors and Gold Plating Thickness for Pogo Pins\.

\#\#\# Comparison of Magnet and Contact Plating

Feature \| N52 Magnet \| Pogo Pin Electrical Contact 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Typical coating \| Ni–Cu–Ni \| Nickel \+ Gold 
Main objective \| Corrosion protection \| Electrical contact reliability 
Base material \| NdFeB \| Copper alloy or other approved conductive material 
Primary risk \| Rust\, coating damage\, magnet cracking \| Oxidation\, contact wear\, resistance increase 
Key mechanical concern \| Brittle fracture \| Compression\, contact force\, mating wear 
Relevant testing \| Corrosion\, plating integrity\, impact \| Contact resistance\, plating thickness\, mating cycles 

A reliable magnetic connector requires both systems to perform properly\.

Better magnet coating does not compensate for poor Pogo Pin contact design\.

Likewise\, gold plating on the Pogo Pins cannot prevent corrosion of a damaged NdFeB magnet\.

\#\# 11\. How Can Engineers Verify Ni–Cu–Ni Coating Quality\?

Visual appearance alone is not sufficient to determine coating quality\.

A plated magnet can appear smooth and bright while still containing defects that affect long\-term corrosion resistance\.

\#\#\# Coating Thickness Inspection

Coating thickness should be evaluated using a measurement method appropriate for the substrate and layer structure\.

X\-ray fluorescence \(XRF\) may be useful for suitable multilayer coatings\.

Cross\-sectional analysis may also be used when individual layers and coating boundaries need to be examined\.

\#\#\# Adhesion Evaluation

Adhesion testing helps identify weak bonding between the coating and substrate\.

The appropriate method should be selected according to part geometry and the applicable coating specification\.

\#\#\# Surface and Edge Inspection

Microscopic inspection can help identify pinholes\, cracks\, incomplete coverage\, and coating damage\.

Edges deserve special attention because geometric features may affect plating distribution and mechanical durability\.

\#\#\# Salt Spray Testing

Salt spray tests are commonly used to compare corrosion resistance under controlled laboratory conditions\.

Important reference methods include\:

These methods provide controlled test conditions\.

They do not independently establish universal pass\/fail criteria or predict a fixed service lifetime\.

A 48\-hour salt spray specification must therefore be interpreted together with the product requirements\, inspection criteria\, and test results\.

\#\#\# Connector\-Level Durability Testing

Mechanical cycling\, magnetic retention\, electrical contact resistance\, and environmental exposure should also be evaluated\.

In some cases\, impact damage may create coating cracks even when the plating process itself is satisfactory\.

For N52 magnetic connectors\, mechanical design and plating integrity should be reviewed together\.

\#\# 12\. Real SUNMON Magnetic Pogo Pin Connector Examples

SUNMON product specifications illustrate how N52 magnets\, Ni–Cu–Ni coating\, gold\-plated electrical contacts\, and environmental requirements are combined in practical connector designs\.

\#\#\# Example 1\: 903\-00025 \/ 903\-00067 — 2Pin Magnetic Connector

This connector series is designed for compact charging and docking applications\.

Published specifications include\:

Parameter \| Specification 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Contact count \| 2Pin 
Electrical rating \| DC 5V \/ 1A 
Magnet \| N52 NdFeB 
Magnet coating \| Ni–Cu–Ni 
Pogo Pin coating \| 0\.125 μm gold 
Contact resistance \| 50 mΩ maximum per pin 
Mechanical life \| 10\,000 cycles minimum 
Salt spray test \| 24 hours 

The N52 magnets provide magnetic alignment and retention\, while the Ni–Cu–Ni layers help protect the magnets\.

The gold\-plated Pogo Pins provide the electrical connection\.

\#\#\# Example 2\: 904\-00020 \/ 903\-00015 — 8Pin Magnetic Connector

This connector pair provides eight electrical contact positions for charging and signal applications\.

Published specifications include\:

Parameter \| Specification 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Contact count \| 8Pin 
Electrical rating \| DC 12V \/ 1A maximum 
Magnet \| N52 NdFeB 
Magnet coating \| Ni–Cu–Ni 
Pogo Pin coating \| 0\.25 μm gold 
Contact resistance \| 50 mΩ maximum at working height 
Ingress protection specification \| IP65 
Magnet salt spray requirement \| 48 hours 
Female Pogo Pin salt spray requirement \| 72 hours 

These specifications illustrate why magnet protection and electrical contact protection are evaluated separately\.

The magnet coating must address corrosion sensitivity\, while the Pogo Pin plating must support stable electrical contact\.

For further details\, explore the 904\-00020 \/ 903\-00015 8Pin Magnetic Connector\.

The published test requirements apply to the specified product configurations and should not be generalized to every SUNMON connector\.

\#\# 13\. Common Signs of Magnet Plating Failure

When a magnetic connector develops corrosion\, discoloration\, or unreliable operation\, engineers should identify the underlying failure mechanism before selecting a corrective action\.

Observed Symptom \| Possible Cause \| Recommended Investigation 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Copper\-colored exposure \| Outer nickel coating worn through \| Check coating thickness and surface damage 
Dark surface discoloration \| Tarnishing\, contamination\, or oxidation \| Identify the affected coating material 
Green deposits \| Possible copper corrosion compounds \| Inspect for moisture and exposed copper 
Rust\-colored deposits \| Possible substrate or adjacent ferrous\-material corrosion \| Locate the source of corrosion 
Coating blistering \| Corrosion beneath the coating or adhesion failure \| Inspect coating interfaces and substrate condition 
Magnet chipping \| Mechanical impact \| Review magnet clearance and housing stops 
Reduced magnetic holding force \| Gap changes\, damage\, or alignment problems \| Test magnetic retention in the assembled connector 
Intermittent charging \| Contact contamination\, wear\, or insufficient compression \| Measure Pogo Pin contact resistance 

A damaged coating should not be repaired simply by polishing the visible surface\.

Where corrosion has spread beneath a multilayer coating\, replacement and further engineering evaluation may be necessary\.

For repeated failures\, the investigation should include coating specifications\, assembly conditions\, environmental exposure\, and mechanical design\.

\#\# 14\. Frequently Asked Questions

\#\#\# Does copper plating tarnish\?

Yes\. Exposed copper plating can tarnish when it reacts with oxygen\, moisture\, sulfur compounds\, or other environmental contaminants\. The surface may turn brown\, black\, or green depending on the corrosion products formed\.

\#\#\# Why does copper plating sometimes appear to rust\?

Copper itself does not produce iron rust\. When a copper coating is applied over an iron\-containing substrate\, scratches or pores may allow the substrate to corrode\. In NdFeB magnets\, defects in the protective coating can also expose corrosion\-sensitive material and lead to rust\-colored deposits or coating deterioration\.

\#\#\# Why is nickel plated over copper\?

Nickel plating provides an additional exterior barrier that reduces exposure of the copper layer to the environment\. In Ni–Cu–Ni\-coated magnets\, the outer nickel layer helps limit copper oxidation and protect the NdFeB substrate from moisture and corrosion\.

\#\#\# Does nickel plating completely prevent copper oxidation\?

No\. Nickel improves corrosion resistance when the coating is continuous and properly applied\, but cracks\, pores\, abrasion\, or aggressive environments can compromise its protective performance\.

\#\#\# Does copper plating wear off\?

Yes\. Copper plating can be removed through repeated abrasion\, friction\, or mechanical damage\. In a Ni–Cu–Ni coating\, the copper layer is normally protected by the outer nickel layer\.

\#\#\# How durable is copper plating\?

Durability depends on coating thickness\, adhesion\, environmental exposure\, mechanical loading\, and the complete coating structure\. For neodymium magnets\, the durability of the Ni–Cu–Ni system matters more than the copper layer alone\.

\#\#\# How long does copper plating last\?

There is no universal lifetime\. A properly protected copper layer can remain functional for many years under suitable conditions\, but scratches\, humidity\, salt exposure\, and coating defects may shorten its service life\.

\#\#\# How does copper plating prevent corrosion\?

Copper can contribute to corrosion resistance when used as part of a properly designed multilayer coating\. In a Ni–Cu–Ni system\, it acts as an intermediate layer that supports the protective structure\. Exposed copper alone should not be regarded as a complete corrosion barrier\.

\#\#\# Will copper plating corrode in brine water\?

Yes\. Exposed copper plating can corrode in chloride\-containing water\. A Ni–Cu–Ni\-coated magnet offers additional protection\, but coating defects may allow saltwater to reach the substrate\.

\#\#\# How can copper plating be protected from oxidation\?

A suitable nickel topcoat\, effective coating thickness\, controlled porosity\, careful handling\, and protection from moisture can reduce oxidation risk\. In highly corrosive environments\, additional sealing or encapsulation may be necessary\.

\#\#\# Why does SUNMON use N52 magnets\?

N52 NdFeB magnets provide strong magnetic attraction in a compact size\, supporting alignment and retention in magnetic Pogo Pin connectors\. Their corrosion sensitivity and brittleness require suitable surface protection and mechanical design\.

\#\#\# Why should powerful magnets have clearance when mating\?

A controlled magnet\-to\-magnet clearance can help prevent direct impact between brittle magnets\. Mechanical stops and recessed magnet positioning may reduce chipping or fracture\, provided that sufficient magnetic holding force and correct Pogo Pin compression are maintained\.

\#\#\# Is Ni–Cu–Ni magnet plating the same as nickel and gold plating on Pogo Pins\?

No\. Ni–Cu–Ni primarily protects the magnet from corrosion\, while nickel and gold plating on electrical contacts supports stable conductivity and contact durability\.

\#\#\# Can Ni–Cu–Ni\-coated magnets be used underwater\?

They should not automatically be considered suitable for continuous immersion\. Water exposure requirements must be evaluated at the complete assembly level\, with appropriate coating\, sealing\, and qualification testing\.

\#\# 15\. Conclusion\: Why Copper Plating Needs Nickel Protection in Magnetic Connectors

Copper plating can tarnish and corrode when exposed to moisture\, oxygen\, salts\, and environmental contaminants\.

In plated components\, corrosion may also originate from scratches\, connected pores\, inadequate coating thickness\, or deterioration of the underlying substrate\.

When the base material corrodes beneath a coating\, expanding corrosion products may cause blistering\, cracking\, and peeling\.

For corrosion\-sensitive N52 neodymium magnets\, relying on an exposed copper coating is therefore not always appropriate\.

SUNMON uses a Nickel–Copper–Nickel \(Ni–Cu–Ni\) coating structure in selected magnetic connector designs\.

The inner nickel layer establishes a protective foundation\, the intermediate copper layer contributes to the multilayer coating structure\, and the outer nickel layer helps protect the copper and magnet from environmental exposure\.

This structure improves corrosion resistance but does not make the magnet indestructible or completely waterproof\.

Because N52 magnets are mechanically brittle\, reliable connector design must also consider magnet\-to\-magnet clearance\, impact protection\, appropriate housing geometry\, and correct Pogo Pin compression\.

Long\-term magnetic connector reliability depends on combining suitable material selection\, multilayer plating\, mechanical protection\, and application\-specific testing\.

Need a magnetic connector that balances corrosion protection\, strong magnetic retention\, and reliable electrical contact\?

records.body_text:
PECC Summit: Coherent Sees Chip-to-Chip Optics as the Next Frontier
Coherent CTO Dr. Julie Eng outlines coexisting pluggable, CPO and NPO architectures and a longer-term path to optical compute-and-memory connectivity.
Optical connectivity is moving progressively closer to the compute core, with chip-to-chip links and new memory architectures emerging as the next frontier after optical scale-up networks, according to Dr. Julie Sheridan Eng, EVP, Optical Components and Chief Technology Officer at Coherent. Speaking at PECC Summit on October 20, Eng outlined a future in which pluggable transceivers, co-packaged optics (CPO) and near-packaged optics (NPO) coexist, with different technologies addressing distinct requirements for reach, power, bandwidth density and serviceability.
Eng traced that progression from long-haul telecommunications through enterprise and hyperscale data centers to today’s AI infrastructure. Enterprise networks adopted multimode fiber and gallium arsenide VCSELs, while hyperscale facilities expanded demand for single-mode fiber, indium phosphide devices and silicon photonics. Multiple optical lanes, PAM4 modulation and digital signal processing subsequently increased transceiver capacity. AI now places greater pressure on bandwidth density and energy efficiency as optics becomes part of the fabric connecting distributed computing resources.
For scale-out networks, Eng described a continuing roadmap for pluggable optics built around higher lane speeds and denser packaging. Coherent has demonstrated 400G-per-lane links using differential electro-absorption modulated lasers and silicon-photonics modulators. At the recent ECOC exhibition in Málaga, the company demonstrated a 3.2T architecture in an OSFP-size package using eight 425G PAM4 optical lanes. These are technology demonstrations supporting the next generation of pluggables, rather than announcements of general product availability.
For scale-up connectivity, Eng emphasized the trade-offs between CPO and NPO. Placing optical engines beside a switch ASIC or accelerator shortens electrical connections, supporting signal integrity and potentially lower power. NPO places the optical engine on the circuit board near the processor, offering greater serviceability and flexibility while requiring signals to traverse additional board traces and connectors. Eng expects NPO deployments in 2027 and identified Coherent’s participation in the Open CPX MSA as part of the effort to develop a socketed ecosystem.
The longer-term opportunity is moving optical links inside advanced packages as bandwidth requirements between compute and memory increase. Eng’s presentation illustrated an optical interposer connecting XPUs and high-bandwidth memory, with external laser sources, wavelength-division multiplexing and circulators. Candidate implementations include silicon photonics powered by external ultra-high-power or integrated high-power InP lasers, alongside high-density VCSEL arrays connected through fiber arrays or multicore fiber. Eng placed these emerging chip-to-chip and memory-disaggregation applications toward the end of the decade.
Manufacturing remains central to that transition. During the discussion, Eng identified electrical crosstalk and matching driver pitch to dense optical arrays as practical challenges, alongside optical crosstalk and fiber integration. She also stressed that wafer-level integration must deliver reproducible performance and sufficiently high yields to achieve its cost advantages. On supply, Eng said Coherent’s InP capacity was essentially sold out through the end of 2027, with expansion underway to address demand.
• Pluggables: Higher lane speeds and denser packaging extend the scale-out roadmap.
• CPO: Short electrical paths support bandwidth density and power efficiency.
• NPO: Socketed optical engines offer serviceability and implementation flexibility; Eng expects deployments in 2027.
• Chip-to-chip: Optical compute-and-memory connections represent a longer-term opportunity toward decade-end.
• Technology choice: Silicon photonics, InP and VCSEL architectures address different reach, density, power and cost requirements.
Analysis
Eng’s presentation points to several optical transitions occurring simultaneously. Higher-speed pluggables continue to address scale-out fabrics while CPO and NPO bring optical conversion closer to switching and accelerator silicon. Coherent’s published demonstrations reflect that breadth: its OFC portfolio included a 6.4T silicon-photonics CPO implementation, a VCSEL-based multimode approach and a 400G-per-lane InP modulator. The company’s PhotonLink platform brings together technologies and assembly capabilities for these different implementations.
Chip-to-chip optics introduces a deeper architectural change because it extends optical connectivity into the relationship between processors and memory. The slide’s emphasis on multiple wavelengths, multiplexers and circulators also shows that increasing bandwidth alone is insufficient: designers must manage fiber count, routing complexity and packaging density. Eng’s discussion identifies the practical milestones to watch—driver integration, crosstalk control, optical coupling and manufacturing yield—before these architectures can progress from demonstrations to repeatable production.

\# PECC Summit\: Coherent Sees Chip\-to\-Chip Optics as the Next Frontier

Coherent CTO Dr\. Julie Eng outlines coexisting pluggable\, CPO and NPO architectures and a longer\-term path to optical compute\-and\-memory connectivity\.

Optical connectivity is moving progressively closer to the compute core\, with chip\-to\-chip links and new memory architectures emerging as the next frontier after optical scale\-up networks\, according to Dr\. Julie Sheridan Eng\, EVP\, Optical Components and Chief Technology Officer at Coherent\. Speaking at PECC Summit on October 20\, Eng outlined a future in which pluggable transceivers\, co\-packaged optics \(CPO\) and near\-packaged optics \(NPO\) coexist\, with different technologies addressing distinct requirements for reach\, power\, bandwidth density and serviceability\.

Eng traced that progression from long\-haul telecommunications through enterprise and hyperscale data centers to today’s AI infrastructure\. Enterprise networks adopted multimode fiber and gallium arsenide VCSELs\, while hyperscale facilities expanded demand for single\-mode fiber\, indium phosphide devices and silicon photonics\. Multiple optical lanes\, PAM4 modulation and digital signal processing subsequently increased transceiver capacity\. AI now places greater pressure on bandwidth density and energy efficiency as optics becomes part of the fabric connecting distributed computing resources\.

For scale\-out networks\, Eng described a continuing roadmap for pluggable optics built around higher lane speeds and denser packaging\. Coherent has demonstrated 400G\-per\-lane links using differential electro\-absorption modulated lasers and silicon\-photonics modulators\. At the recent ECOC exhibition in Málaga\, the company demonstrated a 3\.2T architecture in an OSFP\-size package using eight 425G PAM4 optical lanes\. These are technology demonstrations supporting the next generation of pluggables\, rather than announcements of general product availability\.

For scale\-up connectivity\, Eng emphasized the trade\-offs between CPO and NPO\. Placing optical engines beside a switch ASIC or accelerator shortens electrical connections\, supporting signal integrity and potentially lower power\. NPO places the optical engine on the circuit board near the processor\, offering greater serviceability and flexibility while requiring signals to traverse additional board traces and connectors\. Eng expects NPO deployments in 2027 and identified Coherent’s participation in the Open CPX MSA as part of the effort to develop a socketed ecosystem\.

The longer\-term opportunity is moving optical links inside advanced packages as bandwidth requirements between compute and memory increase\. Eng’s presentation illustrated an optical interposer connecting XPUs and high\-bandwidth memory\, with external laser sources\, wavelength\-division multiplexing and circulators\. Candidate implementations include silicon photonics powered by external ultra\-high\-power or integrated high\-power InP lasers\, alongside high\-density VCSEL arrays connected through fiber arrays or multicore fiber\. Eng placed these emerging chip\-to\-chip and memory\-disaggregation applications toward the end of the decade\.

Manufacturing remains central to that transition\. During the discussion\, Eng identified electrical crosstalk and matching driver pitch to dense optical arrays as practical challenges\, alongside optical crosstalk and fiber integration\. She also stressed that wafer\-level integration must deliver reproducible performance and sufficiently high yields to achieve its cost advantages\. On supply\, Eng said Coherent’s InP capacity was essentially sold out through the end of 2027\, with expansion underway to address demand\.

• Pluggables\: Higher lane speeds and denser packaging extend the scale\-out roadmap\.

• CPO\: Short electrical paths support bandwidth density and power efficiency\.

• NPO\: Socketed optical engines offer serviceability and implementation flexibility\; Eng expects deployments in 2027\.

• Chip\-to\-chip\: Optical compute\-and\-memory connections represent a longer\-term opportunity toward decade\-end\.

• Technology choice\: Silicon photonics\, InP and VCSEL architectures address different reach\, density\, power and cost requirements\.

\#\#\# Analysis

Eng’s presentation points to several optical transitions occurring simultaneously\. Higher\-speed pluggables continue to address scale\-out fabrics while CPO and NPO bring optical conversion closer to switching and accelerator silicon\. Coherent’s published demonstrations reflect that breadth\: its OFC portfolio included a 6\.4T silicon\-photonics CPO implementation\, a VCSEL\-based multimode approach and a 400G\-per\-lane InP modulator\. The company’s PhotonLink platform brings together technologies and assembly capabilities for these different implementations\.

Chip\-to\-chip optics introduces a deeper architectural change because it extends optical connectivity into the relationship between processors and memory\. The slide’s emphasis on multiple wavelengths\, multiplexers and circulators also shows that increasing bandwidth alone is insufficient\: designers must manage fiber count\, routing complexity and packaging density\. Eng’s discussion identifies the practical milestones to watch—driver integration\, crosstalk control\, optical coupling and manufacturing yield—before these architectures can progress from demonstrations to repeatable production\.

Nvidia targets 15x more optics capacity for AI data centers by 2027: Report
The initiative involves several global suppliers, including Amkor, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Unimicron. On the networking side, Nvidia confirmed plans with Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL). SPIL will expand its manufacturing capacity 15-fold for optical engines used in co-packaged optics (CPO) by mid-2027.
E
- Published On Oct 22, 2026 at 08:18 AM IST
Highlights
- Nvidia plans to boost its optical engine manufacturing capacity by 15 times by mid-2027, with a further doubling aimed by late 2028.
- The expansion involves key global suppliers like Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL), Amkor, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Unimicron.
- This move supports Nvidia's Spectrum-6 CPO switch, designed for AI data centers and offering 409.6 Tb/s bandwidth.
- The initiative addresses extraordinary demand for AI supercomputing systems and capacity constraints in electro-absorption modulated lasers.
NEW DELHI: Nvidia is significantly expanding its supply chain, aiming to scale its optics capacity fifteen-fold by 2027. This aggressive move, driven by "extraordinary demand" for AI supercomputing systems, includes a further doubling by the end of 2028, according to an SDxCentral report on Wednesday.
The initiative involves several global suppliers, including Amkor, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Unimicron. On the networking side, Nvidia confirmed plans with Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL). SPIL will expand its manufacturing capacity 15-fold for optical engines used in co-packaged optics (CPO) by mid-2027.
Nvidia’s new Spectrum-6 CPO switch is a key building block for scale-out networking in Vera Rubin DSX AI factories. Ian Buck, Nvidia’s VP and GM of hyperscale and high-performance computing (HPC), highlighted excitement about integrating co-packaged optics into AI data centers. He noted the collaboration with SPIL and other partners to boost capacity.
The Spectrum-6 switch line was formally unveiled in July this year. It offers both standard copper and CPO versions. The optical iteration provides 409.6 Tb/s of bandwidth across 512 ports, each operating at 800 Gb/s.
This supply chain expansion is consistent with Nvidia's past actions. The company has signed multiple deals throughout 2026 with optics firms such as Corning, Lumentum, and Finisar's parent, Coherent. These agreements ensure adequate supply amid ongoing capacity concerns related to electro-absorption modulated lasers (EMLs).
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang further emphasised the scale of the current buildout, stating, "Demand is extraordinary. Capacity is the constraint." He expressed gratitude to supply chain partners for expanding production globally to deliver AI supercomputing systems.

records.title: Transferability of laser powder bed fusion parameters optimized for dense specimens to thin-walled Zr-based bulk metallic glass gyroids
records.source_name: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology
records.summary: This study tested whether a laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) parameter set previously optimized for dense, X-ray-amorphous Zr35Ti30Be27.5Cu7.5 (at%) cubes could be applied unchanged to thin-walled sheet-based gyroid lattices. Three geometrically scaled gyroids (G100, G200, G300) with nominal wall thicknesses of 100, 200 and 300 μm, unit-cell sizes of 1.5, 3.0 and 4.5 mm, and a designed relative density of 20% were built and compared against CAD cross-sections using spatial deviation maps and the Dice coefficient. The contour-only G100 design showed poor structural continuity with extensive missing material (Dice 0.479–0.564) but no resolvable crystalline reflections in XRD, whereas G200 and G300 (contour plus hatch exposure) showed better geometric agreement (Dice 0.643–0.769 and 0.764–0.865) but wall thickening and XRD-detectable crystallinity. Pore area fraction was 0.51% for both G200 and G300 versus 0.06% for G100, while mean microhardness was similar across gyroids and the dense reference (555–574 HV0.3). The authors conclude that geometry-specific optimization is needed to achieve structural continuity while retaining an X-ray-amorphous state.
records.why_it_matters: Process parameters validated on dense bulk coupons cannot be assumed to transfer to thin-walled lattice geometries; wall thickness and exposure strategy must be re-optimized per geometry to balance geometric fidelity against crystallization.

Transferability of laser powder bed fusion parameters optimized for dense specimens to thin-walled Zr-based bulk metallic glass gyroids
- ORIGINAL ARTICLE
- Published:
Abstract
Laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) enables fabrication of Zr-based bulk metallic glass components with complex geometries, but parameters optimized for dense specimens may not transfer directly to thin-walled structures. This study applied without modification a parameter set previously optimized for dense, X-ray-amorphous Zr35Ti30Be27.5Cu7.5 (at%) cubes to three geometrically scaled sheet-based gyroids. The designs, denoted G100, G200, and G300, had nominal wall thicknesses of 100, 200, and 300 μm, corresponding unit-cell sizes of 1.5, 3.0, and 4.5 mm, and a designed relative density of 20%. Structural continuity and geometrical agreement were assessed by comparing optical-microscopy cross-sections with cross-sections extracted from the computer-aided design model, using spatial deviation maps and the Dice coefficient. Metallographic pore area fraction, microstructure, microhardness, and phase state were evaluated by optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, Vickers testing, and X-ray diffraction (XRD), respectively. The contour-only G100 design showed poor continuity and extensive missing-material regions (Dice = 0.479–0.564), while its XRD pattern showed no resolvable crystalline reflections. The G200 and G300 designs, produced using contour and hatch exposure, showed better agreement (Dice = 0.643–0.769 and 0.764–0.865, respectively) but also wall thickening. Both had a pore area fraction of 0.51%, compared with 0.06% for G100, and contained crystalline material detectable by XRD. The gyroids and the dense reference had similar mean microhardness values (555–574 HV0.3). Thus, dense-optimized parameters produced different outcomes across the scaled gyroids. Geometry-specific optimization is needed to achieve structural continuity while retaining an X-ray-amorphous state.

\#\# Abstract

Laser powder bed fusion \(PBF\-LB\) enables fabrication of Zr\-based bulk metallic glass components with complex geometries\, but parameters optimized for dense specimens may not transfer directly to thin\-walled structures\. This study applied without modification a parameter set previously optimized for dense\, X\-ray\-amorphous Zr35Ti30Be27\.5Cu7\.5 \(at\%\) cubes to three geometrically scaled sheet\-based gyroids\. The designs\, denoted G100\, G200\, and G300\, had nominal wall thicknesses of 100\, 200\, and 300 μm\, corresponding unit\-cell sizes of 1\.5\, 3\.0\, and 4\.5 mm\, and a designed relative density of 20\%\. Structural continuity and geometrical agreement were assessed by comparing optical\-microscopy cross\-sections with cross\-sections extracted from the computer\-aided design model\, using spatial deviation maps and the Dice coefficient\. Metallographic pore area fraction\, microstructure\, microhardness\, and phase state were evaluated by optical microscopy\, scanning electron microscopy\, Vickers testing\, and X\-ray diffraction \(XRD\)\, respectively\. The contour\-only G100 design showed poor continuity and extensive missing\-material regions \(Dice \= 0\.479–0\.564\)\, while its XRD pattern showed no resolvable crystalline reflections\. The G200 and G300 designs\, produced using contour and hatch exposure\, showed better agreement \(Dice \= 0\.643–0\.769 and 0\.764–0\.865\, respectively\) but also wall thickening\. Both had a pore area fraction of 0\.51\%\, compared with 0\.06\% for G100\, and contained crystalline material detectable by XRD\. The gyroids and the dense reference had similar mean microhardness values \(555–574 HV0\.3\)\. Thus\, dense\-optimized parameters produced different outcomes across the scaled gyroids\. Geometry\-specific optimization is needed to achieve structural continuity while retaining an X\-ray\-amorphous state\.

records.body_text:
Controlled resin coating and image-based transparency assessment for VPP-printed components
- ORIGINAL ARTICLE
- Open access
- Published:
Abstract
Additive manufacturing of transparent polymer components produced by vat photopolymerization (VPP) is often limited by surface roughness and internal optical inhomogeneities, which degrade light transmission and visual quality. In this work, a controlled resin-coating post-processing strategy and a quantitative image-based framework for transparency assessment were developed to improve the optical performance. The effects of layer height (50, 100 μm) and printing angle (0°, 15°, 30°) were investigated. The coating process reduced surface roughness from values up to ~ 10 μm to below 0.15 μm, increasing optical transmittance from as low as 3–6% to ~ 86–89%, largely independent of the initial printing conditions. However, image-based metrics revealed that transparency quality remained strongly distance-dependent: haze increased from ~ 10% to over 40% as the air-gap distance increased from 20 mm to 60 mm, while sharpness metrics showed significant degradation, indicating persistent internal scattering effects. The results are consistent with a transition from a predominantly surface-dominated optical regime in the as-printed condition toward a regime in which bulk and interfacial effects become increasingly relevant after coating. While surface smoothing effectively restores transmitted intensity, the persistent degradation of contrast and image fidelity suggests a residual contribution from internal layer interfaces and refractive-index inhomogeneities. The proposed framework links manufacturing parameters and post-processing to optical performance and supports the design of transparent VPP-printed components.
