1 Introduction and background
Additive Manufacturing (AM) of transparent polymer components is attracting growing interest due to the possibility of creating geometrically complex and customized shapes with tailored optical properties. Consequently, innovative applications have emerged across the medical field, optical engineering, and consumer products, where enhanced visualization of internal structures plays a crucial role. Transparent parts, for example, can be used to perform flow measurements [1], as in the case of hollow vessel replicas to assess the mechanical behaviour of endovascular devices [2] or for microfluidic devices [3, 4]. Traditionally, glass has been widely adopted for applications requiring high transparency. Nevertheless, its inherent brittleness makes it vulnerable to cracking during post-processing procedures, including grinding and polishing, that are typically performed to enhance optical clarity. For these reasons, the fabrication of complex and customized geometries using transparent polymer materials represents a viable alternative for producing see-through prototypes. Polymers are particularly suitable for these applications owing to their advantageous properties, including transparency in the visible and infrared spectral ranges, low weight, adaptable mechanical properties, and tunable refractive index [5].
Among polymer additive manufacturing (AM) technologies, Vat Photopolymerization (VPP), including Stereolithography (SLA), Digital Light Processing (DLP), and LCD-based systems, generally provides higher optical quality than filament-based approaches, as it avoids filament deposition and the associated inter-raster and inter-layer voids. These voids entrap air, whose refractive index markedly differs from that of the surrounding polymer, thereby causing light scattering and, consequently, a reduction in optical transparency [6,7,8]. Nevertheless, obtaining truly transparent VPP parts remains a challenging task. The layer-by-layer nature of the 3D printing process can introduce both surface and internal optical inhomogeneities. Surface roughness generated by the staircase effect enhances diffuse scattering, while local variations in the degree of polymerization may produce refractive-index discontinuities, particularly at layer interfaces and in pixelated exposure systems (e.g., DLP systems) [9]. In many resins, the refractive index increases with the degree of curing, further contributing to these optical inhomogeneities. In this context, post-curing protocols (e.g., UV, thermal, or vacuum treatments) may improve mechanical properties and wear resistance but generally have limited influence on optical transparency, indicating that surface finishing remains a dominant factor in determining the final optical quality [10].
The morphology of VPP-printed parts is strongly governed by the printing parameters adopted during fabrication, making this aspect crucial for any meaningful assessment of transparent printed components. Among these parameters, layer height [11, 12] and printing angle play a major role, as they influence both the amplitude of the staircase effect, and consequently the resulting surface roughness, and the orientation of the interfaces between adjacent layers with respect to the optical path [13, 14]. Aligning interlayer boundaries with the optical path can increase light scattering and refractive-index discontinuities. Therefore, these parameters influence not only the transparency of the as-printed part, but also the effectiveness of subsequent post-processing treatments. Common post-processing techniques include sanding, polishing, coating with transparent resins, and chemical treatments [15]. Among them, resin-based coating approaches have proven particularly promising because they can fill surface valleys, reduce asperities, and limit surface-induced light scattering. Spin coating, performed using the same or a compatible resin, has been successfully employed to reduce surface roughness and improve the transparency of optical lenses, achieving surface roughness values as low as Ra = 13–28 nm (arithmetical mean deviation of the profile) and optical performance approaching that of commercial glass, particularly for short focal lengths [16, 17]. Dip coating using the same printing resin was proposed in [18], yielding nanometre-scale surface roughness and highly transparent, low-loss optical components. Similarly, Vaidya and Solgaard demonstrated that UV-curable polymer smoothing can transform as-printed surfaces with micrometre-scale roughness into nanometre-smooth optics, enabling high-quality reflective and transmissive elements [19]. Mechanical or chemical polishing and varnish coating are also used, although they may be less effective for complex geometries and can introduce inhomogeneities or alter surface curvature [11].
Despite these advances, several challenges remain in the effective implementation of coating-based post-processing for transparent VPP components. Coating thickness and uniformity can be difficult to control, especially on large or complex geometries, and defects or surface waviness may arise during deposition and curing. Manual or semi-manual operations may also introduce operator-dependent variability [17]. Achieving coatings with minimal surface defects and waviness requires careful control of resin viscosity, temperature, and curing conditions [18]. Even recent efforts toward automation, such as the conversion of consumer-grade 3D printers into dip-coating systems [20], have primarily focused on improving process accessibility rather than enabling a fully controlled and dedicated coating environment. In addition to process-related limitations, the evaluation of optical performance in the literature is often restricted to bulk metrics such as optical transmittance or surface roughness. While these parameters provide useful information, they do not fully capture the effective visual quality of transparent components, which is influenced by light diffusion, contrast degradation, and loss of image sharpness when observing objects through the material. Beyond bulk transmission, the perceived transparency of a component is also distance-dependent, since image degradation becomes progressively more pronounced as the distance between the specimen and the target object increases. Consequently, a comprehensive and quantitative assessment of transparency quality beyond simple light transmission is still lacking.
Overall, existing studies clearly demonstrate the feasibility of resin-based coating strategies for improving transparency, but provide limited solutions in terms of process control, reproducibility, and advanced optical characterization, all of which are essential for engineering applications requiring predictable and quantitatively assessable optical performance.
On this basis, the present study aims to develop and validate a controlled post-processing workflow for VPP-printed components based on resin coating, combined with a quantitative image-based framework for transparency assessment. This work provides a twofold contribution: first, a controlled coating process for surface smoothing enabled by a purpose-built apparatus integrating vertical translation and multi-axis rotation; second, a distance-dependent optical characterization methodology that links process parameters and material morphology to functional transparency.
The coating system enables controlled immersion, improved resin distribution, and effective removal of excess material, addressing key limitations related to coating uniformity and reproducibility. In parallel, a dedicated optical setup was designed to acquire images of a reference target through the specimens at controlled air-gap distances, enabling the quantitative evaluation of contrast and sharpness degradation in addition to conventional transmittance measurements. Furthermore, the influence of layer height and printing angle was systematically investigated to elucidate how as-printed morphology affects both the coating outcome and the final optical response. By correlating surface roughness, optical transmittance, and image-based transparency metrics, the study establishes a multi-scale framework for linking manufacturing parameters to functional optical performance, supporting the engineering design and qualification of transparent VPP-printed components.
2 Materials and methods
2.1 3D printing and design of experiments
Prismatic specimens were designed and manufactured using Vat Photopolymerization (VPP) technology to investigate the influence of printing parameters and post-processing conditions on optical transparency.
Manufacturing was performed using an Anycubic Photon Mono M7 Pro 3D printer operating with LCD (Liquid Crystal Display) technology (pixel size: 16.8 × 24.8 µm2). The specimen geometry (Fig. 1) consisted of square plates measuring 35 × 35 × 2 mm³, incorporating a small integrated tab to facilitate handling during the coating post-processing stage. In addition, a dedicated base region was included to provide a non-measuring surface for support placement. A High Transparency Photopolymer resin supplied by JAMG HE (Shenzhen Yongchanghe Technology Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, China) was selected to maximize the optical clarity achievable directly from the printing process, thereby establishing a benchmark for evaluating subsequent post-processing improvements.
The experimental plan for analysing thickness, transmittance, and surface roughness was defined according to a 2 × 3 full factorial design of experiments (DOE), varying two key process parameters: the layer height and the printing angle of the specimen with respect to the building platform. Specifically, the layer height was set to 50 μm and 100 μm, while the printing angles investigated were 0°, 15°, and 30°. For each factor combination, four independent specimens were analysed. All specimens were characterized both before and after the application of the coating, allowing for a paired comparison of the measured properties.
Statistical analysis was performed using a mixed-design analysis of variance (ANOVA), with layer height and printing angle treated as between-subject factors and coating condition (as-printed (AP) vs. coated (C)) as a within-subject factor. Effect sizes were quantified using partial eta-squared (ηp2). This approach enabled the assessment of both the initial distribution of properties in the as-printed condition and its modification after coating. When significant effects or interactions involving coating condition were observed, separate analyses of the AP and C conditions were also considered to support their interpretation. Statistical significance was assessed at a 95% confidence level (α = 0.05).
In addition to the measurements described above, optical transparency was analysed in terms of haze and sharpness. The analysis excluded the as-printed and 0° coated specimens because their corresponding images did not satisfy the applicability criterion defined in Sect. 2.5.
A full factorial DOE was implemented to investigate the effect of process parameters on haze and sharpness. The factors considered were air-gap distance (20, 40, and 60 mm), printing angle (15° and 30°), and layer height (50 μm and 100 μm), resulting in a total of 12 experimental conditions (3 × 2 × 2). The same four specimens adopted in the previous experimental campaign were used for all conditions. Statistical analysis was performed using a three-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), including main effects and all interaction terms up to the third order. Statistical significance was assessed at a 95% confidence level (α = 0.05). When significant effects were identified, post-hoc comparisons were carried out using Tukey’s HSD test.
The printing parameters were defined and optimized using the Anycubic Photon Workshop software, in accordance with the manufacturer’s guidelines for the selected photopolymer resin, with the dual objective of minimizing build time and ensuring high part quality. Accordingly, the exposure time was set to 2.5 s for a layer height of 50 μm and 5 s for 100 μm.
2.2 Coating post-processing
The coating treatment was conducted using a custom-designed apparatus, specifically developed for this study and shown in Fig. 2. The system consisted of a vertically translating central body, actuated by two lead screws driven by stepper motors, which converted the rotational motion of the motors into precise linear displacement along the Z-axis. A linear guide was integrated into the system to enhance motion stability and minimize lateral clearance, ensuring accurate and repeatable positioning during the coating cycle. The central unit was supported by a rigid frame and equipped with a mechanical clamping device that securely held the specimen during the coating, allowing controlled immersion into the resin bath at predefined speeds.
The same commercial transparent photopolymer resin used for specimen fabrication (High Transparency Resin, JAMG HE, Shenzhen Yongchanghe Technology Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, China) was also used as the coating material. The resin is compatible with UV radiation in the 385–405 nm wavelength range and, according to the manufacturer’s technical data sheet, has a viscosity of 1000–1300 mPa·s and a density of 1.05–1.25 g cm⁻³. All coating operations were performed under laboratory ambient conditions at approximately 25 °C and 50% relative humidity.
The coating process started with the specimen being lowered toward the resin bath at a moderate speed of 31.25 mm/s. As the specimen approached the resin surface, the downward speed was reduced to 0.78 mm/s to ensure controlled immersion and minimize air entrainment and bubble formation. The motion continued until the specimen was fully submerged in the resin bath. Once immersion was completed, the carriage paused for 5 s and then was retracted by 80 mm until the specimen was completely withdrawn from the resin bath at the same speed of 0.78 mm/s. The clamping unit then initiated a rapid rotational phase at approximately 1400 rpm for a total time of 20 s. This stage ensured a uniform distribution of the coating layer and facilitated removal of excess resin by centrifugal action. Upon completion, the carriage returned to its initial position at a speed of 31.25 mm/s, marking the end of the coating cycle.
After coating, the specimens were carefully removed from the clamping device and placed in a first-generation Form Cure unit (Form Cure V1, Formlabs Inc., Somerville, MA, USA), equipped with thirteen multidirectional 405 nm LEDs, with a nominal LED power of 39 W and a total radiant output of 9.1 W, as well as a reflective chamber and a rotating turntable. The chamber temperature was set to 40 °C and, after reaching the target temperature, the specimens underwent simultaneous UV irradiation and heating for 15 min. The same curing cycle was applied to all coated specimens. During this stage, the liquid resin underwent photopolymerization, resulting in the formation of a solid crosslinked network. The specimens were then immersed in isopropyl alcohol (IPA) for 20 min to remove residual unpolymerized resin from the surface. This final cleaning step was included as an integral part of the post-processing workflow because a tacky surface associated with residual unpolymerized resin would promote the accumulation of dust and fingerprints during handling, thereby progressively impairing optical transparency and limiting the practical usability of the components.
2.3 Thickness and roughness
The specimen thickness was measured using a micrometre at five different locations on each specimen, and the average value was used for analysis in order to minimize local measurement variability.
Surface roughness measurements were carried out using a contact profilometer (Jenoptik Waveline W812R), equipped with a TKU400 stylus probe. The instrument was operated with a scanning length of 4.8 mm and a traverse speed of 0.1 mm/s, acquiring a total of 9600 data points per measurement to ensure high spatial resolution of the surface profile.
The roughness parameter Ra (arithmetical mean deviation of the profile) was selected as the reference metric for surface characterization. Measurements were performed on specimens produced with both investigated layer heights (50 μm and 100 μm) and for all build orientations (0°, 15°, and 30°), considering both AP and C conditions.
Surface roughness measurements and the statistical interpretation of process effects were primarily performed along the y′-direction on the specimen surface (Fig. 3), corresponding to the direction most directly affected by the layer-by-layer process and therefore selected as the most significant direction for assessing the staircase effect induced by additive manufacturing. Measurements along the orthogonal x′-direction were additionally considered as a complementary characterization of the directional surface morphology.
On each specimen, three measurements were taken per surface, and the reported Ra value corresponds to the average of these measurements. All measurements were performed under controlled environmental conditions, and care was taken to ensure proper stylus alignment and consistent contact with the specimen surface.
2.4 Optical transmittance
Optical transmittance was measured for all specimen conditions, namely in the AP and C states, for the three printing angles (0°, 15°, and 30°) and the two investigated layer heights (50 and 100 μm). Measurements were performed using a Linshang LS116 light transmittance meter (Shenzhen Linshang Technology Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, China), operating over the 380–760 nm spectral range. The instrument operates with a parallel-beam optical configuration: a visible-light source illuminates the specimen, while a detector placed on the opposite side records the transmitted light intensity. Before the measurements, the emitting and receiving probes were aligned without a specimen between them, and the instrument completed its automatic calibration to 100% transmittance. The unobstructed air path was thus used as the measurement reference. During each measurement, the specimen was positioned between the emitting and receiving probes under orthogonal alignment and constant probe spacing. Following calibration, transmittance was determined as the ratio between the light intensity measured through the specimen (I) and the reference intensity established using the unobstructed air path (I0), expressed as a percentage: T(%) = I/I0× 100. For each experimental condition, measurements were repeated at three locations on the specimen surface (Fig. 3), and the mean values were used for the analysis. According to the manufacturer, the LS116 provides an accuracy of ± 1% for colourless and uniformly transparent materials, with a resolution of 0.001% in the 0–10% range and 0.01% in the 10–100% range. Transmittance was evaluated at the actual thickness of each specimen and treated as a component-level optical property. All specimens had the same nominal thickness of 2 mm, while the measured thickness values and their variation among the investigated conditions were independently characterized and analysed in Sect. 3.1. This reporting approach captures the effective optical response of the specimens in their AP and C conditions, including the contributions associated with surface morphology and internal layer interfaces.
2.5 Transparency characterization
The optical transparency of the 3D printed specimens was evaluated by considering two parameters that reflect the human visual perception of contrast loss and edge acuity: the illumination diffusion haze (ID-haze) and the illumination diffusion sharpness (ID-sharpness) as defined by Busato et al. [21].
The haze was defined as the scattering of light by a specimen responsible for the contrast reduction of target objects viewed through it, while the sharpness was defined as the ability to reproduce fine details and clear edges. The variation of transparency was evaluated as a function of the distance (air-gap) between the specimen and a target object consisting of a black-and-white checkerboard pattern. The experimental setup for specimen transparency characterization consisted of a digital camera (monochrome sensor; 1280 × 960 pixels) and the black-and-white checkerboard pattern (1.5 × 1.5 mm squares) mounted on a 3 mm-thick glass plate, backlit by an LED light source. A specimen holder was used to ensure a parallel placement of the specimen with respect to the checkerboard. Three distances (d = 20, 40 and 60 mm) between the specimen and the checkerboard were considered using three slots in the base to place the specimen holder (Fig. 4). The experimental setup was 3D printed using PETG-HS and a Bambu Lab X1E 3D printer.
All images were acquired sequentially during the same measurement session in a darkened laboratory, with the backlighting LED as the only illumination source. LED operating conditions and camera settings were kept unchanged throughout the experimental campaign. No additional signal amplification was used, and the exposure time was set to 1/370 s, so that the white checkerboard regions remained below sensor saturation. Focus was adjusted manually only once, using the reference configuration without a specimen, in which the camera directly imaged the checkerboard pattern, and was then kept unchanged for all subsequent acquisitions. The checkerboard brightness was not independently calibrated using a photometric instrument; however, its effective brightness was controlled by using the same LED source under unchanged operating conditions.
The transparency metrics were computed over five regions of interest (ROIs) to account for spatial non-uniformities across the field of view. Each ROI was defined by a pair of checkerboard squares, horizontally or vertically arranged, in order to include a single transition between adjacent black and white squares: one ROI at the centre of the image and four ROIs near the four image corners (upper left, upper right, lower left, and lower right) (Fig. 5).
ROI locations and dimensions were defined from the reference image and kept unchanged for all experimental conditions. An image was excluded when structured distortion prevented one or more predefined ROIs from containing an unambiguous pair of adjacent black and white squares separated by a single transition; ROI relocation or resizing was not allowed, as it would introduce operator-dependent selection.
Following Busato et al. [21], the illumination diffusion haze was determined as:
$$\:{H}\_{ID}=\left(1-\frac{{C}\_{sample}}{{C}\_{ref}}\right)\times\:100$$
where Cref and Csample denote the Michelson contrast values measured from images acquired without and with the specimen placed between the camera and the checkerboard pattern, respectively. For a given ROI, the Michelson contrast value C was computed as:
$$\:C=\left(\frac{{\overline{I}}\_{white}-{\overline{I}}\_{black}}{{\overline{I}}\_{white}+{\overline{I}}\_{black}}\right)$$
where \(\:{\overline{I}}\_{white}\) and \(\:{\overline{I}}\_{black}\:\)represent the mean grayscale intensity values of the white and black squares, respectively. To avoid the influence of partial-intensity pixels, the edge region corresponding to the white-black transition was explicitly excluded from the contrast computation. Only pixels belonging to the interior regions of the white and black squares were considered for the evaluation of the mean intensity values.
The sharpness of the transition between the white and black squares was quantified using an edge-based modulation transfer function (MTF) analysis. For each bright-dark edge, 11 profiles (5 above, 1 central, 5 below the ROI centre) perpendicular to the edge were extracted and averaged to reduce noise, resulting in the edge spread function (ESF). The ESF was then numerically differentiated to obtain the line spread function (LSF), which describes the spatial blurring introduced by the specimen. The modulation transfer function (MTF) was computed as the magnitude of the Fourier transform of the LSF and normalized to unity at zero spatial frequency (MTF0 = 1), so that higher MTF values at intermediate and high spatial frequencies correspond to sharper black-white transitions.
To obtain scalar sharpness metrics, the MTF was analysed in a specific spatial frequency band expressed in line pairs per millimetre (lp mm− 1). Given the pixel size of the imaging system (0.03 mm), the selected frequency range lies well below the Nyquist limit and corresponds to visually relevant detail scales. In particular, the average MTF values were computed over the band 2–6 lp mm− 1. Additionally, the spatial frequency at which the MTF dropped to 50% of its zero-frequency value (MTF50) was extracted as an auxiliary sharpness indicator.
The illumination diffusion sharpness (SID) was determined as:
$$\:{S}\_{ID}=\frac{{\overline{MTF}}\_{sample,band}}{{\overline{MTF}}\_{ref,band}}\times\:100$$
where \(\:{\overline{MTF}}\_{sample,band}\) and \(\:{\overline{MTF}}\_{ref,band}\) are the average MTF values obtained for a specific frequency band for the images acquired with and without the specimen, respectively. Accordingly, a SID value of 100 corresponds to no sharpness degradation with respect to the reference configuration, while lower SID values indicate increasing diffusion-induced loss of edge sharpness.
3 Results
Figure 6 presents a preliminary qualitative comparison of the optical response of the investigated specimens, considering both AP and C conditions across different printing orientations (0°, 15°, and 30°). The use of a USAF 1951 resolution test chart enables a direct visual assessment of feature distinguishability and overall transparency. AP specimens exhibit significant light scattering, limiting the visibility of fine details, whereas C specimens show a clear enhancement in transmitted image clarity and edge definition. Although these observations suggest the effectiveness of the coating-based post-processing and a potential influence of printing orientation, a comprehensive evaluation requires quantitative analysis. The following sections provide a quantitative assessment of these effects.
3.1 Thickness
Figure 7 reports the results obtained from thickness measurements carried out on the specimens in the different investigated conditions. Repeated measurements performed at different locations on the same specimen showed low within-specimen variability for both AP and C conditions, with standard deviations typically ranging between 0.006 and 0.070 mm, confirming the high repeatability of the measurement procedure.
Considering the mean value for each specimen, thickness in the AP condition was strongly influenced by printing angle, which showed a highly significant effect (F(2, 18) = 123.33, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.932). In contrast, layer height did not significantly affect thickness (p = 0.186), while a weak but significant interaction between layer height and angle was detected (F(2, 18) = 3.67, p = 0.046, ηp2 = 0.290).
These results indicate that the initial thickness distribution was mainly governed by printing angle, with the 30° condition showing markedly higher values than 0° and 15°. After coating, printing angle remained a significant factor affecting thickness (F(2, 18) = 26.03, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.743), whereas neither layer height nor the interaction term showed statistically significant effects (p = 0.436 and p = 0.824, respectively). These results indicate that the dependence of thickness on printing angle persisted after coating, although the effect was less pronounced than in the as-printed (AP) state.
Considering coating condition as the within-subject factor, the mixed-design ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of coating on specimen thickness (F(1, 18) = 238.69, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.930), confirming an overall increase in thickness after coating. However, the coating-induced change did not significantly depend on layer height (condition × layer height: F(1, 18) = 3.42, p = 0.081, ηp² = 0.159), printing angle (condition × printing angle: F(2, 18) = 1.35, p = 0.284, ηp² = 0.130), or their interaction (condition × layer height × printing angle: F(2, 18) = 0.60, p = 0.562, ηp² = 0.062).
Therefore, coating shifted the thickness values upward without substantially altering their dependence on the printing parameters and produced comparable thickness increases across the investigated process conditions (Fig. 7).
The mean coating-induced thickness increments were 0.10 ± 0.02, 0.12 ± 0.02, and 0.08 ± 0.04 mm for the 50 μm layer height at 0°, 15°, and 30°, respectively; and 0.08 ± 0.02, 0.08 ± 0.04, and 0.07 ± 0.04 mm for the corresponding conditions at 100 μm (mean ± SD). These values represent the combined thickness increase across the two opposite coated faces. The coating configuration was nominally symmetric with respect to the two main specimen faces, since the specimen was centrally clamped and rotated about its central axis during the centrifugal removal of excess resin, thus promoting a comparable coating distribution on both faces.
3.2 Surface roughness
Figure 8 provides representative 3D topographical maps of the surface morphology of an LH100-30° specimen before and after coating. The maps were generated by combining the individual line profiles acquired with the profilometer, enabling the direct visualization of the initial surface roughness and the subsequent coating-induced smoothing effect. The as-printed condition exhibits a pronounced directional pattern associated with the layer-wise fabrication process, whereas the coated surfaces show a markedly reduced amplitude and a more uniform topography.
In the AP condition, surface roughness (Ra) showed a strong dependence on both layer height and printing angle (Fig. 9). Ra increased monotonically with printing angle for both layer heights, rising from 0.283 to 3.650 μm for LH50 and from 2.300 to 10.50 μm for LH100. These results highlight the combined effect of thicker layers and larger printing angles in amplifying the staircase effect. This interpretation is supported by the ANOVA, which revealed highly significant main effects of layer height (F(1, 18) = 7224.7, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.998) and printing angle (F(2, 18) = 4243.5, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.998) together with a strong interaction between the two factors (F(2, 18) = 740.7, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.988).
After coating, Ra was drastically reduced under all conditions, falling within 0.028–0.140 μm for LH50 and 0.045–0.063 μm for LH100. Thus, even surfaces with initial roughness above 10 μm were smoothed to approximately 0.1 μm, demonstrating the very high effectiveness of the coating treatment. Although both main effects and their interaction remained statistically significant after coating (p < 0.001 for all; ηp2 = 0.60, 0.76 and 0.75 for layer height, printing angle and their interaction, respectively), their influence on absolute roughness was markedly attenuated, and all coated specimens exhibited low roughness values.
Considering coating condition as the within-subject factor, the mixed-design ANOVA revealed a highly significant main effect of coating on surface roughness along the y′-direction (F(1, 18) = 26210.72, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.999), confirming the marked reduction in Ra after coating. Significant interactions were also observed between condition and layer height (F(1, 18) = 7240.47, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.998), between condition and printing angle (F(2, 18) = 4106.66, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.998), and for the condition × layer height × printing angle interaction (F(2, 18) = 765.25, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.988). These results indicate that, although coating consistently reduced surface roughness, the magnitude of the absolute reduction depended strongly on the initial processing condition.
The roughness change was defined as Δ = C − AP. Consistent with the significant interactions involving coating condition, the largest absolute reductions were observed for the roughest as-printed surfaces, particularly at larger printing angles and for the 100 μm layer height. Overall, the coating acted as an effective smoothing mechanism, drastically reducing Ra while substantially mitigating the process-dependent differences observed in the AP condition.
To complement the primary characterization performed along the y’-direction, additional measurements were conducted along the orthogonal x′-direction to further assess the surface morphology. Mean Ra values were markedly reduced after coating, ranging from approximately 1.27–2.47 μm in the AP condition to 0.028–0.095 μm after coating. The mixed-design ANOVA confirmed a significant main effect of coating condition (F(1, 18) = 181.90, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.910), showing a strong smoothing effect also along the x′-direction.
3.3 Optical transmittance
Optical transmittance showed a strong dependence on both layer height and printing angle in the AP condition (Fig. 10). For LH50 specimens, transmittance decreased from about 45% at 0° to 14% at 15° and 6.5% at 30°, whereas for LH100 specimens it dropped from about 21% to 5% and 3%, respectively. These marked reductions are consistent with the roughness results and indicate progressively stronger light scattering at higher build angles and larger layer heights. This interpretation is supported by the ANOVA, which revealed highly significant main effects of layer height (F(1, 18) = 1910.6, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.991) and printing angle (F(2, 18) = 4219.7, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.998), as well as a strong interaction between the two factors (F(2, 18) = 502.0, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.982).
After coating, transmittance values increased substantially and became much more uniform across all conditions, ranging between approximately 86% and 89%. Thus, specimens with initial transmittance as low as 3% increased to values close to 88%, demonstrating the high effectiveness of the coating in suppressing surface-induced optical losses. Although layer height and printing angle remained statistically significant (layer height: p = 0.0038, ηp2 = 0.380; printing angle: p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.622), their effects were markedly attenuated compared to the AP condition, and the interaction between the two factors was no longer significant (p = 0.074).
Considering coating condition as the within-subject factor, the mixed-design ANOVA revealed a highly significant main effect of coating on optical transmittance (F(1, 18) = 143685.06, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.9999), confirming the substantial increase observed after coating. Significant interactions were also found between condition and layer height (F(1, 18) = 807.96, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.978), between condition and printing angle (F(2, 18) = 2197.56, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.996), and for the condition × layer height × printing angle interaction (F(2, 18) = 247.56, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.965). These results indicate that the magnitude of the transmittance increase depended strongly on the initial processing condition.
The transmittance gain was defined as Δ = C − AP. Consistent with the significant interactions involving coating condition, Δ was larger for specimens exhibiting lower initial AP transmittance values. Consequently, conditions characterized by the poorest initial optical performance showed the greatest absolute increase after coating, leading to a substantial reduction in variability across the dataset.
3.4 Transparency
Figure 11 shows representative examples of the checkerboard pattern acquired by the camera in the absence of the specimen (reference condition, Fig. 11a) and with the specimen placed between the camera and the checkerboard. These images qualitatively illustrate the impact of specimen interposition, air-gap distance, and printing orientation on the transmitted image, highlighting progressive changes in pattern visibility, contrast, and sharpness. For instance, Fig. 11b shows the checkerboard pattern acquired by the camera with an as-printed specimen placed between the camera and the checkerboard, while Fig. 11c-e correspond to images acquired with a coated specimen printed with a layer height of 50 μm and a printing angle of 0°. In the 0° coated condition, a spatially non-uniform distortion organized in approximately horizontal bands smeared, displaced, or replicated the checkerboard transitions within the predefined ROIs. Since obtaining valid profiles would have required repositioning the ROIs toward less-affected regions, the 0° condition was excluded according to the criterion defined in Sect. 2.5, and only 15° and 30° printing angles were evaluated for haze and sharpness.
3.4.1 Haze
Illumination diffusion haze (HID) increased monotonically with air-gap distance under all investigated conditions (Fig. 12), indicating a progressive loss of image contrast as the distance between the specimen and the target increased because of increased light scattering. At the same time, haze was consistently higher at a layer height of 100 μm than at 50 μm, and at a printing angle of 30° than at 15°. The combined effect of these factors led to a marked cumulative degradation of transparency, with HID rising from about 11% for the 50 μm-15° condition at 20 mm to 43% for the 100 μm-30° condition at 60 mm. This trend suggests that increasing air-gap amplifies the perceptual effect of light scattering, while larger layer height and higher printing angle further intensify haze because of the more pronounced structural discontinuities introduced by the layer-by-layer process.
These observations are supported by the three-way ANOVA, which showed significant main effects of layer height (F(1, 36) = 332.41, p < 0.001), printing angle (F(1, 36) = 134.93, p < 0.001), and air-gap (F(2, 36) = 117.39, p < 0.001). Among them, layer height exhibited the largest effect size (η2 = 0.43), followed by distance (η2 = 0.30) and printing angle (η2 = 0.17), indicating that layer height-related morphology was the dominant factor governing haze. In addition to the main effects, all two-way interactions were statistically significant, including layer height × angle (p < 0.001), layer height × distance (p = 0.005), and angle × distance (p = 0.029), suggesting that the influence of each factor is partially dependent on the levels of the others. Conversely, the three-way interaction was not significant (p = 0.497).
Post-hoc comparisons (Tukey HSD) further revealed that haze increased significantly from 20 mm to both 40 mm and 60 mm, whereas the difference between 40 mm and 60 mm was not significant when averaged across all conditions. Overall, these results indicate that HID is governed by a combined effect of air-gap distance and process parameters, with thicker layers and larger printing angles exacerbating the distance-dependent degradation of optical transparency.
3.4.2 Sharpness
The illumination diffusion sharpness (SID) was computed for each image by considering the five ROIs shown in Fig. 5 to obtain a global sharpness value. To enable direct comparison between reference and sample conditions, relative ID-sharpness indices were defined as the ratio between the sharpness metrics measured with and without the specimen. Figure 13 reports an example of the results obtained for the edge spread function and the line spread function computed from the images in Fig. 11f-h. It is worth noting that the use of multiple profiles for the ESF estimation ensured consistent averaging across ROIs and imaging conditions, thereby reducing the influence of manual ROI size selection. Moreover, ESF and LSF profiles in Fig. 13 were aligned with respect to the peak of the LSF to allow a fair comparison and averaging of edge responses obtained by considering different ROIs.
Figures 14 and 15 report SID and MTF50 values, respectively, expressed as a percentage with respect to the reference condition. Sharpness metrics showed a consistent degradation with increasing air-gap distance, confirming a progressive loss of image quality as the specimen was moved farther from the target pattern. However, the effect of process parameters depended strongly on edge orientation. For vertically oriented edges, both SID and MTF50 decreased monotonically with air-gap under all investigated conditions. In this case, layer height was the dominant process parameter, whereas printing angle had a limited influence. For example, at 50 μm, vertical SID decreased from about 75% at 20 mm to 23–31% at 60 mm, while vertical MTF50 dropped from about 69–70% to 34–35%. At 100 μm, the decrease with distance remained evident, but both SID and MTF50 were consistently higher, indicating a better preservation of spatial frequency content in the vertical direction. This interpretation is supported by the ANOVA. For vertical SID, significant main effects were observed for layer height (F(1, 36) = 169.46, p < 0.001) and air-gap (F(2, 36) = 114.40, p < 0.001), with air-gap showing the largest contribution (η² = 0.45), followed by layer height (η² = 0.33). In contrast, printing angle did not exhibit any statistically significant effect. Similarly, vertical MTF50 was significantly affected by both layer height (F(1, 36) = 73.59, p < 0.001) and air-gap (F(2, 36) = 84.31, p < 0.001), with air-gap representing the dominant contribution (η² = 0.54), followed by layer height (η² = 0.24), while the effect of printing angle was not significant (p = 0.059). In both cases, post-hoc comparisons confirmed a progressive reduction with increasing air-gap.
A markedly different behaviour emerged for horizontally oriented edges, which exhibited substantially stronger degradation and a clearer sensitivity to both layer height and printing angle. At 50 μm, horizontal SID and MTF50 were relatively high at short air-gap distances, reaching about 84% and 80%, respectively, at 20 mm for the 15° condition, but decreased sharply as distance increased. For the 100 μm specimens, both SID and MTF50 values were significantly lower, especially at larger air-gap distances, reaching values as low as about 20% at 60 mm. The printing angle also influenced the transparency results, although to a lesser extent than layer height. In general, a 30° angle tended to yield lower SID and MTF50 values for horizontal edges, while its effect was less systematic for vertical edges, indicating that the orientation of the printed structure contributed to the optical degradation. The statistical analysis confirmed this stronger parameter dependence in the horizontal direction. For horizontal SID, all three main factors were significant, layer height (F(1, 36) = 171.28, p < 0.001), printing angle (F(1, 36) = 65.81, p < 0.001), and air-gap (F(2, 36) = 230.32, p < 0.001), with air-gap exhibiting the dominant effect (η² = 0.50), followed by layer height (η² = 0.19) and printing angle (η² = 0.07). Likewise, horizontal MTF50 was significantly affected by layer height (F(1, 36) = 386.04, p < 0.001), air-gap (F(2, 36) = 191.38, p < 0.001), and printing angle (F(1, 36) = 43.17, p < 0.001). Layer height and air-gap exhibited comparable effect sizes (η² ≈ 0.42), while the contribution of the printing angle was smaller (η² ≈ 0.047). Significant layer height × air-gap interactions (p < 0.001) were observed for both horizontal SID and MTF50, indicating that the effect of distance depended on the printed morphology. Post-hoc analysis showed significant differences between 20 mm and the larger air-gaps, while the difference between 40 mm and 60 mm was not significant, suggesting a partial plateau in MTF degradation at higher distances.
A direct comparison between SID and MTF50 measurements reveals a consistent behaviour in terms of the influence of process parameters, but differences emerge in the sensitivity to printing angle. While SID, especially in the horizontal direction, exhibits a pronounced dependence on angle, MTF appears comparatively less sensitive to this parameter, particularly in the vertical component. This suggests that, although both metrics are related to image quality, SID is more sensitive to anisotropic effects introduced by the layer-wise structure, while MTF reflects a more averaged response of the system.
Overall, the sharpness results reveal a clear anisotropic optical response. While vertical edges were mainly governed by air-gap and layer height, horizontal edges were more severely degraded and more sensitive to printing angle, suggesting that the layer-by-layer architecture introduces direction-dependent scattering and blur. In particular, increasing air-gap produced the most systematic reduction in both SID and MTF50, whereas layer height controlled the magnitude and anisotropy of the response. These results indicate that surface smoothing alone is not sufficient to fully preserve visual quality, as the internal structure generated during printing continues to affect sharpness in an orientation-dependent manner.
4 Discussion
The results presented in this study can be interpreted within a unified framework in which the optical behaviour of VPP-printed transparent components is consistent with a transition between different dominant mechanisms across multiple scales. In particular, the experimental evidence indicates a shift from a surface-dominated optical regime in the AP condition to a bulk/interface-dominated regime after coating, with additional effects introduced by light propagation conditions.
In the AP condition, the optical response is primarily governed by surface morphology. Both layer height and printing angle strongly affect surface roughness, which increases monotonically with increasing printing angle and layer height due to the staircase effect inherent to layer-by-layer fabrication [11, 14]. In this study, Ra values increase from sub-micrometric levels (~ 0.28 μm for LH50 at 0°) up to more than 10 μm (~ 10.5 μm for LH100 at 30°), confirming the strong process dependence of surface morphology. The direct correspondence between roughness and transmittance observed in the results indicates that surface-induced scattering is likely the dominant mechanism controlling optical performance in this regime. As the amplitude of surface asperities increases, diffuse scattering at the air-polymer interface becomes more pronounced, leading to a substantial reduction in transmitted light intensity. Consistently, transmittance decreases from approximately 45% (LH50, 0°) to values as low as 3–6% at higher layer height and printing angles. Similar trends were reported in additively manufactured optical polymers, where surface irregularities are identified as the primary source of optical losses [6,7,8]. Consequently, process parameters such as layer height and printing angle influence optical properties mainly through their effect on surface morphology.
The application of the resin coating markedly alters this behaviour. The coating process leads to a drastic reduction in surface roughness across all investigated conditions, bringing Ra down to the sub-micrometric range (~ 0.03–0.15 μm), substantially mitigating surface-induced scattering. As a result, optical transmittance increases significantly and becomes nearly independent of the initial process parameters, reaching values in the range of approximately 86–89% for all configurations. These values approach those reported for conventional optical materials. For comparison, an uncoated N-BK7 glass window of comparable thickness (~ 2 mm), supplied by Edmund Optics Inc., exhibits a transmittance of approximately 92–93% under similar conditions.
However, despite this proximity in bulk transmission, the coated VPP specimens still exhibit significant image degradation, highlighting that high transmittance alone is not sufficient to ensure optical-grade performance. Importantly, the coating does not simply act as a uniform additive layer. Although the measured thickness increment is comparable across all conditions, the resulting optical improvement is not uniform. Specimens characterized by higher initial roughness and lower as-printed transmittance exhibit larger gains after coating, with transmittance increases exceeding 80% points in the most critical cases. This indicates that comparable overall thickness increments across process conditions do not imply uniform functional improvement. Rather, by smoothing surface irregularities, the coating yielded the largest gains for the most critical initial condition and reduced variability in the final optical response. Similar smoothing-driven improvements have been reported for resin-based finishing techniques, where surface levelling plays a dominant role in restoring optical clarity [16,17,18,19]. From a physical point of view, this behaviour is consistent with a transition from a predominantly surface-dominated regime toward one in which bulk and interfacial effects become more relevant. Once surface irregularities are strongly reduced, residual optical degradation is therefore more plausibly associated with internal features of the material.
The UV curing step was primarily intended to solidify the newly deposited resin coating rather than to post-cure the printed specimens. Nevertheless, the underlying substrate was also subjected to additional UV exposure and heating, and a contribution of this treatment to the optical response cannot be completely excluded. However, the close correspondence between the reduction in surface roughness and the increase in transmittance supports surface levelling as the main mechanism responsible for the observed optical improvement.
Despite the high and nearly constant transmittance achieved after coating, the image-based transparency analysis reveals that optical performance is not fully restored. The progressive increase in haze and the reduction in sharpness with increasing air-gap distance demonstrate that residual light scattering persists within the material. Quantitatively, haze values increase from approximately 10–11% at short air-gap distances (20 mm, LH50-15°) up to more than 40% (~ 43% for LH100-30° at 60 mm), indicating a degradation of contrast despite high transmitted intensity. This behaviour suggests that internal structure plays a major role in the coated condition. In particular, refractive index variations and interlayer interfaces generated during the printing process are likely to introduce localized optical discontinuities that may cause light deviation, as also discussed in studies on refractive index distributions in additively manufactured optics [9]. Unlike surface scattering, these effects are not eliminated by coating, as they originate from the bulk of the material. Therefore, after coating, the persistence of image degradation despite the strong reduction in surface roughness suggests an increasingly important contribution from internal scattering mechanisms. This explains why transmittance alone is not sufficient to describe functional optical performance, in agreement with recent perception-based transparency frameworks [21].
A key result of this study is the strong dependence of transparency metrics on the air-gap distance. Both haze and sharpness metrics show systematic degradation as the distance between the specimen and the target increases. This behaviour can be interpreted in terms of light propagation: even small angular deviations introduced by internal scattering mechanisms lead to progressively larger spatial displacements as light travels through free space. As a result, contrast is reduced (haze increase) and edge definition is degraded (sharpness reduction). For instance, SID values decrease from approximately 70–80% at 20 mm to values as low as 20–30% at 60 mm, depending on the process parameters, while MTF50 shows a comparable reduction trend. This finding highlights that transparency is inherently a distance-dependent property, as also emphasized by Busato et al. [21]. Materials exhibiting high transmittance may still produce significant image degradation under realistic observation conditions. Therefore, optical performance must be evaluated in relation to the intended application geometry, rather than relying solely on bulk transmission measurements.
The sharpness analysis further reveals a pronounced anisotropic optical behaviour. Vertical and horizontal edges exhibit different sensitivities to process parameters, with horizontal features showing a stronger degradation and a more pronounced dependence on both layer height and printing angle. This anisotropy can be attributed to the orientation of interlayer interfaces relative to the optical path. The layer-by-layer architecture introduces preferential directions for light scattering and refraction, resulting in direction-dependent image degradation. In particular, interfaces aligned with the optical path may act as scattering planes, affecting spatial frequency transfer differently depending on the observed feature orientation. The statistical analysis confirms this behaviour, showing that printing angle has a negligible effect on vertical sharpness metrics, while it significantly affects horizontal ones. This result provides indirect evidence that internal structure affects not only the magnitude of optical degradation, but also its directional characteristics.
An important outcome of the study is the non-trivial role of layer height. While lower layer heights improve surface quality in the AP condition by reducing roughness and enhancing transmittance, the results obtained after coating indicate a more complex behaviour. In particular, thicker layers may, in some cases, better preserve spatial frequency content, especially in specific orientations. This apparent contradiction may reflect a trade-off between surface quality and internal interface density. Thinner layers produce smoother external surfaces but are also associated with a greater number of internal interfaces along the optical path, potentially amplifying cumulative scattering effects. Conversely, thicker layers are associated with fewer interfaces, although each individual interface may introduce stronger local optical discontinuities. Therefore, layer height cannot be considered a parameter with a uniformly positive or negative effect on transparency. Its influence depends on the balance between surface morphology and internal structural effects, which become more relevant after coating.
From an engineering perspective, the results demonstrate that the optical performance of transparent VPP-printed components must be interpreted within a multi-scale framework involving surface morphology, internal structure, and light propagation conditions. Surface finishing is a necessary step to achieve high transmittance, as it suppresses surface-induced scattering and is consistent with a shift toward an optical regime in which bulk and interfacial contributions become increasingly relevant.However, this is not sufficient to guarantee full optical functionality. Internal structure and air-gap distance play a critical role in determining the final visual performance, particularly for applications involving image transmission or visualization. The results also indicate that coating can substantially reduce the dependence of optical transmittance on manufacturing parameters, allowing greater flexibility in process optimization. At the same time, anisotropic effects and distance-dependent degradation must be explicitly considered in design, especially when directional image quality is relevant. Overall, the findings highlight that the design of transparent VPP components cannot rely on single-parameter optimization. Instead, a multi-scale approach is required, in which process parameters, post-processing strategies, and application-specific optical requirements are considered simultaneously.
5 Conclusions
In this study, a controlled resin coating process and an image-based optical characterization framework were developed to investigate the transparency of VPP-printed polymer components. The main findings can be summarized as follows:
surface roughness was strongly associated with optical performance in the AP condition, with Ra increasing up to ~ 10 μm and transmittance decreasing to values below 10% as a function of layer height and printing angle;
the coating process drastically reduced surface roughness (Ra < 0.15 μm) and increased transmittance to ~ 86–89%, effectively suppressing surface-induced scattering and reducing the influence of printing parameters;
despite high transmittance, transparency quality remained limited, and the observed distance-dependent increase in haze (up to ~ 40%) and reduction in sharpness are consistent with a contribution from internal scattering mechanisms;
the overall results support a mechanistic interpretation in which coating shifts the optical response from a predominantly surface-controlled regime toward one in which bulk and interfacial effects become increasingly relevant, suggesting an important role of interlayer interfaces and internal structure in governing functional optical performance;
the results suggest a potential trade-off associated with layer height, in which reduced surface roughness (thin layers) competes with increased interface density, affecting directional sharpness preservation;
from an engineering perspective, these results demonstrate that achieving high optical performance in VPP components requires a multi-scale design approach combining process parameter selection, surface finishing, and application-specific evaluation of transparency.
While the proposed methodology was successfully applied under the investigated conditions, the present study focused on a single photopolymer resin and a specific coating formulation, and the observed behaviour may therefore depend on material properties such as refractive index and curing characteristics. Furthermore, the coating process was validated on planar specimens, providing a solid baseline for future investigations on more complex geometries.
Future studies could focus on extending the proposed coating methodology to geometrically complex components, where curvature, internal channels, or variable thickness could affect coating uniformity and optical behaviour. In addition, the influence of different photopolymer resins and coating formulations could be investigated to assess the role of refractive index matching and curing behaviour on transparency performance.
