Oct 22, 2026 View: 106 Leave a message
Most Common Surface Plating Types for Pogo Pin Connectors
Alice Smith
Alice is a senior R&D engineer at Dongguan Xinteng Electronics Co., Ltd. With over 8 years of experience in the field of Pogo Pin connectors, she specializes in the research of high - current and miniaturization scenarios. She has contributed to many of the company's patented products and more than 300 solutions.
Gold, nickel, tin and silver can serve different functions in a pogo pin connector. The appropriate finish depends on the surface being coated: a plunger tip, an internal sliding surface and a soldering terminal may have different requirements.
For the mating contact, the main concerns are stable electrical resistance, wear and corrosion. For a termination, solderability may be the priority. The coating specification should therefore describe the complete layer structure and its location rather than assign one finish to the entire connector without further detail.
Plating type | Typical role | Main benefit | Key consideration
---|---|---|---
Gold | Mating contacts and other surfaces requiring stable electrical contact | Resistance to oxidation and reliable contact behavior | Wear, thickness, coverage and the underlying coating
Nickel | Underlayer beneath gold or another contact finish; exposed finish where suitable | Barrier protection and support for the coating system | Surface films can affect exposed electrical contacts
Tin | Solderable terminations and selected contact applications | Solderability and comparatively economical processing | Oxide films, contact design and repeated mating
Silver | Selected power contacts and other suitable electrical interfaces | High electrical conductivity | Tarnishing and compatibility with the operating environment
Gold is a common choice for pogo pin mating surfaces, particularly where the connection operates with limited contact force or carries low-level signals. Its resistance to oxidation helps maintain an electrically stable surface.
Gold does not provide the highest bulk conductivity of these metals. Its usefulness in many connectors comes from the behavior of the contact interface, where surface films and contamination can matter as much as the conductivity of the metal underneath.
The gold deposit also needs to suit the mechanical duty. Hard gold formulations can be considered where repeated contact and wear are important. Soft gold has different properties and may suit particular connection or manufacturing requirements. Neither should be specified solely by color or a general description such as "gold finish."
Thickness is one part of the requirement. Coverage, porosity, adhesion, substrate preparation and the condition of the mating surface also influence performance. A thicker coating cannot correct poor alignment or an unsuitable contact structure.
Nickel is frequently used beneath gold on copper-alloy components. It can limit copper diffusion toward the surface and provide support for the coating system. Its thickness and integrity should be specified with the top layer rather than treated as an incidental manufacturing detail.
An exposed nickel surface behaves differently from a gold contact surface. Nickel can develop surface films that affect electrical contact, particularly where available force or movement is limited. Its suitability must therefore be evaluated for the actual interface.
A component plated with nickel is not automatically equivalent to one plated with gold over nickel. The exposed surface determines what meets the mating contact, while the underlying layers contribute to the overall coating performance.
The preparation sequence depends on the base material and selected process. A copper intermediate layer may be appropriate in some constructions, but it is not a universal requirement for every steel component. The process specification should identify the approved sequence.
Tin is useful where solderability is important, including suitable connector terminations. It can also be used in contact systems designed to accommodate its surface behavior.
Tin forms an oxide film, so the mating geometry, contact force and any wiping action need to be considered. There is no single minimum force that qualifies every tin-plated pogo contact. The required force depends on the contact area, movement, finish condition and electrical acceptance criteria.
Repeated movement can also affect tin surfaces. A finish suitable for a solder tail should not automatically be transferred to a frequently mated plunger tip. Evaluating those locations separately can produce a more appropriate and economical coating specification.
Tin should therefore not be described simply as a low-quality finish. Its value depends on whether it is used for a function that suits its properties.
Silver offers high electrical conductivity and can be considered for selected power-contact designs. However, the conductive coating is only one part of the current path. Contact geometry, pressure, base material and terminations still determine the performance of the assembled connector.
Silver's characteristic tarnishing is commonly associated with sulfur-containing contaminants. Describing this only as "easy oxidation" misses an important environmental consideration.
Tarnish can affect contact behavior, so the expected atmosphere, storage conditions and mating mechanism should be included in the evaluation. A silver-plated power contact and a lightly loaded signal contact may need different acceptance criteria.
Silver is neither a universal replacement for gold nor a finish that should be dismissed solely because it can tarnish. Selection requires evidence from the intended contact arrangement and exposure conditions.
Palladium-nickel, sometimes discussed alongside nickel plating, is a separate alloy finish. It should be identified accurately in the specification. Substitution between nickel, palladium-nickel and gold-based coating systems requires a review of electrical behavior, wear, mating compatibility and manufacturing conditions.
Different finishes may be appropriate on different parts of one pogo pin. For example, the mating surface may need a wear-resistant contact finish while the termination needs a solderable surface. This distinction should be included in the drawing and agreed with the manufacturer.
Working from customer drawings, we can develop custom pogo pin and magnetic connector assemblies with coordinated contact materials, coating specifications, precision machining and terminations. Where different surfaces have different functions, the design review can establish which areas require each finish and how the finished parts will be inspected.
Coating thickness also affects dimensions. Deposits on an external shaft increase its diameter, while deposits inside a barrel reduce the available opening. The machining allowance and coating variation must leave sufficient clearance for smooth plunger movement.
Drawings should state whether critical dimensions apply before or after plating. They should also identify the relevant coated areas, layer sequence, thickness limits and inspection locations. A thickness measured on an accessible outer surface may not represent the coating inside a narrow barrel.
Operating temperature cannot be assigned from the plating name alone. The base material, spring, housing, termination and any other assembly components also have limits. A temperature quoted for a particular coated metal should not be presented as the rating of a complete pogo pin connector.
The same principle applies to corrosion resistance and service life. A coating can help preserve the interface, but the finished assembly needs evaluation under the specified compression, electrical load, mating cycles and environmental exposure.
Useful verification includes:
- Coating thickness and coverage at defined locations.
- Adhesion and surface condition.
- Finished dimensions and plunger movement.
- Solderability where relevant.
- Contact resistance before and after the required tests.
- Electrical and mechanical performance after wear or environmental exposure.
The result should be a finish specification tied to the connector's function. This gives manufacturing and purchasing teams a clearer basis for controlling quality than a general request for "better plating."
1. Which plating is commonly used on pogo pin contact surfaces?
Gold over a nickel underlayer is a common arrangement. It combines an oxidation-resistant contact surface with an underlying barrier layer. Suitability still depends on the required force, wear, environment and electrical performance.
2. Is tin plating unsuitable for pogo pin connectors?
No. Tin can be appropriate for solderable terminations and contact designs developed around its properties. A tin-plated solder tail and a repeatedly mated plunger tip have different requirements and should be evaluated separately.
3. Why does silver plating tarnish?
Silver can react with sulfur-containing contaminants in the environment, producing surface tarnish. Its effect on the connection depends on the contact design and operating conditions. Storage and environmental exposure should be included in the assessment.
4. How should plating thickness be selected?
Define the contact function, mating conditions, wear requirement, environment and dimensional limits first. Then specify the complete coating system, including individual layers, thickness limits and measurement locations. Current rating or product category alone is insufficient.

records.abstract: Which Contact Finishes Help Reduce Corrosion and Wear ... Gold can support stable low-level contact, but a plated surface can still wear or become contaminated. ... Cleaning may remove some foreign contamination, but it cannot restore missing plating or repair a fatigued dome. ... Does gold plating prevent every contact failure? No.
records.summary: This vendor blog post from metal-domes.com explains that metal dome keypad failures can occur when the tactile click still feels normal but the dome-to-PCB contact interface has corroded chemically or worn mechanically. It distinguishes corrosion (chemical/electrochemical surface change), wear (mechanical removal of finish), foreign contamination, mechanical fatigue and fretting corrosion, and recommends inspecting both the dome and the mating PCB pad rather than assuming a single cause. For measurement it recommends a controlled actuation fixture and four-wire resistance measurement (R = V/I) with specified test current and open-circuit voltage limits, recording force, actuator position, dwell time and first-closure versus later readings. It notes that debouncing cannot restore a damaged contact surface and that cleaning may remove contamination but cannot restore missing plating or a fatigued dome. How Can You Prevent Switch Contact Corrosion and Wear in Metal Dome Keypads?
Posted on October 21, 2026 by li
Table of Contents
Toggle
Switch Contact Corrosion and Wear can make a metal dome keypad miss presses even when its tactile click still feels normal. Corrosion changes the contact surface chemically; wear removes or damages it mechanically. Preventing repeat failures means checking both the dome and its PCB contact pad, controlling contamination and movement, and testing electrical closure after the expected operating and storage conditions.
What Causes Corrosion on Metal Dome Switch Contacts?
Moisture, corrosive contaminants and residues can produce films or attack exposed metal at the dome-to-pad interface. A keypad may still snap mechanically while the small conducting areas no longer make reliable electrical contact. Electrical contact corrosion therefore cannot be ruled out simply because the button feels normal.
Preventing switch corrosion starts with finding the route into the assembly as well as the affected surface. Liquid can enter through an enclosure opening, a damaged overlay edge or an exposed vent path. Residues may already be present when the array is laminated. Condensation is different from high humidity without condensation: cooling below the dew point can place liquid directly on surfaces that were dry during assembly. Switch contact oxidation is one possible surface change, but not every insulating deposit is an oxide.
For a failed keypad, keep its storage history, cleaning-agent exposure and time in service with the sample. Several adjacent failed keys near an entry point suggest a different investigation from one heavily used key in an otherwise clean assembly. Neither pattern alone proves the cause.
How Is Contact Wear Different from Corrosion?
Contact wear results from mechanical interaction between mating surfaces. Repeated actuation, unintended rubbing or trapped particles can remove a finish or change the contact area. Corrosion is a chemical or electrochemical change. The two can combine: wear may expose underlying material, while corrosion products can interfere with later contact.
Condition | What to examine | What it does not prove
---|---|---
Surface corrosion or tarnish | Deposits, discoloration, local attack and exposure history | Color alone does not identify the material or chemical species
Mechanical wear | Repeated contact tracks, scratches, coating loss and corresponding marks on the mating pad | A visible track is not automatically an electrical failure
Foreign contamination | Fibers, dust, adhesive transfer, oils or process residues | All residue is not corrosion
Mechanical fatigue | Permanent deformation, cracking, changed return or force behavior | Fatigue and surface wear are not the same failure
Fretting corrosion involves very small repeated relative movement at a loaded contact interface. It should be considered when vibration or thermal movement is relevant, not used as a label for every worn dome. Establish whether movement occurred at the actual contact before assigning that diagnosis.
What Are the Symptoms of Worn or Corroded Switch Contacts?
Common symptoms include missed keypresses, intermittent continuity, higher closed-state resistance or a response that changes with pressing position. Some faults appear only after storage or environmental exposure. Repeatedly pressing a failed key before measurement can alter its contact condition and hide the original symptom.
Observed behavior | Useful next check | Avoid assuming
---|---|---
Normal click but missed input | Raw switch signal and closed-contact resistance | The tactile click guarantees electrical closure
Works only with off-center pressure | Dome position, actuator alignment and local contact marks | More actuation force is the correct repair
Intermittent after humid storage | Uncleaned surface condition and moisture entry routes | Humidity alone identifies the corrosion mechanism
Failure after many cycles | Both contact surfaces, return behavior and cycle history | Only the dome can be worn
Several keys fail together | Shared trace, connector, contamination path and scan circuit | Every dome failed independently
Compare an affected key with a known-good key using the same fixture and electrical settings. Record the unmodified result before cleaning, replacing parts or changing debounce settings.
How Do You Inspect a Metal Dome and Its PCB Pad?
Start with the assembled keypad. Record the failed key location, overlay condition, alignment and any entry path before opening it. Disconnect power and follow the product's ESD and service procedures. Preserve at least one sample in its received condition when a failure investigation is required.
Under suitable magnification, compare the dome's contacting regions with the corresponding pad. Look for transferred residue, exposed base material, a shifted contact track or damage to the retaining film. Keep photographs of both surfaces with consistent lighting and scale. Reflections can resemble surface damage, so change the illumination angle before drawing a conclusion.
Opening a bonded array can disturb the evidence and change its mechanical behavior. The assembly photograph shows why the carrier, dome and board should be considered together; it is not a photograph of a proven corrosion failure. If deposit identification is necessary, retain the sample for appropriate materials analysis rather than identifying corrosion from color alone.
How Do You Measure Metal Dome Contact Resistance?
Use a controlled actuation fixture and a resistance measurement appropriate to the expected range. A four-wire measurement separates the current leads from the voltage-sensing leads, reducing lead-resistance error. Place the sense connections close to the switch terminals and document any board trace resistance included in the result.
The calculation is R = V / I: measured voltage drop divided by test current. For low-level contacts, specify the test current and open-circuit voltage limit before testing. An unsuitable test stimulus can change a surface film and make a degraded contact appear better than it was. Use an agreed dry-circuit method where preserving that condition is necessary.
Record the force, actuator position, dwell time and whether the reading is from first closure or later operations. A continuity buzzer is useful for a basic open/closed check, but it is not a substitute for a resistance limit or a record of intermittent interruptions. Test the application input separately when the complaint is a missed digital event.
Can Debouncing Fix Corroded Contacts?
No. Debouncing filters brief transitions around actuation or release; it does not restore a damaged conducting surface. Increasing the debounce interval may hide some transitions, but cannot guarantee detection if the contact never reaches a valid electrical state.
Check the raw input before the software filter. With a pull-up input, excessive series resistance can stop a pressed switch from pulling the node below the specified logic-low threshold. The relevant limits come from the actual circuit, not from a universal debounce delay. Keep the surface-failure investigation separate from button debounce and switch bounce testing.
Do not add a large discharge capacitor or raise switching current to burn through contamination without reviewing the switch rating and circuit. That can change the failure mechanism instead of correcting it.
Which Contact Finishes Help Reduce Corrosion and Wear?
Choose the switch contact material, dome finish and PCB pad finish as a mating pair. Resistance to surface films, thickness, hardness, porosity and operating conditions all matter. A gold-colored pad does not establish whether it has a wear-oriented electrodeposited finish or a thin immersion finish.
Our four-leg metal domes include stainless-steel, nickel and gold options across a 5–20 mm size range. The appropriate option depends on the selected part and the mating circuit; an available finish is not a guarantee of lifetime in every keypad.
Gold can support stable low-level contact, but a plated surface can still wear or become contaminated. Nickel and stainless steel may suit other requirements when the completed assembly meets its electrical limits. For PCB pads, compare the specified finish and thickness with the required actuation count. ENIG should not be assumed equivalent to hard gold for repeated mechanical contact.
Specify the finish on both drawings and test the pair. Changing only one surface without tracking the other makes later results difficult to interpret.
How Do Dome Arrays Help Keep Contamination Away from Contacts?
A carrier holds domes in position and limits direct handling of the contact surfaces. Its adhesive pattern, spacer and air paths also influence how contaminants might reach the dome cavity. Protection must be assessed at the assembled keypad, including its perimeter and enclosure.
Our double-layer dome arrays use a spacer beneath the dome layer with air paths for actuation. The carrier can reduce exposure, but a double-layer construction alone does not establish a waterproof or hermetic seal.
Keep adhesive away from the active contact region and control residues before lamination. Avoid touching the dome underside or pad with bare fingers. Review vent endpoints rather than blocking all vents: a trapped-air problem and an ingress problem require different solutions. Where liquid exposure is expected, assess the overlay, enclosure seal and vent routing together.
How Can Assembly Design Reduce Contact Wear?
Keep the actuator aligned with the intended pressing region and support the PCB so that the board does not become an uncontrolled spring. Excessive travel, a tilted plunger or a displaced dome can create localized loading and inconsistent contact.
Check the complete tolerance stack: button position, plunger geometry, dome placement, carrier thickness and board location. A drawing that controls each part independently can still allow an unfavorable assembled condition. Compare contact marks after cycling with the original intended geometry.
Prevent particles from becoming trapped under the dome during assembly. A harder press is not a substitute for correct placement, and hand-bending a dome to restore its feel does not establish a reliable repair. For a design change, confirm both the force–travel response and electrical performance.
Can You Clean Corroded Metal Dome Contacts?
Switch contact repair depends on what has failed. Cleaning may remove some foreign contamination, but it cannot restore missing plating or repair a fatigued dome. Preserve the original evidence first, then use only a cleaning method compatible with the PCB finish, carrier, adhesive and overlay.
Do not treat household abrasives, contact sprays or scraping as a general production repair. Abrasion can remove a thin finish; liquid can carry residues into an array or affect its adhesive. An opened carrier may also need replacement rather than reattachment.
If the approved service procedure permits cleaning, compare resistance and input behavior before and after it, then check whether the fault returns under relevant conditions. Temporary continuity is not evidence that the underlying ingress or wear problem has been removed. Replace damaged parts or assemblies according to the product's repair criteria.
How Should You Test Long-Term Contact Reliability?
Test the finished switch stack under the electrical load and mechanical arrangement it will actually use. Separate cycle wear from storage exposure, then combine them when the intended service includes both. Include the first operation after a dwell period, not only readings taken during continuous cycling.
Test element | Record | Reason
---|---|---
Baseline | Part lot, pad finish, initial resistance and raw input behavior | Establishes the starting condition
Cycling | Actuation count, force, travel, position and rate | Relates wear to the actual mechanical input
Environmental exposure | Temperature, humidity or relevant contaminants, duration and recovery conditions | Avoids treating different exposures as interchangeable
Electrical checks | Test current, voltage limit, resistance and intermittent events | Makes before/after results comparable
Final inspection | Mating surface photographs, carrier condition and return behavior | Connects the symptom with physical evidence
Define acceptance criteria before the test: allowable resistance, missed events, mechanical return and any permitted physical changes. Salt-spray hours do not translate directly into years of service, and a dome's cycle rating does not establish the life of an arbitrary pad and enclosure combination.
At EBest Circuit(Best Technology), we supply custom dome arrays with specified dome locations, cutouts and carrier outlines. Send the layout, mating-pad finish, electrical operating conditions, expected cycles and exposure details to sales@metal-domes.com when discussing a new array or a repeat failure. Include uncleaned sample photographs and the measured symptom so the configuration can be reviewed against the actual problem.
Switch Contact Corrosion and Wear FAQs
Does a metal dome need visible rust to have a contact problem?
No. A thin surface film or contamination can affect a low-level connection without obvious rust. Electrical results and the condition of both mating surfaces matter more than appearance alone.
Does gold plating prevent every contact failure?
No. Gold does not prevent incorrect alignment, excessive travel, contamination or wear-through of an unsuitable finish. Validate the complete dome-to-pad interface.
Why can a keypad work again after several presses?
Repeated operation can change an intermittent interface. That observation is useful evidence, but it does not identify the mechanism or establish a permanent repair. Record the first-press behavior before repeatedly actuating the key.
Should you replace the dome or the PCB?
Inspect both. A new dome cannot restore a worn pad, and a new board cannot correct a damaged carrier or fatigued dome. Use the inspection and electrical results to select the repair scope.
Preventing Switch Contact Corrosion and Wear requires a clean, compatible contact pair, controlled assembly and validation after relevant exposure. Preserve failure evidence first; then correct the identified surface, mechanical or ingress problem rather than masking the symptom with more force or a longer debounce delay.

\# TPS Elektronik at The Battery Show North America 2026

Detroit\, USA \| October 12–15\, 2026

TPS Elektronik GmbH participated as an exhibitor at The Battery Show North America 2026\, held at Huntington Place in Detroit\, Michigan\. Bringing together professionals from the battery\, electric vehicle\, and energy storage industries\, the event provided an international platform for exploring technologies and solutions shaping the future of electrification\.

For TPS Elektronik\, a Germany\-based specialist in power electronics and electronics manufacturing services \(EMS\)\, the exhibition represented an opportunity to strengthen its international industry presence and highlight its capabilities in electrical engineering\, power conversion\, and customized manufacturing solutions\.

\#\# Supporting the Evolution of Battery and Power Electronics Technologies

As battery technology continues to advance\, the requirements placed on electrical and electronic systems are becoming increasingly demanding\. Reliable power conversion\, efficient energy distribution\, precise testing\, and effective thermal management are essential considerations across battery\-related applications\.

With more than 25 years of experience in power electronics and an international manufacturing and distribution network\, TPS Elektronik offers a broad portfolio of products and services addressing these technical requirements\.

The company’s capabilities extend from individual electrical components to customized electronic assemblies and complete systems\, supporting customers throughout different stages of product development and manufacturing\.

\#\# Power Electronics Solutions for Modern Energy Applications

TPS Elektronik’s portfolio includes several technologies relevant to the battery and electrification industries\.

Power Supplies and Power Conversion

TPS provides industrial power supply solutions\, programmable power equipment\, and bidirectional power modules\. Its expertise also covers AC\/DC applications\, battery charging and discharging systems\, and power conversion technologies used in industrial and energy\-related applications\.

Bidirectional power systems are particularly relevant where electrical energy must be transferred in both directions\, such as in certain battery testing\, charging\, and energy storage applications\.

Busbars and Electrical Power Distribution

Reliable power distribution is essential for electrical systems operating with high currents\. TPS Elektronik offers busbar solutions designed for compact\, efficient power distribution\, with options for application\-specific electrical and mechanical requirements\.

Such components are relevant to battery systems\, industrial power electronics\, and energy storage equipment\, where current\-carrying capacity\, electrical performance\, and space\-efficient integration are important design considerations\.

Transformers and Inductive Components

Transformers\, inductors\, and chokes are fundamental components in many power conversion systems\. TPS Elektronik supports the development\, manufacturing\, and testing of customized magnetic components for a range of electrical and electronic applications\.

These components can contribute to voltage conversion\, filtering\, and electromagnetic compatibility in power electronic equipment\.

Thermal Management and Cooling Solutions

Effective thermal management plays an important role in maintaining the performance and service life of electronic components\.

TPS Elektronik provides passive heat sinks\, active cooling solutions\, and liquid\-cooling options for applications requiring controlled heat dissipation\. Depending on system requirements\, these technologies can support thermal management in power supplies\, converters\, and other electronic assemblies\.

\#\# From Components to Customized Electronics Manufacturing

Beyond its product portfolio\, TPS Elektronik offers electronics manufacturing services covering development\, component procurement\, assembly\, testing\, and production\.

Its manufacturing capabilities include PCB assembly\, magnetic components\, mechanical processing\, and system integration\.

This combination enables TPS to support customers seeking application\-specific solutions\, whether for individual components\, electronic assemblies\, or more complex industrial systems\.

By integrating technical development with manufacturing expertise\, TPS helps customers address design requirements\, production considerations\, and the transition from prototypes to series production\.

\#\# Connecting with the International Battery Industry

The Battery Show North America brings together organizations working across battery manufacturing\, electric mobility\, energy storage\, and related technologies\.

Participation in an international exhibition of this kind reflects TPS Elektronik’s interest in the technical requirements and developments influencing these industries\.

For companies operating in power electronics\, such events provide an opportunity to follow emerging industry priorities\, understand evolving application needs\, and explore potential areas for technical cooperation\.

TPS Elektronik’s participation in Detroit forms part of its broader international business activities and its focus on supporting industrial customers with specialized electrical and electronic solutions\.

\#\# Looking Ahead\: Engineering Solutions for Future Requirements

As electrification progresses across industrial and energy applications\, dependable electrical components and adaptable manufacturing capabilities remain essential\.

TPS Elektronik continues to focus on customer\-specific engineering solutions\, combining expertise in power electronics\, component manufacturing\, and electronics manufacturing services\.

Are you developing a battery\-related\, energy storage\, or power electronics application\?

Explore our products and EMS capabilities or contact the TPS Elektronik team to discuss your technical requirements and customized solutions\.

records.title: Plasma-Enhanced Multilayer Coatings on Metal Bipolar Plates for Corrosion Resistance and High Electrical Conductivity
records.abstract: Abstract Metal bipolar plates are central to lowering the cost and weight of proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) stacks, yet their long-term use is limited by aggressive corrosion in the acidic, humid, low-pH cathode environment. Multilayer protective coatings combining adhesion-promoting metal interlayers with chemically inert graphitic carbon are widely regarded as a promising solution, but they have historically been deposited slowly and from precursors such as titanium tetrachloride that are difficult to scale safely. Here, we report the design and operation of a showerhead plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) reactor that deposits Ti/TiCx/amorphous-carbon (a-C) multilayer coatings on 304 stainless steel using the comparatively safe titanium isopropoxide (TiPO) precursor in combination with a hydrogen plasma. Both continuous radio frequency (RF) and nanosecond-pulsed glow discharges were tested at 10 W and at substrate temperatures up to 300 °C. Cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and Raman scattering confirm uniform, pinhole-free multilayers in which Ti is reduced from TiPO by atomic hydrogen and the carbon top layer is sp2-rich and graphitic. Carbon deposition rates of 200–237 nm min–1 were obtained, matching or exceeding the best values reported in the literature. A coupled plasma kinetics and showerhead transport model rationalizes these rates, the distinct microstructures obtained under continuous and nanosecond-pulsed excitation, and the measured coating uniformity. The best carbon coatings reach interfacial contact resistance (ICR) values of 5.4–13.5 mΩ·cm2 at 1.10 MPa, with the lowest well below the 2025 U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) target of 10 mΩ·cm2. The coatings showed no detectable Raman or morphological degradation after accelerated thermal cycling between 30 and 100 °C in pH 3 H2SO4, demonstrating their potential as a fast, safe, and scalable coating route for next-generation PEMFC bipolar plates.

records.title: Effect of lubricant oxidation on tribological performance of gear contact interfaces in three gorges ship lift: experiments and simulation
records.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to investigate the high-temperature degradation behavior of lubricating oils used in the gearboxes of the Three Gorges ship lift, which operate under harsh environmental conditions. The study seeks to understand the correlation between the evolution of physicochemical properties, oxidation mechanisms and the resulting tribological performance to address excessive gear wear. Design/methodology/approach High-temperature oxidation experiments were conducted to simulate the degradation process. The evolution of physicochemical properties was characterized by monitoring color, acid number and kinematic viscosity. Oxidation products were analyzed using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy and GC-MS chromatography. Furthermore, ReaxFF reactive molecular dynamics simulations were used to reveal microscopic reaction pathways. Finally, the tribological performance of the degraded oil was evaluated using a friction tester and a 3D profilometer and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was performed on the worn surface to characterize the compositional changes of the friction film, thereby revealing the friction-induced damage mechanism of the oxidized lubricating oil. Findings The results indicate that thermal oxidation leads to the formation of acidic polar molecules, such as carboxylic acids, aldehydes and esters, resulting in an increasing trend in both acid number and kinematic viscosity. ReaxFF simulations revealed that high-temperature oxidation proceeds through multiple specific reaction pathways. Crucially, the study confirms that the decline in tribological performance is directly related to these physicochemical changes and the accumulation of oxidation products. Originality/value This study uniquely combines macroscopic experimental characterization with microscopic ReaxFF molecular dynamics simulations to provide a comprehensive understanding of lubricant degradation in the specific context of large-scale ship lift gearboxes. The findings offer theoretical support for optimizing oil monitoring indicators and maintenance strategies for critical hydraulic engineering equipment.

The authors conducted high-temperature oxidation experiments and tracked color, acid number and kinematic viscosity, while analyzing oxidation products with FTIR and GC-MS chromatography. ReaxFF reactive molecular dynamics simulations were used to probe microscopic reaction pathways. Tribological performance of the degraded oil was evaluated with a friction tester, a 3D profilometer and XPS analysis of worn surfaces to characterize friction-film compositional changes. The abstract reports that thermal oxidation forms acidic polar molecules such as carboxylic acids, aldehydes and esters, with increasing acid number and kinematic viscosity, and states that declining tribological performance is directly related to these physicochemical changes and accumulated oxidation products. Only the abstract was available, so detailed numerical results and full experimental data could not be verified.

CASSIDA FM GEAR OIL TLS 150
Specialty gear fluid for use in food manufacturing equipment
Description
CASSIDA FM GEAR OIL TLS 150 is a specialty anti-wear gear fluid which is specifically designed for use in the food and beverage canning industry.
This product is based on careful blend of fluids and selected additives chosen for their ability to meet the stringent requirements of food and beverage industry.
Certified by NSF for ISO 21469 and registered by NSF (Class H1) for use where there is potential for incidental food contact. This product is produced according to FUCHS quality standards, in facilities where HACCP audit and Good Manufacturing Practice have been implemented and form part of the quality and hygiene management systems ISO 9001 and ISO 21469.
Certifications and Specifications
- NSF H1
- NSF ISO 21469
- Kosher
- Halal
- DIN 51517 CLP
Performance Features
- The base fluid has been selected for its ability to provide superior lubrication under variety of applications
- Specially formulated to provide good lubrication even when operating in locations where it is subject to contamination with water, juice and food, which is held in suspension, thus protecting metal surfaces from wear and corrosion.
- Neutral odor and taste
- Good anti-oxidant properties. Resists the formation of deposits and sludge even at elevated temperatures, resulting in long equipment life
Applications
- Lubrication of rotary can seaming machines equipped with total loss systems
- Circulating and bearing oil systems where contamination with water or food juice can occur, such as citrus juice extraction machines
- Can be used on drives and transport chains in the food Industry. Easily applied by either brush, through baths or by automatic lubrication system.
Seal and paint compatibility
Compatible with the elastomers, gaskets, seals and paints such as poly-urethane and two part epoxy resin paints, frequently used on machinery and in lubrication systems employed in the food processing industry.
Handling and storage
All food grade lubricants should be stored separately from other lubricants, chemical substances and foodstuffs and out of direct sunlight or other heat sources. Store between 32 °F and 100 °F. Provided that the product has been stored under these conditions we recommend that the product be used within 5 years from the date of manufacture. Upon opening a pack, the product must be used within 2 years (or within 5 years of the date of manufacture, whichever is sooner).
Industries
- Food
Note
The information shown on this side is based on the experience and expertise of the FUCHS Group in the development and manufacture of lubricants and represents the current state of the art. The performance of our products can be influenced by a series of factors, especially the specific use, the method of application, the operational environment, component pretreatment, possible external contamination, etc. For this reason, universally valid statements about the function of our products are not possible. Our products must not be used in aircraft/spacecraft or parts thereof. This does not apply if the products can be removed again before the components are fitted in an aircraft/spacecraft. The information given here represents general, non-binding guidelines. No warranty expressed or implied is given concerning the properties of the product or its suitability for any given application. We therefore recommend that you consult a FUCHS Group application engineer to discuss application conditions and the performance criteria of the products before the products are used. It is the responsibility of the user to test the functional suitability of the products and to use them with the corresponding care. Our products are subject to continuous further development. We therefore retain the right to change our product range, the products, and their manufacturing processes as well as all details on this side at any time and without warning, provided that no customer-specific agreements exist that require otherwise.

Applications

Metal Forming Lubricants
The metal forming industry is undergoing rapid transformation driven by the use of lighter and stronger materials, increasingly complex production processes, and stricter environmental regulations.
In this context, metal forming lubricants play a critical role in ensuring process efficiency, part quality, and tool protection across industrial applications.
Manufacturers are increasingly working with advanced materials such as high-strength steels (AHSS), aluminium, and lightweight alloys, particularly in sectors such as automotive and industrial manufacturing. While these materials offer clear advantages in terms of weight reduction and performance, they also introduce new challenges in metal forming processes. These include increased tool wear, a higher risk of edge cracking, springback effects, and overall greater process complexity. To successfully address these challenges, it is essential to use high-performance metal forming lubricants that ensure process stability, part quality, and operational efficiency.
Modern metal forming lubricants must meet multiple technical and operational requirements:
Material compatibility: Today’s processes involve a wide range of metals, including ferrous materials, aluminum, and coated substrates, requiring versatile lubrication solutions.
Performance under demanding conditions: Lubricants must deliver excellent friction reduction and tool protection in operations such as deep drawing, stamping, and in-die tapping.
Post-process compatibility: Residues must be compatible with cleaning, painting, or assembly processes to ensure seamless production flow.
Health, safety, and sustainability: There is growing demand for chlorine-free lubricants and environmentally friendly solutions that reduce impact on operators and the environment.
FUCHS offers a comprehensive portfolio of metalworking lubricants designed to optimize forming processes:
Chlorine-free lubricants: Efficient alternatives to traditional oils, delivering high performance while reducing environmental impact.
Synthetic lubricants: Ideal for demanding applications, providing enhanced tool protection and reducing or eliminating cleaning requirements.
Water-miscible lubricants and neat oils: Versatile solutions suitable for a wide range of forming operations, offering excellent lubrication and corrosion protection.
Choosing the right metal forming lubricant delivers key operational advantages:
- Extended tool and die life
- Reduced maintenance and operating costs
- Improved part quality
- Enhanced process stability and efficiency
- Compliance with environmental and safety regulations

Abstract:
Thermal gradients in co-packaged optics (CPO) increase thermal crosstalk in densely integrated multi-chip stacks and accelerate reliability wear-out. Fast prediction of three-dimensional (3D), multi-layer temperature distributions is therefore critical for early-stage package exploration and thermal-aware layout decisions. This paper presents a physics-informed deep learning framework that predicts volumetric temperature fields in heterogeneous CPO assemblies by embedding the steady-state variable-conductivity heat equation into the training objective via a finite-difference residual. A 3D U-Net maps voxelized thermal-conductivity and heat-source tensors to the 3D temperature distribution, while the physics loss enforces consistency with governing heat transfer without requiring extensive labeled datasets. Validation against ANSYS Icepak on both a photonic chip region and system-level multi-chip layouts demonstrates accurate hotspot prediction and inter-chip heat transfer modeling, achieving an average temperature-field prediction accuracy of 89%.
Date of Conference: 26-29 May 2026
Date Added to IEEE Xplore: 17 June 2026
Conference Location: Orlando, FL, USA
Funding Agency:
I. Introduction
Co-packaged optics (CPO) is widely regarded as a key packaging approach to scale bandwidth density and improve energy efficiency by colocating photonic and electronic components and shortening electrical I/O distances [1]. However, this tight integration makes thermal behavior a first-order system constraint. Temperature rise and spatial gradients can increase thermal crosstalk across nearby devices and layers, reduce reliability margins, and complicate package-level design closure. As emphasized by recent silicon photonics roadmaps, robust packaging- and system-level thermal modeling is increasingly important as integration density and heterogeneity continue to grow [2].

Fast prediction of three\-dimensional \(3D\)\, multi\-layer temperature distributions is therefore critical for early\-stage package exploration and thermal\-aware layout decisions\. This paper presents a physics\-informed deep learning framework that predicts volumetric temperature fields in heterogeneous CPO assemblies by embedding the steady\-state variable\-conductivity heat equation into the training objective via a finite\-difference residual\. A 3D U\-Net maps voxelized thermal\-conductivity and heat\-source tensors to the 3D temperature distribution\, while the physics loss enforces consistency with governing heat transfer without requiring extensive labeled datasets\. Validation against ANSYS Icepak on both a photonic chip region and system\-level multi\-chip layouts demonstrates accurate hotspot prediction and inter\-chip heat transfer modeling\, achieving an average temperature\-field prediction accuracy of 89\%\.

Date Added to IEEE Xplore\: 17 June 2026

Conference Location\: Orlando\, FL\, USA

\#\#\# I\. Introduction

Co\-packaged optics \(CPO\) is widely regarded as a key packaging approach to scale bandwidth density and improve energy efficiency by colocating photonic and electronic components and shortening electrical I\/O distances \[1\]\. However\, this tight integration makes thermal behavior a first\-order system constraint\. Temperature rise and spatial gradients can increase thermal crosstalk across nearby devices and layers\, reduce reliability margins\, and complicate package\-level design closure\. As emphasized by recent silicon photonics roadmaps\, robust packaging\- and system\-level thermal modeling is increasingly important as integration density and heterogeneity continue to grow \[2\]\.

Lithium Battery Pack Busbar Design and Current Density Limits
When a customer asks me to push more current through a lithium battery pack, the cells are rarely the bottleneck. In my fifteen years designing packs at Horizon Power, the component that quietly decides whether a 100 A or 200 A rating is realistic is the busbar. A busbar is the solid metal strip that links cells or modules together, and its cross-section, material, and connection method set a hard ceiling on current density. Get it wrong and you get hot spots, voltage sag, and in the worst case a thermal event that no amount of cell-level protection can fix.
In this guide I will walk through how we size busbars for lithium battery packs, the current density limits we use in production, and the safety margins that keep a pack within UN38.3 and IEC 62133 expectations.
Why Busbar Design Defines Pack Current Capability
A lithium battery pack is only as strong as its weakest series link. The busbar carries the full pack current between parallel groups, so every amp that leaves the pack also crosses every busbar joint. Unlike a wire, a busbar is a fixed geometry: its resistance is set the moment you choose the material, thickness, and width. We model it early in the mechanical layout because changing it later means re-tooling the cell holder and the laser-welding fixture.
The first number I look at is not capacity but continuous current divided by busbar cross-section. That ratio, current density, tells me whether the strip will stay cool or slowly cook the pack. A drone battery that draws 60 A peak through a 2 mm thick, 10 mm wide nickel strip is already running near the edge, which is why high-rate packs move to copper or nickel-plated copper busbars.
Current Density Limits for Lithium Battery Busbars
For nickel-plated steel busbars, which are common in cylindrical cell holders, we hold continuous current density to about 4 A per square millimeter and peak, sixty second, to about 8 A per square millimeter. Pure nickel is better at roughly 6 A per square millimeter continuous. Copper busbars, with conductivity near 58 megasiemens per meter, comfortably carry 8 to 10 A per square millimeter continuous and 15 to 20 A per square millimeter for short pulses. Aluminum sits between, around 5 to 6 A per square millimeter continuous, but it needs careful surface treatment to stop oxidation at the joint.
These are not arbitrary numbers. They come from balancing temperature rise against the pack enclosure’s ability to shed heat. Inside a sealed case with still air, a strip running at 10 A per square millimeter in copper still climbs several degrees per minute, so we derate for duty cycle. A custom battery solution that runs a thirty percent duty cycle can use a higher density than one running flat out for an hour.
Material Choices: Copper, Aluminum, and Nickel-Plated Steel
Copper is the default for high-current lithium battery packs. It is expensive and heavy, but its low resistance means thin bars can carry serious current. We use tin or nickel plating on copper to stop verdigris and to make ultrasonic or laser welding consistent.
Nickel-plated steel is the workhorse of consumer 18650 and 21700 packs because spot welding nickel to the cell cap is fast and reliable. The trade-off is higher resistance, so you need more cross-section for the same current. Aluminum is lighter and cheaper than copper but demands ferrite or laser cleaning at the joint; a dirty aluminum interface can double contact resistance overnight.
For an LFP battery used in stationary storage, weight matters less than cost, so we often choose thick tinned copper. For a NCM battery in a mobile device where every gram counts, aluminum busbars with plated joints earn their place.
Cross-Section Sizing and the 4 A per Square Millimeter Rule
The quick field rule I teach new engineers is 4 A per square millimeter of busbar cross-section for nickel-based strip under continuous load. A 2 mm by 10 mm strip gives 20 square millimeters, so it is good for about 80 A continuous. If the application is a 12v lithium battery in a trolling motor pulling 50 A, that strip has comfortable margin. If it is a 120 A power pack, we double the section or switch to copper.
Sizing is not just area. Width spreads heat better than thickness because more surface faces the air. We prefer wide, thin bars over narrow, thick ones when space allows. The section must also survive the weld: a 0.2 mm foil welds cleanly, while a 3 mm bar needs a pre-weld and a penetration check.
Connection Methods: Welding, Bolting, and Busbar Rivets
How the busbar meets the cell decides whether your calculated resistance is real. Laser welding gives the lowest, most repeatable resistance on prismatic terminals and is our choice for automotive-grade lithium ion battery modules. Ultrasonic welding suits foil-to-busbar tabs and leaves no heat-affected zone in the cell. Resistance spot welding is cheap for nickel strip on cylindrical cans but drifts with electrode wear, so we audit weld strength weekly.
Bolted joints are serviceable and let you open the pack, but every bolt is a resistance point. We specify spring washers and a torque window, then verify with a milliohm test. Busbar rivets are a middle path for modular packs that must be field-repairable without special welders.
Busbar Layout: Series, Parallel, and Hybrid Topologies
The geometry of the busbar matters as much as its material. In a series layout the same current runs through every link, so each busbar must carry the full pack current and the section is uniform. In a parallel group the current splits, so the busbar that collects the group current is the thick one while the intra-group links carry only a share. I have seen packs where the parallel busbar was sized for the cell current and then used as the series link by mistake, overheating on the first full discharge.
Hybrid topologies, common in a high-voltage lithium ion battery module, use wide copper bars to gather many parallel strings and thin nickel links between series groups. The rule is simple: draw the current path, find the highest current any one bar carries, and size that bar first. We color-code the current path in the CAD model so a reviewer can see the peak at a glance before the first prototype is cut.
Thermal Rise, Voltage Drop, and Safety Margins
Two numbers close the loop. First, voltage drop: I equals V over R, and a busbar at 1 milliohm dropping 0.1 V at 100 A is wasting 10 W as heat. Second, temperature rise: we simulate the strip in still air and derate until the steady-state surface stays below 60 degrees Celsius inside the case. That 60 degree figure protects the cell seals and the surrounding polymer parts.
We also watch the joint, not just the bar. A perfect copper bar with a poor weld can carry half its rated current before the joint glows. Our production test is a four-wire milliohm measurement across every series busbar after welding; any joint above the design limit is cut and reworked. This step is cheap insurance against field failures that no battery management system can see until it is too late.
Safety margins are where experience shows. We never run a busbar at its calculated limit. A thirty percent margin on current density covers plating variation, dust on contacts, and the day the cooling fan fails. This discipline is what lets a pack pass IEC 62619 and UL 1973 abuse tests without the busbar becoming the failure point.
Frequently Asked Questions
What current density is safe for a lithium battery busbar?
For nickel-plated steel we hold about 4 A per square millimeter continuous and 8 A per square millimeter peak. Copper busbars are safe near 8 to 10 A per square millimeter continuous. Always derate for duty cycle and enclosure heat.
How do I size a busbar for a 100 A lithium battery pack?
Plan for at least 25 square millimeters of cross-section in copper, or about 50 square millimeters in nickel strip, then verify with a temperature-rise test in the real enclosure. The 4 A per square millimeter rule gives a 120 A rating on a 30 square millimeter nickel bar, leaving margin.
Is copper or aluminum better for battery busbars?
Copper carries more current per gram and per millimeter, welds cleanly, and resists corrosion with plating. Aluminum is lighter and cheaper but needs surface preparation at joints. Choose copper for high-rate packs and aluminum when weight and cost dominate.
Can busbar current limits affect UN38.3 or IEC 62133 compliance?
Yes. A busbar that overheats or develops a high-resistance joint can trigger the thermal and short-circuit tests in UN38.3 and the safety requirements in IEC 62133. Proper sizing and welding are part of passing those standards.
How does busbar resistance impact pack runtime?
Every milliohm in the busbar wastes energy as heat instead of reaching the load. A pack with 2 milliohm of busbar loss at 100 A sheds 20 W, which shortens runtime and heats the case. Lower-resistance copper busbars recover that capacity.

\#\#\# Is copper or aluminum better for battery busbars\?

Copper carries more current per gram and per millimeter\, welds cleanly\, and resists corrosion with plating\. Aluminum is lighter and cheaper but needs surface preparation at joints\. Choose copper for high\-rate packs and aluminum when weight and cost dominate\.

\#\#\# Can busbar current limits affect UN38\.3 or IEC 62133 compliance\?

Yes\. A busbar that overheats or develops a high\-resistance joint can trigger the thermal and short\-circuit tests in UN38\.3 and the safety requirements in IEC 62133\. Proper sizing and welding are part of passing those standards\.

\#\#\# How does busbar resistance impact pack runtime\?

Every milliohm in the busbar wastes energy as heat instead of reaching the load\. A pack with 2 milliohm of busbar loss at 100 A sheds 20 W\, which shortens runtime and heats the case\. Lower\-resistance copper busbars recover that capacity\.

records.body_text:
Battery Temperature Monitoring in BESS: From Sensing Points to System Protection
2026-10-20
Temperature monitoring is a basic function in a battery energy storage system, but the value of the measurement depends heavily on where the temperature is measured and how the data is used.
In a BESS, heat does not come from the battery cells alone. Current-carrying connections, busbars, contactors, fuses, cables and other electrical components can also become local heat sources. A temperature value taken from one location may therefore tell only part of the story.
For battery racks and high-voltage electrical systems, temperature monitoring needs to be considered as part of the wider monitoring and protection architecture.
Where Should Temperature Be Measured?
There is no single temperature point that can represent the condition of an entire battery rack.
Different parts of the system can experience different thermal conditions.
At the battery level, temperature monitoring may focus on cells or modules because battery temperature affects charging, discharging and overall operating conditions.
At the electrical level, other locations can also deserve attention:
Busbar connections
Cable terminals
High-current connection points
DC contactors
Fuse installation points
Other components inside the battery rack or electrical enclosure
These locations do not necessarily have the same thermal behavior as the battery cells.
A rack can therefore have a normal average temperature while a particular connection point is running significantly hotter than the surrounding area.
This is one reason why sensor placement matters as much as the sensor itself.
A Hotspot Can Be More Important Than Average Temperature
Battery thermal monitoring is sometimes viewed mainly as a way to detect an overall rise in temperature.
For system protection, however, the location of the temperature rise can be just as important.
A localized increase may be associated with:
Increased contact resistance
A loose or degraded connection
High current concentration
Poor heat dissipation
Abnormal loading
Component aging
A temperature sensor installed at an appropriate electrical connection can therefore provide information that would not be visible from a general ambient-temperature measurement.
This is particularly relevant in compact BESS designs where high-current components are installed close together.
The objective is not to place sensors everywhere. It is to identify the points where temperature data can provide useful information about battery and electrical-system conditions.
Battery Temperature and Electrical Temperature Are Different Measurements
Battery temperature and electrical-component temperature should not automatically be treated as the same thing.
A battery cell may be operating within its expected temperature range while a cable terminal or busbar connection is experiencing abnormal local heating.
The reverse can also occur. A battery module may experience a temperature increase because of its operating condition while the surrounding electrical connections remain within their normal range.
This distinction matters when temperature data is used for protection decisions.
The monitoring system needs to know what each measurement represents rather than treating all temperature values as interchangeable.
For this reason, the physical location of each sensing point should be considered when defining the monitoring architecture.
From Sensor Data to BMS Decisions
Temperature measurement becomes more useful when it is connected to the BMS and the wider control system.
A BMS can use temperature information together with other battery parameters such as cell voltage, pack voltage and charge/discharge current to determine whether the battery is operating within its defined limits.
Temperature can affect several decisions, including:
Whether charging or discharging should continue
Whether current should be limited
Whether an abnormal condition should trigger an alarm
Whether a protection threshold has been reached
Whether the battery needs to enter a different operating state
The important point is that the sensor does not make the protection decision by itself.
The sensor provides the measurement. The BMS interprets the data according to the configured protection and control logic.
This distinction becomes increasingly important as battery systems use more monitoring points and more detailed operating information.
Temperature Difference Can Also Carry Useful Information
Absolute temperature is not always the only useful value.
The difference between sensing points can provide additional information about the condition of the battery system.
For example, if several comparable battery sections operate under similar conditions but one location shows a persistent temperature difference, that variation may deserve further investigation.
The same principle can apply to electrical connection points.
A single temperature value may appear acceptable when viewed on its own, while a comparison between multiple points can reveal an abnormal pattern.
This makes multi-point temperature monitoring useful not only for protection, but also for condition monitoring and maintenance.
The quality of the monitoring architecture therefore depends on both the sensor performance and the way the collected data is interpreted.
Wired and Wireless Temperature Monitoring
The choice between wired and wireless sensing depends on the physical structure of the system.
Wired sensors can provide a straightforward connection to the monitoring system, but a larger number of sensing points can increase wiring requirements.
In a battery rack with many modules and multiple monitoring locations, cable routing can become a practical design consideration.
Wireless temperature monitoring can reduce the amount of signal wiring required between sensing points and the data collection system. This can be useful where installation space is limited or where monitoring points are distributed across a larger electrical structure.
Wireless sensing can also be relevant when monitoring is required at locations such as busbars, cable connections or other electrical interfaces where adding additional wiring is inconvenient.
The choice should still be based on the complete system requirements, including communication method, installation environment, measurement accuracy, power supply and maintenance requirements.
Temperature Monitoring Beyond the Battery Cell
As BESS electrical architectures become more compact, temperature monitoring does not necessarily stop at the battery module.
The electrical path around the battery can also contain important thermal information.
For example, a high-current connection may experience additional heating because of contact resistance. A fuse may operate in an enclosure where the local temperature is considerably different from the external ambient temperature. A contactor may also experience its own thermal conditions depending on continuous current and installation environment.
These measurements can help engineers distinguish between a battery-related thermal issue and a problem associated with the electrical path.
This is also why temperature monitoring and component selection should not be treated as completely separate design tasks.
The thermal environment around a protection or switching component can affect its operating margin, while the component itself can contribute to the local thermal environment.
Sensor Placement Should Follow the Electrical and Thermal Architecture
Sensor placement is best considered together with the physical layout of the BESS.
A useful approach is to identify:
Where heat is generated → where heat can accumulate → where temperature changes can indicate an abnormal condition
This may lead to different sensing priorities in different parts of the system.
Battery modules may require temperature monitoring for battery operating limits.
Busbars and terminals may require monitoring because they carry high current.
Connection points may deserve attention because local resistance can create concentrated heat.
Other components may need monitoring when their operating temperature has a direct relationship with reliability or protection requirements.
This approach is more useful than simply increasing the number of sensors.
More data does not automatically mean better monitoring. The sensing points need to provide information that can be acted upon.
Temperature Monitoring and BESS Protection Work Together
Temperature monitoring is one layer of a larger protection system.
In a BESS, electrical protection may involve fuses, DC contactors, insulation monitoring, current measurement and BMS protection functions.
Temperature monitoring provides another source of information that can help identify abnormal operating conditions.
These functions have different roles.
A temperature sensor detects a physical condition.
The BMS evaluates that condition together with other battery information.
A control system can then determine the appropriate response.
A fuse or contactor, depending on the system architecture and fault condition, may provide the physical isolation or interruption function.
Keeping these roles clear is important when designing the complete protection strategy.
It also prevents a common design mistake: expecting one monitoring device or one protection component to solve a system-level problem on its own.
Temperature Data Becomes More Valuable Over Time
A temperature measurement is useful at the moment it is taken, but recorded temperature data can provide additional value.
Continuous monitoring can show how a particular point behaves under different charging and discharging conditions.
Over time, engineers may be able to identify:
Repeated temperature rises at the same location
Differences between battery sections
Changes in thermal behavior under similar loads
Abnormal temperature patterns
Conditions that occur before a fault or maintenance event
This moves temperature monitoring beyond simple alarm generation.
It can also support maintenance decisions by helping engineers identify locations that require closer inspection.
For larger or more complex battery systems, this historical information can become increasingly useful because the operating condition of the system changes over its service life.
Designing the Monitoring Layer Alongside the Battery Rack
Temperature monitoring works best when it is considered during the battery rack design rather than added after the electrical architecture has already been fixed.
The battery modules, busbars, high-current connections, protection components, cooling system and sensing points occupy the same physical space and interact thermally.
The monitoring architecture therefore needs to reflect the actual rack structure.
This is consistent with the broader approach to high-voltage battery rack design: battery monitoring, thermal management, protection and electrical integration need to work together rather than being treated as separate tasks.
For BESS developers, the practical question is not simply how many temperature sensors are required. It is which locations need to be monitored, what information each point provides, and how that information will be used by the BMS or system controller.
That is where temperature sensing becomes part of the system design rather than just another component installed inside the rack.

records.abstract: A small number of Captur and Symbioz crossovers are being recalled in Europe because of a potentially compromised busbar-to-relay connection inside the traction battery. ... Regarding the problem per se, the busbar is the conductive bar that carries current within the battery. A relay creates resistance at the joint, and resistance turns current into heat. Too much of it...
records.summary: This autoevolution news article reports a Renault recall (campaign code 0FDZ) affecting a small number of Captur and Symbioz hybrid crossovers built at the Valladolid, Spain plant between December 1, 2025 and February 6, 2026, per the European Commission's Safety Gate rapid alert system. The reported defect is a potentially compromised busbar-to-relay connection inside the traction battery: the busbar carries current within the battery, and resistance at the relay joint converts current into heat, which the Safety Gate description says may cause abnormal heating of the connection and battery cells and result in a fire. The article states no such fires have been reported in Europe thus far, and that Renault's local subsidiaries will send registered letters asking owners to book a service appointment. The piece is publisher reporting of a regulatory alert, not a peer-reviewed experiment, and it does not describe the remedy procedure or any measured failure rates.
records.why_it_matters: For battery-pack and high-voltage connection design, the case illustrates that joint resistance at busbar-to-relay interfaces is a thermal-runaway precursor, so contact quality and joint resistance control in traction-battery assembly are safety-critical rather than merely performance-related.

records.body_text:
Per the European Commission's Safety Gate rapid alert system for dangerous non-food products, the recall covers Captur and Symbioz hybrids produced between December 1, 2025, and February 6, 2026. The French automaker uses 0FDZ to identify said campaign.
The vehicles in question are based on the CMF-B platform, with both the Captur and Symbioz hailing from the Valladolid plant in Spain. Although they are identical in many respects, the Captur is a bit shorter than its brother. Featuring an extended overhang, the wagon-like Symbioz offers a bit more luggage space while retaining the Captur's wheelbase.
Regarding the problem per se, the busbar is the conductive bar that carries current within the battery. A relay creates resistance at the joint, and resistance turns current into heat. Too much of it, and the lithium-ion battery could very well sign off in a ball of fire.
The Safety Gate description of the problem reads that abnormal heating of the connection and battery cells may result in a fire, but no such fires have been reported thus far in the European space. Renault's local subsidiaries will send owners registered letters asking them to book a service appointment.
Instead of 29,990 euros for the Eco-G with the manual box, the full-hybrid model retails at 34,400 euros. The Captur sits below it, with prices kicking off at 26,800 euros for the Eco-G and 27,300 euros for the TCe. Upgrading to the noticeably more frugal hybrid means 30,500 euros from the outset.
Competing against the Peugeot 2008, Toyota Yaris Cross, and the Volkswagen T-Roc, the Captur is one of the best-selling crossovers in France. It and the Symbioz maintain consistent placement in the country's top 20 best sellers, with Renault being the leading automotive brand in France.
The group as a whole experienced a successful year in 2025, driven by strong demand for electrified vehicles in the core brand's home market. Renault alone sold more than a million vehicles across the continent, ranking second overall, while French registrations totaled nearly 285,600 vehicles in 2025. When it comes to best-selling passenger vehicle overall in France, the Renault Clio made easy work of second-placed Peugeot 208 and third-placed Dacia Sandero.

Competing against the Peugeot 2008, Toyota Yaris Cross, and the Volkswagen T-Roc, the Captur is one of the best-selling crossovers in France. It and the Symbioz maintain consistent placement in the country's top 20 best sellers, with Renault being the leading automotive brand in France.
The group as a whole experienced a successful year in 2025, driven by strong demand for electrified vehicles in the core brand's home market. Renault alone sold more than a million vehicles across the continent, ranking second overall, while French registrations totaled nearly 285,600 vehicles in 2025. When it comes to best-selling passenger vehicle overall in France, the Renault Clio made easy work of second-placed Peugeot 208 and third-placed Dacia Sandero.

records.title: Development of a low-temperature curable sodium silicate-based inorganic binder for binder jetting with enhanced jetting performance and bonding strength
records.abstract: Purpose This study aims to improve the jetting performance and low-temperature bonding strength of a sodium silicate-based inorganic binder for binder jetting (BJ) applications through silicate network structure enhancement and curing reaction control. Design/methodology/approach Silica sol, NaOH and a phosphate-based curing agent were incorporated into a sodium silicate binder system to increase the Si–O–Si network density and promote rapid curing. The developed binder was evaluated in terms of jetting suitability, bonding behavior with sand, thermal stability and practical printability. Flexural strength was measured after curing at 120, 150 and 180 °C, and the chemical network structure was analyzed using FT-IR spectroscopy. Findings The developed N-binder exhibited significantly improved low-temperature bonding strength compared with the conventional sodium silicate binder (S-binder). In particular, the strength increased markedly from 1.42 MPa to 6.80 MPa at 120 °C, demonstrating superior low-temperature curing behavior. At 150 °C and above, both binders showed comparable strength levels, while the N-binder maintained slightly higher mechanical performance. FT-IR analysis suggested modification of the local silicate network, including increased Na?-associated non-bridging oxygen sites, which contributed to improved curing behavior, penetration performance, and flexural strength. Originality/value This study proposes an effective strategy for improving the printability and low-temperature bonding strength of inorganic binders for BJ through control of silicate network formation and phosphate-assisted curing behavior, providing practical insights for industrial binder development.

The authors added silica sol, NaOH and a phosphate-based curing agent to a sodium silicate binder to raise Si–O–Si network density and promote rapid curing, then evaluated jetting suitability, sand bonding, thermal stability and printability. Flexural strength was measured after curing at 120, 150 and 180 °C, and FT-IR was used to examine the silicate network. The abstract reports that the developed N-binder reached 6.80 MPa at 120 °C versus 1.42 MPa for the conventional S-binder, with comparable strength at 150 °C and above and slightly higher values for the N-binder. Only the abstract was available, so the summary is limited to the authors' reported findings and does not include full experimental detail.
