\# How to Diagnose and Address BMW B38 Boost Control Connector Corrosion

Corrosion at a boost\-control electrical connector can interrupt the signal or power that the engine management system needs to regulate turbocharger boost\.
This guide explains how to identify the likely connector\, inspect it safely\, clean minor contamination\, and decide when a damaged terminal or separate boost\-control fault needs professional diagnosis\.

\#\# What the boost\-control connector does

The BMW B38 is a turbocharged three\-cylinder engine used in several BMW and MINI models\.
Depending on the exact vehicle\, model year\, and engine configuration\, boost control may involve an electronically controlled actuator or a solenoid\, along with pressure sensors and related wiring\.
The connector at one of these components carries electrical power or control signals\; it does not itself control boost mechanically\.

A loose\, wet\, corroded\, or poorly repaired connection can cause an intermittent electrical circuit\.
Possible symptoms include a warning light\, reduced engine power\, uneven acceleration\, or a fault code referring to a boost\-control circuit or actuator\.
These symptoms are not proof of connector corrosion\.
A split charge pipe\, vacuum or pressure leak\, faulty sensor\, damaged wire\, actuator problem\, or software issue can produce overlapping complaints\.

BMW uses different engine and wiring configurations across vehicles\.
Identify the component using the VIN\-specific wiring diagram or a reliable repair manual before unplugging anything\.
Do not assume that a connector shown for one B38\-equipped car is in the same location or has the same pinout on another\.

\#\# Signs that justify an inspection

Look for a pattern that changes with rain\, washing\, temperature\, or vibration\, such as an intermittent warning or power loss\.
A stored diagnostic trouble code can help identify the affected circuit\, but a code is a starting point\, not a parts\-replacement instruction\.

Check for these visible clues\:

\- Green\, blue\, white\, or powdery deposits on exposed metal contacts\.
\- Moisture\, dirt\, or oily residue inside the connector shell\.
\- A cracked housing\, broken lock\, bent pin\, or terminal pushed backward into the connector\.
\- Chafed\, stretched\, brittle\, or previously spliced wiring near the plug\.
\- A connector that does not latch firmly or separates with very little force\.

Corrosion may be hidden inside a sealed connector or under insulation\.
Conversely\, a dirty exterior does not prove that the electrical contacts are corroded\.
Avoid disturbing wiring just to look for a problem if there are no symptoms or relevant codes\.

\#\# Gather tools and make the car safe

You will need the vehicle\-specific service information\, a scan tool that can read BMW\-relevant engine codes\, a flashlight\, eye protection\, and suitable electrical contact cleaner\.
A small nylon detailing brush can help with light surface contamination\.
If terminal repair is needed\, use the correct terminal release tool and replacement contacts specified for the connector\; improvised picks can spread or break the locking features\.

Before working\:

\- Park on a level surface\, select Park or a gear\, apply the parking brake\, and let the engine and nearby exhaust parts cool\.
\- Switch off the ignition and remove the key or keep the key away from the vehicle\. Follow the model\-specific procedure for disconnecting the battery if the repair information requires it\. Some electrical systems require a waiting period before service\.
\- Keep metal tools\, liquids\, and loose hardware away from belts\, fans\, and other moving parts\. Electric cooling fans can start unexpectedly on some vehicles\, even after shutdown\.
\- Confirm the connector identity from service information\. Do not probe terminals or unplug an unknown sensor based only on location or wire color\.

If you are uncertain about battery isolation\, airbag\-adjacent wiring\, or how to access the component\, stop and consult a qualified technician\.
Avoid working on orange high\-voltage cables in hybrid or electric vehicles\; those are outside this repair procedure\.

\#\# Inspect the connector without damaging it

Photograph the connector and wire routing before disconnecting it\.
This gives you a reference for reassembly and helps document the condition if the repair needs to be escalated\.

Release the connector by its locking tab or secondary lock as designed\.
Pull on the connector body\, not the wires\.
If it will not release\, check for a secondary latch and use the specified tool rather than levering against the housing\.
Once apart\, inspect both halves under good light\.

Look for corrosion on the metal contact surfaces\, but also check the plastic shell\, seals\, and wire entry points\.
A swollen seal\, missing weather seal\, cracked housing\, or damaged lock can let contamination return\.
Gently compare the terminals\: they should sit at a similar depth and should not look spread\, bent\, blackened\, or loose\.
Do not scrape contacts with a knife\, sandpaper\, or steel brush\; removing plating can make future corrosion and poor contact more likely\.

If the connector is wet\, identify how water could enter\.
Nearby damaged covers\, an incorrectly routed harness\, a missing seal\, or a prior repair may be the underlying cause\.
Cleaning without correcting water entry often provides only temporary improvement\.

\#\# Clean light corrosion and reassemble

Only attempt cleaning when the contamination is minor and the terminals\, seals\, and housing remain intact\.
Use an electronics\-safe contact cleaner labeled for automotive electrical connectors\, and follow its product directions\.
Avoid household acids\, vinegar\, baking soda mixtures\, carburetor cleaner\, brake cleaner\, and general\-purpose lubricants\.
They may attack plastics\, seals\, coatings\, or leave residue\.

\- Keep the connector disconnected and protect nearby painted or sensitive surfaces from overspray\.
\- Apply a small amount of contact cleaner to the affected contacts\. Do not flood the harness or force liquid deep into a sealed assembly\.
\- If needed\, use a clean\, soft nylon brush on accessible light deposits\. Do not bend terminals or insert anything that can widen the female contact\.
\- Allow the connector to dry completely for the time stated on the cleaner label\. Do not use a flame\, heat gun\, or compressed air at excessive pressure\.
\- Inspect again\. If deposits remain\, contact surfaces are pitted\, or a terminal has lost tension\, stop cleaning and arrange terminal or connector replacement\.
\- Reconnect the plug squarely until its primary and secondary locks engage\. Check that the harness is routed as before and is not under tension or rubbing on adjacent parts\.

Use dielectric grease only if the vehicle repair instructions or connector manufacturer specifies it\, and only in the manner directed\.
It is generally applied to seals or used as specified for connector protection\; it should not be packed onto contact surfaces as a substitute for clean\, correctly tensioned terminals\.
Never use grease to conceal a loose or damaged connection\.

Connector condition \| Suitable next step 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Dry\, clean\, secure\, no visible damage \| Reconnect and continue diagnosis based on codes and symptoms 
Minor removable surface contamination\; sound pins and seals \| Clean with suitable contact cleaner\, dry\, and reassemble 
Pitted\, loose\, bent\, or heat\-discolored terminal \| Replace the affected terminal or connector using the correct repair parts 
Cracked housing\, failed seal\, water entry\, or damaged wire \| Repair the cause and replace compromised components 

\#\# Troubleshoot after the repair

Clear a stored code only after recording it and its freeze\-frame information\, if available\.
The code can help show when and under what conditions the fault occurred\.
Then follow the vehicle’s service procedure to confirm that the connector is seated and that any repair is recognized by the engine control system\.

If you have a capable scan tool\, review live data and relevant fault status while following the manufacturer’s diagnostic procedure\.
Do not run the engine with hands\, tools\, or loose clothing near moving components\.
A basic code reader may show a generic description but may not provide BMW\-specific details or guided tests\.

If the same fault returns\, work through the circuit instead of repeatedly cleaning the plug\:

\- Check the harness\: Look for abrasion\, a broken conductor near the connector\, tension\, or a poor prior splice\. A wire can break internally while its insulation still looks normal\.
\- Verify electrical supply and ground\: Use the correct wiring diagram and specified test points\. Back\-probing or probing the wrong terminal can damage a seal or short a circuit\. Avoid applying battery voltage to control wires\.
\- Check the actuator or solenoid\: A connector fault and a failed component can produce similar codes\. Use model\-specific resistance\, output\, or functional tests rather than guessing from a generic code description\.
\- Check boost plumbing and pressure readings\: A boost leak or implausible sensor reading may cause underboost or reduced power even when the electrical connector is sound\.
\- Consider intermittent faults\: If the symptom comes and goes with movement or moisture\, a technician may need to monitor the circuit during a controlled harness movement test\. Do not tug on the harness with the engine running\.

Do not replace a turbocharger\, actuator\, sensor\, or engine computer solely because a warning mentions boost\.
Diagnose the circuit and mechanical system in the order specified for the exact vehicle\.

\#\# When connector repair is not a DIY cleaning job

Cleaning is not enough if a terminal is loose\, deeply pitted\, overheated\, bent\, or partially withdrawn\.
Replace the affected terminal with the correct part and crimp tool\, or replace the connector repair lead or housing as the manufacturer specifies\.
A poor crimp or mismatched terminal can create resistance and heat\, leading to another failure\.

Seek professional help when the connector is inaccessible\, several wires are damaged\, water has entered a control module\, the wiring diagram is unavailable\, or the fault persists after a careful inspection\.
A BMW specialist can use the VIN to identify the correct circuit and repair procedure\, test the actuator and wiring\, and determine whether programming or adaptation is required after component replacement\.

Avoid driving if the vehicle has severe power loss\, repeated stalling\, a flashing engine warning\, burning electrical odor\, visible smoke\, or signs of overheating\.
Arrange recovery or prompt inspection\.
For a mild intermittent warning\, follow the vehicle’s manual and avoid hard acceleration or sustained boost until the fault is diagnosed\; reduced power can make merging or passing unsafe\.

\#\# Preventing repeat corrosion

After a successful repair\, keep the connector and its seals intact\.
Make sure any covers\, clips\, and splash shields removed for access are refitted\, and route the harness through its original supports\.
Do not direct a pressure washer at engine\-bay connectors\.
During routine service\, look for chafing\, cracked protective covering\, or a harness pulled tight after other work\.

If the connector repeatedly becomes wet\, trace the water path and repair the source rather than applying more cleaner or grease\.
Record the fault codes\, the connector condition\, and the repair performed\.
That history helps a technician distinguish a recurring moisture problem from a separate boost\-control fault\.

Home/ICT/Data Centers/Co-Packaged Optics and Optical Engines for AI Data Centers Market
The Co-Packaged Optics and Optical Engines for AI Data Centers Market is forecast to grow at a CAGR of 85.0%, reaching USD 3,400.0 million in 2032 from USD 85.0 million in 2026.
Highlights:
- 1NVIDIA reports that Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics entered production in May 2026, while Broadcom disclosed shipments of 102.4 Tb/s CPO-enabled switching technology.
- 2High-speed electrical channel loss and retimer power make photonic integration more attractive as switch bandwidth and the number of links rise.
- 3TSMC is beginning production of COUPE-on-substrate technology in 2026, creating a repeatable foundry and packaging route for integrated photonics.
- 4Serviceable external lasers, removable fiber interfaces and package-level testing remain commercial qualification requirements, not secondary engineering details.
- 5Scale-out switches provide the initial installed base, while photonic I/O for custom accelerators and multi-rack scale-up domains represents a later adoption path.
- 6CPO competes with continuously improving 800G, 1.6T and higher-speed pluggable technologies and therefore does not replace all data-center optical connections.
Market Overview
At high electrical lane rates, sending signals across a circuit board and through faceplate connectors creates insertion loss, equalization, and retiming requirements. The penalties rise with lane rate, physical distance, and switch radix. CPO moves the optical-electrical conversion closer to the ASIC so the longest path is optical. The resulting power saving is especially valuable when every additional kilowatt devoted to networking competes with accelerator capacity inside a constrained AI factory.
NVIDIA states that Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics provides materially better power efficiency than conventional transceiver-based designs. Broadcom is commercializing its own high-radix CPO-enabled Ethernet switching platforms. The platforms differ in optical bandwidth, engine configuration, port reach, topology, and field-service requirements. Operators therefore evaluate the entire network power budget, network topology and operational risks rather than purchase optics against a nominal cost per terabit alone.
The packaging transition changes supplier bargaining power. Photonic engines must align with electrical SerDes, laser wavelengths, fiber arrays, thermal performance, and high-yield package assembly. TSMC has identified 2026 production for COUPE on substrate; Coherent has demonstrated a socketed 6.4 Tb/s CPO engine paired with an external laser. The socketed design adds a serviceability option, while volume production will depend on package yield, component reliability, and customer qualification.
The next adoption decision concerns optical connections associated with accelerators rather than network switches alone. Ayar Labs, Lightmatter and other developers are integrating optical I/O with system or accelerator packaging, with production volumes dependent on system-level qualification and design wins. Commercial adoption will depend on optical-link reliability, fabric compatibility and the economics of replacing copper. Customer production schedules will determine the timing of volume ramps.
Market Drivers
Increasing Cost of Electrical Reach
The decisive constraint is the shortening usable reach of high-speed electrical links, not optical speed in isolation. Additional retiming can preserve a front-panel architecture, but it adds power, board area, heat, and component count. Moving optical conversion closer to the switch silicon changes the design trade-off: the system accepts more difficult package assembly to reduce recurring network electricity and board-level signal conditioning. This improves CPO economics first in the largest and most heavily utilized AI fabrics.
AI Fabric Bandwidth and Accelerator Utilization
Large AI training domains demand synchronized communication and predictable throughput across many network hops. Congestion and electrical link constraints can lower the useful compute delivered by expensive accelerators. CPO supports higher optical bandwidth density, while procurement decisions increasingly depend on sustained network performance and energy per delivered bit rather than peak interface throughput alone. Buyers may retain pluggables wherever replacement access, price competition and incremental installation are more valuable.
Packaging and External Laser Supply
As optical engines move inside the system, manufacturing yield and external laser supply become procurement risks. A photonic defect at final assembly may affect an expensive system package, while a hard-to-service laser could raise lifecycle costs. Socketed engines, external light sources and detachable fiber arrays preserve serviceability, creating opportunities for specialized optics and connector suppliers. Capacity investments by NVIDIA, Coherent and Corning reflect increasing demand for a reliable, qualified photonics supply chain.
Market Restraints
Yield, Qualification and Repair Economics
CPO raises the cost of incomplete optical testing. Yield losses can multiply when photonics, packaging and high-value switch electronics are integrated before defects are detected. Operators also require clear repair procedures because an optical fault may take an entire switch out of service rather than a single transceiver port. Test-at-source, detachable fiber interfaces and field-replaceable lasers directly influence procurement acceptance and supplier margins.
Strong Pluggable Optics Competition
Transceiver suppliers are improving density and power efficiency at 800G and 1.6T, with higher-speed roadmaps continuing. Pluggables provide multivendor flexibility, straightforward field replacement and incremental port deployment. CPO is therefore more likely to gain penetration in high-port-count configurations with sustained bandwidth use than in small AI pods or enterprise networks where operational simplicity has greater value.
Segment Analysis
By Integration Target
Switch-ASIC CPO constitutes the initial commercial installation base because Ethernet and InfiniBand switching platforms already have identified products and production programs. It concentrates optical subsystems next to a high-radix switch ASIC and requires careful integration of thermal control, laser distribution, and fiber routing. Accelerator/XPU optical I/O is an emerging adjacent opportunity, with a wider set of possible architectures from directly co-packaged optical chiplets to near-package systems. Its commercial growth depends on accelerator and fabric qualification, not simply the number of AI GPUs sold.
By Component
Photonic engines and optical control electronics account for the main subsystem content, while external light sources are critical to lifetime reliability and serviceability. Fiber-array units, connector systems and assembly/test providers influence manufacturability and cost even when their individually invoiced value is smaller. Greater integration can simplify procurement while concentrating component-sourcing and manufacturing risk at the optical-engine supplier.
By Network Role and Customer
Scale-out switching is the near-term deployment center, led by hyperscalers and major AI-platform vendors. Scale-up optical interconnects potentially extend photonics across accelerator trays and racks, but face strict latency, power, error-rate and fabric-control requirements. System OEMs often make integration and qualification decisions, while cloud operators influence architectures and purchasing terms. Consequently, equipment specifications are often set jointly by cloud buyers and system vendors, while component purchasing is concentrated among platform integrators.
Regional Analysis
North America
North America leads architectural decisions through NVIDIA, Broadcom, hyperscale AI operators, photonic-engine specialists and large network-equipment programs. The commercial opportunity is shaped by demand for high-bandwidth AI fabrics and by access to supply chains in Taiwan and other Asian electronics hubs. Taiwan remains essential to foundry, packaging and system assembly even where AI systems are ultimately deployed in the United States. Consequently, manufacturing investment in Asian supply chains can expand even when North America remains the principal end market.
Near-term investment includes suppliers of laser sources, photonics, fiber handling and system test. NVIDIA announced a multiyear optics agreement with Coherent and separately expanded its optical-connectivity partnership with Corning. These partnerships strengthen access to optical components and manufacturing capacity as AI networking platforms adopt higher-bandwidth architectures.
Competitive and Technology Landscape
NVIDIA and Broadcom lead identifiable switch-level CPO commercialization. Marvell supplies optical and custom-compute semiconductor capabilities; Coherent, Lumentum and Ayar Labs focus on active optical engines or light-source technology; Lightmatter and Intel participate in optical I/O architectures. TSMC is a foundry and packaging enabler, while Corning, SENKO and Sumitomo Electric serve fiber attachment and connector requirements. Competition therefore differs across integrated switching systems, photonic-engine development, advanced packaging and passive optical connectivity.
The wider CPO supply chain also depends on network-equipment design, advanced assembly and high-volume manufacturing. Arista, Cisco, Celestica, Foxconn Interconnect Technology, Fabrinet and others remain relevant ecosystem participants where they qualify integrated hardware or contribute packaging, assembly and supply capacity.
Recent Developments
September 2026: Ayar Labs disclosed additional funding to expand manufacturing capability and advance customer qualification of optical-I/O technology.
May 2026: NVIDIA stated that Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics had entered production with Vera Rubin systems.
April 2026: TSMC announced 2026 production for COUPE on substrate, a photonic engine integrated within advanced packages.
March 2026: Coherent demonstrated a 6.4 Tb/s socketed CPO optical engine with an external laser source and a separate 400G-lane technology path.
March 2026: Broadcom confirmed production shipments of the 102.4 Tb/s Tomahawk 6 family; its CPO-enabled Davisson configuration was announced separately.
March 2026: NVIDIA and Coherent announced a multi-year optics partnership that includes purchase commitments and manufacturing investment.

Home\/ICT\/Data Centers\/Co\-Packaged Optics and Optical Engines for AI Data Centers Market

The Co\-Packaged Optics and Optical Engines for AI Data Centers Market is forecast to grow at a CAGR of 85\.0\%\, reaching USD 3\,400\.0 million in 2032 from USD 85\.0 million in 2026\.

\#\#\# Highlights\:

\- 1NVIDIA reports that Spectrum\-X Ethernet Photonics entered production in May 2026\, while Broadcom disclosed shipments of 102\.4 Tb\/s CPO\-enabled switching technology\.
\- 2High\-speed electrical channel loss and retimer power make photonic integration more attractive as switch bandwidth and the number of links rise\.
\- 3TSMC is beginning production of COUPE\-on\-substrate technology in 2026\, creating a repeatable foundry and packaging route for integrated photonics\.
\- 4Serviceable external lasers\, removable fiber interfaces and package\-level testing remain commercial qualification requirements\, not secondary engineering details\.
\- 5Scale\-out switches provide the initial installed base\, while photonic I\/O for custom accelerators and multi\-rack scale\-up domains represents a later adoption path\.
\- 6CPO competes with continuously improving 800G\, 1\.6T and higher\-speed pluggable technologies and therefore does not replace all data\-center optical connections\.

\#\# Market Overview

At high electrical lane rates\, sending signals across a circuit board and through faceplate connectors creates insertion loss\, equalization\, and retiming requirements\. The penalties rise with lane rate\, physical distance\, and switch radix\. CPO moves the optical\-electrical conversion closer to the ASIC so the longest path is optical\. The resulting power saving is especially valuable when every additional kilowatt devoted to networking competes with accelerator capacity inside a constrained AI factory\.

NVIDIA states that Spectrum\-X Ethernet Photonics provides materially better power efficiency than conventional transceiver\-based designs\. Broadcom is commercializing its own high\-radix CPO\-enabled Ethernet switching platforms\. The platforms differ in optical bandwidth\, engine configuration\, port reach\, topology\, and field\-service requirements\. Operators therefore evaluate the entire network power budget\, network topology and operational risks rather than purchase optics against a nominal cost per terabit alone\.

The packaging transition changes supplier bargaining power\. Photonic engines must align with electrical SerDes\, laser wavelengths\, fiber arrays\, thermal performance\, and high\-yield package assembly\. TSMC has identified 2026 production for COUPE on substrate\; Coherent has demonstrated a socketed 6\.4 Tb\/s CPO engine paired with an external laser\. The socketed design adds a serviceability option\, while volume production will depend on package yield\, component reliability\, and customer qualification\.

The next adoption decision concerns optical connections associated with accelerators rather than network switches alone\. Ayar Labs\, Lightmatter and other developers are integrating optical I\/O with system or accelerator packaging\, with production volumes dependent on system\-level qualification and design wins\. Commercial adoption will depend on optical\-link reliability\, fabric compatibility and the economics of replacing copper\. Customer production schedules will determine the timing of volume ramps\.

\#\# Market Drivers

Increasing Cost of Electrical Reach

The decisive constraint is the shortening usable reach of high\-speed electrical links\, not optical speed in isolation\. Additional retiming can preserve a front\-panel architecture\, but it adds power\, board area\, heat\, and component count\. Moving optical conversion closer to the switch silicon changes the design trade\-off\: the system accepts more difficult package assembly to reduce recurring network electricity and board\-level signal conditioning\. This improves CPO economics first in the largest and most heavily utilized AI fabrics\.

AI Fabric Bandwidth and Accelerator Utilization

Large AI training domains demand synchronized communication and predictable throughput across many network hops\. Congestion and electrical link constraints can lower the useful compute delivered by expensive accelerators\. CPO supports higher optical bandwidth density\, while procurement decisions increasingly depend on sustained network performance and energy per delivered bit rather than peak interface throughput alone\. Buyers may retain pluggables wherever replacement access\, price competition and incremental installation are more valuable\.

Packaging and External Laser Supply

As optical engines move inside the system\, manufacturing yield and external laser supply become procurement risks\. A photonic defect at final assembly may affect an expensive system package\, while a hard\-to\-service laser could raise lifecycle costs\. Socketed engines\, external light sources and detachable fiber arrays preserve serviceability\, creating opportunities for specialized optics and connector suppliers\. Capacity investments by NVIDIA\, Coherent and Corning reflect increasing demand for a reliable\, qualified photonics supply chain\.

\# Market Restraints

Yield\, Qualification and Repair Economics

CPO raises the cost of incomplete optical testing\. Yield losses can multiply when photonics\, packaging and high\-value switch electronics are integrated before defects are detected\. Operators also require clear repair procedures because an optical fault may take an entire switch out of service rather than a single transceiver port\. Test\-at\-source\, detachable fiber interfaces and field\-replaceable lasers directly influence procurement acceptance and supplier margins\.

Strong Pluggable Optics Competition

Transceiver suppliers are improving density and power efficiency at 800G and 1\.6T\, with higher\-speed roadmaps continuing\. Pluggables provide multivendor flexibility\, straightforward field replacement and incremental port deployment\. CPO is therefore more likely to gain penetration in high\-port\-count configurations with sustained bandwidth use than in small AI pods or enterprise networks where operational simplicity has greater value\.

\#\# Segment Analysis

\#\#\# By Integration Target

Switch\-ASIC CPO constitutes the initial commercial installation base because Ethernet and InfiniBand switching platforms already have identified products and production programs\. It concentrates optical subsystems next to a high\-radix switch ASIC and requires careful integration of thermal control\, laser distribution\, and fiber routing\. Accelerator\/XPU optical I\/O is an emerging adjacent opportunity\, with a wider set of possible architectures from directly co\-packaged optical chiplets to near\-package systems\. Its commercial growth depends on accelerator and fabric qualification\, not simply the number of AI GPUs sold\.

\#\#\# By Component

Photonic engines and optical control electronics account for the main subsystem content\, while external light sources are critical to lifetime reliability and serviceability\. Fiber\-array units\, connector systems and assembly\/test providers influence manufacturability and cost even when their individually invoiced value is smaller\. Greater integration can simplify procurement while concentrating component\-sourcing and manufacturing risk at the optical\-engine supplier\.

\#\#\# By Network Role and Customer

Scale\-out switching is the near\-term deployment center\, led by hyperscalers and major AI\-platform vendors\. Scale\-up optical interconnects potentially extend photonics across accelerator trays and racks\, but face strict latency\, power\, error\-rate and fabric\-control requirements\. System OEMs often make integration and qualification decisions\, while cloud operators influence architectures and purchasing terms\. Consequently\, equipment specifications are often set jointly by cloud buyers and system vendors\, while component purchasing is concentrated among platform integrators\.

\#\# Regional Analysis

\#\#\# North America

North America leads architectural decisions through NVIDIA\, Broadcom\, hyperscale AI operators\, photonic\-engine specialists and large network\-equipment programs\. The commercial opportunity is shaped by demand for high\-bandwidth AI fabrics and by access to supply chains in Taiwan and other Asian electronics hubs\. Taiwan remains essential to foundry\, packaging and system assembly even where AI systems are ultimately deployed in the United States\. Consequently\, manufacturing investment in Asian supply chains can expand even when North America remains the principal end market\.

Near\-term investment includes suppliers of laser sources\, photonics\, fiber handling and system test\. NVIDIA announced a multiyear optics agreement with Coherent and separately expanded its optical\-connectivity partnership with Corning\. These partnerships strengthen access to optical components and manufacturing capacity as AI networking platforms adopt higher\-bandwidth architectures\.

\#\# Competitive and Technology Landscape

NVIDIA and Broadcom lead identifiable switch\-level CPO commercialization\. Marvell supplies optical and custom\-compute semiconductor capabilities\; Coherent\, Lumentum and Ayar Labs focus on active optical engines or light\-source technology\; Lightmatter and Intel participate in optical I\/O architectures\. TSMC is a foundry and packaging enabler\, while Corning\, SENKO and Sumitomo Electric serve fiber attachment and connector requirements\. Competition therefore differs across integrated switching systems\, photonic\-engine development\, advanced packaging and passive optical connectivity\.

The wider CPO supply chain also depends on network\-equipment design\, advanced assembly and high\-volume manufacturing\. Arista\, Cisco\, Celestica\, Foxconn Interconnect Technology\, Fabrinet and others remain relevant ecosystem participants where they qualify integrated hardware or contribute packaging\, assembly and supply capacity\.

\#\# Recent Developments

September 2026\: Ayar Labs disclosed additional funding to expand manufacturing capability and advance customer qualification of optical\-I\/O technology\.

May 2026\: NVIDIA stated that Spectrum\-X Ethernet Photonics had entered production with Vera Rubin systems\.

April 2026\: TSMC announced 2026 production for COUPE on substrate\, a photonic engine integrated within advanced packages\.

March 2026\: Coherent demonstrated a 6\.4 Tb\/s socketed CPO optical engine with an external laser source and a separate 400G\-lane technology path\.

March 2026\: Broadcom confirmed production shipments of the 102\.4 Tb\/s Tomahawk 6 family\; its CPO\-enabled Davisson configuration was announced separately\.

March 2026\: NVIDIA and Coherent announced a multi\-year optics partnership that includes purchase commitments and manufacturing investment\.

records.body_text:
Co-Packaged Optics Clears System-Level Proof: Wiwynn Runs Live AI Rack at OCP Summit
Ayar Labs Optical Chiplets Stream Live Rack Telemetry at OCP Summit, Crossing Hyperscale Proof Gate
Co-packaged optics has crossed the milestone hyperscale data center operators have been waiting for. At the OCP Global Summit in San Jose this past week, Wiwynn, Ayar Labs, and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC) jointly ran the most complete live demonstration of a co-packaged optics (CPO) rack system to date — a working compute platform with a GUC ASIC, Ayar Labs TeraPHY optical engines, and SuperNova external laser sources transmitting real-time health telemetry in an Open Rack V3 (ORV3) enclosure. The demo, staged at the San Jose Convention Center during the summit's October 12–15 run, marked what the three companies described as CPO's transition from "architectural validation to system-level functional proof" — the specific engineering gate that separates lab credibility from procurement relevance.
Why System-Level Proof Is the Hyperscale Gate
To understand why that phrase carries weight, it helps to know what the earlier milestones were not. Optical components functioning correctly in a lab, or in a purpose-built testbed, demonstrate physics. A running system — with a real ASIC, a real rack form factor, open-standard die-to-die interfaces, and a multi-vendor fiber plant — demonstrates deployment feasibility. These are different claims, and hyperscalers wait for the second kind before committing qualification resources.
Three features of the OCP demonstration make it the second kind. First, the GUC XPU multi-chip package (MCP) uses UCIe-S chiplet links (Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express Standard) at 64 Gbps per lane to connect Ayar Labs' TeraPHY optical engines to I/O chiplets, and UCIe-A (Advanced) at 64 Gbps per lane via LSI bridges to connect I/O chiplets to the main AI compute die. UCIe is an open standard; using it rather than a proprietary interface lets a hyperscaler add multiple chiplet suppliers to the same platform without renegotiating license terms.
Second, the rack platform is built to ORV3, the OCP open rack standard already deployed in major hyperscaler facilities. Third, the fiber and connector partners in the demonstration—Corning and Senko at OCP, plus Browave, FOCI, Molex, and TE Connectivity at Computex in May—represent the kind of multi-vendor supply chain hyperscalers require before committing to a new interconnect architecture.
OCP Summit 2026 dedicated a full technical track — "Short Reach Optical Interconnect" — to CPO standardization across 22 total summit tracks, signaling that the open-standards consortium is treating CPO as an active priority, not a roadmap aspiration.
From Blueprint to Running System
The OCP demonstration was the third public proof point in a nine-month progression.
Ayar Labs and Wiwynn announced their strategic partnership in March 2026 at the Optical Fiber Communication Conference (OFC) in Los Angeles, where they presented a joint architecture targeting an HVDC (High Voltage Direct Current)-enabled rack-level system designed to scale to 1,024 accelerators with more than 100 Tbps of optical connectivity per XPU package. That announcement was a design commitment — a shared vision for what the architecture should look like.
By May, at Computex 2026 in Taipei, Wiwynn expanded the demonstration to a broader fiber and connectivity ecosystem, bringing in Browave, Corning, FOCI, Molex, Senko, and TE Connectivity alongside Ayar Labs and GUC. The wider supplier roster reflected the practical engineering complexity of routing fiber at rack scale: CPO is not merely a chip-level problem, but a full-stack infrastructure challenge.
At OCP in October, the goal shifted from integration design to operational proof. For the first time, the three companies demonstrated a live Wiwynn compute system with a GUC ASIC, Ayar Labs TeraPHY optical engines, and SuperNova light sources, transmitting health telemetry data in real time.
Inside TeraPHY: Why Shortening the Electrical Path Changes the Economics
Co-packaged optics integrates photonic integrated circuits (PICs) with electronic integrated circuits (EICs) inside the same package, positioning the optical modulator within millimeters (roughly 0.2 inches) of the ASIC rather than at the end of the 15–30 centimeter (5.9–11.8 inch) electrical trace that runs from a switch chip to a faceplate pluggable transceiver. At 1.6 terabit-per-second data rates and above, every centimeter of that electrical trace requires signal amplification; the DSP retimer chip responsible for that amplification in a pluggable module alone consumes 10–15 watts per port.
Ayar Labs' TeraPHY optical engine uses CW-WDM (Continuous Wave Wavelength Division Multiplexing) across 8 wavelengths in the O-band (around 1310 nm), each carrying 256 Gbps, for 2 Tbps per direction and 4 Tbps total bidirectional bandwidth per chiplet, across 8 ports. The continuous-wave laser light is provided by a separate component — the SuperNova external laser source — in the ELSFP (External Laser Small Form Factor Pluggable) form factor. Separating the heat-intensive laser from the heat-sensitive photonic modulator addresses one of CPO's most persistent engineering challenges: photonic components are far more temperature-sensitive than digital CMOS, and co-locating a laser with a high-power AI accelerator creates thermal management complications. Wiwynn developed custom liquid-cooling infrastructure for SuperNova as part of the system design.
The aggregate target for the GUC XPU multi-chip package is more than 100 Tbps bandwidth of full-duplex optical bandwidth per package — a figure that is physically impossible to achieve with copper at this board geometry.
The power economics are straightforward. A conventional pluggable transceiver at 1.6T draws approximately 30 watts per port; the equivalent CPO path draws approximately 9 watts per port, a roughly 70% reduction. At the scale of a 100,000-GPU AI training cluster — where each accelerator needs an optical port — that 21-watt-per-port difference sums to approximately 2.1 megawatts of interconnect power that CPO eliminates, representing millions of dollars annually in direct operating cost savings at commercial power rates.
That arithmetic explains the urgency behind the $650 million in primary capital Ayar Labs raised in 2026 alone — by far the largest annual fundraising in the company's history — reflecting investor conviction that CPO is approaching a commercial inflection point, not a longer-horizon research bet.
What Was Shown
The OCP demo covered three interlocking layers: rack-level fiber routing, patch panel integration, and multi-vendor fiber management, along with a live optical engine telemetry demonstration.
The fiber-handling side of the demonstration is notable in its own right. AI scale-up clusters require dozens — potentially hundreds — of fiber runs per rack, and the mechanical problem of routing, connecting, and managing that optical infrastructure alongside high-density liquid cooling is one of the unsolved engineering challenges that has slowed CPO's path from lab to data center floor. The OCP demo brought fiber routing and patch panel integration into the same room as the live optical telemetry, signaling that the team is treating the full system stack — not just chip-level optics — as the deliverable.

The demo\, staged at the San Jose Convention Center during the summit\'s October 12–15 run\, marked what the three companies described as CPO\'s transition from \"architectural validation to system\-level functional proof\" — the specific engineering gate that separates lab credibility from procurement relevance\.

To understand why that phrase carries weight\, it helps to know what the earlier milestones were not\. Optical components functioning correctly in a lab\, or in a purpose\-built testbed\, demonstrate physics\. A running system — with a real ASIC\, a real rack form factor\, open\-standard die\-to\-die interfaces\, and a multi\-vendor fiber plant — demonstrates deployment feasibility\. These are different claims\, and hyperscalers wait for the second kind before committing qualification resources\.

Three features of the OCP demonstration make it the second kind\. First\, the GUC XPU multi\-chip package \(MCP\) uses UCIe\-S chiplet links \(Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express Standard\) at 64 Gbps per lane to connect Ayar Labs\' TeraPHY optical engines to I\/O chiplets\, and UCIe\-A \(Advanced\) at 64 Gbps per lane via LSI bridges to connect I\/O chiplets to the main AI compute die\. UCIe is an open standard\; using it rather than a proprietary interface lets a hyperscaler add multiple chiplet suppliers to the same platform without renegotiating license terms\.

Second\, the rack platform is built to ORV3\, the OCP open rack standard already deployed in major hyperscaler facilities\. Third\, the fiber and connector partners in the demonstration—Corning and Senko at OCP\, plus Browave\, FOCI\, Molex\, and TE Connectivity at Computex in May—represent the kind of multi\-vendor supply chain hyperscalers require before committing to a new interconnect architecture\.

OCP Summit 2026 dedicated a full technical track — \"Short Reach Optical Interconnect\" — to CPO standardization across 22 total summit tracks\, signaling that the open\-standards consortium is treating CPO as an active priority\, not a roadmap aspiration\.

records.summary: The paper reports a sulfonate-oleylammonium ionic covalent organic framework (soa-TADA) designed as a lubricant additive for precision lubrication. The concept addresses the trade-off between physically adsorbed films, which lack anchoring strength, and tribochemical films, which grow uncontrollably and deplete. In soa-TADA, immobilized sulfonate anions provide electrostatic anchoring to metal surfaces, oleylammonium cations aid oil dispersibility, and the rigid covalent skeleton supplies mechanical robustness, enabling self-limiting assembly of a compact physical adsorption film. The authors report that in 500 SN base oil, soa-TADA reduced friction by 64% and wear volume by 89.5% at 200 N, reached a load-carrying capacity of 400 N, and maintained lubrication under varying speeds and prolonged operation, whereas 500 SN alone and a non-ionic analogue failed. Combined tribological testing, interfacial characterization, and DFT calculations were used to support an 'electrostatically anchored, reinforced physical adsorption' mechanism involving lower electron-transfer barriers, p-d orbital hybridization via sulfonate groups, and hard acid-hard base interactions.
records.why_it_matters: The design suggests a molecular-engineering route to lubricant additives that combine electrostatic surface anchoring with a rigid framework, potentially avoiding the uncontrolled growth and depletion associated with tribochemical films while improving on weak physical adsorption.

records.body_text:
Published by: Elsevier
Published by
Highlights
- •Ionic covalent organic frameworks (iCOFs) are designed as lubricant additives.
- •Sulfonate anchors enable robust physical adsorption on metal surfaces.
- •Friction and wear volume decrease by 64% and 89.5% at 200 N.
- •DFT reveals strong p-d hybridization and hard acid-hard base interactions.
Abstract
Precision lubrication demands interfacial films with strong adhesion, high load-bearing capacity, and long-term durability. However, conventional physically adsorbed films lack anchoring strength, while tribochemical films suffer from uncontrollable growth and consumption. Here, we revealed that ionic covalent organic framework (iCOF) could enable an electrostatically anchored, robust physical adsorption film to overcome shortcomings. A sulfonate-oleylammonium iCOF additive (soa-TADA) is designed, in which immobilized sulfonate anions provide instantaneous electrostatic anchoring to metal surfaces, oleylammonium cations ensure oil dispersibility, and the rigid covalent skeleton delivers mechanical robustness. The electrostatic manipulation drives self-limiting assembly into a compact, robust and cohesive physical adsorption film, where covalent skeleton imparts high load-bearing strength and ionic moieties facilitate inter-sheet shear. Consequently, soa-TADA reduces friction by 64% and wear volume by 89.5% at 200 N, also achieves load-carrying capacity of 400 N and maintains unchanged lubrication under varying speeds and prolonged operation, where both 500 SN and non-ionic analogue fail. Combined experimental and DFT calculations elucidate an “electrostatically anchored, reinforced physical adsorption” mechanism. The lower electron-transfer barrier, stronger p-d orbital hybridization via sulfonate groups, and favorable hard acid-hard base interactions ensure rapid formation and exceptional durability. This iCOF-enabled strategy provides a molecular engineering route for precision lubrication where both surface integrity and interfacial stability are paramount.

Keywords
Ionic covalent organic frameworks
;
Electrostatic anchoring
;
Precision lubrication
;
Physical adsorption film
Introduction
Under harsh boundary lubrication regimes, the ability to construct an interfacial film with superior mechanical strength, persistent adhesion stability and adaptability to varying operational conditions at the contact interfaces of moving components dictates the systemic efficiency, lifespan and reliability of machinery [1], [2], [3]. Ideally, such interfacial film not only possesses low shear strength to effectively reduce friction, but also exhibits high load-bearing capacity, strong film-substrate adhesion and excellent shear durability to maintain structural integrity and functional continuity under the synergistic impact of extreme pressure, cyclic shear and triboheat. As aerospace, precision manufacturing or machining and new micro/nano-device systems advance toward high-speed, heavy-load, extreme-precision, and long-term stable operation conditions, traditional lubrication systems containing organic modifiers and anti-wear additives face profoundly limitations, because these systems predominantly rely on molecular physical adsorption or tribochemical reactions to form interfacial films [4], [5]. The adsorption film fed by the former (organic modifiers) presents weak bonding forces that are prone to desorption under higher loads or temperatures, while the tribofilm created by the latter (anti-wear additives) requires a high activation energy, often grows uncontrollable film configuration and consumes continuously active components. The intense operational dependence, unpredictability and unsustainable supply in lubricating performance render their unavailability to meet the urgent demands of modern equipment for the stability, predictability and low environmental dependence of lubrication interface.
Over the past two decades, ionic liquids (ILs) have been emerging as versatile lubricants that spontaneously adsorb via electrostatic interactions, yet while film formation proceeds through tribochemical pathways. Thus, ILs inherit the typical drawbacks of reaction-based films: uncontrollable growth, potential corrosion, and progressive depletion (Scheme 1) [6], [7]. Meanwhile, two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have drawn attention as “pre-designable” solid lubricants due to their layered structures, tunable interlayer interactions, and exceptional mechanical strength [8], [9]. However, their lubrication films are assembled predominantly through weak van der Waals, ion-π, or coordination forces, resulting in critically insufficient adhesion to the substrate. Under high loads or variable frequencies, these films are prone to slippage or delamination, preventing their intrinsic mechanical properties from translating into effective interfacial protection (Scheme 1) [10], [11], [12]. Therefore, a fundamental contradiction persists: physical adsorption films lack sufficient anchoring strength, while tribochemical films suffer from poor controllability and consumptive nature, which presents the limitation of strategies relying solely on structural mechanical enhancement while neglecting interfacial force engineering.
To resolve this contradiction, herein, we propose a molecular interfacial engineering strategy that integrates the strong interfacial anchoring capability of immobilized ionic groups with the robust mechanical framework of COFs. A sulfonate-oleylammonium ionic pair-functionalized COF (soa-TADA) was rationally designed and fabricated, wherein the fixed sulfonate anions serve as powerful electrostatic anchors that bind instantly to positively charged metal surfaces, while the rigid covalent skeleton provides structural support and prevents the migration and depletion typical of liquid-phase ions. This synergy enables the formation of a “reinforced physical adsorption film” with excellent adhesion, structural integrity, and shear/compressive resistance. When applied in 500 SN base oil, soa-TADA reduces the coefficient of friction by 64% and wear volume by 89.5%, and boosts the load-carrying capacity to 400 N, far surpassing the non-ionic analogue TADA (150 N). The film also exhibits exceptional adaptability under variable frequencies, elevated temperatures, and prolonged operation. Combined with systematic tribological tests, multi-scale interfacial characterizations, and DFT quantum chemical calculations, the structure–performance correlation and electronic-level reinforcement mechanism of electrostatically anchored lubrication are thoroughly uncovered. This work not only provides a high-efficiency and multi-environment adaptive lubricant additive for precision lubrication, but also offers a universal molecular design principle for developing advanced functional COF materials toward interfacial friction regulation.

\#\# Introduction

Under harsh boundary lubrication regimes\, the ability to construct an interfacial film with superior mechanical strength\, persistent adhesion stability and adaptability to varying operational conditions at the contact interfaces of moving components dictates the systemic efficiency\, lifespan and reliability of machinery \[1\]\, \[2\]\, \[3\]\. Ideally\, such interfacial film not only possesses low shear strength to effectively reduce friction\, but also exhibits high load\-bearing capacity\, strong film\-substrate adhesion and excellent shear durability to maintain structural integrity and functional continuity under the synergistic impact of extreme pressure\, cyclic shear and triboheat\. As aerospace\, precision manufacturing or machining and new micro\/nano\-device systems advance toward high\-speed\, heavy\-load\, extreme\-precision\, and long\-term stable operation conditions\, traditional lubrication systems containing organic modifiers and anti\-wear additives face profoundly limitations\, because these systems predominantly rely on molecular physical adsorption or tribochemical reactions to form interfacial films \[4\]\, \[5\]\. The adsorption film fed by the former \(organic modifiers\) presents weak bonding forces that are prone to desorption under higher loads or temperatures\, while the tribofilm created by the latter \(anti\-wear additives\) requires a high activation energy\, often grows uncontrollable film configuration and consumes continuously active components\. The intense operational dependence\, unpredictability and unsustainable supply in lubricating performance render their unavailability to meet the urgent demands of modern equipment for the stability\, predictability and low environmental dependence of lubrication interface\.

Over the past two decades\, ionic liquids \(ILs\) have been emerging as versatile lubricants that spontaneously adsorb via electrostatic interactions\, yet while film formation proceeds through tribochemical pathways\. Thus\, ILs inherit the typical drawbacks of reaction\-based films\: uncontrollable growth\, potential corrosion\, and progressive depletion \(Scheme 1\) \[6\]\, \[7\]\. Meanwhile\, two\-dimensional covalent organic frameworks \(COFs\) have drawn attention as “pre\-designable” solid lubricants due to their layered structures\, tunable interlayer interactions\, and exceptional mechanical strength \[8\]\, \[9\]\. However\, their lubrication films are assembled predominantly through weak van der Waals\, ion\-π\, or coordination forces\, resulting in critically insufficient adhesion to the substrate\. Under high loads or variable frequencies\, these films are prone to slippage or delamination\, preventing their intrinsic mechanical properties from translating into effective interfacial protection \(Scheme 1\) \[10\]\, \[11\]\, \[12\]\. Therefore\, a fundamental contradiction persists\: physical adsorption films lack sufficient anchoring strength\, while tribochemical films suffer from poor controllability and consumptive nature\, which presents the limitation of strategies relying solely on structural mechanical enhancement while neglecting interfacial force engineering\.

To resolve this contradiction\, herein\, we propose a molecular interfacial engineering strategy that integrates the strong interfacial anchoring capability of immobilized ionic groups with the robust mechanical framework of COFs\. A sulfonate\-oleylammonium ionic pair\-functionalized COF \(soa\-TADA\) was rationally designed and fabricated\, wherein the fixed sulfonate anions serve as powerful electrostatic anchors that bind instantly to positively charged metal surfaces\, while the rigid covalent skeleton provides structural support and prevents the migration and depletion typical of liquid\-phase ions\. This synergy enables the formation of a “reinforced physical adsorption film” with excellent adhesion\, structural integrity\, and shear\/compressive resistance\. When applied in 500 SN base oil\, soa\-TADA reduces the coefficient of friction by 64\% and wear volume by 89\.5\%\, and boosts the load\-carrying capacity to 400 N\, far surpassing the non\-ionic analogue TADA \(150 N\)\. The film also exhibits exceptional adaptability under variable frequencies\, elevated temperatures\, and prolonged operation\. Combined with systematic tribological tests\, multi\-scale interfacial characterizations\, and DFT quantum chemical calculations\, the structure–performance correlation and electronic\-level reinforcement mechanism of electrostatically anchored lubrication are thoroughly uncovered\. This work not only provides a high\-efficiency and multi\-environment adaptive lubricant additive for precision lubrication\, but also offers a universal molecular design principle for developing advanced functional COF materials toward interfacial friction regulation\.

FUCHS LUBRICANTS SOUTH AFRICA Achieves GBCSA Net Zero Carbon Level 2 Certification
20.10.2026 - 10:00
As businesses face increasing pressure to reduce their environmental impact, FUCHS LUBRICANTS SOUTH AFRICA is demonstrating what sustainable industrial development can look like in practice. The company's headquarters in Isando has been rated Net Zero Carbon Level 2 certification by the Green Building Council South Africa (GBCSA), placing it among a select group of buildings recognised for their commitment to low-carbon operations and sustainable design.
The achievement was recently commemorated through a plaque handover ceremony, recognising FUCHS' ongoing efforts to reduce emissions while creating a high-performance workplace aligned with its long-term sustainability ambitions.
Developed as part of the FUCHS Net-Zero Carbon Strategy, the headquarters was designed to maximise energy efficiency while enhancing employee comfort and wellbeing. Key sustainability features include high-performance double glazing, passive design principles that reduce reliance on mechanical cooling, intelligent fresh-air ventilation systems, comprehensive energy monitoring and a 100% electrification approach that creates opportunity for renewable energy use through our solar PV system.
Together, these measures help reduce the building's carbon footprint while supporting more efficient and resilient operations.
The certification was achieved with support from sustainability consultancy Solid Green Consulting, which served as the Accredited Professional on the project, and Brundtland Consulting, which provided carbon credit specialist expertise.
According to Esther Seabi, Sustainability Director at FUCHS LUBRICANTS SOUTH AFRICA, the recognition reflects the company's long-term commitment to responsible business practices. “This certification demonstrates how sustainability can be integrated into everyday business operations and infrastructure decisions. As a company, we continue to pursue practical solutions that reduce environmental impact while supporting operational excellence and long-term resilience.”
The GBCSA Net Zero Carbon certification recognises projects that achieve highly energy-efficient operations while balancing or eliminating carbon emissions associated with building performance. Level 2 certification extends beyond base building emissions to include occupant operational energy use, reflecting a broader and more comprehensive sustainability approach.
Managing Director Paul Deppe said the recognition aligns with the wider sustainability objectives of both the local business and the global FUCHS Group. “Sustainability is becoming increasingly important across every sector we serve. records.abstract: Abstract Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is highly vulnerable to a range of process-induced defects that can adversely part quality, structural integrity, dimensional accuracy and long-term reliability, thereby limiting broader industrial adoption. This work presents a feasibility investigation into automated detection of defect-related surface patterns in LPBF using a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based image classification framework. Classical image-processing techniques were initially found to be insufficient for reliable defect detection due to their limited robustness to variations in surface morphologies and image characteristics. To address these limitations, a CNN-based image classification framework was developed and trained using surrogate-labeled LPBF surface images to evaluate the viability of deep learning for automated surface condition classification and recognition. The proposed and developed model achieved a validation accuracy of approximately 84% while exhibiting stable convergence behavior during training, indicating that meaningful classification of LPBF surface patterns is achievable under limited labeling conditions, demonstrating the potential of deep learning for automated LPBF surface condition assessment. This work establishes a foundation for future work focused on incorporating physically verified defect labels, improved imaging fidelity, and integration with in-situ monitoring framework to enable real-time defect detection in LPBF process conforming for quality assurance.
records.summary: This paper reports a feasibility study of CNN-based image classification for defect-related surface patterns in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). The authors first evaluated classical image-processing approaches (histogram analysis, contrast enhancement/thresholding, edge detection, and grid/tiled analysis) and found them insufficiently robust to illumination variation, surface roughness, and multi-scale defect morphology. They then trained a sequential CNN in TensorFlow/Keras on real LPBF surface images from a previously published dataset, using surrogate class labels derived from preprocessing/annotation groupings rather than physically verified defect types. Images were resized to 128×128 pixels, normalized to [0,1], and split 80/20 (about 2,674 training and 540 validation images). The model reached approximately 84% validation accuracy with stable convergence, and three independent training runs gave a mean validation accuracy of 83.14% ± 0.48% and mean validation loss of 0.2594 ± 0.0121. The authors frame the work as proof-of-concept rather than validated defect detection.
