\# A vision\-based deep convolutional neural network framework for surface defect detection in laser powder bed fusion \(LPBF\)

\- ORIGINAL ARTICLE
\- Open access
\- Published\:

\#\# Abstract

Laser Powder Bed Fusion \(LPBF\) is highly vulnerable to a range of process\-induced defects that can adversely part quality\, structural integrity\, dimensional accuracy and long\-term reliability\, thereby limiting broader industrial adoption\. This work presents a feasibility investigation into automated detection of defect\-related surface patterns in LPBF using a convolutional neural network \(CNN\)\-based image classification framework\. Classical image\-processing techniques were initially found to be insufficient for reliable defect detection due to their limited robustness to variations in surface morphologies and image characteristics\. To address these limitations\, a CNN\-based image classification framework was developed and trained using surrogate\-labeled LPBF surface images to evaluate the viability of deep learning for automated surface condition classification and recognition\. The proposed and developed model achieved a validation accuracy of approximately 84\% while exhibiting stable convergence behavior during training\, indicating that meaningful classification of LPBF surface patterns is achievable under limited labeling conditions\, demonstrating the potential of deep learning for automated LPBF surface condition assessment\. This work establishes a foundation for future work focused on incorporating physically verified defect labels\, improved imaging fidelity\, and integration with in\-situ monitoring framework to enable real\-time defect detection in LPBF process conforming for quality assurance\.

\#\#\# Similar content being viewed by others

\#\# 1 Introduction

Laser Powder Bed Fusion \(LPBF\) is one of the highest impact metal powder\-bed additive manufacturing processes that enables the fabrication of complex\, lightweight\, high\-performance metallic components with near\-net\-shape components having complex geometries through selective laser melting of powder layers that are difficult or impossible to realize by conventional machining or casting as shown in Fig\. 1\.

Despite its industrial adoption in aerospace\, biomedical\, and energy sectors\, LPBF remains highly quality sensitive to processing parameters and thermal dynamics\, leading to the formation of manufacturing defects such as lack\-of\-fusion pores\, keyhole pores\, cracks\, balling\, denudation\, spatter\-related surface damage\, recoating anomalies\, and geometric distortion can degrade density\, dimensional accuracy\, ductility\, fracture resistance\, and especially fatigue performance that degrade mechanical performance and structural integrity enabling the idea that defect detection is a core enabler of reliability and certification \[3\, 4\, 12\, 22\]\.

As mentioned earlier\, defects such as lack\-of\-fusion porosity\, keyhole porosity\, gas\-induced pores\, cracking\, and spatter are commonly observed in LPBF\-produced parts\. These defects originate from unstable melt pool dynamics\, insufficient or excessive energy input\, and complex thermal gradients during rapid melting and solidification\. Conventional quality assurance methods that rely on post\-build destructive or volumetric inspection techniques such as optical microscopy\, X\-ray computed tomography\, and destructive testing\, are expensive and unsuitable for real\-time process monitoring \[8\, 10\]\. In\-situ monitoring systems and layer\-wise monitoring techniques capable of capturing optical and thermographic images using optical and thermal imaging devices\, melt\-pool cameras\, photodiodes\, pyrometers\, optical tomography\, acoustic emission\, and multimodal sensor fusion now provide layer\- or track\-resolved process signatures during LPBF builds have emerged as promising tools for defect detection\.However\, manual interpretation of such data is impractical due to signal noise\, large volume and complexity of generated images\. Classical image\-processing techniques\, including histogram analysis\, contrast enhancement\, and edge detection\, have been applied in industrial inspection but exhibit limited robustness for LPBF defect detection due to noise\, illumination variations\, and multi\-scale defect morphology as these signals are affected by spatter\, plume emission\, perspective distortion\, f\-theta lens distortion\, chromatic aberration\, changing light levels\, limited depth of field\, and imperfect alignment between in\-situ sensing and ex\-situ ground truth\. These problems are why handcrafted or purely threshold\-based image analysis often has trouble working well across different builds\, materials\, machines\, and process maps \[7\]\. Recent advances in deep learning\, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks \(CNNs\)which have progressed from finding anomalies in powder beds and clustering morphology to using transfer learning\, and explainability techniques\, provide a data\-driven framework for automated defect detection in manufacturing\. The existing literature shows that deep models can find defect\-relevant features that are hard to encode by hand\. However\, it also shows that there are still not many public\, physically annotated datasets and that generalization\, interpretability\, registration\, and deployment\-readiness are still open problems\. CNNs can learn hierarchical spatial features directly from image data\, enabling robust classification of complex surface and subsurface defect patterns\.

Recent advances in deep learning\, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks \(CNNs\)which have progressed from finding anomalies in powder beds and clustering morphology to using transfer learning\, and explainability techniques\, provide a data\-driven framework for automated defect detection in manufacturing\. The existing literature shows that deep models can find defect\-relevant features that are hard to encode by hand\. However\, it also shows that there are still not many public\, physically annotated datasets and that generalization\, interpretability\, registration\, and deployment\-readiness are still open problems\. CNNs can learn hierarchical spatial features directly from image data\, enabling robust classification of complex surface and subsurface defect patterns \[9\, 16\]\.

This present study presents a CNN\-based framework for image\-driven LPBF defect detection where the most justifiable framing is not “solved defect detection\,” but “feasible defect\-related surface pattern classification under limited labels\.” This framing is especially important because the current work uses surrogate labels that includes the evaluation of fundamental detection techniques\, dataset preprocessing\, model architecture design\, implementation details\, and experimental results instead of physically annotated defect labels\, where the specific imaging modality wasn’t given\.

\#\# 2 Background and related work

\#\#\# 2\.1 LPBF and defect mechanisms

Laser Powder Bed Fusion \(LPBF\) is a metal additive manufacturing process in which a high\-energy laser selectively melts successive layers of powder to fabricate three\-dimensional components\. The process involves powder spreading\, laser scanning\, melt pool formation\, solidification\, and layer\-by\-layer consolidation as shown in Fig\. 2\.

LPBF enables complex geometries\, material efficiency and tailored microstructures but is highly sensitive to processing conditions and thermal history\. LPBF has become a key process for high\-value industries where weight\, complexity\, and performance are important\, such as turbomachinery\, medical implants\, propulsion hardware\, and heat\-management structures\. LPBF is powerful because of the steep thermal gradients\, fast melt\-pool dynamics\, repeated reheating\, and powder\-spreading steps that make it powerful\. But these same things also make it prone to defects and sensitive to the process \[3\, 22\]\.

Figure 3 illustrates how LPBF process parameters\, e\.g\. laser power\, scanning speed\, hatch spacing\, layer thickness\, powder properties and gas flow conditions\, impact the thermal and fluid flow behaviour inside the melt pool\. The interaction of these parameters generates measurable in\-situ process signatures e\.g\. melt pool geometry\, temperature profile\, plume behaviour\, spatters and acoustic emission\; the variation of these signatures directly correlates to the formation of defects and quality metrics \(lack of fusion\, keyholing\, porosity\, cracking\, dimensional accuracy\, surface finish\, mechanical performance and residual stress\) of the final part\. The framework demonstrates the benefits of using in\-situ monitoring and data\-driven measurements for providing intelligent control of the LPBF process\, predicting defects and future digital twin enabled manufacturing systems\.

From literature it has been observed that even with parameter optimization\, the LPBF process is still susceptible to inherent varaition in process parameters that lead to defect formation in LPBF which is primarily governed by melt pool dynamics\, heat transfer\, and powder–laser interactions\. Failure modes commonly cited in reviews include porosity\, poor fusion\, insufficiently fused spots\, keyholes\, cracks\, balling\, surface deformation\, denudation\, and defects associated with the powder bed\/re\-coater process\. These defects do not necessarily occur because of the same underlying cause\. Lack\-of\-fusion \(LOF\) defects occur when insufficient energy density prevents complete melting and bonding between adjacent scan tracks and layers\, resulting in irregularly shaped pores and weak interlayer bonding\. Whereas\, crack formation is connected with thermomechanical stresses and material sensitivity whereas\, while\, balling and spatter are linked to liquid instability and liquid ejection\. Coating are also observed to show imperfections that can lead to defects downstream because they affect coating formation locally\.In contrast\, excessive energy input can lead to keyhole porosity\, where vaporization\-driven recoil pressure forms deep cavities in the melt pool that collapse and trap gas bubbles\, producing near\-spherical pores \[4\, 12\]\.

Figure 4 how different LPBF processing parameters such as laser power and scanning speed can affect the formation of defects and porosity levels in the material processed within the LPBF process window\. The image illustrates that there is an operating range within LPBF that allows for the production of fully dense components\. However\, there are multiple defect driven zones on either side of the operating range due to improper amounts of energy being introduced into the MELT during the melting of a powder particle\.

High laser power and low scan speed produce enough energy locally to create an excessive energy density within the melting pool that allows for the formation of deep vapor depressions in the melting pool\, which produces keyhole melting and produces keyhole porosity\. During rapid solidification\, unstable vapor cavities may collapse and trap gas pores in the consolidated material\. Conversely\, low laser power with high scan speed do not provide sufficient energy input to create full melting and fusion between adjacent scan tracks and layers\, which creates lack of fusion porosity\. Lack of fusion porosity is characterized by incomplete bonding\, irregular voids\, and poor inter\-layer consolidation\.

The figure also outlines the balling regime\, an effect that typically occurs from the Plateau–Rayleigh instability when the scan velocity is too high or when there are instability issues with the melt pool\. The balling process causes the powder to be melted in an uneven manner\, creating a discontinuous melt track and problem with the geometry of the surface that is being deposited upon\. Overall\, the image demonstrates how closely coupled thermal input\, melt pool behaviour and product characteristics are connected in LPBF processes\. These relationships among processing variables and defects are key to process optimisation\, in\-situ monitoring\, machine learning\-based defect prediction\, and digital twin enabled control for manufacturing\.

Gas porosity may originate from entrapped gas in powder particles or shielding gas\, while thermal cracking arises due to large thermal gradients and residual stresses during rapid cooling\. Spatter formation\, driven by melt pool instabilities and vapor plume interactions\, can eject molten material\, contaminate the powder bed\, and induce secondary defects in subsequent layers \[12\]\.

These defect mechanisms are strongly coupled with laser power\, scan speed\, hatch spacing\, layer thickness\, and powder characteristics\, where process induced defects have proven to reduce structural integrity and service reliability\. However\, due to the stochastic nature of powder spreading and melt pool turbulence\, defect formation exhibits spatial and temporal variability\, making deterministic detection and prediction challenging\.

Figure 5 summarizes several commonly used methodologies regarding adjusting parameters to improve the quality of parts produced via LPBF \(Laser Powder Bed Fusion\) and minimize the number of defects in the parts produced through this process\. For each category\, there is a listing of the problems associated with this production process\, including keyhole porosity\, lack of fusion porosity\, compositional variation\, and residual stress\/distortion\, as well as methods to correct these same issues\.

The excessive energy input is what creates unstable vapor cavities within the melt pool leading to keyhole porosity\. Thus\, reducing the laser power is considered the preferred way to mitigate this porosity problem\. However\, increasing the scanning velocity and using remelting or reheating methods are secondary or additional ways to stabilize melt pool behavior\.

Insufficient energy density and non\-fusion melting together create lack of fusion porosity\. Because of this\, the primary ways to mitigate lack of fusion porosity is to reduce scan\-line spacing and\/or layer thickness in order to achieve better melting overlap and interlayer bonding\. The secondary methods would be to reduce scan velocity\, increase laser power and\/or utilize remelting techniques to promote consolidation of materials\.

The illustration also shows how to minimize variance due to composition and how to alleviate residual stress and geometrical distortion\. Reduced scan vector length and preheating the substrate\/chamber will lessen the amount of stress induced by the thermal gradient by moderating the thermal cycling and cooling rates that occur during the fabrication process\. Overall\, the mitigation framework presented\, along with the data shown\, supports a strong link between process parameter optimization and defect control in LPBF machines\.

Intelligent manufacturing relies heavily on understanding the parameter\-defect relationship because it provides critical knowledge necessary for closed\-loop process control\, machine learning\-based optimizations\, defect predictive capabilities\, and the development of digital twin\-enabled additive manufacturing systems\.

This idea captures the core reasoning behind LPBF automated inspection where the detection of any defect\-related signatures will allow transitioning inspection techniques from expensive post\-build evaluation into process awareness\, triage\, and eventually closed\-loop control\. The challenge of accomplishing this objective lies in the ability to develop machine learning algorithms that can successfully differentiate between any defect\-related patterns and those arising simply from normal process behavior\, instrumentation noise\, or other environmental factors associated with build conditions\.

\#\#\# 2\.2 Visual signatures in layer\-wise images

In\-situ monitoring systems for LPBF are dominated by optical cameras and infrared thermographic modalities to capture layer\-wise images during fabrication as they offer non\-contact access to the build surface or process zone\. Two major approaches have been classically used for visual signature\-based studies\, surface or layerwise imaging approach capturing patterns left on the powder bed or newly solidified layer\, naturally aligned with defect\-related surface pattern classification technique or\, process\-zone monitoring observation method looking at short\-lived signals from the melt pool\, plume\, or nearby area\, usually with much better time resolution\. Both paradigms are important\, but they create different kinds of data abstractions and different kinds of labeling problems\.Different techniques utilize instruments such as off\-axis infrared thermography\, visible cameras\, on\-axis melt\-pool cameras\, optical tomography\, and photodiode\/pyrometer systems to analyze melt\-pool dimensions\, thermal and radiance signatures\, overheating zones\, surface morphology\, localized process anomalies\, and porosity related indicators\.

Figure 6 illustrates multiple sensing modalities in the context of LPBF process monitoring to observe the melt pool and process behavior in real time\, this schematic demonstrates how high\-speed images\, photodiodes\, and thermal images can be integrated into one system to capture signatures related to defect development and thermal instability during additive manufacturing\.

The configuration illustrated in 6\(a\) depicts a LPBF monitoring arrangement using an on\-axis\, high\-speed camera and both on\- and off\-axis photodiodes as monitoring elements\. The monitored optical emissions created by the melt pool and the interaction between the laser and material are captured using optical filters and quartz glass windows in this configuration\. The on\-axis configuration allows direct observation of the melt\-pool shape and plume characteristics along the axes of the laser\, while the off\-axis photodiodes give further insight into the intensity of the emission and transient perturbations in the process being monitored\.

Configuration \(b\) is another monitoring architecture that uses an off\-axis high\-speed camera and combined with the thermographic imaging\. The thermographic camera is used to capture the spatial and temporal temperature distributions of the melt\-pool as it evolves and the heat transfer behavior\. The off\-axis high\-speed camera records melt\-pool geometry\, the ejected material from the melt pool\, and any phenomena that affect the melting process\. By combining multiple types of sensing strategies\, all the complementary information about the process can be collected\, from the thermal gradients to the ejection of material\, plume dynamics and methods of defect formation\.

Intelligent LPBF process control and data\-driven manufacturing analysis relies upon multimodal monitoring systems to create the underlying structure of the process\. The measurement of the process signatures allows for correlations to be made with the defect regimes of keyholing\, lack\-of\-fusion porosity\, balling instability\, and residual stresses\. Additionally\, these sensing frameworks also provide valuable datasets that will enable machine learning to predict defects\, detect anomalies in real\-time\, optimize processes adaptively and ultimately create future digital twin\-enabled additive manufacturing systems\.

Lack\-of\-fusion defects often manifest as discontinuities in melt tracks\, unmelted powder regions\, or irregular surface textures in optical images\. Keyhole porosity is associated with intense localized heating and elongated melt pools\, which can be observed in thermographic data\. Gas pores may appear as small circular depressions or brightness anomalies\, while cracks manifest as linear high\-contrast features\. Spatter appears as scattered bright or dark particles across the powder bed and may accumulate across layers\. However\, LPBF defect signatures are often subtle\, localized\, and embedded within complex surface textures\. The resolution of monitoring sensors\, illumination conditions\, and surface reflectivity further complicate visual interpretation\. As a result\, manual inspection and threshold\-based detection methods are unreliable for large\-scale LPBF monitoring applications \[7\, 20\, 21\, 28\]\.

\#\#\# 2\.3 Limitations of classical image processing techniques

Classical image\-processing techniques in LPBF commonly rely on thresholding\, contrast segmentation\, morphology\, edge detection\, handcrafted texture descriptors\, or contour rules have been widely applied in industrial inspection and machine vision applications\. Recent high\-fidelity optical monitoring research has found that standard LPBF optical paths can have problems like barrel distortion from f\-theta lenses\, chromatic aberration\, off\-axis perspective distortion\, a limited depth of focus\, and detection limits that are still important compared to critical pore scales\. These methods are still useful for visualization and pointing out simple defects\, but they don’t work well when the image statistics are changing the defect signatures are subtle\, or the relevant evidence is spatially contextual rather than local\. Thermographic imaging measurements are also known to be affected by attenuation\, distortion\, changing optical path length\, and other light sources\, which makes it harder to understand them directly\. These methods are employed in applications such as camera autofocus systems\, surface inspection in manufacturing\, and automated optical inspection\. However\, LPBF monitoring images present unique challenges due to complex textures\, multi\-scale defects\, noise\, and illumination variability\. Histogram\-based methods using evaluation of global pixel intensity distributions to detect anomalies\, while contrast enhancement and thresholding methods amplify intensity differences between defective and non\-defective regions of lack spatial awareness\, contrast\-based methods require manual tuning\, and edge\-based methods produce false positives due to inherent surface roughness\. Consequently\, classical approaches exhibit limited robustness for LPBF defect detection tasks\. Edge detection algorithms\, such as Sobel and Canny filters\, identify geometric discontinuities associated with cracks and surface irregularities\. Grid\-based or tiled image analysis divides images into smaller patches to localize defects spatially\. Because of this\, the literature has been moving away from manually defined image rules and toward representation learning\. This trend is evident in the progression of the Scime–Beuth line of research\: initial powder\-bed analysis illustrated the efficacy of trained computer vision for anomaly detection\, while later investigations transitioned to multi\-scale CNNs and melt\-pool\-signature learning to obtain more comprehensive\, hierarchical defect\-related data\. As such\, these reasons directly explain why data\-driven models are necessary\, why registering for ex\-situ inspection is difficult\, and why a feasibility study based on surface pattern classification is a good next step instead of an end point \[14\, 20\, 27\, 28\, 29\, 33\]\.

\#\#\# 2\.4 Deep learning for manufacturing defect detection

Deep learning\, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks \(CNNs\)\, has emerged as a powerful approach for automated image\-based defect detection\. CNNs learn hierarchical spatial features directly from raw pixel data through convolutional and pooling operations\, enabling robust recognition of complex patterns without manual feature engineering \[16\, 9\]\. The modern LPBF computer\-vision literature can be organized into four waves\. The first wave was about finding strange things in powder\-bed images using either trained or unsupervised methods\. The groundbreaking paper by Scime and Beuth demonstrated that powder\-spreading anomalies could be automatically identified and categorized from image patches\, validating the applicability of computer vision for LPBF monitoring\. The second wave went from scoring anomalies to clear deep architectures\, especially multi\-scale CNNs that made it easier to find and classify anomalies in LPBF images on their own\. The third wave was to relate in\-situ sensing and the construction of physical defects more directly\, Scime and Beuth demonstrated that high\-speed visible\-light imaging of melt pools \(during the layer\-based process\) could be used to extract signatures indicating the occurrence of defects \(e\.g\.\, balling and keyholing\)\. Simultaneously to this work\, there were studies using thermographic and optical\-tomography techniques that were beginning to connect in\-situ feature locations to CT\-derived pore classifications \(i\.e\.\, labels\) or probability maps\, respectively\. Mohr et al\.\, compared thermographic and optical tomography to CT\, while Estalaki et al\.\, successfully predicted voxel level defects using in\-situ thermal imaging features\. The authors suggest that thermography and optical tomography may be useful for assessing layer\-based manufacturing processes when used in conjunction with CT\> Pore Labeling and Porosity Probability Maps\. Finally\, in the fourth generation\, which is the current wave of deep learning\, includes examples such as the detection of defects using thermography with Convolutional Neural Networks \(CNN\)\, the ability to classify different types of defects using 3D Convolutional Neural Networks \(3D\-CNN\) based on in\-situ light intensity data that has been spatially organized\, the use of a CNN\-Long Short Term Memory \(LSTM\) architecture to combine multiple time\-scales of heterogeneous optical and acoustic signals\, and the use of transfer learning to adapt a model trained on porosity to identify surface deformation\. The results of these studies indicate that monitoring of Laser Powder Bed Fusion \(LPBF\) will benefit increasingly from the use of architecture designed to leverage either spatial hierarchy\, temporal context\, or both\. Table 1 shows a descriptive review of prior representative studies \[21\, 27\, 28\, 29\, 2\, 6\, 17\, 1\, 25\, 26\]\.

In manufacturing\, CNNs have been successfully applied to surface defect inspection\, weld defect detection\, semiconductor inspection\, and additive manufacturing monitoring\. For LPBF\, CNNs can learn spatial patterns associated with melt track irregularities\, porosity signatures\, and surface texture anomalies\, providing improved robustness compared to rule\-based image processing \[35\]\.

\#\# 3 Problem definition and objectives

\#\#\# 3\.1 Problem definition

Several gaps have come to surface as research moves forward in LPBF image databases\. First\, labeling remains an issue where many LPBF image databases are either unlabeled\, poorly labeled\, or only loosely connected to the physical defects of the part being built\. Second\, registration can be difficult due to various coordinates and resolutions between process and inspection data that cause confusion when training models on how to register the two forms of data\. Third\, cross\-domain generalization of LPBF images is poor\. Different camera settings\, scan patterns\, materials\, and machine architectures will change the data distribution significantly\; therefore\, training models on one camera’s output will not yield good results when applied to a different camera’s output\. Fourth\, there is inconsistency with models’ interpretability and reliability when using model predictions in qualification\-related applications\. Fifth and finally\, real\-time deployment of LPBF model predictions requires computationally efficient systems and decision\-engineering conversions \(decision logic\) that can be understood by human users\. Considering the above identified gaps\, the objective of this work was scoped to evaluate the feasibility of automated defect\-related surface pattern detection in Laser Powder Bed Fusion \(LPBF\) using image\-based deep learning methods\. The problem is formulated as a supervised image classification task\, where layer\-wise optical images are used as input and categorical labels are used to represent surface condition classes associated with defect\-related patterns\. In this framework\, each LPBF monitoring image is treated as an independent sample\, and the classification model is trained to distinguish between different surface condition categories\. Due to limitations in available datasets\, the labels used in this study are treated as surrogate classification categories rather than direct physical defect mechanisms\. These surrogate categories are sufficient to validate the end\-to\-end detection pipeline\, including data preprocessing\, model training\, and evaluation\. The classification task is intended to demonstrate the technical feasibility of CNN\-based defect detection for LPBF monitoring\. The model output represents the predicted surface condition class for each input image\, enabling automated identification of abnormal surface patterns that may be correlated with defect formation\. The proposed framework is designed to be extensible to physically labeled defect datasets in future studies\. The defect detection problem is defined as mapping layer\-wise optical images to categorical surface condition labels using a convolutional neural network\.

\#\#\# 3\.2 Research objectives

The primary research objectives of this study are\:

\- 1\.
To evaluate the feasibility of CNN\-based image classification for LPBF defect\-related surface patterns\.

\- 2\.
To investigate fundamental image\-processing techniques and assess their limitations for LPBF defect detection\.

\- 3\.
To design and implement a CNN architecture for automated classification of LPBF monitoring images\.

\- 4\.
To analyze training and validation performance metrics to assess model generalization behavior\.

\- 5\.
To establish a reproducible workflow for dataset preprocessing\, model training\, and evaluation suitable for future LPBF monitoring applications\.

Secondary objectives include identifying challenges related to dataset labeling\, image resolution\, class imbalance\, and model interpretability\, which are critical for transitioning from feasibility studies to deployable industrial monitoring systems\.

\#\#\# 3\.3 Scope and assumptions

This study is conducted as a feasibility demonstration using an existing dataset previously reported in the literature for LPBF defect\-related image analysis\. The dataset contains real LPBF surface images but is organized by preprocessing and annotation categories rather than explicit physical defect types\. For the purpose of this work\, these categories are treated as surrogate classification labels to validate the deep learning pipeline\. The scope of this work is limited to image\-based classification and does not include real\-time process control\, defect localization\, or closed\-loop parameter optimization\. Additionally\, the model is trained on resized two\-dimensional images and does not incorporate three\-dimensional volumetric data or temporal sequence analysis\. The results are intended to demonstrate methodological feasibility and provide a foundation for future research involving physically labeled defect datasets\, higher\-resolution imaging\, and integrated LPBF monitoring frameworks \[7\, 19\, 35\]\.

\#\# 4 Research methodology

\#\#\# 4\.1 Research flow and detection pipeline

The overall research methodology was designed to evaluate automated defect\-related surface pattern detection in LPBF through a progressive investigation of image\-processing and deep learning techniques\. The study followed a structured pipeline consisting of image acquisition\, exploratory classical detection techniques\, deep learning model development\, training and validation\, and result interpretation\. Initially\, fundamental image\-processing approaches were explored to establish baseline detection strategies and to understand the limitations of handcrafted feature extraction in LPBF monitoring images\. Subsequently\, a CNN\-based approach was implemented to automatically learn hierarchical spatial features from the image data\. The methodological flow reflects a realistic engineering research process in which classical techniques are evaluated prior to adopting data\-driven deep learning models\.The end\-to\-end pipeline consists of\:

\- 1\.
input LPBF layerwise images\,

\- 2\.
preprocessing and normalization\,

\- 3\.
CNN\-based feature extraction\,

\- 4\.
classification of surface condition categories\, and\.

\- 5\.
evaluation of model performance using validation metrics\.

\#\#\# 4\.2 Study of detection techniques

Prior to implementing deep learning methods\, several fundamental image\-processing techniques were investigated to assess their suitability for LPBF defect detection\. First\, histogram analysis was initially explored to identify statistical differences in pixel intensity distributions between defective and non\-defective regions\. Histogram\-based methods are widely used in industrial inspection systems for anomaly detection and image enhancement\. However\, histograms represent only global intensity statistics and do not preserve spatial information\. In LPBF monitoring images\, defects are highly localized and embedded within complex textures\, making histogram\-based detection ineffective and highly sensitive to illumination variations\. Second\, contrast enhancement and thresholding techniques were investigated to highlight potential defect regions\. Contrast\-based methods are commonly used in camera autofocus systems and machine vision applications to identify regions of interest\. However\, LPBF defects often exhibit subtle intensity variations that overlap with normal surface roughness\. Fixed thresholding strategies failed to generalize across different layers and process conditions\, limiting their applicability for robust defect detection\. Third\, edge detection techniques were evaluated to identify geometric discontinuities associated with cracks\, spatter boundaries\, and melt track irregularities\. While edge detection can effectively identify sharp features\, LPBF surfaces inherently contain high\-frequency roughness and noise\, resulting in excessive false\-positive detections\. Significant parameter tuning was required\, reducing the practicality of this approach for automated monitoring\. Finally\, a grid\-based or tiled image analysis strategy was explored to localize defects by dividing large images into smaller patches\. This approach improves sensitivity to localized anomalies and reduces computational complexity for downstream analysis\. However\, grid\-based segmentation still requires robust feature extraction and classification methods to distinguish defects from normal surface variations\.

\#\#\# 4\.3 Limitations of classical techniques

The investigation of classical image\-processing methods revealed significant limitations for LPBF defect detection\. Histogram\-based methods lack spatial awareness\, contrast\-based methods are sensitive to illumination and process variability\, and edge\-based methods generate excessive false detections due to inherent surface roughness\. Grid\-based analysis improves localization but does not provide a discriminative classification mechanism\. LPBF defects exhibit complex\, multi\-scale spatial patterns influenced by melt pool dynamics and thermal gradients\, which are difficult to capture using handcrafted features\. These limitations motivated the transition toward data\-driven deep learning approaches capable of learning hierarchical spatial representations directly from data \[7\]\.

\#\#\# 4\.4 Selection of CNN\-based detection

Based on the observed limitations of classical techniques\, a CNN\-based approach was selected for automated defect\-related surface pattern detection\. CNNs are well\-suited for image\-based tasks due to their ability to learn local spatial features through convolutional filters and to build hierarchical representations through multiple network layers\. CNNs have demonstrated superior performance in manufacturing defect detection\, including surface inspection\, weld defect analysis\, and additive manufacturing monitoring \[16\, 18\, 35\]\. Unlike classical methods\, CNNs do not require manual feature engineering and can adapt to complex textures\, noise\, and illumination variations present in LPBF monitoring images\.

\#\#\# 4\.5 End\-to\-End Data Flow \(Image → Model → Output\)

The implemented defect detection framework follows an end\-to\-end data\-driven workflow\. Layerwise LPBF images are first resized and normalized to ensure consistent input dimensions and numerical stability\. The preprocessed images are then passed through the CNN\, where convolutional layers extract low\-level features such as edges and textures\, followed by deeper layers that capture higher\-level defect\-related spatial patterns\. The extracted feature representations are subsequently processed by fully connected layers to produce classification outputs corresponding to surface condition categories\. The model outputs class probability scores\, enabling automated identification of abnormal surface patterns associated with defect formation\. The performance of the detection framework is evaluated using training and validation accuracy and loss metrics to assess convergence and generalization behavior\.

\#\# 5 Dataset and preprocessing

\#\#\# 5\.1 Dataset source and characteristics

The dataset used in this study was obtained from a previously published LPBF defect imaging research work and consists of real layerwise LPBF surface images \[34\]\. The images were originally collected for defect\-related surface analysis and contain representative surface texture patterns associated with LPBF processing conditions\. The dataset primarily consists of grayscale optical images\, with some images stored in three\-channel format due to preprocessing pipelines and image storage conventions\. Due to the absence of a publicly available\, large\-scale\, physically labeled LPBF defect dataset\, the images in this work were organized into categorical surrogate classes based on preprocessing and annotation groupings reported in the reference study\. These surrogate labels were used to validate the feasibility of the CNN\-based defect detection pipeline rather than to perform direct physical defect taxonomy classification\. The dataset contains thousands of images\, enabling supervised training and validation of the deep learning model\. Each image represents a layerwise or surface region of an LPBF\-manufactured component\, capturing surface texture variations\, melt track morphology\, and defect\-related visual patterns\. Such datasets are commonly used in feasibility studies for additive manufacturing monitoring due to the scarcity of standardized defect\-labeled benchmarks \[2\, 7\]\.

\#\#\# 5\.2 Ethical and scientific dataset selection reasoning

The dataset was selected based on its relevance to LPBF surface condition analysis and its suitability for demonstrating the feasibility of deep learning–based defect detection\. Although the surrogate class labels do not correspond directly to physical defect mechanisms such as lack\-of\-fusion or keyhole porosity\, the dataset provides representative defect\-related visual patterns necessary for validating the detection pipeline\. Using surrogate labels for methodological validation is a common practice in early\-stage research\, particularly when physically labeled industrial datasets are unavailable due to proprietary restrictions or experimental costs\. The primary objective of this study is to demonstrate the technical feasibility of CNN\-based classification for LPBF monitoring imagery\, with the expectation that future work will incorporate physically annotated defect datasets and in\-situ sensor data for full defect taxonomy classification\.

\#\#\# 5\.3 Image resizing and normalization

All images were resized to a fixed resolution of 128 × 128 pixels to standardize the input dimensions for the CNN model and to reduce computational complexity\. Resizing ensures consistent tensor dimensions and enables efficient batch processing during training\. Pixel intensities were normalized to the range \[0\, 1\] using a rescaling operation\, which improves numerical stability and accelerates convergence during gradient\-based optimization\. Although the images are predominantly grayscale\, they were processed in three\-channel format to maintain compatibility with standard CNN architectures and image loading pipelines\. Resizing to a moderate resolution represents a trade\-off between spatial detail preservation and computational efficiency\. While higher resolutions may capture finer defect features\, the selected resolution is sufficient for feasibility evaluation and proof\-of\-concept validation\.

\#\#\# 5\.4 Data splitting strategy

The dataset was partitioned into training and validation subsets using an 80\/20 split\. The training set consisted of approximately 2\,674 images\, while the validation set contained approximately 540 images\. A fixed random seed was used to ensure reproducibility of the data split\. The training dataset was used to optimize the CNN parameters\, while the validation dataset was used to evaluate model generalization on unseen data\. This split strategy is widely used in supervised learning to prevent overfitting and to provide an unbiased estimate of model performance\.

\#\#\# 5\.5 Potential data augmentation

Data augmentation techniques such as random rotations\, flips\, and intensity perturbations can improve model robustness by increasing dataset diversity and reducing overfitting\. Although data augmentation was not extensively applied in this feasibility study\, it represents an important future improvement for LPBF defect detection frameworks\. Augmentation is particularly relevant for LPBF monitoring datasets\, where defect instances may be rare and class imbalance is common\.

\#\# 6 Model architecture and design

Convolutional Neural Networks \(CNNs\) were selected as the primary model architecture due to their demonstrated effectiveness in image\-based pattern recognition and manufacturing defect detection\. CNNs employ convolutional filters to learn spatially localized features and hierarchical representations\, making them well\-suited for identifying surface texture anomalies and defect\-related patterns in LPBF monitoring images\. The implemented CNN architecture follows a sequential design consisting of three convolutional blocks followed by fully connected layers for classification\. Each convolutional block includes a convolutional layer with a 3 × 3 kernel and Rectified Linear Unit \(ReLU\) activation\, followed by a max pooling layer with a 2 × 2 window\. The convolutional layers contain 32\, 64\, and 128 filters\, respectively\, enabling progressive extraction of low\-level\, mid\-level\, and high\-level spatial features\. Early layers capture fundamental patterns such as edges and surface textures\, while deeper layers capture more complex defect\-related morphological features\. After convolutional feature extraction\, the feature maps are flattened into a one\-dimensional vector and passed through a dense layer with 128 neurons to perform non\-linear classification\. Dropout regularization with a rate of 0\.3 is applied to reduce overfitting by randomly deactivating neurons during training\. The output layer consists of three neurons with sigmoid activation\, producing independent probability scores for each surface condition category\. This formulation enables probabilistic scoring of class membership and supports surrogate multi\-class feasibility classification\. The model was trained using the Adam optimizer\, which adapts learning rates during training and is widely used in deep learning applications due to its fast convergence properties\. Binary cross\-entropy loss was used to optimize the classification objective\. Training and validation accuracy and loss metrics were monitored across epochs to assess convergence behavior and model generalization\. The selected architecture represents a balance between model complexity and computational efficiency\. A moderate\-depth CNN was chosen to avoid excessive overfitting given the dataset size while maintaining sufficient representational capacity to capture defect\-related surface patterns\. This design is suitable for feasibility evaluation and can be extended in future work through deeper architectures\, transfer learning\, or segmentation\-based frameworks for defect localization \[9\, 16\]\.

The present work was conceived as a proof\-of\-concept study to assess the feasibility of utilizing a CNN\-based image classification framework for detecting defect\-indicative surface patterns in LPBF images\. While a comparison with classical feature\-based ML approaches \(e\.g\.\, SVM with HOG features\) or pretrained CNN models \(e\.g\.\, VGG16 transfer learning\) would provide additional insight into the performance of the proposed framework\, this was not performed here for brevity\. This decision was also motivated by the fact that the available dataset is limited in size and relies on surrogate labels rather than physically verified defect classes\, and thus\, a direct comparison between models would imply a degree of benchmark validation beyond the scope of this preliminary feasibility study\.

\#\#\# 6\.1 Mathematical formulation of the CNN framework

The proposed LPBF surface\-classification framework was implemented using a convolutional neural network \(CNN\) architecture developed in TensorFlow\/Keras\. CNNs are widely used for image\-based classification because they can automatically learn hierarchical spatial features from raw image data through convolutional\, pooling\, and nonlinear activation operations \[9\, 15\]\. In the present study\, the model was designed to extract defect\-relevant surface morphology and texture features from LPBF image data\.

Let the dataset be represented as

\$\$\\\:\\mathcal\{D\}\=\{\\left\\\{\\left\(\{x\}\^\{\\left\(n\\right\)\}\,\{y\}\^\{\\left\(n\\right\)\}\\right\)\\right\\\}\}\_\{n\=1\}\^\{N\}\,\$\$

where

\$\$\\\:\{x\}\^\{\\left\(n\\right\)\}\\in\\\:\{\\mathbb\{R\}\}\^\{128\\times\\\:128\\times\\\:3\}\$\$

denotes an RGB LPBF surface image\, and

\$\$\\\:\{y\}\^\{\\left\(n\\right\)\}\\in\\\:\\\{\{e\}\_\{1\}\,\{e\}\_\{2\}\,\{e\}\_\{3\}\\\}\\subset\\\:\{\\mathbb\{R\}\}\^\{3\}\$\$

represents the corresponding one\-hot encoded class label vector associated with the defect category\. The image dataset was partitioned into training and validation subsets using an 80\/20 split strategy through TensorFlow’s image\_dataset\_from\_directory utility\.

Prior to feature extraction\, each image was normalized using a rescaling layer according to

\$\$\\\:\{a\}\^\{\\left\(0\\right\)\}\=\\frac\{x\}\{255\}\,\$\$

thereby mapping pixel intensities from the range \\\(\\\:\[0\,255\]\\\) to \\\(\\\:\[0\,1\]\\\)\. This normalization improves optimization stability and accelerates gradient\-based learning \[9\]\.

The CNN architecture consisted of three convolutional blocks followed by fully connected dense layers\. For a generic convolutional layer\, the pre\-activation feature map at spatial coordinate \\\(\\\:\(i\,j\)\\\) and channel \\\(\\\:k\\\) is expressed as

\$\$\\\:\{z\}\_\{i\,j\,k\}\^\{\\left\(\\mathcal\{l\}\\right\)\}\=\{b\}\_\{k\}\^\{\\left\(\\mathcal\{l\}\\right\)\}\+\\sum\\\:\_\{u\,v\,c\}\{W\}\_\{u\,v\,c\,k\}\^\{\\left\(\\mathcal\{l\}\\right\)\}\\hspace\{0\.17em\}\{a\}\_\{i\+u\,j\+v\,c\}\^\{\(\\mathcal\{l\}\-1\)\}\,\$\$

where

\$\$\\\:\{W\}\^\{\\left\(\\mathcal\{l\}\\right\)\}\$\$

denotes the learnable convolution kernel weights and

\$\$\\\:\{b\}\_\{k\}\^\{\\left\(\\mathcal\{l\}\\right\)\}\$\$

represents the bias associated with output channel \\\(\\\:k\\\)\. Each convolution operation utilized \\\(\\\:3\\times\\\:3\\\) kernels with Rectified Linear Unit \(ReLU\) activation functions\. The use of convolutional layers enables localized feature extraction and parameter sharing\, which are central characteristics of CNN\-based image recognition frameworks \[9\, 15\]\.

The nonlinear activation operation is given by

\$\$\\\:\{a\}\_\{i\,j\,k\}\^\{\\left\(\\mathcal\{l\}\\right\)\}\=\\text\{m\}\\text\{a\}\\text\{x\}\\left\(0\,\{z\}\_\{i\,j\,k\}\^\{\\left\(\\mathcal\{l\}\\right\)\}\\right\)\,\$\$

which introduces nonlinearity into the feature\-learning process while maintaining efficient gradient propagation during optimization\. ReLU activation functions are commonly used in deep neural networks due to their computational efficiency and favorable gradient behavior \[9\, 23\]\.

Spatial dimensionality reduction was achieved through max\-pooling operations using \\\(\\\:2\\times\\\:2\\\) pooling windows and stride 2\. The pooling operation is mathematically represented as

\$\$\\\:\{p\}\_\{i\,j\,k\}\=\\underset\{0\\le\\\:u\,v\<2\}\{\\text\{m\}\\text\{a\}\\text\{x\}\}\{a\}\_\{2i\+u\,2j\+v\,k\}\.\$\$

The progressive convolution\-pooling operations enabled the network to learn increasingly abstract representations of LPBF surface features\, ranging from localized intensity variations to higher\-order morphological defect signatures \[9\, 15\]\.

The spatial evolution of the feature maps throughout the CNN architecture is summarized as follows\:

\$\$\\\:128\\times\\\:128\\times\\\:3\\to\\\:126\\times\\\:126\\times\\\:32\\to\\\:63\\times\\\:63\\times\\\:32\$\$

\$\$\\\:63\\times\\\:63\\times\\\:32\\to\\\:61\\times\\\:61\\times\\\:64\\to\\\:30\\times\\\:30\\times\\\:64\$\$

\$\$\\\:30\\times\\\:30\\times\\\:64\\to\\\:28\\times\\\:28\\times\\\:128\\to\\\:14\\times\\\:14\\times\\\:128\.\$\$

Following the final pooling stage\, the feature tensor was flattened into a one\-dimensional vector of size

\$\$\\\:14\\times\\\:14\\times\\\:128\=25\,088\.\$\$

This flattened representation was subsequently processed by a fully connected dense layer containing 128 neurons\:

\$\$\\\:\{z\}\^\{\\left\(4\\right\)\}\=\{W\}\^\{\\left\(4\\right\)\}\{h\}\^\{\\left\(0\\right\)\}\+\{b\}\^\{\\left\(4\\right\)\}\,\$\$

followed by ReLU activation\:

\$\$\\\:\{h\}\^\{\\left\(1\\right\)\}\=\\text\{m\}\\text\{a\}\\text\{x\}\(0\,\{z\}\^\{\\left\(4\\right\)\}\)\.\$\$

To improve generalization capability and suppress overfitting\, dropout regularization with rate

\$\$\\\:r\=0\.3\$\$

was incorporated\. Dropout is a widely used regularization strategy that reduces co\-adaptation among neurons by randomly deactivating a subset of units during training \[30\]\. During training\, the hidden activations were randomly masked according to

\$\$\\\:\\stackrel\{\\sim\}\{h\}\=\\frac\{m\\odot\\\:\{h\}\^\{\\left\(1\\right\)\}\}\{1\-r\}\,\$\$

where

\$\$\\\:\{m\}\_\{j\}\\sim\\\:\\text\{Bernoulli\}\(1\-r\)\$\$

is a stochastic binary mask and \\\(\\\:\\odot\\\:\\\) denotes elementwise multiplication\.

The final output layer mapped the learned feature representation into a three\-dimensional output vector\:

\$\$\\\:\{z\}\^\{\\left\(5\\right\)\}\=\{W\}\^\{\\left\(5\\right\)\}\{h\}\^\{\\left\(1\\right\)\}\+\{b\}\^\{\\left\(5\\right\)\}\,\$\$

followed by elementwise sigmoid activation\:

\$\$\\\:\{p\}\_\{j\}\=\\sigma\\\:\\left\(\{z\}\_\{j\}\\right\)\=\\frac\{1\}\{1\+\{e\}\^\{\-\{z\}\_\{j\}\}\}\,\\\:\\\:j\=1\,2\,3\.\$\$

The resulting output vector represents the predicted classification scores associated with the LPBF surface\-defect categories\.

The CNN model was trained using binary cross\-entropy loss\, expressed as

\$\$\\\:\{\\mathcal\{l\}\}\_\{\\text\{B\}\\text\{C\}\\text\{E\}\}\(y\,p\)\=\-\\frac\{1\}\{3\}\\sum\\\:\_\{j\=1\}\^\{3\}\\left\[\{y\}\_\{j\}\\text\{l\}\\text\{o\}\\text\{g\}\\left\(\{p\}\_\{j\}\\right\)\+\(1\-\{y\}\_\{j\}\)\\text\{l\}\\text\{o\}\\text\{g\}\(1\-\{p\}\_\{j\}\)\\right\]\.\$\$

For a mini\-batch \\\(\\\:\{B\}\_\{t\}\\\)\, the empirical objective function becomes

\$\$\\\:\{J\}\_\{\{B\}\_\{t\}\}\\left\(\{\\Theta\\\:\}\\right\)\=\\frac\{1\}\{\\left\|\{B\}\_\{t\}\\right\|\}\\sum\\\:\_\{\(x\,y\)\\in\\\:\{B\}\_\{t\}\}\{\\mathcal\{l\}\}\_\{\\text\{B\}\\text\{C\}\\text\{E\}\}\\left\(y\,\{f\}\_\{\{\\Theta\\\:\}\}\\left\(x\\right\)\\right\)\,\$\$

where

\$\$\\\:\{\\Theta\\\:\}\$\$

represents the complete set of trainable network parameters\.

Optimization of the CNN parameters was performed using the Adam optimizer\, an adaptive stochastic gradient\-based optimization algorithm commonly used in deep learning applications \[13\]\. Adam updates the first and second gradient moments according to

\$\$\\\:\{m\}\_\{t\}\=\{\\beta\\\:\}\_\{1\}\{m\}\_\{t\-1\}\+\(1\-\{\\beta\\\:\}\_\{1\}\)\{g\}\_\{t\}\,\$\$

\$\$\\\:\{v\}\_\{t\}\=\{\\beta\\\:\}\_\{2\}\{v\}\_\{t\-1\}\+\(1\-\{\\beta\\\:\}\_\{2\}\)\{g\}\_\{t\}\^\{2\}\,\$\$

with bias\-corrected moment estimates

\$\$\\\:\{\\widehat\{m\}\}\_\{t\}\=\\frac\{\{m\}\_\{t\}\}\{1\-\{\\beta\\\:\}\_\{1\}\^\{t\}\}\,\\\:\\\:\{\\widehat\{v\}\}\_\{t\}\=\\frac\{\{v\}\_\{t\}\}\{1\-\{\\beta\\\:\}\_\{2\}\^\{t\}\}\.\$\$

The parameter update equation is therefore

\$\$\\\:\{\{\\Theta\\\:\}\}\_\{t\+1\}\=\{\{\\Theta\\\:\}\}\_\{t\}\-\\alpha\\\:\\frac\{\{\\widehat\{m\}\}\_\{t\}\}\{\\sqrt\{\{\\widehat\{v\}\}\_\{t\}\}\+\\epsilon\\\:\}\,\$\$

where \\\(\\\:\\alpha\\\:\\\) denotes the learning rate and \\\(\\\:\\epsilon\\\:\\\) is a numerical stabilization parameter \(Kingma and Ba 2014\)\.

The model performance was evaluated using categorical accuracy\, computed as

\$\$\\\:\\text\{Accuracy\}\=\\frac\{1\}\{\{N\}\_\{\\text\{v\}\\text\{a\}\\text\{l\}\}\}\\sum\\\:\_\{n\=1\}\^\{\{N\}\_\{\\text\{v\}\\text\{a\}\\text\{l\}\}\}1\\left\[\\text\{a\}\\text\{r\}\\text\{g\}\\underset\{j\}\{\\text\{m\}\\text\{a\}\\text\{x\}\}\{y\}\_\{j\}\^\{\\left\(n\\right\)\}\=\\text\{a\}\\text\{r\}\\text\{g\}\\underset\{j\}\{\\text\{m\}\\text\{a\}\\text\{x\}\}\{p\}\_\{j\}\^\{\\left\(n\\right\)\}\\right\]\,\$\$

where

\$\$\\\:1\[\\cdot\\\:\]\$\$

denotes the indicator function\. The resulting framework demonstrates the feasibility of utilizing convolutional neural networks for automated LPBF surface\-defect classification and establishes a foundation for future integration with intelligent monitoring and digital twin–based manufacturing systems\.

\#\# 8 Results

The CNN\-based defect detection model demonstrated consistent learning behavior during training and validation\. Training and validation accuracy curves indicate that the model successfully learned discriminative features from LPBF surface images\, while loss curves suggest stable convergence without severe overfitting\.

\#\#\# 8\.1 Training and validation accuracy curves

The training and validation accuracy trends obtained during CNN training are presented in Fig\. 7\. The model exhibited a gradual improvement with increasing epochs\, with the stablization of validation accuracy being acheieved at 84\% demonstrating a successful learning of defect\-related surface morphology features from the LPBF image datset\.

The relatively close agreement between the training and validation accuracy curves shows that the developed CNN architecture has reasonable generalization capability on unseen validation samples\. The training process\, however\, exhibited a small oscillatory behavior\, specifically in the validation accuracy profile\, but these are commonly seen in stochastic gradient\-based optimization and are a common result of the variability of heterogeneous manufacturing image datasets\.In LPBF\, variations in illumination conditions\, powder\-bed texture\, surface irregularities\, and localized defect morphology can contribute to minor epoch\-to\-epoch prediction variability during training\. The classification accuracy gradually increases\, indicating that the convolutional layers can gradually extract hierarchical spatial features related to surface characteristics relevant to defects\. Lower\-level convolutional filters likely captured local geometric and intensity based patterns\, while deeper layers yielded higher\-level feature abstraction related to anomaly\-associated morphology\. The observed convergence behaviour shows that the proposed CNN framework has learned discriminative representations relevant to LPBF surface\-condition classification\.

Furthermore\, the training and validation accuracies being close together indicates that the model was not overfitted by the architecture or training conditions shown by the absence of substantial divergence between the training and validation accuracy curves\. Another important contribution to model stability \(and suppression of overfitting to training features\) is the use of pooling layers and dropout regularization which likely improved model stability and suppression of excessive memorization of training\-specific features\. This type of performance is very important to a ML framework that has to generalize well across real\-time\, in situ applications in the area of industrial manufacturing and intelligent process control\.

The performance achieved during validation supports that the feasibility of deep learning with CNNs for LPBF surface defect analysis can be utilized in practice\; although this is an initial proof of concept\, the results have strong promise for the future integration with real\-time monitoring\, multimodal sensing\, and digital twin\-assisted manufacturing systems for adaptive process optimization and defect prediction\.

\#\#\# 8\.2 Loss curve interpretation

The training and validation loss behavior observed during the CNN training process is presented in Fig\. 8\. Both curves for training and validation loss exhibited an overall decreasing trend across the epochs\, suggesting stable optimization and progressive convergence of the deep learning framework\. There was a decrease in loss value over time\, meaning that the CNN has improved its ability to classify LPBF surface defects\.

The training and validation loss profiles were observed to be in close agreement to each other\, supporting the notion that our model did not learn all training\-specific features\, but was able to generalize reasonably well\. Such a finding suggests that the learning dynamics were stable and that the selected architecture demonstrated an ability to generate meaningful spatial representations of the manufacturing images\, while retaining the ability to make predictions about previously unseen validation samples\. During the intermediate and later training epochs of the validation loss\, a minor\"oscillatory” behavior was observed\. This type of behavior is typical for many deep learning\-based applications that use different images from different sources along with different types of algorithms to optimize the images used in training\. The small amount of variance in the validation results from epoch to epoch found in this particular LPBF surface defect classification example may result from differences in the texture of the powder bed\, localized geometry of defects\, differences in the illumination while taking an image of the part\, and differences in the datasets used to train and validate\. Furthermore\, the random sampling of batches and unequal distribution of verified classes in training will also have an effect on the transient nature of validation loss through training\.

Even though there were some fluctuations with the metrics\, the validation loss stayed relatively steady compared to the training loss\, and there was no prolonged misalignment between the curves\. There was no significant gap between the two curves which strongly suggests that the model was at risk of severe overfitting and that the risk was prevented with the training configuration used to train the model\. The pooling operations and dropout regularization would have helped to limit the sensitivity of excessive parameters and improve the robustness of the model\.

The observed convergence characteristics confirm that the CNN architecture being evaluated and associated training hyperparameters are suitable for the current feasibility study related to the automatic classification of LPBF surface defects\. In addition\, there are stable optimization characteristics that support possible future implementation of monitoring systems utilizing deep learning in the intelligent manufacturing and additive manufacturing environments enabled through digital twins\.

\#\#\# 8\.3 Qualitative prediction results

Qualitative prediction results were generated by evaluating the model on a subset of validation images and comparing predicted class probability vectors with true labels\. The model produced high\-confidence predictions for most samples\, indicating effective separation of surrogate surface condition categories\. The predicted probability vectors provide insight into the model’s confidence in classification decisions and demonstrate the potential of CNN\-based approaches for automated LPBF monitoring\. Although the surrogate labels do not correspond directly to physical defect mechanisms\, the qualitative results confirm that the CNN successfully learned discriminative surface texture patterns\.

\#\#\# 8\.4 Model reproducibility in independent training trials

To assess the repeatability and robustness of our CNN\-based classification framework\, the model was trained three times on a random subset of data with different random seeds\, but with identical data\, preprocessing\, network architecture\, and training parameters\. The goal was to observe the variation in results when using different randomly initialized models\, and confirm that the reported result was not an anomaly\. The results from the three independent training processes had a mean validation accuracy of 83\.14\% ± 0\.48\% and a mean validation loss of 0\.2594 ± 0\.0121\. Observing the relatively low variance in both validation accuracy and loss\, we conclude that our CNN\-based surface classification framework performs consistently within the limited scope of the proof\-of\-concept data sample\.

For each fold in the training process\, both training accuracy and loss\, as well as their validation counterparts\, were recorded\. When plotted with the standard deviation\, the three learning curves show similar patterns across epochs\. The validation loss was consistently improving over the epochs while the validation accuracy was fluctuating in a small range as shown in in Fig\. 9\.

Subsequently\, the model was able to consistently learn the visual patterns in the surrogate labeled data corresponding to the LPBF surface imperfections\. Due to the limited size of the labeled sample\, however\, the k\-fold cross\-validation was not implemented\, and the result could not be generalized to a larger sample size\. In future research\, the CNN classification framework will be tested on a more substantial physically labeled data set and evaluated using various validation techniques\, including k\-fold cross\-validation\, classical machine learning approaches\, and transfer learning\, to assess its performance further\.

\#\#\# 8\.5 Observed strengths and limitations

The primary strength of the implemented framework is its ability to automatically learn hierarchical spatial features from LPBF surface images without manual feature engineering\. The CNN demonstrated robustness to surface texture variability and achieved reliable classification performance using a moderate\-depth architecture and limited computational resources\. However\, several limitations were identified\. The dataset used in this study employed surrogate classification labels rather than physically annotated defect categories\, limiting direct interpretation of results in terms of specific defect mechanisms\. Additionally\, resizing images to 128 × 128 pixels may have reduced fine\-scale defect feature resolution\. Class imbalance and limited dataset diversity may also affect model generalization\. Despite these limitations\, the results demonstrate the technical feasibility of CNN\-based defect\-related surface pattern detection for LPBF monitoring applications\. The analysis of repeatability across 3 independent training trials strengthens the evidence for the proposed CNN framework’s robustness in the scope of the current proof of concept\. Small variations of the validation accuracy and loss between the trials and absence of significantly better performing training runs suggest that model performance is not driven by random factors but is consistent across different random seeds\. This is an important feature of the model\, which enables more confident assessment of the classification performance\. However\, as it was discussed in the main part of the paper\, such assessment is currently limited by the size of available data and the use of the surrogate labels instead of the physically verified defect classes\. Thus\, while the analysis contributes to the understanding of the model performance by excluding random factors\, it will be important to perform multiple experiments with bigger dataset and physically verified labels to establish a consistent performance metric for the proposed CNN\, evaluate its performance across k\-fold validation\, and compare it to classical models and transfer learning approaches\.

\#\# 9 Discussion

\#\#\# 9\.1 Why the model works

CNN\-based models are well\-suited for LPBF defect\-related surface pattern detection due to their ability to learn hierarchical spatial features from image data\. Convolutional layers capture low\-level features such as edges and surface textures\, while deeper layers encode complex spatial structures associated with melt track morphology and surface irregularities\. Unlike classical image\-processing methods\, CNNs do not rely on handcrafted features and can adapt to variations in illumination\, surface roughness\, and noise inherent in LPBF monitoring images Sample body text\. The hierarchical receptive fields in CNNs implicitly perform localized feature extraction\, analogous to grid\-based inspection\, while maintaining global contextual awareness\. This capability is critical for LPBF applications\, where defect signatures are localized but influenced by surrounding melt pool dynamics and surface conditions\.

\#\#\# 9\.2 Failure modes

Several failure modes were identified in the implemented framework\. First\, the dataset employed surrogate classification labels rather than physically annotated defect categories\, limiting direct correlation between model predictions and specific defect mechanisms such as lack\-of\-fusion or keyhole porosity\. Second\, resizing images to 128 × 128 pixels may have reduced spatial resolution\, potentially obscuring fine\-scale defect features\. Third\, class imbalance and limited dataset diversity can introduce bias and reduce generalization performance\. Additionally\, the model does not incorporate temporal information or melt pool sensor data\, which are known to be critical for robust defect detection in LPBF systems \[7\]\.

\#\#\# 9\.3 Comparison with classical methods

Compared to classical image\-processing methods\, the CNN\-based approach demonstrated superior robustness and adaptability\. Histogram\-based and contrast\-based techniques lacked spatial awareness and were sensitive to illumination variations\. Edge\-based detection generated excessive false positives due to inherent surface roughness\. Grid\-based analysis improved localization but still required discriminative feature extraction methods\. In contrast\, the CNN automatically learned discriminative features from data\, eliminating the need for manual parameter tuning and enabling scalable automated defect detection\.

\#\# 10 Conclusion

This study investigated the feasibility of automated defect\-related surface pattern detection in Laser Powder Bed Fusion using a convolutional neural network framework\. Fundamental image\-processing techniques\, including histogram\-based\, contrast\-based\, edge\-based\, and grid\-based approaches\, were initially evaluated and found to be insufficient for robust LPBF defect detection due to their sensitivity to illumination\, noise\, and complex surface textures\. A CNN\-based approach was subsequently implemented to automatically learn hierarchical spatial features from LPBF surface images\. The developed CNN architecture demonstrated stable training behavior and achieved approximately 84\% validation accuracy on surrogate classification categories\. Training and validation loss trends indicated convergence without severe overfitting\, confirming the suitability of the selected model architecture and training strategy for feasibility evaluation\. The implementation established a reproducible workflow for dataset preprocessing\, model training\, evaluation\, and model persistence\, providing a foundation for future LPBF monitoring research\. Despite the promising results\, the study is limited by the use of surrogate classification labels rather than physically annotated defect categories\, moderate image resolution\, and dataset size constraints\. Future work should focus on acquiring physically labeled LPBF defect datasets\, increasing image resolution\, incorporating data augmentation\, and extending the framework to defect localization using segmentation models\. Integration of temporal data and in\-situ sensor signals\, such as melt pool monitoring and thermographic imaging\, is also recommended to enable real\-time defect detection and closed\-loop process control\.

Future work should include benchmarking the proposed CNN framework against classical machine learning methods\, such as SVM with HOG features\, and pretrained transfer learning models\, such as VGG16\, using larger datasets with physically verified defect labels\.

records.summary: The paper addresses how varying thermal boundary conditions in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)—such as substrate temperature changes, heat accumulation in adjacent tracks, and reduced heat dissipation in overhanging zones—cause melt pool fluctuations when constant laser parameters are used, contributing to material and part-scale defects. The authors use a finite element analysis (FEA) model to simulate a multi-track laser scan on a single layer of solid Inconel 625 (IN625) substrate, first with constant laser power to examine effects on melt pool characteristics, particularly transverse area. They then apply a laser power profile computed by a nonlinear sliding mode controller in a feedforward strategy across eight bidirectional laser tracks. The abstract reports that this feedforward control stabilized the melt pool transverse area, particularly in thermally unstable regions such as laser turnarounds, and that the simulation captured the targeted melt pool dynamics. records.body_text:
Computational modeling of melt pool evolution in laser powder bed fusion with laser power control
- ORIGINAL ARTICLE
- Published:
Abstract
Variations in thermal boundary conditions during the Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) process, such as changes in substrate temperature, heat accumulation in adjacent tracks, and reduced heat dissipation in overhanging zones, can lead to fluctuations in melt pool characteristics when constant laser parameters are applied, which is a common practice. These variations have been reported to contribute to the formation of a range of material and part-scale defects. Controlling, therefore, laser parameters can substantially improve print quality and help avoid the initiation of such defects. In this work, a finite element analysis (FEA) approach is used to simulate a multi-track laser scan on a single layer of a solid Inconel 625 (IN625) substrate, aiming to investigate fundamental variations in melt pool behavior under varying process parameters and evolving substrate thermal conditions caused by adjacent printed tracks while simultaneously adjusting the laser profile. The FEA model first simulates constant laser power to examine its effect on melt pool characteristics, and particularly its transverse area. This study is then followed by the implementation of a laser profile, computed by a nonlinear sliding mode controller, using a feedforward strategy across eight bidirectional laser tracks. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the attempted feedforward control in stabilizing the melt pool transverse area during printing, particularly in thermally unstable regions such as laser turnarounds. This simulation approach is shown to be capable of capturing the targeted melt pool dynamics and provides insights related to the correlation between laser power modulation and melt pool behavior in LPBF.

Highlights
- •Low-carbon steel samples were fabricated via GMAW-based WAAM with 100% CO₂.
- •Boriding was applied to low-carbon steel samples manufactured via WAAM.
- •Boride layer degradation was found for boriding treatment at 1000 °C for 6 h.
- •Surface hardness improved significantly in all WAAM samples, except at 1000 °C - 6 h.
- •Borided WAAM samples matched borided AISI 1018 samples in tribological performance.
Abstract
Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) method enables the fabrication of customized layer-by-layer structures. Low-carbon steels are particularly attractive feedstock materials for WAAM because of their low cost, excellent weldability, and reliable deposition behavior. However, their inherently low surface hardness and poor wear resistance restrict their use in tribological applications. Surface modification techniques offer a potential solution to address these limitations. This study evaluates the effect of boriding on the surface properties and tribological performance of low-carbon steel samples manufactured via WAAM. Low-carbon steel (ER70S-6) plates were fabricated using a voltage of ~19.7 V, a current of ~67 A, and a gas flow rate of 20 L/min of 100% CO₂. Samples were extracted from the upper and lower regions of the WAAM-built plates to evaluate possible variations in the response to boriding along the build direction. AISI 1018 steel samples manufactured by conventional processing were used as a reference material. Powder pack boriding treatment was performed at 900 °C and 1000 °C for 2 h and 6 h. The morphology, phase composition, hardness, and tribological performance of the boride layers formed on WAAM-fabricated low-carbon steel were evaluated and compared with those formed on conventionally manufactured AISI 1018 steel. The results indicate that borided WAAM samples can achieve performance on par with AISI 1018 samples. However, at higher temperatures and longer exposure times during boriding (1000 °C for 6 h), degradation of the boride layer was observed in all samples.
