\# 2026 Energy Storage PACK Busbar Selection Guide\: Conductive Copper Components for Battery Packs

Energy storage systems are moving from pilot projects to gigawatt\-scale deployment across Europe\, and the battery pack remains the cost and safety center of gravity\. Inside every PACK\, copper busbars and conductive connecting components carry hundreds of amps between cells\, modules and terminals\. A busbar that is undersized\, poorly plated or sourced from an unqualified supplier can drive contact resistance up\, create hot spots and\, in the worst case\, contribute to thermal runaway\. This guide sets out what procurement and engineering teams should evaluate in 2026 when selecting copper busbars for energy storage PACKs\, from material specification through supplier vetting\, compliance\, logistics and in\-service maintenance\.

The market context matters\. European buyers are balancing cost pressure from Chinese and Southeast Asian suppliers against the incoming requirements of the EU Batteries Regulation\, which tightens documentation\, carbon footprint disclosure and due diligence across the battery value chain\. At the same time\, PACK designs are converging on higher current densities\, more compact module layouts and liquid\-cooled architectures\, all of which raise the demands on busbar geometry\, insulation and joint quality\. Buyers who treat busbars as a commodity item rather than an engineered component tend to discover the cost of that assumption during commissioning or\, worse\, in the field\.

Use the table below as a starting checklist when building a technical specification or evaluating quotations from competing suppliers\.

Selection Area \| What to Specify \| Procurement and Risk Notes 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Copper material \| T2 or TU1 oxygen\-free copper\; conductivity typically ≥ 99\.9\% IACS\; hardness and temper stated on the drawing \| Request mill certificates and conductivity test reports per lot\; verify that the grade on the certificate matches the purchase order 
Surface treatment \| Nickel plating \(typical 3–8 µm\)\, tin plating\, or bare copper with antioxidant treatment depending on joint design and environment \| Plating thickness and adhesion should be measurable\; thin or porous plating is a common cause of rising contact resistance in humid or coastal installations 
Cross\-section and current rating \| Current\-carrying capacity with defined temperature rise limit \(for example ≤ 65 K above ambient\)\, plus short\-circuit withstand \| Do not accept supplier ratings without test conditions\; confirm the calculation basis and request thermal test data 
Insulation and spacing \| Heat\-shrink or powder coating\, dielectric strength\, creepage and clearance distances for the system voltage class \| Insulation must be compatible with the cooling method \(air or liquid\) and with the PACK\'s expected operating temperature range 
Joint and connection design \| Bolt size\, torque values\, contact surface flatness\, use of Belleville washers\, anti\-seize or conductive paste \| Define torque in the assembly work instruction and audit it at the supplier\; loose joints are a leading field failure mode 
Dimensional tolerances \| Hole position\, bend radius\, flatness and twist limits tied to the module stack\-up \| Request first\-article inspection reports and CMM data\; tolerance stack\-up errors cause assembly line stoppages 
Compliance and documentation \| RoHS and REACH declarations\, material traceability\, UL 1973 or IEC 62619 alignment at system level\, IEC 61439 where applicable to assemblies \| Keep declarations on file per shipment\; EU Batteries Regulation due diligence expectations are increasing\, so supplier documentation quality is a selection criterion 
Supplier capability \| In\-house stamping\, bending\, plating and inspection\; ISO 9001 and preferably IATF 16949 where automotive\-grade discipline is required \| Audit plating lines in person or by video\; outsourced plating is a frequent weak point in the supply chain 
Logistics and packaging \| Anti\-oxidation wrapping\, moisture barrier bags\, shock\-resistant cartons\, pallet configuration \| Copper is a theft target and plating is sensitive to humidity\; agree Incoterms\, insurance and packaging standards in the contract 
Maintenance and service life \| Inspection intervals for torque and thermal imaging\, spare parts availability\, replacement part traceability \| Build busbar inspection into the PACK maintenance schedule\; require the supplier to hold spare capacity or stock for the contract term 

On material selection\, T2 and TU1 copper grades are the common baseline for energy storage busbars\, with conductivity verified against the ≥ 99\.9\% IACS expectation\. Buyers should insist on lot\-level mill certificates and\, for high\-current joints\, independent conductivity or resistance testing\. Plating choice depends on the joint and environment\: nickel plating offers good wear and corrosion resistance for bolted joints\, tin plating supports solderability and lower contact resistance in some designs\, and bare copper with antioxidant treatment can be acceptable in sealed\, dry enclosures\. The specification should state plating thickness with a tolerance band and a measurable adhesion test\, because plating quality varies widely between suppliers and is difficult to assess from a datasheet alone\.

Sizing is where many procurement errors originate\. Suppliers frequently quote a current rating without stating the allowable temperature rise\, ambient conditions\, mounting orientation or cooling assumptions\. A defensible specification defines the temperature rise limit\, the short\-circuit withstand current and duration\, and the test method used to verify both\. For liquid\-cooled PACKs\, the busbar and insulation must be qualified for direct or indirect contact with the coolant and for the operating temperature window\. For high\-voltage systems\, creepage and clearance distances should be calculated for the system voltage class and confirmed against the relevant standards rather than copied from a previous project\.

Joint design deserves the same rigor as the busbar itself\. Bolt size\, torque\, contact surface flatness and the use of Belleville washers or conductive paste all influence long\-term contact resistance\. Procurement teams should require the supplier to document torque values and to demonstrate that assembly instructions are controlled and audited\. Where possible\, request joint resistance and thermal cycling test data\, since a busbar that passes a static resistance test can still degrade under repeated thermal cycling in the field\.

Supplier selection in 2026 should combine commercial and technical due diligence\. Look for manufacturers with in\-house stamping\, bending and plating\, because outsourced plating is one of the most common sources of quality escapes\. ISO 9001 is the minimum\; IATF 16949 certification signals automotive\-grade process discipline that transfers well to energy storage\. Ask for first\-article inspection reports\, CMM dimensional data\, plating thickness measurements and references from comparable PACK projects\. Where possible\, audit the plating line and the final inspection station in person or by live video\. Established connector and busbar specialists\, as well as tier\-one automotive suppliers expanding into storage\, are worth shortlisting\, but verify capability rather than relying on brand recognition alone\.

Compliance documentation is now a selection criterion\, not an afterthought\. RoHS and REACH declarations should accompany every shipment\, and material traceability should allow a finished busbar to be linked back to a copper mill lot\. At system level\, UL 1973 and IEC 62619 alignment is expected by many European customers\, and IEC 61439 applies where busbars form part of an assembly\. The EU Batteries Regulation is raising expectations for carbon footprint disclosure and supply chain due diligence\, so suppliers who can provide consistent environmental and traceability documentation will be easier to onboard and less likely to create compliance gaps later\.

Logistics and packaging protect both quality and margin\. Copper is a theft target in transit\, and plated surfaces are sensitive to humidity\, so contracts should specify moisture\-barrier packaging\, anti\-oxidation wrapping and shock\-resistant cartons\, along with Incoterms\, insurance and inspection rights\. For European buyers sourcing from Asia\, build in incoming inspection for plating thickness\, dimensions and conductivity on the first lots\, and consider a pre\-shipment inspection for high\-value orders\.

Finally\, plan for maintenance\. Busbar joints should be included in the PACK inspection schedule\, with periodic torque checks and thermal imaging to detect rising resistance before it becomes a failure\. Agree spare parts availability and replacement lead times in the supply contract\, and keep replacement busbars traceable to the original specification\. Teams that treat busbars as engineered\, documented and maintained components rather than commodity hardware will see fewer commissioning delays\, lower field failure rates and a cleaner compliance position as European requirements tighten through 2026 and beyond\.

records.summary: This review article, published in Lubricants (MDPI, 2026), systematically surveys lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids used in coal-mine hydraulic support systems in China. It organizes additives into liquid types (fatty alcohol ether-based, vegetable oil-based, and ionic liquid-based) and nanoparticle types (inorganic nanoparticles and organic–inorganic composite particles), and analyzes molecular structure design strategies, lubrication mechanisms, and performance regulation pathways for each. The authors argue that additive development should move toward multifunctional integration and environmental friendliness to meet the demands of intelligent coal mining and green mine construction. They further propose that improved dilution-water quality and more mature cylinder anticorrosion technology would enable single-component or few-component hydraulic fluids, and call for deeper structure–performance understanding to support engineering application of high-performance, low-dose, degradable green additives. Only the abstract and page metadata were retrieved, so this summary reflects the review's stated scope rather than its detailed findings.

Abstract
Water-based hydraulic fluids serve as the power transmission medium for hydraulic support systems in coal mines, and the performance of their lubricant additives directly affects the stable operation of the supports. This paper provides a systematic review of research progress on lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids in China, focusing on two main categories: liquid and nanoparticle lubricant additives. Liquid lubricant additives are categorized into fatty alcohol ether-based, vegetable oil-based, and ionic liquid-based additives; nanoparticle-based additives include inorganic nanoparticles and organic–inorganic composite particles. This article analyzes the molecular structure design strategies, lubrication mechanisms, and performance regulation pathways of various additives. In response to the demands of intelligent coal mining and green mine construction, it is proposed that the development of lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids should target multifunctional integration and environmental friendliness. Improvements in the quality of the dilution water and the maturity of cylinder anticorrosion technology will create favorable conditions for the development of single-component (or few-component) hydraulic fluids. In the future, research should deepen understanding of the structure–performance relationships of lubricant additives, so as to facilitate the engineering application of high-performance, low-dose, degradable green lubricant additives and provide technical support for intelligent coal mine construction and ecological protection in the Yellow River Basin.

records.body_text:
Published by: Elsevier
Published by
Highlights
- •Frequent material switching incurs production overhead in multi-material AM.
- •Material switching is internalized directly into the structural design phase.
- •Alternating material-stage mapping is introduced to define the fabrication sequence.
- •Overhang, nozzle collision, and length scale constraints ensure printability.
- •Experiments verify less waste and time than conventional layer-by-layer fabrication.
Abstract
Multi-material additive manufacturing (AM) offers considerable design freedom for realizing complex structures with heterogeneous material distributions. However, current multi-material AM processes are hindered by substantial overheads due to frequent material switching, which increases production time and material purging waste. While existing post-processing approaches attempt to mitigate these issues at the process planning stage, they are limited as the geometry is pre-determined. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel stagewise multi-material topology optimization framework that internalizes material switching considerations directly into the structural design phase. Building upon the concept of a pseudo-time field, the proposed method introduces an explicit formulation to define the multi-material fabrication sequence. By mapping the spatial material distribution onto discretized time stages, the framework facilitates continuous deposition, thereby reducing material switches compared to conventional layer-by-layer processes. Furthermore, the framework integrates spatial manufacturing constraints, including overhang angles, nozzle collisions, and minimum length scales, to ensure manufacturability. Numerical examples demonstrate that the proposed method suppresses material switching while satisfying the imposed constraints. Moreover, its extension to multi-axis AM, explicit material switching minimization, and systems with multiple material phases is presented. Finally, experimental fabrication verifies the manufacturing efficiency of the proposed framework, achieving simultaneous reductions in material switching, purging waste, and production time.

Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM) is a layer-by-layer fabrication process that can realize structures with complex geometry and topology, which are difficult to produce using conventional machining techniques [1], [2]. A prominent application is a multi-material structure, in which materials with distinct properties are distributed within a single component [3], [4], [5], [6]. Manufacturing of such structures necessitates multi-material additive manufacturing that deposits multiple materials during a single process. The fabrication of such multi-material structures is being actively explored across various AM technologies, including fused deposition modeling (FDM) and directed energy deposition (DED), primarily through alternating material deposition strategies [7], [8], [9]. This capability provides a high degree of design freedom for developing advanced structures with customized functionalities and superior mechanical performance.
Despite these advantages in geometric flexibility, the practical implementation of multi-material processes faces significant challenges regarding process efficiency due to the mechanics of switching between multiple materials. In typical multi-material systems, a purge operation is required whenever a material needs to be alternated within a single layer, removing residual material within the nozzle and resetting process parameters [10], [11]. These operations not only cause delays in overall production time but also result in unnecessary material waste [12], [13]. Furthermore, the frequent interruption and resumption of material supply induce extrusion instability, which is a primary cause of surface defects and dimensional inaccuracies at the transition zones [14], [15]. Although hardware improvements such as multi-nozzle systems have been introduced, their compatibility with existing equipment is limited [16], [17], [18]. Consequently, minimizing the number of material switches remains a critical challenge to ensuring the productivity and quality of multi-material additive manufacturing.
To date, efforts to mitigate the issues associated with material switching have predominantly focused on process planning stages, such as slicing and path planning, aiming to reduce the purging waste by reordering deposition paths through grouping same-material regions or localizing transition zones [13], [19], [20]. However, these post-processing approaches face a fundamental limitation as they operate under the premise of an already fixed design. Moreover, in the approaches that group same-material layers into batches, the height deposited in a single batch is restricted by potential collisions between the nozzle and the previously deposited neighboring regions, which limits the attainable reduction in tool changes [13]. If the initial geometric design inherently requires highly fragmented material distributions and frequent intersections, process optimization alone cannot effectively reduce the number of material switches without altering the design intent. Therefore, to fundamentally alleviate the burden of material switching, this issue must be addressed directly during the structural design phase rather than being treated solely as a post-processing task in manufacturing [21].
Topology optimization has been actively adopted as a core methodology for determining complex multi-material distributions during the structural design phase [22], [23], [24], [25], [26]. It enables the derivation of optimal material layouts that satisfy given conditions. However, conventional multi-material topology optimization techniques tend to focus primarily on maximizing structural performance [27], [28], [29], [30]. To achieve these theoretical optima, these approaches often create fragmented material layouts, leading to highly scattered or frequently alternating material distributions. This tendency fundamentally disregards the cost of transitioning between material phases. Consequently, these complex layouts significantly increase the required number of material switches during the multi-material manufacturing process, thereby hindering manufacturability and escalating production costs. To ensure manufacturability, various geometric and process considerations [31], [32], [33], [34], such as overhangs [35], [36], [37], [38], [39], build orientations [40], [41], [42], length scales [43], [44], [45], collisions [46], [47], [48], and build volume limits [49], [50], [51], have been widely integrated. However, these considerations act only on the spatial geometry of the design and thus do not explicitly account for the operational overheads arising from material switching during deposition. A similar limitation applies to spatial regularization strategies such as perimeter control [52], which restrict the total interface length of the design and can thereby suppress the fragmentation of the material layout. The number of material switches is nevertheless determined by where the materials coexist along the build orientation and by the order in which they are deposited, which cannot be captured by such spatial regularizations alone. While recent process-aware multi-material formulations have begun to reflect process-specific restrictions, including the dimensional limits on material components and the build volume [53], [54], as well as the interfacial behavior between different materials [55], [56], the deposition sequence and the number of material transitions have yet to be incorporated into the design formulation, and research addressing material switching in multi-material environments thus remains limited.
Recently, space–time topology optimization has been developed to incorporate the fabrication process into the structural design by introducing a pseudo-time field as an additional design variable, enabling the concurrent optimization of the structural layout and the fabrication sequence [57], [58]. Building upon this concept, the fabrication sequence has been designed to account for process-dependent structural conditions, including the self-weight of intermediate structures and deposition-induced material anisotropy [47], [59], [60], to control process-induced thermomechanical effects, such as distortion and residual stresses [61], [62], [63], and to ensure manufacturability in multi-axis and hybrid manufacturing environments through stagewise build orientations, curved-layer slicing, and the scheduling of additive and subtractive operations [46], [64], [65], [66]. Related sequence-aware formulations have also been extended to fiber-reinforced composites, in which curved layers and deposition paths are optimized concurrently with the structural topology [67], [68]. As summarized in Table 1, however, all of these formulations design the fabrication sequence of a single prescribed material system. Consequently, neither the deposition sequence of multiple materials nor the number of material transitions has been treated as a design quantity in existing sequence-aware formulations.
To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel stagewise multi-material topology optimization framework that directly internalizes material switching into the structural design formulation. As conceptually compared in Fig. 1, unlike conventional layer-by-layer approaches that inevitably require frequent material switching to avoid nozzle collisions, the proposed approach proactively optimizes the structural geometry to ensure that the feature angle
θ does not exceed the nozzle angle ᾱ. This spatial consideration prevents interference and creates an environment where continuous deposition is geometrically feasible. To systematically realize and control this continuous printing process, this study employs the pseudo-time field as a design variable during the optimization process to determine the fabrication sequence of alternating multi-material depositions. By doing so, the framework naturally induces the continuous deposition of each material in a single stage wherever possible, thereby effectively tuning and restricting the number of material switches, as depicted in Fig. 2. In this process, an alternating mapping between materials and stages, a stage elimination mechanism, and a differentiable switching measure are newly introduced. Furthermore, essential geometric constraints specific to multi-material processes, including material-dependent overhang limitations, nozzle collision avoidance, and minimum feature sizes, are concurrently integrated into the optimization problem to prevent potential manufacturing defects in advance. As a result, the proposed methodology derives optimized multi-material designs that balance process efficiency and structural performance. Physical fabrication using a multi-material AM system further confirms these benefits, reducing material switching, purging waste, and production time compared to conventional layer-by-layer processes.
This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the fundamental concepts of the proposed stagewise multi-material topology optimization and the sequence-based deposition model. Section 3 details the mathematical formulation of the manufacturing constraints introduced to ensure manufacturability, including overhang angle limitations, collision avoidance, and length scale constraints. Section 4 presents the formulation of the optimization problem and its numerical implementation. Section 5 demonstrates the effectiveness and validity of the proposed framework through various numerical examples. Section 6 experimentally validates the manufacturing efficiency of the proposed framework using a multi-material AM system. Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper and summarizes its primary contributions.

\#\# Published by\: Elsevier

\#\#\# Published by

\#\# Highlights

\- •Frequent material switching incurs production overhead in multi\-material AM\.
\- •Material switching is internalized directly into the structural design phase\.
\- •Alternating material\-stage mapping is introduced to define the fabrication sequence\.
\- •Overhang\, nozzle collision\, and length scale constraints ensure printability\.
\- •Experiments verify less waste and time than conventional layer\-by\-layer fabrication\.

\#\# Abstract

Multi\-material additive manufacturing \(AM\) offers considerable design freedom for realizing complex structures with heterogeneous material distributions\. However\, current multi\-material AM processes are hindered by substantial overheads due to frequent material switching\, which increases production time and material purging waste\. While existing post\-processing approaches attempt to mitigate these issues at the process planning stage\, they are limited as the geometry is pre\-determined\. To address these challenges\, this paper proposes a novel stagewise multi\-material topology optimization framework that internalizes material switching considerations directly into the structural design phase\. Building upon the concept of a pseudo\-time field\, the proposed method introduces an explicit formulation to define the multi\-material fabrication sequence\. By mapping the spatial material distribution onto discretized time stages\, the framework facilitates continuous deposition\, thereby reducing material switches compared to conventional layer\-by\-layer processes\. Furthermore\, the framework integrates spatial manufacturing constraints\, including overhang angles\, nozzle collisions\, and minimum length scales\, to ensure manufacturability\. Numerical examples demonstrate that the proposed method suppresses material switching while satisfying the imposed constraints\. Moreover\, its extension to multi\-axis AM\, explicit material switching minimization\, and systems with multiple material phases is presented\. Finally\, experimental fabrication verifies the manufacturing efficiency of the proposed framework\, achieving simultaneous reductions in material switching\, purging waste\, and production time\.

\#\# Introduction

Additive manufacturing \(AM\) is a layer\-by\-layer fabrication process that can realize structures with complex geometry and topology\, which are difficult to produce using conventional machining techniques \[1\]\, \[2\]\. A prominent application is a multi\-material structure\, in which materials with distinct properties are distributed within a single component \[3\]\, \[4\]\, \[5\]\, \[6\]\. Manufacturing of such structures necessitates multi\-material additive manufacturing that deposits multiple materials during a single process\. The fabrication of such multi\-material structures is being actively explored across various AM technologies\, including fused deposition modeling \(FDM\) and directed energy deposition \(DED\)\, primarily through alternating material deposition strategies \[7\]\, \[8\]\, \[9\]\. This capability provides a high degree of design freedom for developing advanced structures with customized functionalities and superior mechanical performance\.

Despite these advantages in geometric flexibility\, the practical implementation of multi\-material processes faces significant challenges regarding process efficiency due to the mechanics of switching between multiple materials\. In typical multi\-material systems\, a purge operation is required whenever a material needs to be alternated within a single layer\, removing residual material within the nozzle and resetting process parameters \[10\]\, \[11\]\. These operations not only cause delays in overall production time but also result in unnecessary material waste \[12\]\, \[13\]\. Furthermore\, the frequent interruption and resumption of material supply induce extrusion instability\, which is a primary cause of surface defects and dimensional inaccuracies at the transition zones \[14\]\, \[15\]\. Although hardware improvements such as multi\-nozzle systems have been introduced\, their compatibility with existing equipment is limited \[16\]\, \[17\]\, \[18\]\. Consequently\, minimizing the number of material switches remains a critical challenge to ensuring the productivity and quality of multi\-material additive manufacturing\.

To date\, efforts to mitigate the issues associated with material switching have predominantly focused on process planning stages\, such as slicing and path planning\, aiming to reduce the purging waste by reordering deposition paths through grouping same\-material regions or localizing transition zones \[13\]\, \[19\]\, \[20\]\. However\, these post\-processing approaches face a fundamental limitation as they operate under the premise of an already fixed design\. Moreover\, in the approaches that group same\-material layers into batches\, the height deposited in a single batch is restricted by potential collisions between the nozzle and the previously deposited neighboring regions\, which limits the attainable reduction in tool changes \[13\]\. If the initial geometric design inherently requires highly fragmented material distributions and frequent intersections\, process optimization alone cannot effectively reduce the number of material switches without altering the design intent\. Therefore\, to fundamentally alleviate the burden of material switching\, this issue must be addressed directly during the structural design phase rather than being treated solely as a post\-processing task in manufacturing \[21\]\.

Topology optimization has been actively adopted as a core methodology for determining complex multi\-material distributions during the structural design phase \[22\]\, \[23\]\, \[24\]\, \[25\]\, \[26\]\. It enables the derivation of optimal material layouts that satisfy given conditions\. However\, conventional multi\-material topology optimization techniques tend to focus primarily on maximizing structural performance \[27\]\, \[28\]\, \[29\]\, \[30\]\. To achieve these theoretical optima\, these approaches often create fragmented material layouts\, leading to highly scattered or frequently alternating material distributions\. This tendency fundamentally disregards the cost of transitioning between material phases\. Consequently\, these complex layouts significantly increase the required number of material switches during the multi\-material manufacturing process\, thereby hindering manufacturability and escalating production costs\. To ensure manufacturability\, various geometric and process considerations \[31\]\, \[32\]\, \[33\]\, \[34\]\, such as overhangs \[35\]\, \[36\]\, \[37\]\, \[38\]\, \[39\]\, build orientations \[40\]\, \[41\]\, \[42\]\, length scales \[43\]\, \[44\]\, \[45\]\, collisions \[46\]\, \[47\]\, \[48\]\, and build volume limits \[49\]\, \[50\]\, \[51\]\, have been widely integrated\. However\, these considerations act only on the spatial geometry of the design and thus do not explicitly account for the operational overheads arising from material switching during deposition\. A similar limitation applies to spatial regularization strategies such as perimeter control \[52\]\, which restrict the total interface length of the design and can thereby suppress the fragmentation of the material layout\. The number of material switches is nevertheless determined by where the materials coexist along the build orientation and by the order in which they are deposited\, which cannot be captured by such spatial regularizations alone\. While recent process\-aware multi\-material formulations have begun to reflect process\-specific restrictions\, including the dimensional limits on material components and the build volume \[53\]\, \[54\]\, as well as the interfacial behavior between different materials \[55\]\, \[56\]\, the deposition sequence and the number of material transitions have yet to be incorporated into the design formulation\, and research addressing material switching in multi\-material environments thus remains limited\.

Recently\, space–time topology optimization has been developed to incorporate the fabrication process into the structural design by introducing a pseudo\-time field as an additional design variable\, enabling the concurrent optimization of the structural layout and the fabrication sequence \[57\]\, \[58\]\. Building upon this concept\, the fabrication sequence has been designed to account for process\-dependent structural conditions\, including the self\-weight of intermediate structures and deposition\-induced material anisotropy \[47\]\, \[59\]\, \[60\]\, to control process\-induced thermomechanical effects\, such as distortion and residual stresses \[61\]\, \[62\]\, \[63\]\, and to ensure manufacturability in multi\-axis and hybrid manufacturing environments through stagewise build orientations\, curved\-layer slicing\, and the scheduling of additive and subtractive operations \[46\]\, \[64\]\, \[65\]\, \[66\]\. Related sequence\-aware formulations have also been extended to fiber\-reinforced composites\, in which curved layers and deposition paths are optimized concurrently with the structural topology \[67\]\, \[68\]\. As summarized in Table 1\, however\, all of these formulations design the fabrication sequence of a single prescribed material system\. Consequently\, neither the deposition sequence of multiple materials nor the number of material transitions has been treated as a design quantity in existing sequence\-aware formulations\.

To address these limitations\, this paper proposes a novel stagewise multi\-material topology optimization framework that directly internalizes material switching into the structural design formulation\. As conceptually compared in Fig\. 1\, unlike conventional layer\-by\-layer approaches that inevitably require frequent material switching to avoid nozzle collisions\, the proposed approach proactively optimizes the structural geometry to ensure that the feature angle
θ does not exceed the nozzle angle ᾱ\. This spatial consideration prevents interference and creates an environment where continuous deposition is geometrically feasible\. To systematically realize and control this continuous printing process\, this study employs the pseudo\-time field as a design variable during the optimization process to determine the fabrication sequence of alternating multi\-material depositions\. By doing so\, the framework naturally induces the continuous deposition of each material in a single stage wherever possible\, thereby effectively tuning and restricting the number of material switches\, as depicted in Fig\. 2\. In this process\, an alternating mapping between materials and stages\, a stage elimination mechanism\, and a differentiable switching measure are newly introduced\. Furthermore\, essential geometric constraints specific to multi\-material processes\, including material\-dependent overhang limitations\, nozzle collision avoidance\, and minimum feature sizes\, are concurrently integrated into the optimization problem to prevent potential manufacturing defects in advance\. As a result\, the proposed methodology derives optimized multi\-material designs that balance process efficiency and structural performance\. Physical fabrication using a multi\-material AM system further confirms these benefits\, reducing material switching\, purging waste\, and production time compared to conventional layer\-by\-layer processes\.
This paper is organized as follows\. Section 2 introduces the fundamental concepts of the proposed stagewise multi\-material topology optimization and the sequence\-based deposition model\. Section 3 details the mathematical formulation of the manufacturing constraints introduced to ensure manufacturability\, including overhang angle limitations\, collision avoidance\, and length scale constraints\. Section 4 presents the formulation of the optimization problem and its numerical implementation\. Section 5 demonstrates the effectiveness and validity of the proposed framework through various numerical examples\. Section 6 experimentally validates the manufacturing efficiency of the proposed framework using a multi\-material AM system\. Finally\, Section 7 concludes the paper and summarizes its primary contributions\.

records.summary: This Han's Laser knowledge-page article describes an integrated laser cleaning and welding gantry system intended for copper busbars in EV battery packs, electronic control units, power distribution units, and battery module connections. The article frames the problem as copper's surface contamination (oxide layers, oil residues, paint, insulating coatings) plus its high thermal conductivity and infrared reflectivity, which complicate stable weld formation. The proposed mechanism is a single gantry platform combining a laser cleaning unit and a laser welding unit, with dual left-right workstations, real-time laser distance measurement at each station, and automated welding data recording for traceability. The source is a vendor product description and does not report measured weld quality, conductivity, throughput, or comparative performance data.

Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding System for Automotive Busbars
Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding System for Automotive Busbars
- October 16, 2026
Copper busbars are essential components in electric vehicle (EV) power distribution systems and electronic control units. They carry high currents between batteries, power electronics, and electrical connections. Consistent weld quality is critical to electrical conductivity, connection reliability, and overall system safety.
However, laser welding copper presents two major challenges: surface contamination and the material’s high thermal conductivity and reflectivity at infrared wavelengths. Oxide layers, oil residues, paint, and insulating coatings can interfere with laser energy absorption and weld formation. Copper also dissipates heat rapidly, making stable energy input and precise positioning essential.
Han’s Laser Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding Gantry System for Automotive Busbars combines surface cleaning and laser welding in one machine. By integrating both processes with dual workstations, laser distance measurement, and welding data tracking, the system helps streamline production and improve process consistency.
Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding
The system combines a laser cleaning unit and a laser welding unit on a single gantry platform. The left-right dual-station configuration allows cleaning and welding operations to be organized in alternating or coordinated production cycles, depending on the application.

records.body_text:
Combined Environmental Reliability Testing for EV Busbars: Temperature, Humidity, and 3-Axis Random Vibration
Oct 17, 2026 View: 112
EV battery-pack busbars cannot be qualified reliably through temperature, humidity, or vibration tests performed in isolation. A combined environmental profile exposes the actual interaction between thermal expansion, moisture, mechanical preload loss, fretting at bolted interfaces, and insulation stress, allowing failure mechanisms to be identified before vehicle-level durability testing.
For high-voltage battery applications, Apollo evaluates busbar assemblies under customer-defined combined profiles that can include -40°C to 125°C temperature cycling, up to 95% RH, and 3-axis random vibration, with vibration methodology referenced to ISO 16750-3 where applicable. Electrical resistance, fastening integrity, insulation condition, and post-test dimensional characteristics are correlated with the environmental load history.
-40°C to 125°C Thermal Cycling and 95% RH: Why Single-Factor Testing Misses Busbar Failures
Thermal Expansion at ΔT = 165°C: Copper, Aluminum, Insulation, and Fasteners
A busbar assembly contains materials with different coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE).
A temperature range from -40°C to 125°C produces a thermal span of 165°C. Copper, aluminum, polymer insulation, stainless-steel fasteners, and plated interfaces respond differently to this temperature change.
This differential expansion can generate:
Bolt preload variation
Contact-interface shear
Localized bending stress
Insulation movement
Cracking around formed sections
Fretting at bolted joints
A busbar that passes a static resistance test at 23°C may therefore show a different resistance profile after repeated thermal cycling.
95% RH and Condensation: Corrosion and Interface Degradation
High relative humidity creates an additional mechanism at exposed interfaces.
Potential failure locations include:
Plated copper terminals
Bolt and washer interfaces
Exposed conductor edges
Insulation defects
Crimped or welded transition areas
Moisture combined with temperature variation can accelerate surface oxidation and corrosion products. At a bolted electrical interface, even a small increase in contact resistance becomes significant at hundreds of amperes because
That 16 W is generated locally at the connection rather than distributed along the entire busbar.
ISO 16750-3 Vibration and Environmental Interaction: Mechanical Loading
ISO 16750-3 addresses mechanical loads for road vehicles and provides vibration-test approaches according to component location and vehicle application.
For an EV battery-pack busbar, the relevant mechanical environment may contain:
Broadband random vibration
Multiple vibration axes
Road-induced shocks
Resonance amplification
Fastener excitation
Local bending of flexible sections
The test profile must be established from the vehicle location, mounting structure, mass, and customer durability specification rather than assigning one universal vibration spectrum to every battery busbar.
3-Axis Random Vibration and 165°C Thermal Span: Combined Test Architecture
Three-Axis Excitation at X/Y/Z: Replicating Battery-Pack Mechanical Loads
A production busbar assembly should be mounted using the same:
Fasteners
Torque specification
Insulation components
Support brackets
Connector interfaces
Mounting points
used in the vehicle or battery-pack configuration.
The three principal directions are normally evaluated as:
Axis | Typical Mechanical Concern | Busbar Failure Mechanism
---|---|---
X-axis | Longitudinal excitation | Terminal/interface shear
Y-axis | Lateral excitation | Fastener loosening and bending
Z-axis | Vertical excitation | Support fatigue and resonance
Combined sequence | Multi-directional loading | Interaction of thermal and mechanical stresses
The objective is not simply to demonstrate that the copper conductor survives vibration. The complete assembly must maintain electrical and mechanical functionality.
Random Vibration PSD at Vehicle-Specific Frequencies: Resonance Control
Random vibration is normally defined using a power spectral density (PSD) profile in:
The highest mechanical stress may occur near a natural frequency rather than at the highest nominal acceleration.
For this reason, engineering validation should identify:
Natural frequency
Resonance frequency
Damping ratio
Mode shape
Acceleration response
Relative displacement between mounting points
A busbar with a long unsupported copper span can exhibit significantly higher dynamic displacement than a short rigid conductor.
Thermal-Vibration Interaction at -40°C and 125°C: Structural Resonance Shift
Temperature changes can alter polymer modulus, copper stress state, insulation flexibility, and joint stiffness.
At low temperature:
Polymer insulation may become less compliant
Flexible support elements can stiffen
Thermal contraction increases interface displacement
At high temperature:
Polymer modulus can decrease
Insulation may soften
Fastener preload can change
Differential thermal expansion increases
The vibration test should therefore include temperature states representative of the intended vehicle environment rather than relying exclusively on room-temperature vibration.
Fastener Preload at 400–800V and mΩ Resistance: Monitoring Bolted Busbar Interfaces
Belleville Washer Preload at High Vibration: Preventing Joint Loosening
Bolted busbar connections depend on stable clamping force.
A typical joint consists of:
Bolt → Belleville washer → terminal → busbar → mating terminal → nut
The preload creates the normal force required to maintain a low-resistance electrical interface.
A Belleville washer can provide controlled elastic displacement as the joint stack-up changes through thermal expansion and vibration.
Compared with a rigid flat washer, the spring characteristic of a Belleville washer can provide greater compensation for small changes in joint compression.
Preload Loss After 3-Axis Vibration: Torque Is Not Enough
Initial bolt torque does not prove long-term joint integrity.
Torque is an indirect indicator of preload because friction at the thread and bearing surface consumes a large portion of applied torque.
For reliability validation, Apollo can correlate:
Initial tightening torque
Initial bolt preload
Thermal cycling
Vibration exposure
Final preload
Contact resistance
Interface wear
A useful engineering acceptance criterion is therefore based on measured preload retention and electrical resistance, not torque alone.
Fretting Wear at <1 mΩ Interfaces: Resistance Growth Detection
Microscopic relative movement between two contacting surfaces can cause fretting.
The process may generate:
Removal of plating
Oxide formation
Metallic debris
Reduced real contact area
Increased contact resistance
Localized Joule heating
The failure can develop gradually, making continuous or periodic four-wire resistance measurement more informative than visual inspection alone.
For high-current EV busbars, resistance changes should be tracked against:
Cycle count
Temperature
Vibration axis
RMS acceleration
Joint preload
Interface condition
Flexible Copper Foil and Braided Transition Sections: Reducing Resonance-Induced Shear Stress
Multi-Layer Copper Foil at High Flexibility: Strain Distribution
Rigid copper busbars are efficient for short, fixed-distance connections but can transmit mechanical displacement directly between mounting points.
A flexible transition section changes the mechanical load path.
Common structures include:
Multi-layer copper foil
Laminated copper foil
Copper braided conductor
Stamped flexible links
Braided copper expansion connectors
The flexible section absorbs relative displacement between battery modules, busbar terminals, and structural supports.
Flexible Braided Copper at 100% IACS-Class Conductivity: Electrical and Mechanical Trade-Off
Electrical conductivity and mechanical flexibility must be evaluated together.
Structure | Electrical Path | Flexibility | Vibration Accommodation | Typical Use
---|---|---|---|---
Rigid C1100 copper bar | Low resistance | Low | Low | Fixed connection
Multi-layer copper foil | Low resistance | High | High | Battery interconnect
Braided copper conductor | Low resistance | Very high | Very high | Expansion/vibration transition
Laminated busbar | Low inductance potential | Medium | Medium | Power electronics
Flexible stamped copper link | Low resistance | Medium–High | High | Compact battery modules
High-purity copper such as C1100 can provide conductivity approaching 100% IACS, depending on material condition and specification.
Stray Inductance <10nH: Flexible Geometry in High-Speed Power Switching
For high-current switching systems, mechanical flexibility does not remove electrical design requirements.
A laminated or closely coupled conductor geometry can reduce loop area and associated parasitic inductance.
Even a small inductance becomes relevant when (di/dt) is high.
Therefore, flexible sections used around inverter or battery switching structures should be evaluated for both:
Mechanical strain relief
Electrical loop geometry
The final geometry depends on current rating, switching frequency, insulation system, mounting envelope, and customer electromagnetic compatibility requirements.
Insulation Sleeve at 125°C and Dielectric Strength >15kV/mm: Detecting Environmental Cracking
Thermal Stress at -40°C to 125°C: Polymer Insulation Failure Points
Busbar insulation can fail even when the copper conductor remains electrically functional.
High-risk locations include:
Sharp stamped edges
Formed corners
Bolt holes
Terminal transitions
Molded supports
Areas under mechanical compression
Repeated thermal expansion and contraction can produce tensile strain in the polymer.
At the same time, random vibration can create cyclic bending around the same location.
The combined mechanism is more severe than either load alone.
UL 94 V-0 Insulation and High-Voltage Dielectric Testing
For EV battery applications, insulation material selection may involve:
Operating temperature rating
Dielectric strength
Flame resistance
Chemical resistance
Tracking resistance
Environmental aging
Where specified by the material system, UL 94 V-0 can be used as a flammability classification.
A dielectric strength specification such as >15 kV/mm must be treated as a material or system-specific requirement and verified under the applicable test method.
The test program should also examine insulation after environmental exposure for:
Cracks
Pinholes
Delamination
Edge lifting
Abrasion
Carbonized areas
Post-Test Insulation Resistance at 400–800V: Electrical Safety Verification
Environmental testing should be followed by electrical inspection.
Depending on the customer's validation specification, measurements can include:
Insulation resistance
Dielectric withstand
Leakage current
Hi-pot test
Visual insulation inspection
Continuity testing
The electrical acceptance limits should be established from the vehicle architecture and applicable safety standard.
CMM Inspection at ±0.01mm and Resistance Mapping: Pre-Test and Post-Test Correlation
CMM Measurement at ±0.01mm: Detecting Permanent Deformation
Environmental testing should not end with a pass/fail electrical result.
A busbar may retain electrical continuity while experiencing permanent mechanical deformation.
CMM inspection can measure:
Terminal position
Hole-to-hole distance
Flatness
Bend angle
Mounting height
Flexible-section geometry
Connector alignment
Pre-test and post-test measurements are compared to identify permanent dimensional drift.
Four-Wire Resistance at mΩ Resolution: Mapping Joint Degradation
A four-wire Kelvin measurement separates voltage-sensing leads from current-carrying leads, reducing measurement error caused by lead resistance.
For busbar qualification, resistance should be recorded:
Before test → during defined intervals → after test
This creates a resistance-versus-cycle profile.
A resistance increase should then be correlated with:
Fastener preload loss
Fretting marks
Oxidation
Plating wear
Copper deformation
Thermal exposure
Cross-Section Analysis and Microscopy: Identifying Fretting and Fatigue
When resistance increases after vibration, destructive analysis can locate the failure mechanism.
Typical analysis includes:
Optical microscopy
Metallographic cross-section
SEM where required
Plating thickness measurement
Surface morphology analysis
Joint fracture analysis
The objective is to distinguish between electrical interface degradation and bulk conductor fatigue.
ISO 16750-3 Vibration and EV Battery Validation: From Component Test to Vehicle Durability
Battery-Pack Mounting at -40°C to 125°C: Test Fixture Fidelity
A test fixture must reproduce the mechanical boundary conditions of the production installation.
Fixture design should account for:
Mounting-point stiffness
Fastener type
Torque
Support spacing
Cable routing
Busbar mass
Connector constraints
An overly rigid fixture can suppress real vibration modes. An overly flexible fixture can introduce artificial resonance.
Therefore, fixture modal behavior should be checked before interpreting component test data.
Combined Environmental Test Matrix: Temperature × Humidity × Vibration
A structured validation matrix may be organized as follows:
Test Stage | Temperature | Humidity | Vibration | Primary Measurement
---|---|---|---|---
Baseline | 23°C | Ambient | None | Resistance + dimensions
Low-temperature exposure | -40°C | Defined by profile | Defined PSD | Resistance + function
High-temperature exposure | 125°C | Defined by profile | Defined PSD | Resistance + insulation
High-RH exposure | Defined by profile | Up to 95% RH | Defined PSD | Corrosion + insulation
Combined profile | -40°C to 125°C | Up to 95% RH | X/Y/Z random | Full electrical/mechanical data
Post-test | 23°C | Ambient | None | CMM + resistance + visual
Not every program requires simultaneous maximum temperature, maximum humidity, and maximum vibration. The test matrix should reflect the vehicle duty cycle and customer specification.
Failure Mode Analysis at IATF 16949: PFMEA-Driven Reliability Testing
Environmental reliability testing becomes more useful when each test condition is linked to a predefined failure mode.
For an automotive busbar program, PFMEA can identify:
Joint loosening
Fretting corrosion
Conductor fatigue
Insulation cracking
Plating degradation
Terminal deformation
Resistance increase
Dielectric failure
The Control Plan can then define the corresponding production controls and inspection frequencies.
This creates a closed engineering loop:
Design → FEA → Prototype → Environmental Test → Failure Analysis → DFM → Tooling → SPC → PPAP Level 3 → Mass Production
Apollo EV Busbar Reliability Engineering: C1100 Copper, Flexible Links, and PPAP Level 3
C1100 Copper at High Conductivity: Material and Forming Control
Apollo's EV busbar manufacturing process can incorporate precision copper stamping, bending, forming, surface treatment, insulation, and flexible transition structures according to the customer's drawing and electrical specification.
Typical engineering inputs include:
C1100/C10200 copper grades
Copper thickness
Plating specification
Bend radius
Hole diameter
Mounting pitch
Insulation requirement
Current rating
Temperature rise limit
Precision Stamping at ±0.01mm: Geometry and Assembly Fit
Critical busbar dimensions can be monitored using:
CMM inspection
Optical measurement
Go/no-go gauges
Flatness measurement
Burr inspection
SPC
Dimensional tolerances should be assigned according to functional requirements rather than applying ±0.01mm indiscriminately to every feature.
PPAP Level 3 and IATF 16949: Production Validation Documentation
For automotive programs, Apollo can structure project quality documentation around customer PPAP requirements, including:
Process Flow Diagram
PFMEA
Control Plan
Dimensional Inspection Report
Material Certification
MSA documentation
SPC data
Capability studies
Functional test results
Sample submission records
The final submission level and specific documents remain subject to the customer's purchasing and quality requirements.
FAQ
What temperature range should an EV busbar environmental reliability test use?
A customer-defined profile may include -40°C to 125°C for EV battery applications. The actual temperature limits, dwell time, transition rate, and number of cycles should be based on the battery-pack location and vehicle validation specification.
How is EV busbar random vibration testing performed?
The busbar assembly is mounted in its production configuration and exposed to vehicle-specific vibration profiles, commonly including X/Y/Z excitation. ISO 16750-3 can provide the mechanical test framework, while the customer defines the applicable PSD and duration.
How can Apollo detect busbar failure after combined thermal and vibration testing?
Apollo can compare pre- and post-test CMM dimensions, four-wire resistance, fastener preload, insulation condition, and interface wear. Metallographic analysis can then identify fretting, fatigue, corrosion, or joint degradation.

Acceleration response

Relative displacement between mounting points

A busbar with a long unsupported copper span can exhibit significantly higher dynamic displacement than a short rigid conductor\.

Thermal\-Vibration Interaction at \-40°C and 125°C\: Structural Resonance Shift

Temperature changes can alter polymer modulus\, copper stress state\, insulation flexibility\, and joint stiffness\.

At low temperature\:

Polymer insulation may become less compliant

Flexible support elements can stiffen

Thermal contraction increases interface displacement

At high temperature\:

Polymer modulus can decrease

Insulation may soften

Fastener preload can change

Differential thermal expansion increases

The vibration test should therefore include temperature states representative of the intended vehicle environment rather than relying exclusively on room\-temperature vibration\.

\#\# Fastener Preload at 400–800V and mΩ Resistance\: Monitoring Bolted Busbar Interfaces

Bolted busbar connections depend on stable clamping force\.

A typical joint consists of\:

Bolt → Belleville washer → terminal → busbar → mating terminal → nut

The preload creates the normal force required to maintain a low\-resistance electrical interface\.

A Belleville washer can provide controlled elastic displacement as the joint stack\-up changes through thermal expansion and vibration\.

Compared with a rigid flat washer\, the spring characteristic of a Belleville washer can provide greater compensation for small changes in joint compression\.

Preload Loss After 3\-Axis Vibration\: Torque Is Not Enough

Initial bolt torque does not prove long\-term joint integrity\.

Torque is an indirect indicator of preload because friction at the thread and bearing surface consumes a large portion of applied torque\.

For reliability validation\, Apollo can correlate\:

Initial tightening torque

Initial bolt preload

Thermal cycling

Vibration exposure

Final preload

Contact resistance

Interface wear

A useful engineering acceptance criterion is therefore based on measured preload retention and electrical resistance\, not torque alone\.

Fretting Wear at \<1 mΩ Interfaces\: Resistance Growth Detection

Microscopic relative movement between two contacting surfaces can cause fretting\.

The process may generate\:

Removal of plating

Oxide formation

Metallic debris

Reduced real contact area

Increased contact resistance

Localized Joule heating

The failure can develop gradually\, making continuous or periodic four\-wire resistance measurement more informative than visual inspection alone\.

Cycle count

Temperature

Vibration axis

RMS acceleration

Joint preload

Interface condition

Multi\-Layer Copper Foil at High Flexibility\: Strain Distribution

Rigid copper busbars are efficient for short\, fixed\-distance connections but can transmit mechanical displacement directly between mounting points\.

A flexible transition section changes the mechanical load path\.

Common structures include\:

Multi\-layer copper foil

Laminated copper foil

Copper braided conductor

Stamped flexible links

Braided copper expansion connectors

The flexible section absorbs relative displacement between battery modules\, busbar terminals\, and structural supports\.

Electrical conductivity and mechanical flexibility must be evaluated together\.

Structure \| Electrical Path \| Flexibility \| Vibration Accommodation \| Typical Use 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Rigid C1100 copper bar \| Low resistance \| Low \| Low \| Fixed connection 
Multi\-layer copper foil \| Low resistance \| High \| High \| Battery interconnect 
Braided copper conductor \| Low resistance \| Very high \| Very high \| Expansion\/vibration transition 
Laminated busbar \| Low inductance potential \| Medium \| Medium \| Power electronics 
Flexible stamped copper link \| Low resistance \| Medium–High \| High \| Compact battery modules 

High\-purity copper such as C1100 can provide conductivity approaching 100\% IACS\, depending on material condition and specification\.

Stray Inductance \<10nH\: Flexible Geometry in High\-Speed Power Switching

For high\-current switching systems\, mechanical flexibility does not remove electrical design requirements\.

A laminated or closely coupled conductor geometry can reduce loop area and associated parasitic inductance\.

Even a small inductance becomes relevant when \(di\/dt\) is high\.

Therefore\, flexible sections used around inverter or battery switching structures should be evaluated for both\:

Mechanical strain relief

Electrical loop geometry

The final geometry depends on current rating\, switching frequency\, insulation system\, mounting envelope\, and customer electromagnetic compatibility requirements\.

Thermal Stress at \-40°C to 125°C\: Polymer Insulation Failure Points

Busbar insulation can fail even when the copper conductor remains electrically functional\.

High\-risk locations include\:

Sharp stamped edges

Formed corners

Bolt holes

Terminal transitions

Molded supports

Areas under mechanical compression

Repeated thermal expansion and contraction can produce tensile strain in the polymer\.

At the same time\, random vibration can create cyclic bending around the same location\.

The combined mechanism is more severe than either load alone\.

UL 94 V\-0 Insulation and High\-Voltage Dielectric Testing

For EV battery applications\, insulation material selection may involve\:

Operating temperature rating

Dielectric strength

Flame resistance

Chemical resistance

Tracking resistance

Environmental aging

Where specified by the material system\, UL 94 V\-0 can be used as a flammability classification\.

A dielectric strength specification such as \>15 kV\/mm must be treated as a material or system\-specific requirement and verified under the applicable test method\.

The test program should also examine insulation after environmental exposure for\:

Cracks

Pinholes

Delamination

Edge lifting

Abrasion

Carbonized areas

Post\-Test Insulation Resistance at 400–800V\: Electrical Safety Verification

Environmental testing should be followed by electrical inspection\.

Depending on the customer\'s validation specification\, measurements can include\:

Insulation resistance

Dielectric withstand

Leakage current

Hi\-pot test

Visual insulation inspection

Continuity testing

The electrical acceptance limits should be established from the vehicle architecture and applicable safety standard\.

\#\# CMM Inspection at ±0\.01mm and Resistance Mapping\: Pre\-Test and Post\-Test Correlation

CMM Measurement at ±0\.01mm\: Detecting Permanent Deformation

Environmental testing should not end with a pass\/fail electrical result\.

A busbar may retain electrical continuity while experiencing permanent mechanical deformation\.

CMM inspection can measure\:

Terminal position

Hole\-to\-hole distance

Flatness

Bend angle

Mounting height

Flexible\-section geometry

Connector alignment

Pre\-test and post\-test measurements are compared to identify permanent dimensional drift\.

Four\-Wire Resistance at mΩ Resolution\: Mapping Joint Degradation

A four\-wire Kelvin measurement separates voltage\-sensing leads from current\-carrying leads\, reducing measurement error caused by lead resistance\.

For busbar qualification\, resistance should be recorded\:

Before test → during defined intervals → after test

This creates a resistance\-versus\-cycle profile\.

A resistance increase should then be correlated with\:

Fastener preload loss

Fretting marks

Oxidation

Plating wear

Copper deformation

Thermal exposure

Cross\-Section Analysis and Microscopy\: Identifying Fretting and Fatigue

When resistance increases after vibration\, destructive analysis can locate the failure mechanism\.

Typical analysis includes\:

Optical microscopy

Metallographic cross\-section

SEM where required

Plating thickness measurement

Surface morphology analysis

Joint fracture analysis

The objective is to distinguish between electrical interface degradation and bulk conductor fatigue\.

\#\# ISO 16750\-3 Vibration and EV Battery Validation\: From Component Test to Vehicle Durability

Battery\-Pack Mounting at \-40°C to 125°C\: Test Fixture Fidelity

A test fixture must reproduce the mechanical boundary conditions of the production installation\.

Fixture design should account for\:

Mounting\-point stiffness

Fastener type

Torque

Support spacing

Cable routing

Busbar mass

Connector constraints

An overly rigid fixture can suppress real vibration modes\. An overly flexible fixture can introduce artificial resonance\.

Therefore\, fixture modal behavior should be checked before interpreting component test data\.

Combined Environmental Test Matrix\: Temperature × Humidity × Vibration

A structured validation matrix may be organized as follows\:

Test Stage \| Temperature \| Humidity \| Vibration \| Primary Measurement 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Baseline \| 23°C \| Ambient \| None \| Resistance \+ dimensions 
Low\-temperature exposure \| \-40°C \| Defined by profile \| Defined PSD \| Resistance \+ function

Conductor fatigue

Insulation cracking

Plating degradation

Terminal deformation

Resistance increase

Dielectric failure

The Control Plan can then define the corresponding production controls and inspection frequencies\.

Design → FEA → Prototype → Environmental Test → Failure Analysis → DFM → Tooling → SPC → PPAP Level 3 → Mass Production

The team built a dedicated rig delivering supercritical CO2 (100 bar, 40 °C, 0.185 kg/min) with lubricant injected at 1 and 4 mL/min through a 0.25 mm nozzle, and ran pin-on-cylinder friction tests on a CNC lathe against Ti6Al4V at 20 and 100 m/min and 100–400 N. records.body_text:
Supercritical CO2 and kitchen-shelf lubricants could transform titanium machining
When carbon dioxide is squeezed past 74 bar and warmed above 31 degrees Celsius, it stops behaving like an ordinary gas or liquid and enters a strange middle state known as the supercritical phase. A team of French researchers at the Arts et Métiers Institute of Technology has now harnessed this exotic fluid to attack one of manufacturing’s most stubborn problems: the friction and heat that plague the machining of Ti6Al4V, the titanium alloy that holds together much of the aerospace industry. Their findings, published in Frontiers in Manufacturing Technology, suggest that cheap, sustainable additives dissolved in supercritical CO2 could rival industrial mineral oils, with ionic liquids delivering the most dramatic friction reductions of all.
The machining industry has long relied on flood coolants, minimum quantity lubrication, and cryogenic sprays such as liquid nitrogen to keep cutting tools alive and machined parts intact. These methods aim to tame the intense friction and heating that occur at the chip-tool and tool-part contact zones, where temperatures can soar high enough to soften the workpiece and destroy the tool edge. Supercritical CO2 has emerged as an intriguing alternative because it acts as a green solvent and, when delivered to the cutting zone, expands with a phase transformation that drops its temperature sharply, cooling both the tool and the part. Previous studies have shown that pairing supercritical CO2 with dissolved soybean oil roughly halved flank wear compared with emulsion flood cooling when milling compacted graphite iron, and that supercritical CO2 plus minimum quantity lubrication outperformed flood coolant in milling Ti6Al4V and turning AISI 1045 steel.
Yet supercritical CO2 alone often performs worse than flood cooling, which is why the lubricant carried within it matters so much. The research team, led by Koffi Samuel Koulekpa, set out to systematically test what happens when different lubricants are introduced into supercritical CO2 and delivered to a titanium-carbide contact under conditions mimicking real machining. They selected ionic liquids, vegetable oils, mineral oil, water, and polyethylene glycol, chosen for their solubility in supercritical CO2, their sustainable character, or their previous performances in machining-related friction analysis. The two ionic liquids tested, BMIM-PF6 and BMIM-BF4, are salts that stay liquid at room temperature and boast negligible volatility, high thermal stability, and non-flammability, making them fascinating candidates for machining applications.
Order Lab Supplies
To deliver these exotic mixtures, the researchers designed and built a dedicated machine that feeds CO2 from pressurized bottles, cools it to ensure a liquid phase before compression, then squeezes it to pressures up to 350 bar and heats it with four cartridges to reach the supercritical state in a mixing chamber. There, lubricants are injected at user-specified rates before the mixture sprays through a 0.25 mm round jet nozzle. For the experiments, the pressure was limited to 100 bar and the temperature set to 40 degrees Celsius, guaranteeing a supercritical state while minimizing CO2 consumption. The supercritical CO2 flowed at 0.185 kg/min, while lubricants were delivered at 1 mL/min and 4 mL/min, rates common in minimum quantity lubrication applications.
Shop Motor Oils
The friction tests themselves took place on a CNC lathe fitted with a Hedenqvist-type pin-on-cylinder tribometer, a setup chosen for easy and quick execution. Cylindrical carbide pins, instrumented with K-type thermocouples connected to a data acquisition system sampling at 2 kHz, pressed against a rotating Ti6Al4V bar with an initial diameter of 120 mm. The normal loads of 100 N, 250 N, and 400 N were selected based on a contact pressure of 1,300 MPa derived from finite element simulations, while sliding velocities of 20 m/min and 100 m/min covered the range of chip sliding velocities typical when machining difficult-to-cut alloys such as Ti6Al4V or Inconel 718. After each test, the workpiece surface was refreshed by a fresh machining pass to obtain a theoretical roughness of Ra 0.5 µm, and the pins were rotated by 25 degrees to expose a new contact surface.
The results revealed a striking pattern. At 20 m/min, adding lubricants to supercritical CO2 decreased friction, but the mixtures never outperformed the dry condition, with friction coefficients staying above the dry baseline for almost all loads. At 100 m/min, however, the story changed dramatically. The team observed a mean decrease of 0.1 in the apparent friction coefficient, and increasing the lubricant flow rate from 1 mL/min to 4 mL/min produced further reductions. The ionic liquids showed their lubricating prowess most clearly at 100 m/min with significant friction decreases at 4 mL/min and 400 N, demonstrating that the combined effect of lubrication by the additives and cooling from supercritical CO2 works best under the most demanding conditions.
The adhesive behavior of Ti6Al4V, notorious for sticking to counter-materials during friction, provided another revealing metric. After each test, the researchers examined the friction zone under an optical microscope and calculated the sticking area by assimilating it to an ellipse. Once again, the effects of the lubricants were clearly visible at 100 m/min. The ionic liquids, together with polyethylene glycol, led to the lowest sticking area values, with surface reductions of 54 percent and 55 percent for BF4 and PF6 respectively at the 1 mL/min rate. These values climbed to 74 percent at 4 mL/min, showing how strongly the delivery flow rate influences the protective action. The researchers attribute this to an adsorption layer that reduces direct contact between the two materials, and for the ionic liquids, to tribochemical reactions between the liquids and the tool-workpiece materials that form remarkably effective protective films.
Temperature measurements confirmed the cooling credentials of supercritical CO2. Pin temperatures dropped significantly compared with dry tests, with a maximum reduction of 80 degrees Celsius. Interestingly, no significant difference in cooling was provided by the presence of the lubricants compared with supercritical CO2 alone, suggesting that the additives’ contribution to heat removal was not activated under the tested speed conditions, possibly due to suboptimal delivery techniques or solubility issues that the team plans to investigate further.
Perhaps the most commercially significant finding concerns the cheap lubricants. Water, rapeseed oil, and sunflower oil performed similarly to the commonly used machining mineral oil when paired with supercritical CO2, and these biological alternatives are less expensive and less health-threatening than traditional emulsions. This could help develop future low-cost yet effective cooling and lubrication methods for the machining industry, a prospect with real sustainability appeal given that cryogenic minimum quantity lubrication methods have already been highlighted as superior to conventional flood coolants when considering toxicity, power consumption, and ozone depletion. The researchers caution that these lubricants would not suit applications where cleanliness is crucial, such as the biomedical and agri-food industries, but for aerospace-grade titanium machining the outlook is bright.
The study also demonstrates the fundamental need for lubrication when using supercritical CO2 in friction-related applications, since supercritical CO2 alone had almost no lubrication effect. The measured apparent friction coefficients could prove useful for supercritical CO2-assisted finite element simulations of machining processes, helping engineers model cutting operations more accurately. Solubility studies are already under investigation to find suitable supercritical conditions for better dissolving oils in supercritical CO2 and defining new efficient cutting fluids. If successful, this work could usher in a new generation of cutting fluids that combine the cooling power of an abundant, recyclable gas with the lubricating finesse of kitchen-shelf oils or laboratory-designed ionic liquids, transforming how the industry machines its most valuable alloys.

Water\, rapeseed oil\, and sunflower oil performed similarly to the commonly used machining mineral oil when paired with supercritical CO2\, and these biological alternatives are less expensive and less health\-threatening than traditional emulsions\. This could help develop future low\-cost yet effective cooling and lubrication methods for the machining industry\, a prospect with real sustainability appeal given that cryogenic minimum quantity lubrication methods have already been highlighted as superior to conventional flood coolants when considering toxicity\, power consumption\, and ozone depletion\. The researchers caution that these lubricants would not suit applications where cleanliness is crucial\, such as the biomedical and agri\-food industries\, but for aerospace\-grade titanium machining the outlook is bright\.

The study also demonstrates the fundamental need for lubrication when using supercritical CO2 in friction\-related applications\, since supercritical CO2 alone had almost no lubrication effect\. The measured apparent friction coefficients could prove useful for supercritical CO2\-assisted finite element simulations of machining processes\, helping engineers model cutting operations more accurately\. Solubility studies are already under investigation to find suitable supercritical conditions for better dissolving oils in supercritical CO2 and defining new efficient cutting fluids\. If successful\, this work could usher in a new generation of cutting fluids that combine the cooling power of an abundant\, recyclable gas with the lubricating finesse of kitchen\-shelf oils or laboratory\-designed ionic liquids\, transforming how the industry machines its most valuable alloys\.

records.title: Application and Adaptation of Arc-Based Welding Processes to Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing: A Review
records.abstract: Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) has emerged as one of the most industrially scalable arc-based metal additive manufacturing (AM) technologies, using established Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW), Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (GTAW), and Plasma Arc Welding (PAW) processes to deposit metallic material layer-by-layer into near-net-shape components. This review presents a physics-based examination of the adaptation of traditional welding processes for AM applications, with emphasis on: (i) the thermodynamic and metallurgical principles governing melt pool formation, solidification, and solid-state transformations; (ii) the thermal and solidification features that WAAM shares with multi-pass welding and those that are distinctive to WAAM, with particular attention to the temperature gradient-to-solidification-rate ratio (G/R) and its role in controlling grain morphology; (iii) deposition path strategies and their influence on heat distribution and microstructural homogeneity; (iv) arc metal transfer modes and their thermal implications for AM; and (v) mechanisms of defect formation including porosity, solidification cracking, residual stress, and geometric deviation. Unlike general WAAM reviews, this article specifically positions conventional arc welding processes as the metallurgical and thermal foundation of WAAM and critically examines how their operating principles are transformed under repeated layer-by-layer deposition. Key governing equations linking process parameters to microstructure and properties are presented. Among GMAW variants, Cold Metal Transfer (CMT) provides low heat input, controlled droplet transfer, and low spatter, whereas GTAW and PAW allow wire feed and arc power to be set independently; the preferred process therefore depends on the alloy, required deposition rate, geometry, and surface quality. A synthesis of findings across ferrous and non-ferrous alloy systems is presented, together with knowledge gaps and future directions toward closed-loop adaptive WAAM systems.
records.summary: This review examines how established arc welding processes—GMAW, GTAW, and PAW—are adapted for Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM), positioning conventional welding as the metallurgical and thermal foundation of layer-by-layer metal deposition. It covers melt pool thermodynamics, solidification and solid-state transformations, the temperature gradient-to-solidification-rate ratio (G/R) as a grain-morphology control parameter, deposition path strategies, arc metal transfer modes, and defect mechanisms including porosity, solidification cracking, residual stress, and geometric deviation. The authors state that among GMAW variants, Cold Metal Transfer (CMT) offers low heat input, controlled droplet transfer, and low spatter, while GTAW and PAW permit independent setting of wire feed and arc power, so process choice depends on alloy, deposition rate, geometry, and surface quality. The article synthesizes findings across ferrous and non-ferrous alloy systems and identifies knowledge gaps and directions toward closed-loop adaptive WAAM.
