\#\# 1 Introduction

Bolted busbar joints are critical current\-carrying components in switchgear\, but their condition can deteriorate under mechanical relaxation\, surface oxidation\, contamination\, and repeated thermal cycling\. These processes reduce the real conducting area\, increase electrical contact resistance\, intensify current constriction\, and promote localized Joule heating\. The resulting temperature rise can accelerate insulation ageing and material degradation\. Electrical\-contact theory and recent multiphysics studies show that joint heating depends not only on bulk conductor properties\, but also on contact state\, current\-transfer paths\, surface films\, and asperity deformation \(\; \; \)\.

Infrared thermography is widely used for non\-contact condition monitoring of electrical equipment \(\; \; \)\. Automated approaches have further extended thermal inspection to early fault detection\, equipment localization\, smart\-camera diagnosis\, image recognition and fusion\, and machine\-learning\-assisted fault identification \(\; \; \; \; \; \)\. However\, a measured surface temperature is not determined by contact degradation alone\. Load current\, ambient temperature\, enclosure airflow\, conductor geometry\, heat\-transfer conditions\, and contact resistance jointly shape the observed thermal field\. Studies of insulated busbar joints and high\-capacity switchgear have accordingly related accessible surface or enclosure temperatures to internal conductor temperature under specified operating conditions \(\; \)\. This dependence limits the use of a single temperature value as a unique indicator of joint degradation\.

To disentangle these coupled influences and resolve the internal electro\-thermal response beyond surface observations\, finite\-element analysis can be used to calculate current density\, interfacial heat generation\, and three\-dimensional temperature fields in busbar assemblies\. Existing electro\-thermal studies have examined how joint resistance\, contact area\, conductor dimensions\, and cooling affect hotspot formation\. However\, the consistency between the simulated contact heating power and the theoretical relation\, where I denotes the load current and I2Rc the prescribed joint contact resistance\, is rarely verified explicitly\. More detailed contact models have represented rough\-surface deformation\, microcontact conduction\, and coupled resistance–temperature behaviour \(\; \)\. Data\-driven approaches have also been explored for predicting electrical contact resistance under wear\-related conditions \(\)\. These models are valuable for mechanism analysis\, but repeated high\-fidelity calculations become computationally demanding when many combinations of load\, contact state\, and thermal boundary conditions must be evaluated\.Rc

Simulation\-trained surrogate models offer a practical means of reducing this computational burden\. A surrogate learns the input–output mapping generated by a finite\-element model and rapidly approximates the response within the sampled domain\. Previous studies have used machine learning as a finite\-element surrogate\, including graph\-based prediction of engineering responses and surrogate\-supported digital\-twin models for dynamic systems \(\; \; \)\. Such approaches can support parameter exploration\, sensitivity analysis\, and scenario screening\. Their predictions\, however\, inherit the assumptions\, parameter ranges\, and numerical limitations of the parent simulation and do not become experimentally validated merely because the surrogate accurately reproduces finite\-element outputs\.

This distinction is important when positioning the present method relative to physics\-informed machine learning\. Physics\-informed approaches commonly embed governing equations\, conservation laws\, invariants\, or related constraints directly into the loss function\, training procedure\, or model structure \(\; \)\. The present study does not impose such constraints within the learning algorithm\. Instead\, physics enters through finite\-element generation of the training data\, physically defined predictors\, and post hoc numerical consistency checks\. The resulting model is therefore a simulation\-trained forward surrogate with physically interpretable inputs\, rather than a physics\-informed neural network or an inverse diagnostic model\.

Interpretability is nevertheless necessary for engineering use\. Tree\-based ensembles can capture nonlinear interactions among load\, contact state\, and cooling\, but their predictive structure is not transparent from model coefficients\. SHapley Additive exPlanations \(SHAP\) provides a consistent framework for decomposing predictions into feature contributions\, while TreeSHAP enables efficient explanation of tree ensembles and aggregation from local to global behaviour \(\; \)\. SHAP\-based interpretation has also been adopted in engineering condition\-monitoring applications to clarify feature contributions in machine\-learning fault models \(\)\. Such attribution can clarify how a surrogate uses its inputs\, but it does not establish causality\, particularly when predictors are correlated\.

Taken together\, these considerations motivate two requirements\. First\, because the physical consistency between simulated contact heating and the theoretical relation is seldom verified\, the finite\-element implementation should be checked explicitly before its outputs are used for surrogate\-model development\. Second\, a computationally efficient and interpretable surrogate is needed for repeated scenario assessment\, with explicit predictors\, target definition\, leakage controls\, validation procedure\, and applicability domain\.I2Rc

This study develops an interpretable surrogate framework for load\-aware thermal\-risk assessment of bolted switchgear busbar joints\. Its contributions are fourfold\. First\, a three\-dimensional electro\-thermal model is established in which prescribed contact resistance and effective contact ratio are controlled separately\, allowing their roles in power dissipation and current distribution to be examined without treating them as interchangeable degradation indicators\. Second\, numerical consistency is assessed through mesh independence and an effective\-contact power check against the theoretical relation across the complete simulation set\. Third\, leakage\-controlled forward surrogates are trained using five prescribed physical inputs\, and four candidate model families are compared by repeated cross\-validation for continuous temperature\-rise prediction and four\-class simulation\-oriented risk assessment\. Fourth\, TreeSHAP is used to interpret global and local prediction behaviour\, while limitations arising from correlated predictors\, geometry specificity\, internal\-to\-surface temperature mapping\, and the absence of experimental validation are stated explicitly\. The framework is intended to accelerate simulation\-based scenario analysis and clarify how load\, prescribed contact state\, and cooling jointly shape thermal response\; it is not presented as an experimentally validated infrared diagnostic system or as a method for inversely estimating contact degradation from field images\.P≈I2Rc

\#\# 2 Electro\-thermal model of the bolted busbar joint

This section describes the three\-dimensional electro\-thermal finite\-element model of the bolted busbar joint\, the equivalent representation of contact degradation\, the governing equations\, the boundary conditions\, and the model\-consistency assessment\. The central modelling idea is that contact degradation is represented as a contraction of the effective conducting contact area rather than as a single high\-resistance block\, so that the current constriction and the resulting localized Joule heating are reproduced in a physically consistent manner\.

\#\#\# 2\.1 Geometry and materials

The model consists of two overlapping copper busbars connected by steel bolts\, washers and nuts\, as shown in Figure 1B\, which corresponds to the bolted joint of an actual switchgear busbar shown in Figure 1A\. Each busbar is 300 mm long\, 50 mm wide and 8 mm thick\, and the overlap length of the lap joint is Lo \= 80 mm\. The two bolts are spaced 40 mm apart\, each with a shank radius of 5 mm and a washer of 10 mm radius and 2 mm thickness\. A contact layer of thickness 0\.5 mm is inserted between the two busbars over the overlap region to represent the electrical contact interface\, which is further divided into an effective conducting region and a degraded non\-contact region as described in Section 2\.2\. The material properties used in the model are summarized in Table 1\. The densities and specific heat capacities of copper and steel were 8\,960 kg m\-3 and 385 J kg\-1 K−1\, and 7\,850 kg m\-3 and 475 J kg\-1 K−1\, respectively\.

\#\#\# 2\.5 Mesh independence and model\-consistency assessment

A free tetrahedral mesh was used for the three\-dimensional electro\-thermal model\. Because large current\-density and temperature gradients were expected around the effective and degraded contact regions\, bolt holes\, washers\, and adjacent busbar surfaces\, targeted local refinement was applied to these regions\. The mesh used to generate the primary 400\-case dataset is hereafter referred to as the production locally refined mesh\.

Four refinement levels—coarse\, normal\, fine\, and extra fine—were evaluated\. They contained 21\,958\, 54\,394\, 312\,700\, and 368\,625 tetrahedral elements\, respectively\, corresponding to 83\,307\, 190\,271\, 1\,003\,469\, and 1\,155\,331 degrees of freedom\. Solver time was measured as the wall\-clock duration surrounding Study\. run \(\)\, including equation assembly and the stationary solution but excluding mesh generation and post\-processing\. Each level was evaluated in three complete runs\, and the median solver times were 5\.429\, 8\.413\, 37\.292\, and 42\.786 s for the coarse\, normal\, fine\, and extra\-fine meshes\, respectively\.

Using the extra\-fine solution as the reference\, the coarse mesh produced relative differences of 0\.0218\% in the maximum temperature and 0\.4947\% in the effective contact temperature rise Tmax\. The corresponding differences for the normal mesh were 0\.0225\% and 0\.5284\%\, respectively\. The slightly smaller scalar differences obtained with the coarse mesh do not indicate systematically better convergence\, because the differences between the coarse and normal results are within the numerical variability of these global outputs\. The mesh selection was therefore not based on the smallest value of a single scalar error metric or on an asserted optimal accuracy–cost balance\.ΔT

The normal mesh was retained as the production mesh because it provided finer local resolution in the effective contact region\, degraded region\, bolt holes\, and washer regions\, where current constriction and steep thermal gradients were concentrated\. \#\#\# 3\.4 Implications of class distribution for surrogate\-model development

The retained dataset exhibits an imbalanced distribution across the four simulation\-oriented thermal\-risk classes\, with the Normal class containing substantially fewer cases than the Warning\, Serious\, and Critical classes\, as summarized in Table 3 and discussed in Section 3\.1\. This imbalance was preserved rather than corrected through oversampling or synthetic sample generation\, so that the subsequent model evaluation reflects the original distribution produced by the electro\-thermal simulations\.

The four classes are ordered discretizations of the continuous effective\-contact temperature rise\. Consequently\, cases located immediately on opposite sides of a class boundary may have very similar thermal responses even though they are assigned different labels\. Classification performance should therefore be evaluated not only using overall accuracy\, but also using class\-balanced metrics and the structure of the misclassifications\. In particular\, an error between adjacent thermal\-risk classes has a different engineering implication from an error that crosses multiple classes\.ΔT

The relatively small Normal class may also increase the variability of class\-specific performance estimates\. The classification workflow therefore employed stratified repeated cross\-validation and imbalance\-aware weighting\, as described in Section 4\. These measures retain the original simulated samples while reducing the likelihood that model assessment is dominated by the more numerous Warning and Serious classes\.

Because the steady\-state thermal response scales approximately as\, similar temperature\-rise values may arise from different combinations of load current and contact condition\. Regression estimates the underlying temperature\-rise response without imposing discrete class boundaries\, whereas classification provides a compact representation of the simulation\-oriented thermal\-risk class\.

\#\# 4 Surrogate\-model framework

The finite\-element simulations described in Sections 2 and 3 establish physically defined mappings from operating\, environmental\, and contact\-degradation variables to the thermal response of the bolted busbar joint\. However\, repeated solution of the full three\-dimensional electro\-thermal model becomes computationally inefficient when dense evaluations are required across combinations of load current\, contact condition\, ambient temperature\, and cooling intensity\. Each finite\-element case required a median solver time of approximately 8\.4 s on the production mesh\, as reported in Section 2\.5\. Once trained\, a surrogate model evaluates the same prescribed input combination essentially instantaneously relative to the finite\-element solution\, making dense scans over\, I\, Rc\, and ηc computationally practical\.h

The present framework is formulated as a forward surrogate model\. It predicts the simulated thermal response from prescribed operating\, environmental\, and degradation variables\. The prescribed contact quantities are supplied as model inputs through direct measurement\, calibration\, estimation\, or scenario specification\, as summarized in Table 2\.

All predictors represent explicitly defined operating\, environmental\, or degradation quantities\, but the nonlinear mapping learned by the models is not transparent to direct inspection\. SHAP analysis was therefore introduced to quantify global and case\-specific feature attributions and to examine whether the learned relationships were consistent with the underlying electro\-thermal mechanisms\.

Two complementary learning tasks were considered\: continuous prediction of the effective\-contact temperature rise and classification into the simulation\-oriented thermal\-risk classes defined in Section 2\.4\. The following subsections describe the task formulation\, leakage\-controlled predictor design\, candidate algorithms\, validation workflow\, evaluation metrics\, model configurations\, and interpretability procedure\.

\#\#\# 4\.1 Surrogate\-learning tasks

Both surrogate\-learning tasks were developed using the retained 382\-case dataset described in Section 3\.1\.

The first task was a regression problem in which the target variable was the effective\-contact temperature rise\. The regression model approximated the mapping from the five physical predictors—load current ΔT\, prescribed contact resistance I\, effective contact ratio Rc\, ambient temperature ηc\, and convective heat\-transfer coefficient Ta\,C—to the continuous response h\. Retaining a continuous target allows the surrogate to reproduce variations in the simulated thermal response without imposing discrete class boundaries\.ΔT

The second task was a four\-class classification problem\. Its target was the simulation\-oriented thermal\-risk class assigned from using the reference threshold scheme defined in Section 2\.4\. The four classes—Normal\, Warning\, Serious\, and Critical—were encoded as the ordered integers 0\, 1\, 2\, and three for model implementation\.ΔT

Although the labels possess a natural order\, the candidate classifiers were evaluated using a multiclass formulation\. This enabled consistent comparison across the four candidate classifier families within the same modelling framework\. The ordered nature of the labels was assessed separately through the structure of the classification errors\, distinguishing between adjacent\-class errors and errors that crossed multiple thermal\-risk classes\.

The regression and classification tasks serve complementary purposes\. Regression estimates the continuous finite\-element temperature\-rise response\, whereas classification provides a compact representation of the corresponding simulation\-oriented thermal\-risk class\. The classification output should not be interpreted as an independently established field defect grade because the labels are derived from simulation\-oriented thresholds rather than standardized operational alarm limits or experimentally validated maintenance categories\.

Neither task was formulated as an inverse\-identification problem\. In particular\, the models do not estimate or Rc from ηc\, Tmax\, or infrared images\. Instead\, the operating\, environmental\, and degradation variables are specified as inputs\, and the surrogate approximates the resulting finite\-element response\. Practical application of the present model therefore requires the relevant inputs to be measured\, estimated\, calibrated\, or prescribed as scenario values before prediction\.ΔT

\#\#\# 4\.2 Predictor design and target\-leakage control

Both surrogate\-learning tasks used the same five predictors\: the load current\, prescribed contact resistance I\, effective contact ratio Rc\, ambient temperature ηc\, and convective heat\-transfer coefficient Ta\,C\. These quantities define the operating condition\, contact\-degradation scenario\, and thermal boundary condition of each finite\-element case\. They are prescribed before the electro\-thermal solution is obtained and therefore do not contain information derived from the resulting temperature field\.h

In this study\, target leakage refers to the inclusion of any predictor that contains the prediction target\, is calculated from it\, or becomes available only after the target response has been generated\. Such leakage allows the model to access response information that would not be available at the time of forward prediction and can consequently produce unrealistically optimistic performance\. This form of feature leakage is distinct from leakage caused by improper separation of training and evaluation data\, which is addressed through the validation workflow described in Section 4\.3\.

For the regression task\, the target was the effective\-contact temperature rise\. Consequently\, ΔT\, Tmax\, Teff\, and all other quantities extracted from the solved temperature field were excluded from the predictor set\. For the classification task\, the target class was assigned directly from Tref using the reference threshold scheme defined in Section 2\.4\. Any predictor containing ΔT\, or information derived from it\, would therefore reveal information used to construct the class label\.ΔT

As discussed in Section 3\.2\, the load\-normalized descriptors and ΘTmax were retained only for post\-processing and physical interpretation\. In particular\, ΘΔT is calculated directly from ΘΔT\, which is both the regression target and the basis of the thermal\-risk labels\. Its inclusion as a predictor would therefore constitute explicit target leakage\.ΔT

The thermal\-risk label\, high\-temperature boundary\-risk flag\, retained\-subset flag\, and other bookkeeping variables were likewise excluded\. These fields describe target construction\, data screening\, or dataset organization rather than physical conditions available to the forward surrogate\.

The strong physical relationships of\, I\, and Rc with the thermal response do not constitute leakage\. Unlike the excluded quantities\, these variables are prescribed independently of the finite\-element output and represent the conditions whose thermal consequences the surrogate is intended to emulate\. Similarly\, ηc and Ta\,C define the imposed thermal environment before the solution is calculated\. Their differing levels of practical availability\, summarized in Table 2\, affect field deployment but not their methodological status as response\-independent predictors\.h

Accordingly\, both the regression and classification surrogates were trained using only the five original physical inputs\. The regression model predicted\, whereas the classifier predicted the simulation\-oriented thermal\-risk class\.ΔT

\#\#\# 4\.3 Candidate models and validation workflow

Four candidate algorithms were evaluated for each surrogate\-learning task to compare linear and nonlinear model families within a common framework\. For regression\, the candidate models were linear regression\, random\-forest regression\, XGBoost regression \, and support\-vector regression\. For classification\, the candidates were multinomial logistic regression\, random\-forest classification\, XGBoost classification\, and support\-vector classification\. Their evaluation metrics\, principal model configurations\, and imbalance\-handling settings are specified in Section 4\.4\.

The primary performance estimates were obtained using repeated cross\-validation on the retained 382\-case dataset\. Regression used repeated five\-fold cross\-validation with 10 repeats\, and classification used the stratified variant so that class proportions were approximately preserved within each fold\; a random seed of 42 was used solely for reproducibility and has no physical significance\. Across the resulting 50 train–validation iterations\, each candidate model was fitted only on the training portion of the corresponding fold and evaluated on its held\-out validation portion\.

The repeated cross\-validation results were used as the primary basis for comparing the candidate model families\. The reported regression and classification metrics therefore represent the mean and standard deviation across the 50 validation folds rather than the result of a single partition\. The earlier single five\-fold results are retained only as a reproducibility comparison in Supplementary Table S6\.

After the candidate model families had been compared\, a separate stratified 80\/20 split was generated using random seed 42 to support sample\-level visualization and interpretation\. The split contained 305 development cases and 77 held\-out cases\. The model fitted on the 80\% development portion was used to generate the predicted\-versus\-simulated regression plot\, the classification confusion matrix\, and the selected case\-level explanations\. The 77 held\-out cases were not used to fit the model that generated the corresponding predictions\; training isolation therefore holds for these visualizations\.

The 77 cases should not\, however\, be described as an independent or model\-selection\-independent test set\: before the 80\/20 split was constructed\, all 382 cases had already participated in the repeated cross\-validation comparison of the four candidate families\. The two procedures therefore serve different purposes\. The repeated cross\-validation provides the primary quantitative comparison and supplies every performance value reported in the Abstract\, Results\, and Conclusions\, whereas the 80\/20 split supplies sample\-level plots\, a confusion structure\, and representative local explanations\. Because the model family retained for interpretation was selected using the same cross\-validation results\, its reported performance is conditional on that selection\; differences between closely performing models are therefore described cautiously\, and the 80\/20 results are treated as descriptive supporting evidence rather than an estimate of post\-selection generalization\.

No automated hyperparameter search\, grid search\, Bayesian optimization\, or cross\-validation\-guided tuning was performed\. The principal model settings were specified before the final comparison\, while parameters not explicitly set retained their software\-package defaults\, as detailed in Section 4\.4\. This avoids an additional tuning\-induced source of optimism\, although it does not eliminate the model\-family selection bias described above\.

\#\#\# 4\.4 Evaluation and interpretation procedures

\#\#\#\# 4\.4\.1 Evaluation metrics

The regression models were evaluated using the coefficient of determination\, root\-mean\-square error \(RMSE\)\, and mean absolute error \(MAE\)\. The coefficient of determination was calculated as R2\, where R2\=1−∑iyi−y\^i2\/∑iyi−y¯2\, yi\, and y\^i denote the simulated value\, predicted value\, and mean simulated value\, respectively\. RMSE is the square root of the mean squared prediction error\, whereas MAE is the mean absolute prediction error\. Because the regression target was y¯\, RMSE and MAE are reported in kelvin\.ΔT

Classification performance was evaluated using accuracy\, macro precision\, macro recall\, macro F1\, and weighted F1\. For class\, precision was defined as k\, recall as TPk\/TPk\+FPk\, and F1 as the harmonic mean of precision and recall\. Macro metrics are the unweighted means of the four class\-specific values\, whereas weighted F1 weights each class\-specific F1 by its sample count\. Because the retained dataset was imbalanced\, macro F1 and macro recall were emphasized alongside accuracy and weighted F1\. \#\#\#\# 4\.4\.2 Model configurations\, preprocessing\, and imbalance handling

As described in Section 4\.3\, no automated or cross\-validation\-guided hyperparameter search was performed\. The model configurations were fixed before the final repeated\-cross\-validation comparison\, and unspecified parameters retained the defaults of the corresponding software implementation\.

StandardScaler was included in the pipelines for linear regression\, support\-vector regression\, multinomial logistic regression\, and support\-vector classification\. Within each cross\-validation iteration\, the scaler was fitted only on the training fold and then applied to the corresponding validation fold\, preventing preprocessing information from crossing the fold boundary\. Random\-forest and XGBoost models were fitted without feature scaling\.

The principal manually specified settings included 300 estimators for the random\-forest and XGBoost models\, C \= 10 for the support\-vector models\, and the learning\-rate\, tree\-depth\, and subsampling settings reported in Supplementary Table S5\. Logistic regression used max\_iter \= 2000 to support numerical convergence rather than to optimize predictive performance\.

Class imbalance was addressed during model fitting without altering the sample distribution\. Logistic regression\, random\-forest classification\, and support\-vector classification used balanced class weights\, whereas balanced sample weights were supplied to the XGBoost classifier\. No oversampling\, undersampling\, or synthetic sample generation was applied\. Random seed 42 was used where supported to make stochastic estimation and resampling reproducible\; it has no physical significance\. Complete preprocessing\, model\, random\-state\, convergence\, and imbalance\-handling settings are reported in Supplementary Table S5\.

Because nested cross\-validation was not performed\, the results represent the specified configurations rather than globally optimized versions of the candidate algorithms\.

\#\#\#\# 4\.4\.3 SHAP procedure

SHAP was used to interpret the XGBoost regression and classification surrogates \(\; \)\. SHAP decomposes a model output into a baseline and additive predictor contributions\. Positive and negative values indicate contributions that increase or decrease the relevant model output relative to its baseline\.

For regression\, SHAP values are expressed in kelvin and quantify the contribution of each predictor to the predicted\. For multiclass classification\, SHAP values were calculated for each class on the raw model\-output scale\. This scale represents the class\-specific margin\, or log\-odds\-type score\, before conversion to normalized probabilities\; classification SHAP values must therefore not be interpreted as temperature changes or direct probability changes\.ΔT

Global regression importance was calculated as the mean absolute SHAP value across evaluated cases\. Global classification importance was calculated by averaging absolute SHAP values across both cases and the four output classes\, producing one overall value for each predictor\. Class\-specific results\, including those for the Critical class\, were analysed separately and were not combined with the all\-class averages\. Local explanations were generated for representative cases from the 77\-case held\-out visualization subset described in Section 4\.3\.

SHAP analysis was restricted to XGBoost to maintain one attribution procedure across the regression and classification tasks\. Under its adopted feature\-dependence formulation\, TreeSHAP computes exact Shapley values for tree ensembles \(\)\. Applying model\-agnostic KernelSHAP to the support\-vector or linear candidates would require sampling\-based approximation and a different attribution framework\, so the resulting magnitudes would not be directly comparable with the TreeSHAP values\.

Only the five predictors used by the surrogate models were included\. The response\-derived descriptors and ΘTmax were excluded because they were not model inputs\. SHAP values represent attribution within the fitted model rather than causal effects\; correlations among the sampled predictors may share or redistribute their apparent contributions\, as considered in Sections 5\.3 and 5\.5\.ΘΔT

\#\#\# 5\.4 Classification error structure and threshold sensitivity

The ordered structure of the four simulation\-oriented thermal\-risk classes was examined using out\-of\-fold predictions generated by a single stratified five\-fold procedure with shuffling and random seed 42\. Each of the 382 retained cases therefore received exactly one prediction from a classifier that had not been fitted using that case\.

Under the reference thresholds of 5\, 15\, and 30 K\, 21 of the 382 out\-of\-fold predictions were incorrect\. All 21 errors occurred between adjacent classes\, and no case crossed two or more class boundaries\. Thus\, no Normal case was assigned to Serious or Critical\, and no Critical case was assigned to Warning or Normal\. The classifier therefore generally preserved the ordinal structure of the labels when the exact class assignment was incorrect\. However\, adjacency alone does not demonstrate that every misclassified case was located immediately next to a numerical threshold\.

These 21 out\-of\-fold errors should not be confused with the five errors shown in Figure 6\. The former were obtained from the single five\-fold out\-of\-fold analysis covering all 382 retained cases\, whereas the latter arose from the separate 77\-case held\-out visualization subset\. The repeated\-cross\-validation means and standard deviations in Table 6 remain the primary aggregate performance estimates\; the two error counts are used only to characterize prediction behaviour under their respective resampling procedures\.

Threshold sensitivity was assessed using the three schemes defined in Section 2\.4\. Under the lower thresholds of 4\, 12\, and 24 K\, the class counts were 14\, 141\, 138\, and 89\. The corresponding repeated\-cross\-validation accuracy and macro F1 were 0\.9251 ± 0\.0317 and 0\.8960 ± 0\.0511\, respectively\. The single five\-fold out\-of\-fold analysis contained 32 errors\, all between adjacent classes\, with no non\-adjacent error\.

For the reference thresholds of 5\, 15\, and 30 K\, the class counts were 26\, 174\, 123\, and 59\. Accuracy reached 0\.9377 ± 0\.0266\, and macro F1 reached 0\.9407 ± 0\.0337\. The corresponding out\-of\-fold predictions contained 21 adjacent\-class errors and no non\-adjacent error\.

Under the higher thresholds of 6\, 18\, and 36 K\, the class counts became 39\, 195\, 106\, and 42\. Accuracy was 0\.9346 ± 0\.0274\, while macro F1 was 0\.9249 ± 0\.0332\. The out\-of\-fold analysis again produced 21 errors\, all between adjacent classes\. The complete threshold\-sensitivity results are reported in Supplementary Table S2\.

The lower scheme produced a particularly small Normal class of only 14 cases and exhibited both the lowest macro F1 and the greatest fold\-to\-fold variation in that metric\. This result demonstrates why accuracy alone is insufficient for the present imbalanced classification problem\. Raising the thresholds increased the number of Normal cases but reduced the Critical class to 42 cases\, accompanied by a modest reduction in macro F1 relative to the reference scheme\.

The diagnostics from the 5 × 10 repeated stratified cross\-validation further clarify the observed variability\. Across the 50 validation folds\, macro F1 ranged from 0\.794 to 0\.991\. In the lowest\-performing fold \(repeat 8\, fold 3\)\, Normal\-class precision\, recall\, and F1 were 1\.000\, 0\.200\, and 0\.333\, respectively\, whereas the F1\-scores of the Warning\, Serious\, and Critical classes were 0\.901\, 0\.941\, and 1\.000\. Four of the five Normal cases in that fold were assigned to the adjacent Warning class\, while all 12 Critical cases were correctly classified\. The highest\-performing fold \(repeat 3\, fold 4\) reached a macro F1 of 0\.991\, with a Normal\-class F1 of 1\.000\. The low\-to\-high variation therefore reflects the sensitivity of a macro\-averaged metric to the small number of Normal cases within individual folds rather than a change in the dominant error mechanism\.

Their comparatively balanced class distribution and stable macro\-level performance support their use as the principal discretization in the present simulation study\. Across all three schemes\, the absence of non\-adjacent errors indicates that the classifier retained the ordering of simulated thermal severity as the numerical class boundaries changed\. These findings do not convert the classes into standardized field alarm levels\; their operational interpretation\, experimental validation requirements\, and applicability limits are discussed in Section 5\.5\.

\#\#\# 5\.5 Applicability\, limitations\, and validation requirements

The present study establishes a numerically consistent simulation\-to\-surrogate workflow rather than an experimentally validated field\-diagnostic system\. The mesh\-independence assessment\, electrical\-power consistency check\, and comparison between the production mesh and the globally controlled sensitivity mesh support the internal numerical consistency of the finite\-element implementation\. These checks do not constitute experimental validation of the predicted temperatures\, current\-transfer paths\, or contact\-degradation states\. Accordingly\, the reported surrogate performance quantifies reproduction of the finite\-element outputs within the simulated design space\, rather than agreement with measurements from operating switchgear\.

Several modelling assumptions delimit the interpretation of the electro\-thermal results\. The primary 400\-case dataset was generated using constant material properties and one\-way sequential electrical\-to\-thermal coupling\. The temperature\-dependent conductivity sensitivity analysis produced only a small change in under the investigated conditions\, supporting the use of constant copper electrical conductivity for the present parameter study\. This result does not demonstrate that all material properties remain temperature independent\, particularly at elevated temperatures\. Temperature\-dependent thermal conductivity\, heat capacity\, surface\-film properties\, and contact resistance may become increasingly important as the joint condition evolves\.ΔT

The contact state was represented through prescribed values of and Rc\. These quantities were not dynamically updated in response to thermal expansion\, contact\-pressure redistribution\, bolt relaxation\, oxidation\, surface\-film growth\, arcing\, or irreversible material degradation\. The model therefore represents specified contact conditions rather than the time\-dependent evolution of a deteriorating joint\. The 18 cases with ηc were excluded from surrogate development because the adopted physics did not represent the high\-temperature evolution that could occur beyond this applicability boundary\. The resulting surrogate should therefore be used only within the retained input and response domain and should not be extrapolated to thermal\-runaway conditions\.Tmax\>500∘C

The thermal boundary conditions were also simplified\. Convective cooling was represented by a prescribed heat\-transfer coefficient\, while detailed enclosure airflow\, buoyancy\-driven circulation\, radiation exchange\, nearby conductors\, cabinet walls\, and spatially varying ventilation were not explicitly resolved\. These effects may alter both the absolute temperature field and the apparent contribution of h under operating conditions\. In addition\, the steel fasteners were included in the thermal domain but excluded from the electric\-current domain\. This assumption isolates the intended busbar\-to\-busbar current\-transfer paths\, but it may not apply to assemblies in which bolts\, washers\, surface coatings\, or conductive contamination provide non\-negligible parallel electrical paths\.

The finite\-element model describes one busbar geometry\, material system\, bolt arrangement\, contact\-patch representation\, and set of boundary conditions\. A separate sensitivity analysis of the assumed contact\-layer thickness is provided in Supplementary Table S7\. The surrogate is consequently geometry\- and configuration\-specific\. Application to different conductor dimensions\, overlap lengths\, bolt spacings\, materials\, surface treatments\, enclosure designs\, or cooling arrangements would require additional simulations and preferably recalibration against measurements\. Load current and ambient temperature can generally be measured directly\, whereas\, Rc\, and ηc may require dedicated resistance measurements\, calibration\, engineering estimation\, or scenario specification\. Related studies have shown that relating accessible surface temperatures to internal conductor temperatures requires equipment\-specific thermal modelling and controlled calibration \(\; \)\.h

The machine\-learning assessment has further limitations\. The retained dataset comprised 382 simulated cases\, including only 26 Normal cases under the reference threshold scheme\. Repeated stratified cross\-validation reduces dependence on a single partition but cannot replace evaluation on an external dataset\. The learning curves in Supplementary Figure S3 show near\-perfect training performance\, including a classification training accuracy of 1\.000\, whereas validation performance remains lower and the validation curves have not fully plateaued at the largest training fraction\. The remaining train–validation gap indicates that overfitting cannot be ruled out and further motivates evaluation with larger external datasets\. As shown in Section 5\.4\, macro\-averaged performance is also sensitive to the small number of Normal cases within individual folds\, and a larger\, more balanced dataset would be required to establish the stability of this error pattern\.

The XGBoost family was selected after comparing four candidate algorithms on the same retained dataset\, so its reported performance is conditional on that selection rather than a selection\-independent estimate obtained from an external test set\; the scatter plot and confusion matrix are correspondingly post\-selection internal visualizations \(Section 4\.3\)\.

The four thermal\-risk classes were introduced as simulation\-oriented modelling categories\. Their thresholds were not derived from standards\, maintenance records\, insulation limits\, experimentally established failure probabilities\, or utility alarm criteria\. The threshold\-sensitivity analysis showed that the principal classification behaviour was not dependent on one exact set of boundaries\, but this numerical robustness does not convert the labels into operational alarm levels\. Field deployment would require application\-specific thresholds linked to equipment design\, loading history\, allowable temperature limits\, measurement uncertainty\, and maintenance practice\.

The SHAP results likewise require cautious interpretation\. They describe how the fitted XGBoost models distribute prediction attribution among the five inputs within the sampled dataset\. They do not establish causal effects or uniquely identify the physical origin of a hotspot\. Correlations among\, I\, and Rc may share or redistribute attribution among related predictors\. In particular\, the relatively small global contribution assigned to ηc should not be interpreted as evidence that contact\-area contraction is physically unimportant\. It indicates that the area\-averaged target ηc was less sensitive to its independent variation than to the dominant electrical power scale established by ΔT and I\.Rc

Experimental validation should precede operational use\. A controlled laboratory programme should use bolted\-joint specimens with documented geometry\, surface condition\, tightening state\, and independently measured contact resistance\, tested over multiple current levels\, ambient temperatures\, and cooling conditions\. Thermocouples and calibrated infrared imaging would provide\, the effective\-contact temperature\, the reference\-busbar temperature\, Tmax\, and hotspot location\. Simultaneous measurements of current\, voltage drop\, and joint power would allow both the thermal response and the ΔT power consistency to be evaluated\.I2Rc

A second validation stage should examine repeated heating cycles\, bolt relaxation\, oxidation\, and controlled surface degradation to determine whether prescribed and Rc scenarios adequately represent evolving joints\. Measurements from switchgear with different geometries\, ventilation conditions\, and operating histories would then be needed to evaluate transferability and define application\-specific thresholds\. Until these steps are completed\, the proposed framework should be regarded as an interpretable forward surrogate for simulation\-based thermal\-risk assessment and scenario analysis\, rather than a standalone field diagnostic or maintenance\-decision system\.ηc

\#\# 6 Conclusion

This study developed an interpretable simulation\-to\-surrogate framework for load\-aware thermal\-risk assessment of bolted switchgear busbar joints\. A three\-dimensional electro\-thermal finite\-element model was constructed to represent variations in load current\, prescribed contact resistance\, effective contact ratio\, ambient temperature\, and convective cooling\. The contact formulation separately controlled and Rc\, enabling their thermal consequences to be examined without treating them as interchangeable measures of degradation\. Numerical consistency was supported through mesh\-independence assessment and comparison between integrated contact\-region Joule heating and the theoretical ηc value\.I2Rc

Of the 400 simulated cases\, 382 were retained for surrogate development after excluding 18 cases with\, which lay outside the intended applicability domain of the adopted constant\-property\, sequentially coupled model\. Using the five prescribed physical inputs\, the XGBoost regressor achieved Tmax\>500∘C\, R2\=0\.990±0\.005 K\, and MAE RMSE\=1\.877±0\.542 K under \=1\.042±0\.198 repeated cross\-validation\. Its regression performance was comparable with that of random forest rather than demonstrably superior\. For classification\, XGBoost achieved an accuracy of5×10 and a macro F1\-score of0\.938±0\.026\, with a more balanced macro recall than random forest\. It was therefore retained for detailed interpretation because of its combined classification performance\, competitive regression accuracy\, and compatibility with a unified TreeSHAP procedure\.0\.941±0\.033

SHAP analysis showed that load current and prescribed contact resistance dominated both continuous temperature\-rise prediction and simulation\-oriented class assignment\. Convective cooling provided a smaller but physically meaningful contribution\, while the global importance of was comparatively low\. This result does not imply that contact\-area contraction is physically unimportant\; rather\, the area\-averaged target ηc was less sensitive to changes in spatial current distribution than to the electrical power scale established by ΔT and I\. The non\-monotonic dependence of Rc further demonstrated that its contribution varied with the accompanying operating and contact conditions\.ηc

Across the lower\, reference\, and higher threshold schemes\, all out\-of\-fold classification errors occurred between adjacent classes\, with no non\-adjacent error\. The poorest repeated\-cross\-validation fold was primarily affected by upward misclassification of the sparsely represented Normal cases\, while all Critical cases in that fold were correctly identified\. These findings indicate preservation of the ordered thermal\-severity structure\, but they do not establish standardized operational alarm levels\.

The proposed model remains a geometry\-specific forward surrogate of finite\-element outputs\. It does not infer contact condition from infrared measurements and has not been experimentally validated\. Future work should combine controlled bolted\-joint experiments\, calibrated thermal measurements\, independently measured electrical quantities\, evolving degradation states\, and additional switchgear configurations to assess physical accuracy\, transferability\, and application\-specific risk thresholds\. Until such validation is completed\, the framework should be used for simulation\-based scenario assessment and interpretable sensitivity analysis rather than as a standalone field\-diagnostic or maintenance\-decision system\.

Optical illusion: Is co-packaged optics the savior the data center industry has been waiting for?
As demands on data center networks grow, is CPO finally ready to take center stage?
When Cisco took to the stage at the Optical Fiber Conference (OFC) 2023 to demonstrate co-packaged optics (CPO) on a 3.2TB switch, it is fair to say the technology did not receive a rapturous reception.
“I would say the industry response at that time ranged from indifference or a yawn to fairly negative,” Bill Gartner, SVP & GM, optical systems and optics at Cisco, tells DCD.
It wasn’t that three years ago the world didn’t care about the potential benefits of CPO. Rather, as Gartner explains it, the negative response stemmed from a number of concerns, one being that the technology would introduce vendor lock-in to an environment that traditionally allowed for a multi-vendor approach.
“There’s a switch, which makes up the bulk of the router and its costs, and then there are ports on the face plate into which you plug these pluggable optics,” Gartner explains. “But a customer has a choice of which pluggable optic they want to use, and there are many providers of pluggable optics. That gives them negotiating leverage and the ability to make sure that they've got supply chain diversity, which gives them a lot of benefit.”
In 2023, customers were fearful that CPO would force them into an all-Cisco or all Broadcom world, Gartner says, although he stresses that while Cisco is one of the aforementioned providers of pluggable optics, the company is not in the habit of forcing its customers to buy Cisco.
“Multi-vendor gives customers leverage, and customers like that leverage. It gives them peace and comfort that they're not going to be held hostage by a single source.”
While vendor lock-in remains an issue that CPO has yet to fully resolve three years later, it appears that the indifference Gartner witnessed on the OFC stage has vanished, replaced by an industry ready to shrug off all concerns and welcome the technology with open arms.
What is co-packaged optics?
Co-packaged optics emerged as a concept around the start of the decade, when the data center industry began discussing the need for a solution to the power and bandwidth bottlenecks it was increasingly experiencing.
“In the old days, your electrical connections were copper. Your data center networks were connected by Ethernet, and everything was good,” says Roy Chua, founder and industry analyst at AvidThink. “Then, as speeds increased, copper became unable to handle the volume of traffic, so the industry turned to fiber optics,” which Chua notes was also good, until it wasn’t quite good enough anymore.
Fiber optics requires the use of lasers to convert electrical signals into optics, or photons, so they can be transported over the glass fiber, then reconverted from optical signals back to electrical ones when they reach the other side. “So that's all wonderful, except that all takes a certain amount of energy,“ Chua says.
In today’s data center environments, most electrical-to-optical conversions take place via pluggable optical transceivers, known as digital signal processors (DSPs), which connect to the switch. However, DSPs are expensive and power-hungry, meaning that although they have clear benefits over copper interconnects, they are not quite the power-efficient option the industry is looking for.
Enter: Co-packaged optics. On a very basic level, unlike pluggable optics, where the transceivers are kept separate from the main chips, CPO integrates optical and electrical components, such as optical engines and switching ASICs, on a single packaged substrate.
“What co-packaged optics does is move the conversion onto the actual silicon itself. It moves those lasers onto the silicon, eliminating the need for any external units,” Chua explains. “And by putting those lasers inside the silicon, you are able to save power. By co-packaging these elements, it allows for more consolidation while lowering costs and energy use.”
However, while the concept might seem relatively straightforward, the practicalities are less so. “As you can imagine, manufacturing of co-packaged optics can be complicated because you have to manufacture everything – your wave guides and your modulators – all together.”
Therefore, it's unsurprising that another early concern regarding the technology was its potential cost, with Chua noting that “people felt it would not be sufficiently reliable and cost-effective enough to produce and take to market. “
The reliability of the technology has also come under scrutiny from customers, with questions arising as to how to go about replacing a laser that has failed when it's part of a monolithic structure, particularly given the so-called blast radius of optics, and the high failure rate of lasers.
The industry has responded by developing a hot-swappable laser source known as an External Laser Small Form-Factor Pluggable (or ELSFP) while keeping everything monolithically integrated. Gartner says that although this solution certainly helps to address the challenge, it’s something of a half-measure that doesn’t succeed in solving the issue entirely.

According to AvidThink’s Data Center Networking in 2026 report, CPO is one of several new architectures that are driving a “structural shift” in the optical interconnect landscape, namely removing the need for DSPs from optical transceiver modules.
In addition to CPO, there’s what Chua describes as a half-step, known as linear pluggable optics (LPO), and a three-quarter step called near-packaged optics, with LPO currently the most popular of the three. There’s also eXtra-dense pluggable optics, or XPO, which was developed by Arista but described by Chua as less of a pure technology and more of a packaging form factor. [See Box Out].
While co-packaged optics is not a new concept, AvidThink’s report notes that the technology reached a milestone this year, transitioning from “perpetual promise to production deployment,” with both Chua and Gartner agreeing this has been largely driven by announcements made by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at GTC 2026.
At the March conference, Huang indicated that Nvidia’s Spectrum-X CPO switches would be in production in H2 2026, and officially announced that the chip giant’s 2028 Feynman architecture would introduce NVLink 8 CPO, bringing silicon photonics directly to the GPU-to-GPU scale-up interconnect for the first time.
AvidThink says this is architecturally significant as, until now, CPO has been applied to scale-out switch-to-switch connections. Applying it to the latency-critical scale-up domain signals that CPO technology has achieved the maturity and performance required for the most demanding interconnect tier.
“Until Jensen said CPO, no one cared about CPO. No one had any idea what CPO was, and now I get asked that question all the time,” Chua laughs. He also questions whether anyone in the industry would have been saying widespread adoption of the technology would take place in 2028 had Huang not gotten on stage and made the Feynman announcement.
“Without Jensen sort of stoking the fire, I think it would have been the 2027 - 2028 conversation, and Jensen basically made it the 2025 - 2026 conversation,” Chua says, adding that “to be frank, I wasn't expecting it.”
While Chua says Huang has put a rocket under the industry – with Broadcom in particular being incredibly aggressive around its timelines for deployment in the wake of Huang’s comments – the AvidThink report does highlight that there have been a number of other notable CPO announcements from the last 18 months.
These include AMD’s January 2025 acquisition of Enosemi; Lightmatter unveiling Passage L200, the world’s first 3D co-packaged optics product; Broadcom announcing its Tomahawk 6 CPO variant ‘Davisson’; Marvell’s acquisition of Celestial AI; Coherent demonstrating multi-technology CPO at OFC 2026; and Ayar Labs and Wiwynn announcing a joint reference design for optically connected, rack-scale AI systems.
Furthermore, in March 2026, Ciena, Coherent, Marvell, Molex, Samtec, and TeraHop announced the formation of the Open CPX MSA (Open Co-packaging Multi-Source Agreement) to develop the specifications for optical engines “required to enable a broad ecosystem of interoperable co-packaged and near-package interconnect solutions.”
Where are we now?
While all of these announcements appear to indicate significant demand, Gartner says it's important to note that a lot of work in the CPO space was initially vendor, not customer, driven, as demonstrated by those poor early responses.
“[In 2023] Cisco and Broadcom announced these CPO demos and didn't get a great customer response. Then Nvidia announced that they were going to deploy CPO and, quite honestly, stimulated a lot of excitement in the industry – I think maybe irrational exuberance is the way I would characterize it though.”
Although Cisco had already demoed a co-packaged optics prototype back in 2023, Gartner says the company has not yet announced a commercial CPO line, although he says that it does have CPO technology under development.
“We're playing this a bit cautiously,” he explains. “We don't want to come across to our customers like we're not going to give them a choice.”
Gartner says Cisco’s initial CPO offering will likely be in the 100-terabit switch capacity range, and the company will continue to give customers a choice between pluggables and an embedded option, be that CPO or NPO.
“Again, we have not announced a product yet; this is something that's under development, and we're really going to be cautious about launching it based on customer demand. We want to see the customers are really pulling for this, as opposed to it being a vendor push.”
In the meantime, the company is developing LPO options for its Silicon One portfolio, with the first commercially available 800G LPO modules for its Nexus 9000 series switches and 8000 series routers released in February 2026.
“I think the challenge that we have to acknowledge here is that the industry ecosystem is evolving around CPO, but it’s not mature. The ecosystem around silicon is highly mature – we know how to put a package and substrates around silicon, and we know how to do that around optics, and build a pluggable optics module, but we don’t have an ecosystem that’s mature and can put those two together,” Gartner says.
“There's a lot of invention right now around things like connectors for CPO, substrates that support the optics, and optical chiplets, but that's an immature ecosystem, and it really has to mature pretty significantly before we'll see this technology make sense at volume. Anybody can produce a hundred of these things, but when we have to talk about delivering thousands or millions, that ecosystem really needs to be mature, and that's going to take some time.”
Despite all the excitement, Chua also acknowledges that, at the moment, CPO is being deployed at “a very small scale.” However, he says all early signs are promising, and the data show that the technology will be able to scale up and be deployed into production.
In particular, Meta’s deployment of the Broadcom Tomahawk 5 ‘Bailly’ CPO switch in its data centers resulted in a 0.34 percent annual link failure rate during the first million hours of testing, making it roughly five times more reliable than traditional pluggable transceivers that were used as control groups.
As a result, Chua says he can’t see anything on the horizon that would block the mass adoption of co-packaged optics in the near future, and he expects to see some level of volume shipments from Broadcom of its Tomahawk 6 ‘Davisson’ CPO variant.
For Gartner, however, whether the reality of CPO lives up to the hype remains to be seen, especially with regard to the timelines being touted by vendors such as Nvidia and Broadcom. While shiny and new will be enough for some people to jump on board the co-packaged optics train, for him, the real turning point for the technology will be when all the other technologies currently on offer hit their ceiling, making CPO a necessity.
“Today, the SerDers rate coming off the silicon is 200G per line, and at that rate, in my view, it's a toss-up as to whether CPO or LPO makes sense,” he says. “Once we get to 400G per line, then LPO becomes much more challenging ... that is where the ability for LPO to continue serving the market diminishes, and the need for CPO becomes more real.”

Thermal Co-Simulation Testing Of Co-Packaged Optics
Ensuring optical engines can operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors in multi-chip packages.
By Vladimir Stojanovic and Igor Elkanovich
The CPO revolution is at our doorstep. But transforming data center interconnects requires overcoming new challenges in architecture, power delivery, mechanical design, and thermal management. Of these, thermal management has emerged as one of the most critical areas for successfully deploying co-packaged optics (CPO) in hyperscale AI environments.
Thermal instability has been a concern for CPO technology. Ayar Labs and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC) jointly conducted thermal co-simulation of the advanced package design and determined the thermal floor map for the package and subsequent chiplets, including air- and liquid-cooled environments.
Since thermal stability has been raised as a concern for micro-ring-based CPO, we want to address it head-on. Our co-simulation data show that CPO can operate reliably within the thermal envelope of advanced multi-chip packages. We’re sharing these results to give hyperscalers the confidence to move forward with CPO deployments at scale.
Novel design enables over 100 Tbps speeds
Let’s start with the new multi-chip package (MCP) design that integrates Ayar Labs’ TeraPHY optical engines into GUC’s advanced packaging and ASIC workflow. The new XPU MCP design replaces traditional electrical interconnects with Ayar Labs’ optical engines, which are attached directly to the MCP organic substrate. This architecture enables a full-duplex optical interface of more than 100 Tbps from the XPU package, an improvement of more than an order of magnitude over current XPUs.
UCIe-S provides bandwidth between the optical engines and the I/O chiplets over the MCP substrate. UCIe-A, on the other hand, is used for communication between the I/O chiplet and the main AI die over local silicon interconnect (LSI) bridges.
The scale of this design creates thermal challenges we must address. The complete package measures 105mm x 140mm, housing:
- 2 XPUs (25.69mm x 32.40mm each)
- 8 HBM4 memory modules
- 4 I/O chiplets
- 8 TeraPHY optical engines (12.5mm x 13.0mm each)
The +3 kW power envelope in a single package underscores the importance of thermal management and the need for optical engines to operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors. This complex multi-chip architecture requires sophisticated packaging. The design uses a 9-2-9 layer substrate structure to handle the complex routing requirements.
The design also addresses signal and power integrity challenges associated with the large-scale package. We perform thermal optimization at the XPU MCP level, while a stiffener design incorporates optical engines’ requirements and enables detachable fiber connections that meet mechanical stress and warpage requirements.
What is thermal co-simulation and why is it important?
Thermal co-simulation is the combined simulation of electrical behavior and heat flow across a chip. It lets designers predict temperatures, hotspots, and reliability issues in integrated circuits (ICs) and packages under realistic operating conditions. The data ensures the entire system operates within required temperature specifications. This is critical for successful deployment.
In GUC’s thermal integrity design flow, we consider every chip’s power maps and perform thermal crosstalk and dynamic thermal co-simulation to ensure the MCP’s thermal integrity from early-stage through sign-off. This allows us to identify local thermal hotspots and the impact of thermal crosstalk on the optical engine.
Thermal co-simulation is crucial for GUC’s advanced ASIC workflows. In our joint analysis, the MCP includes multiple chiplets to analyze thermal crosstalk between adjacent chiplet dies. Any heat generated by the entire interposer complex may affect the optical engine’s performance.
Thermal modeling is needed to optimize optical engine performance. This joint technical exercise deliberately probes thermal hotspots and thermal crosstalk to evaluate overall CPO thermal stability in a realistic customer package form factor. Rather than avoiding the hard questions, we designed the simulation to stress the system and raise any potential concerns.
These findings are invaluable for assessing advanced packaging designs and collaborating with ecosystem partners to design optimal cooling solutions for AI server and switch applications at the most demanding Thermal Design Power levels. This testing allows us to do just that.
Thermal co‑sim testing
We performed three simulations: an analysis to determine thermal resistance targets for each chip component, plus testing of two different cooling solutions. One solution met spec, and one did not.
3D VC heatsink test
We tested a standard air fin heatsink at airspeeds of 5 m/s and 6 m/s at 25ºC.
Fig. 1: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using heatsink.
This did not meet spec, as the temperature significantly exceeded spec for all components except the I/O die.
Thermal resistance analysis
We analyzed the maximum junction temperature versus resistance curve to determine suitable resistance for the Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate with Local Silicon Interconnect (CoWoS-L) advanced packaging and optical engine to meet the temperature spec.
Fig. 2: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO Thermal Resistance (Rsa) analysis.
The system-level thermal solution successfully meets the specification when RSA-ASIC is ≤ 0.008 K/W and RSA-OE is ≤ 0.15 K/W. The cold plate design achieves these targets with pressure drops of 11.2 kPa for the ASIC cold plate and 18.8 kPa for the optical engine cold plate. This ensures efficient coolant flow while maintaining thermal performance.
Cold plate test
Finally, we tested an impingement-type cold plate thermal solution at 4.5 LPM.
Fig. 3: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using cold plate.
This solution did meet spec. All components were below the temperature specifications.
Cold plate details
We selected the impingement-type cold plate for this application because it enables higher heat flux removal than conventional parallel-channel designs. The design uses optimized fin dimensions (thickness: 0.15mm, height: 2.4mm for the ASIC and 3.0mm for the optical engine) with thermal interface materials (K=5.2 W/mK) to achieve the required thermal performance.
This approach effectively dissipates the concentrated heat from multiple high-power chiplets while maintaining the optical engines within their operational temperature limits.
Key Results
- Determined the thermal resistance design targets for each chiplet for thermal sign-off constraints:
- HBM4 < 95ºC
- SoC < 125ºC
- Optical Engine < 100ºC
- Mapped the location of thermal hotspots.
- Showed that a traditional air heatsink does not work for this solution.
- Demonstrated that a real-world liquid cooling device meets the specifications needed.
These results point to a significant breakthrough in CPO deployment. \# Thermal Co\-Simulation Testing Of Co\-Packaged Optics

Ensuring optical engines can operate reliably alongside high\-power AI processors in multi\-chip packages\.

By Vladimir Stojanovic and Igor Elkanovich

The CPO revolution is at our doorstep\. But transforming data center interconnects requires overcoming new challenges in architecture\, power delivery\, mechanical design\, and thermal management\. Of these\, thermal management has emerged as one of the most critical areas for successfully deploying co\-packaged optics \(CPO\) in hyperscale AI environments\.

Thermal instability has been a concern for CPO technology\. Ayar Labs and Global Unichip Corp\. \(GUC\) jointly conducted thermal co\-simulation of the advanced package design and determined the thermal floor map for the package and subsequent chiplets\, including air\- and liquid\-cooled environments\.

Since thermal stability has been raised as a concern for micro\-ring\-based CPO\, we want to address it head\-on\. Our co\-simulation data show that CPO can operate reliably within the thermal envelope of advanced multi\-chip packages\. We’re sharing these results to give hyperscalers the confidence to move forward with CPO deployments at scale\.

\#\# Novel design enables over 100 Tbps speeds

Let’s start with the new multi\-chip package \(MCP\) design that integrates Ayar Labs’ TeraPHY optical engines into GUC’s advanced packaging and ASIC workflow\. The new XPU MCP design replaces traditional electrical interconnects with Ayar Labs’ optical engines\, which are attached directly to the MCP organic substrate\. This architecture enables a full\-duplex optical interface of more than 100 Tbps from the XPU package\, an improvement of more than an order of magnitude over current XPUs\.

UCIe\-S provides bandwidth between the optical engines and the I\/O chiplets over the MCP substrate\. UCIe\-A\, on the other hand\, is used for communication between the I\/O chiplet and the main AI die over local silicon interconnect \(LSI\) bridges\.

The scale of this design creates thermal challenges we must address\. The complete package measures 105mm x 140mm\, housing\:

\- 2 XPUs \(25\.69mm x 32\.40mm each\)
\- 8 HBM4 memory modules
\- 4 I\/O chiplets
\- 8 TeraPHY optical engines \(12\.5mm x 13\.0mm each\)

The \+3 kW power envelope in a single package underscores the importance of thermal management and the need for optical engines to operate reliably alongside high\-power AI processors\. This complex multi\-chip architecture requires sophisticated packaging\. The design uses a 9\-2\-9 layer substrate structure to handle the complex routing requirements\.

The design also addresses signal and power integrity challenges associated with the large\-scale package\. We perform thermal optimization at the XPU MCP level\, while a stiffener design incorporates optical engines’ requirements and enables detachable fiber connections that meet mechanical stress and warpage requirements\.

\#\# What is thermal co\-simulation and why is it important\?

Thermal co\-simulation is the combined simulation of electrical behavior and heat flow across a chip\. It lets designers predict temperatures\, hotspots\, and reliability issues in integrated circuits \(ICs\) and packages under realistic operating conditions\. The data ensures the entire system operates within required temperature specifications\. This is critical for successful deployment\.

In GUC’s thermal integrity design flow\, we consider every chip’s power maps and perform thermal crosstalk and dynamic thermal co\-simulation to ensure the MCP’s thermal integrity from early\-stage through sign\-off\. This allows us to identify local thermal hotspots and the impact of thermal crosstalk on the optical engine\.

Thermal co\-simulation is crucial for GUC’s advanced ASIC workflows\. In our joint analysis\, the MCP includes multiple chiplets to analyze thermal crosstalk between adjacent chiplet dies\. Any heat generated by the entire interposer complex may affect the optical engine’s performance\.

Thermal modeling is needed to optimize optical engine performance\. This joint technical exercise deliberately probes thermal hotspots and thermal crosstalk to evaluate overall CPO thermal stability in a realistic customer package form factor\. Rather than avoiding the hard questions\, we designed the simulation to stress the system and raise any potential concerns\.

These findings are invaluable for assessing advanced packaging designs and collaborating with ecosystem partners to design optimal cooling solutions for AI server and switch applications at the most demanding Thermal Design Power levels\. This testing allows us to do just that\.

\#\# Thermal co‑sim testing

We performed three simulations\: an analysis to determine thermal resistance targets for each chip component\, plus testing of two different cooling solutions\. One solution met spec\, and one did not\.

\#\#\# 3D VC heatsink test

We tested a standard air fin heatsink at airspeeds of 5 m\/s and 6 m\/s at 25ºC\.

Fig\. 1\: GUC \+ Ayar Labs CoWoS\-L CPO simulation using heatsink\.

This did not meet spec\, as the temperature significantly exceeded spec for all components except the I\/O die\.

\#\#\# Thermal resistance analysis

We analyzed the maximum junction temperature versus resistance curve to determine suitable resistance for the Chip\-on\-Wafer\-on\-Substrate with Local Silicon Interconnect \(CoWoS\-L\) advanced packaging and optical engine to meet the temperature spec\.

Fig\. 2\: GUC \+ Ayar Labs CoWoS\-L CPO Thermal Resistance \(Rsa\) analysis\.

The system\-level thermal solution successfully meets the specification when RSA\-ASIC is ≤ 0\.008 K\/W and RSA\-OE is ≤ 0\.15 K\/W\. The cold plate design achieves these targets with pressure drops of 11\.2 kPa for the ASIC cold plate and 18\.8 kPa for the optical engine cold plate\. This ensures efficient coolant flow while maintaining thermal performance\.

\#\#\# Cold plate test

Finally\, we tested an impingement\-type cold plate thermal solution at 4\.5 LPM\.

Fig\. 3\: GUC \+ Ayar Labs CoWoS\-L CPO simulation using cold plate\.

This solution did meet spec\. All components were below the temperature specifications\.

\#\# Cold plate details

We selected the impingement\-type cold plate for this application because it enables higher heat flux removal than conventional parallel\-channel designs\. The design uses optimized fin dimensions \(thickness\: 0\.15mm\, height\: 2\.4mm for the ASIC and 3\.0mm for the optical engine\) with thermal interface materials \(K\=5\.2 W\/mK\) to achieve the required thermal performance\.

This approach effectively dissipates the concentrated heat from multiple high\-power chiplets while maintaining the optical engines within their operational temperature limits\.

Key Results

\- Determined the thermal resistance design targets for each chiplet for thermal sign\-off constraints\:
\- HBM4 \< 95ºC
\- SoC \< 125ºC
\- Optical Engine \< 100ºC

\- Mapped the location of thermal hotspots\.
\- Showed that a traditional air heatsink does not work for this solution\.
\- Demonstrated that a real\-world liquid cooling device meets the specifications needed\.

These results point to a significant breakthrough in CPO deployment\. Successfully maintaining optical engines under 100ºC while dissipating over 3kW TDP from a single package \(with 1\,500W coming from the AI processors alone\) shows that CPO operates reliably with ample junction\-temperature headroom\, paving the way for the most demanding thermal environments\.

\#\# Future plans

Our next step will focus on dynamic workload simulation to further analyze thermal impact on CPO under real\-world operating conditions\. The tests we’ve shared here were based on static power assumptions\, where each component’s power consumption remains constant\. Systems ramp up from idle\, spike during training or booting\, and fluctuate based on user demand during normal operations\.

Large numbers of users can cause heat spikes\. A dynamic workload simulation will allow us to test our design under conditions more accurate to the real world\. This will help us understand how the optics respond to sudden temperature changes and ensure the systems operate efficiently\.

These thermal co\-simulation test results demonstrate that CPO can operate reliably in high\-power AI systems when paired with appropriate cooling solutions\. As the industry continues to push the boundaries of compute performance and thermal design power\, CPO will play a significant role in overcoming bandwidth and power limitations\.

Igor Elkanovich is the CTO of GUC\.

Stojanovic was recently a professor of EECS at UC Berkeley\, and was one of the key developers of the Rambus high\-speed link technology\. He holds a PhD from Stanford University\.

Celestica DS6005 Puts 102.4Tbps of Co-Packaged Optics and 64 1.6TbE Ports in a 1.5OU Liquid-Cooled ORv3 Switch
by Harold Fritts on October 15, 2026
Celestica introduced the DS6005 at the OCP Global Summit, a co-packaged optics (CPO) data center switch that puts 102.4Tbps of switching capacity and 64 optically enabled 1.6TbE ports in a 1.5OU, fully liquid-cooled chassis for Open Rack v3. It is built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk 6 Davisson, the CPO version of the 102.4T Tomahawk 6, which integrates the optical engines onto the switch package so the front panel carries fiber connectors and laser modules in place of pluggable transceivers. Celestica is aiming it at AI/ML scale-up and scale-out fabrics.
The DS6005 lands in the same week as two other Tomahawk 6 CPO systems. Micas Networks put Davisson in a 1RU box with a Q1 2027 production date, and Supermicro’s 2OU CPO switch takes busbar power in an ORv3 rack. Celestica’s version is the one built for the OCP high-power rack from the start, with liquid cooling as the only cooling option and a chassis labeled for 46 to 56V DC input at 76A on the rear.
Optical Engine Integration
Co-packaging moves the optical engines from the faceplate onto the Tomahawk 6 Davisson package, which Celestica says removes the discrete digital signal processors and the long copper traces between the ASIC and a pluggable module, cutting link-level power and latency.
The lasers stay outside the package: the DS6005 carries 16 ELSFP external laser modules on the front panel that can be swapped in the field, so a failed laser does not take the switch out of service, and the 64 1.6TbE ports terminate in 16 MMC-16 fiber connectors. Celestica also cites CPO-aware software management for the platform, though it has not described what that covers.
“AI infrastructure is driving unprecedented demand for bandwidth, while power, thermal management, latency, and reach are becoming increasingly important constraints,” said Gavin Cato, SVP & GM Portfolio Solutions & AI Platform Engineering at Celestica. “The DS6005 brings co-packaged optics, liquid cooling, field-replaceable external laser modules, and CPO-aware software management together in a compact platform designed to help customers build scalable and power-efficient AI fabrics.”
Celestica has not published power or latency figures for the DS6005, so the savings over a pluggable-optics switch remain something to investigate further. Broadcom’s Manish Mehta, vice president of marketing and operations for its Optical Systems Division, said the partnership covers silicon, optical engines, packaging, thermal design, manufacturing, and system integration, and Dell’Oro Group’s Sameh Boujelbene noted in the same announcement that pluggable, near-package, and co-packaged optics will coexist as the ecosystem matures.
Thermal Management
The DS6005 is fully liquid-cooled in a 1.5OU chassis for ORv3-HPR, the OCP high-power rack, with the coolant quick-disconnects and the DC input on the rear panel. Celestica says the cooling keeps switch-level temperature stable, which improves reliability and allows denser racks, and its product page claims the design prevents thermal throttling. Beyond the switch ASIC and optics, the system runs an AMD Ryzen x86 host CPU with a BMC, carries TPM 2.0, a hardware root of trust, and post-quantum cryptography support, and has IEEE 1588 and SyncE timing hardware.
The switch runs SONiC with ONIE for installation, though Celestica has not named a SONiC release, and its specifications are preliminary and subject to change. The announcement and product documentation do not give sampling, shipping, or general-availability dates.
