Although this test demonstrated that the proposed controller can operate with satisfactory performance during the printing of another layer\, it does not constitute comprehensive validation across different geometries\, parts\, or processing conditions\, as interlayer effects\, such as heat accumulation from previously deposited layers\, were not considered\. The closed\-loop control proposed in this paper consists of two parts\: prediction and control\. The idea behind this was to first predict the future output\, which is the future melt pool emissions in this case\, by estimating the Markov parameters\, and then update the control input accordingly\. The melt pool and laser energy data were recorded by the InfiniAM Spectral system\, which comprises two modules\: the MeltVIEW module with two coaxial photodiodes for recording melt pool data\, and the LaserVIEW module with one photodiode for recording laser energy data\. These data\, collected from a Renishaw RenAM 500 printer\, were used to design a data\-based controller intended for future real\-time deployment and evaluated within a simulated environment in MATLAB R2024b\.

The proposed controller aimed to reduce fluctuations in the melt pool data to decrease the likelihood of LOF and keyhole porosity\, both of which can degrade the quality of spinal cages\, considered in the present study\. The DB\-PFPC successfully reduced these fluctuations and regulated the melt pool data toward the setpoint\. The melt pool intensity setpoint was selected as the mean of the open\-loop signal and was used as a representative reference level for the present simulation study\, with the aim of reducing fluctuations associated with measurement noise and surface changes during scanning\. However\, this choice does not establish the mean as an experimentally validated optimal processing condition\. Instead\, it is considered a nominal statistical reference for assessing the feasibility of the proposed controller in regulating the melt pool intensity and reducing its fluctuations\. Nevertheless\, the controller was also tested with several other setpoints\, and the results showed that it successfully regulated the melt pool emissions towards the tested setpoints\. Therefore\, future investigations should focus on deriving an experimentally validated setpoint or determining an appropriate setpoint based on process\-quality requirements\. This study contributes to the application of control systems in L\-PBF by introducing a data\-based control design methodology that links the estimation of Markov parameters of an FIR model to the future melt pool behaviour within a layer\. This predictive capability enables the controller to update the control input based on predicted process behaviour rather than solely reacting to measured deviations\. It should be noted that a limitation of the present study is that the proposed controller is evaluated in a closed\-loop simulation environment rather than deployed directly on the Renishaw RenAM 500 system\. This is due to current hardware and software constraints that restrict real\-time access to intralayer sensing and control inputs\. Although the proposed controller is formulated for online intralayer operation\, practical real\-time implementation and experimental validation were not performed in the present study\. Instead\, the simulation provides a controlled assessment of the feasibility and closed\-loop behaviour of the proposed approach under the assumption that melt pool measurements and laser energy control are available during the laser scanning of each layer\. Experimental implementation on an L\-PBF system with access to these signals is required to verify the controller’s real\-time performance and its effectiveness in reducing actual defects\.

The stability of the proposed closed\-loop system was analysed under both nominal and uncertain cases\, which helped in tuning and selecting a suitable proportional gain to ensure it remained within the stable region\. Furthermore\, a sensitivity analysis of the closed\-loop performance and stability to variations in the control\-design parameters was conducted to assess the extent to which changes in these parameters affect the closed\-loop performance and stability\. A threshold\-based anomaly detection approach\, inspired by \[85\, 86\]\, was employed to identify melt pool emission excursions that may give rise to LOF and keyhole porosity\, as the dataset does not contain physical defect labels\. Although this study demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed DB\-PFPC in regulating melt pool temperature\, several aspects remain to be explored in the future\. The proposed approach does not constitute direct physical defect detection\. Instead\, it identifies defect\-prone signal conditions using statistically defined thresholds\. The reduction observed in the defect\-prone signal excursions demonstrates the ability of the proposed controller to maintain the melt pool emission within the statistically defined threshold region\. However\, it does not establish a reduction in actual defects\. Therefore\, experimental validation using techniques such as computed tomography \(CT\) scanning or other imaging methods is required to determine validated defect thresholds and assess the proposed anomaly detection method by comparing the identified defect\-prone region with the actual physical defects\.

Another aspect that could be considered is extending this control design into interlayer \(layer\-to\-layer\) control design\, where adjustments are applied between layers by the controller\. Although most studies in the literature have adopted an intralayer approach\, the interlayer approach presents distinct advantages as well as challenges\. This aspect warrants further investigation to assess its effectiveness\, particularly given its greater compatibility with the Renishaw RenAM 500 system for practical implementation\.

Beyond improving the quality of the final spinal cages\, which was the primary focus of this work\, future research could also consider integrating optimisation of energy consumption and CO\\\(\_\{2\}\\\) impact into the control design to enhance environmental sustainability\. This could be achieved by designing a recommender system that serves as a supervisory controller\, balancing and trading off between part quality and environmental impact\.

\#\# Abbreviations

\- Term\:

Definition

\- Control\:

A discipline concerned with regulating the behaviour of dynamical systems using feedback and algorithms \[1\]\.

\- Control signal\:

The controller output that is calculated and applied to the system to achieve the control objective \[2\]\.

\- Control system\:

A group of interacting elements that work together to drive the measured variable toward the desired value \(set point\) \[3\]\.

\- Disturbance\:

An uncontrollable input that is not known accurately in advance and is not manipulable by the control designer\. The control system should therefore be designed to effectively handle and mitigate its effects \[4\]\.

\- Feedback\:

A looped signal or process used to control a system \[5\]\.

\- Reference\:

A desired value of a system \[5\]\.

\- System identification\:

The set of techniques used to derive mathematical models of dynamical systems from measured input–output data \[6\]\.

\- Control law\:

The algorithm or mathematical formula used by the controller to dynamically adjust the control signal\, aiming to drive the system output toward the desired setpoint \[7\]\.

records.title: Hybrid tool electrodes for electrical discharge machining: fused deposition modeling combined with electroless copper plating and copper electroplating
records.abstract: The fabrication of tool electrodes with complex geometries remains a major technological challenge in electrical discharge machining (EDM). This critical review analyzes a hybrid strategy that combines additive manufacturing of a polymer core with subsequent electroless and electrolytic copper deposition to obtain electrically conductive tool electrodes. The principal 3D printing technologies—FDM/FFF, SLA/DLP, SLS, and PolyJet—are compared for polymer core fabrication. By the considered criteria, FDM/FFF and SLA/DLP show the greatest practical potential for polymer cores for subsequent metallization. FDM/FFF offers equipment/material availability and process flexibility; SLA/DLP provides lower surface roughness and higher dimensional accuracy. FDM parameters – layer thickness, nozzle temperature, infill density, and build orientation – are examined for effects on geometric accuracy, surface roughness, and thus metal coating adhesion and uniformity. Primary metallization methods (electroless deposition, physical vapor deposition, conductive pastes) and subsequent copper electroplating are analyzed. A synthesis of experimental data shows that in most studies that included a comparison with a solid copper tool electrode, electrodes with a printed polymer core (mainly ABS) and a copper coating provided comparable material removal rate, wear, and machined surface roughness under finishing and semi-finishing conditions; at the same time, in several studies the hybrid electrodes were inferior to solid copper in material removal rate or wore 1.1–2.8 times faster, and data on the service life of the copper shell are lacking. Optimizing FDM parameters and selecting a metallization method should be treated as interdependent stages of an integrated process chain determining hybrid tool electrode performance.
records.summary: This critical review examines a hybrid route to EDM tool electrodes in which a polymer core is additively manufactured and then metallized by electroless copper deposition followed by copper electroplating. The authors compare FDM/FFF, SLA/DLP, SLS and PolyJet for core fabrication, concluding that FDM/FFF (equipment and material availability, process flexibility) and SLA/DLP (lower surface roughness, higher dimensional accuracy) have the greatest practical potential. FDM parameters such as layer thickness, nozzle temperature, infill density and build orientation are analyzed for their influence on geometric accuracy, surface roughness and hence coating adhesion and uniformity. Synthesizing published experimental data, the review reports that in most studies comparing against solid copper electrodes, printed ABS cores with copper coatings gave comparable material removal rate, wear and machined surface roughness under finishing and semi-finishing conditions, while in several studies hybrid electrodes were inferior in material removal rate or wore 1.1–2.8 times faster. The authors emphasize that FDM parameter optimization and metallization selection are interdependent stages of one process chain, and note that data on copper shell service life are lacking.
records.why_it_matters: For engineers developing additively manufactured EDM electrodes, the review indicates that core printing parameters and metallization method must be co-optimized as a single process chain, since surface finish and dimensional accuracy of the printed core govern coating adhesion and uniformity and thus electrode performance.

Pavel Antipov, Alexander Vaskovsky, Ivan Zubkov, Victor Klushin, Ekaterina Korsunova, Alina Petrenko, Elena Chernyaeva
Abstract
The fabrication of tool electrodes with complex geometries remains a major technological challenge in electrical discharge machining (EDM). This critical review analyzes a hybrid strategy that combines additive manufacturing of a polymer core with subsequent electroless and electrolytic copper deposition to obtain electrically conductive tool electrodes. The principal 3D printing technologies—FDM/FFF, SLA/DLP, SLS, and PolyJet—are compared for polymer core fabrication. By the considered criteria, FDM/FFF and SLA/DLP show the greatest practical potential for polymer cores for subsequent metallization. FDM/FFF offers equipment/material availability and process flexibility; SLA/DLP provides lower surface roughness and higher dimensional accuracy. FDM parameters – layer thickness, nozzle temperature, infill density, and build orientation – are examined for effects on geometric accuracy, surface roughness, and thus metal coating adhesion and uniformity. Primary metallization methods (electroless deposition, physical vapor deposition, conductive pastes) and subsequent copper electroplating are analyzed. A synthesis of experimental data shows that in most studies that included a comparison with a solid copper tool electrode, electrodes with a printed polymer core (mainly ABS) and a copper coating provided comparable material removal rate, wear, and machined surface roughness under finishing and semi-finishing conditions; at the same time, in several studies the hybrid electrodes were inferior to solid copper in material removal rate or wore 1.1–2.8 times faster, and data on the service life of the copper shell are lacking. Optimizing FDM parameters and selecting a metallization method should be treated as interdependent stages of an integrated process chain determining hybrid tool electrode performance.

additive manufacturing; tool electrodes; fused deposition modeling; copper plating; electrical discharge machining (EDM)

Printing technology comparison: FDM/FFF favored for equipment/material availability and flexibility; SLA/DLP favored for lower surface roughness and higher dimensional accuracy; SLS and PolyJet also compared.
FDM parameters examined for effects on accuracy, roughness and coating quality: layer thickness, nozzle temperature, infill density and build orientation.

\#\#\# Hybrid tool electrodes for electrical discharge machining\: fused deposition modeling combined with electroless copper plating and copper electroplating

Pavel Antipov\, Alexander Vaskovsky\, Ivan Zubkov\, Victor Klushin\, Ekaterina Korsunova\, Alina Petrenko\, Elena Chernyaeva

\#\#\#\# Abstract

The fabrication of tool electrodes with complex geometries remains a major technological challenge in electrical discharge machining \(EDM\)\. This critical review analyzes a hybrid strategy that combines additive manufacturing of a polymer core with subsequent electroless and electrolytic copper deposition to obtain electrically conductive tool electrodes\. The principal 3D printing technologies—FDM\/FFF\, SLA\/DLP\, SLS\, and PolyJet—are compared for polymer core fabrication\. By the considered criteria\, FDM\/FFF and SLA\/DLP show the greatest practical potential for polymer cores for subsequent metallization\. FDM\/FFF offers equipment\/material availability and process flexibility\; SLA\/DLP provides lower surface roughness and higher dimensional accuracy\. FDM parameters – layer thickness\, nozzle temperature\, infill density\, and build orientation – are examined for effects on geometric accuracy\, surface roughness\, and thus metal coating adhesion and uniformity\. Primary metallization methods \(electroless deposition\, physical vapor deposition\, conductive pastes\) and subsequent copper electroplating are analyzed\. A synthesis of experimental data shows that in most studies that included a comparison with a solid copper tool electrode\, electrodes with a printed polymer core \(mainly ABS\) and a copper coating provided comparable material removal rate\, wear\, and machined surface roughness under finishing and semi\-finishing conditions\; at the same time\, in several studies the hybrid electrodes were inferior to solid copper in material removal rate or wore 1\.1–2\.8 times faster\, and data on the service life of the copper shell are lacking\. Optimizing FDM parameters and selecting a metallization method should be treated as interdependent stages of an integrated process chain determining hybrid tool electrode performance\.

\#\#\#\# Keywords

additive manufacturing\; tool electrodes\; fused deposition modeling\; copper plating\; electrical discharge machining \(EDM\)

records.title: Facet-Dependent Plating/Stripping Behavior and Crystallographic Evolution during Cycling on Zn Metal Anodes
records.abstract: Abstract Aqueous zinc metal batteries offer a safe and low-cost option for scalable energy storage; however, their practical reversibility is limited by nonuniform Zn plating/stripping and dendritic growth. Here, Zn single-crystal electrodes exposing well-defined (002), (100), and (101) crystalline facets were used to isolate the role of crystallography in Zn metal cycling. Zn deposition is strongly facet-dependent, forming hexagonal, rectangular/prismatic, and corner-defined morphologies on (002), (100), and (101) facets, respectively. Time-dependent SEM further reveals that Zn growth proceeds via discrete edge- or corner-initiated crystallographic units rather than uniform terrace coverage. During stripping, Zn metal is removed via facet-preserved mesoscopic dissolution domains, leaving geometry-defined pits rather than random corrosion-like features. However, these pits are not preferentially refilled during subsequent plating. Repeated cycling redirects Zn growth to protrusions and roughened regions, causing mossy/dendritic accumulation, mixed-texture evolution, and loss of epitaxial reversibility. These findings highlight the need to control both oriented deposition and poststripping surface reconstruction.

The authors used Zn single-crystal electrodes exposing well-defined (002), (100), and (101) facets to isolate crystallographic effects on cycling. Deposition was strongly facet-dependent, producing hexagonal, rectangular/prismatic, and corner-defined morphologies on (002), (100), and (101) facets respectively, and time-dependent SEM indicated growth via discrete edge- or corner-initiated crystallographic units rather than uniform terrace coverage. Stripping removed Zn through facet-preserved mesoscopic dissolution domains, leaving geometry-defined pits rather than random corrosion-like features, but these pits were not preferentially refilled on subsequent plating. Repeated cycling redirected growth to protrusions and roughened regions, causing mossy/dendritic accumulation, mixed-texture evolution, and loss of epitaxial reversibility. This summary is based on the abstract only; the full text was not retrieved.
records.why_it_matters: The finding that stripping pits are not preferentially refilled implies that engineering oriented deposition alone is insufficient; anode or electrolyte designs must also promote post-stripping surface reconstruction to prevent cycling-induced roughening and dendrite formation.

records.body_text:
Lightmatter and Flex Bring 204.8 Tbps Co-Packaged Optics Into Open Racks
Lightmatter unveiled a 204.8 Tbps CPO switch tray built with Flex and a 102.4 Tbps four-XPU tray at the 2026 OCP Global Summit, the first systems to carry Passage co-packaged optics and Guide DR lasers in Open Rack Version 3 and Modular Hardware System designs. Futurum assesses whether open rack standards can pull co-packaged optics into volume production.
What is Covered in this Article
- A 204.8 Tbps CPO switch tray in 1RU developed with Flex as a production validation system
- A 102.4 Tbps XPU tray carrying four accelerator ASICs and two CPUs on DC-MHS chassis infrastructure from a major ODM partner
- The first ORv3 and MHS-based systems with Passage CPO, Guide DR laser modules, and vClick detachable optics
- Fiber connectivity from SENKO and expanded beam PRIZM TMT connector technology from Corning
- The first proof of concept for the Open Silicon Photonics for AI Systems white paper, with the OCP initiative now above 20 companies
- Lightmatter’s roadmap through NPO form factors in 2027-2028 and the Passage M1000 interposer in late 2028
The News: Lightmatter unveiled Passage co-packaged optics (CPO), Guide DR external laser modules, and vClick Optics integrated into a switch tray and an XPU tray built to Open Compute Project (OCP) rack and server specifications at the 2026 OCP Global Summit in San Jose. Flex collaborated with Lightmatter on the 204.8 Tbps CPO switch tray, a 1RU production validation platform that integrates eight Passage CPO bidirectional (BiDi) engines powered by Guide DR laser modules in a liquid-cooled chassis. Separately, Lightmatter developed a 102.4 Tbps CPO XPU tray housing four accelerator ASICs and two CPUs on Data Center Modular Hardware System (DC-MHS) infrastructure provided by another major ODM, with expanded beam PRIZM TMT optical connector technology from Corning and fiber connectivity from SENKO. Both designs follow the Open Rack Version 3 (ORv3) and Modular Hardware System (MHS) specifications, and the XPU tray is the first proof of concept for the “Architecture Vision: Open Silicon Photonics for AI Systems” white paper contributed to OCP.
“In an AI factory, interconnect bandwidth sets the ceiling on compute,” said Nick Harris, Ph.D., Founder and CEO at Lightmatter. “Alignment towards a unified rack architecture for silicon photonics will significantly accelerate adoption.” The companies work together in the Open Silicon Photonics for AI Systems initiative, announced in August, which now includes more than 20 companies.
Lightmatter and Flex Bring 204.8 Tbps Co-Packaged Optics Into Open Racks
Analyst Take: The Lightmatter CPO systems at OCP Global Summit mark the moment co-packaged optics stopped being a technology demonstration and started looking like data center infrastructure. Every CPO rack shown publicly to date, including prototypes from NVIDIA and Broadcom, has been a proprietary design that bears little resemblance to the hardware hyperscalers actually deploy. Lightmatter and Flex built the opposite artifact: a 204.8 Tbps switch tray in a single rack unit that follows ORv3 and MHS specifications, uses DC-MHS chassis infrastructure, and exists specifically so Flex can validate its production design and manufacturing flow for photonic systems. The companion XPU tray carries four accelerators and two CPUs with 102.4 Tbps of scale-up optical bandwidth, with Guide DR laser modules that blind mate as the tray slides into the rack. Lightmatter claims the switch design packs the optical bandwidth of a two-to-four rack unit system into one, with 2-4x better rack faceplate density than conventional ELSFP lasers and unidirectional fiber harnesses. The industry’s CPO conversation is shifting from whether the optics work to whether an ODM can build them in volume, and that shift favors whoever defines the open template first.
Futurum forecasts AI networking spend approaching $350 billion in 2030, and optics can win a significant share of it only on terms cloud operators have already set: chips and switches from different vendors connecting over an open optical interface, with roadmap stability and multi-vendor supply. That is the gap the Open Silicon Photonics for AI Systems initiative is built to close. Launched in August with 19 companies and now above 20, including Celestica, Dell Technologies, Flex, Foxconn Interconnect Technology, Qualcomm, and Quanta Cloud Technology, the initiative published a 300-page architecture vision document that maps a shared MHS-based CPO rack architecture spanning silicon photonics, VCSELs, and micro-LEDs, with first specifications expected in Q4 2026. The white paper incorporates link-layer work from OIF and the OCI MSA, which was first to specify BiDi and DWDM for data center optics, rather than duplicating it. Lightmatter demonstrated BiDi and DWDM in rack validation systems a year before the OCI MSA was announced and reconfigured its 16-wavelength demo to replicate the MSA’s Gen 2 spec at OFC. Standards participation is necessary rather than sufficient. The initiative must now convert a well-regarded document into adopted specifications while NVIDIA ships proprietary CPO switches into the same window.
Flex Turns a Demo Into a Production Validation Exercise
The Flex collaboration is the most commercially meaningful element of the announcement because of what Flex is doing with it. Flex uses the switch tray design to validate its entire production process and production flow for photonics, and that the tray is engineered to look like hardware a hyperscaler build chain could produce in volume. That positions Flex ahead of an ODM field that has mostly waited for photonics to arrive. Celestica dominates the switch ODM arena today on copper infrastructure, and the transition to optics opens share-shift windows that forward-leaning manufacturers want to capture. Dell Technologies, a larger player still by hyperscale data center revenue, is a major contributor to the standard and is presenting jointly with Lightmatter at the summit.
The XPU tray extends the story to compute: it is the industry’s first compute tray to connect four XPUs with 102.4 Tbps of scale-up optical bandwidth in a single rack unit, replacing the copper backplanes that limit scale-up domains to one or two racks today. One caution applies. The switch tray is a validation platform rather than a product; no hyperscaler has publicly committed to deploying either design, and Lightmatter’s first production sampling year is 2027, so an execution gap remains between an OCP booth and a purchase order.
Serviceable Connectors and Laser Supply Address CPO’s Two Hardest Objections
The component debuts answer the objections that have kept operators cautious on CPO. vClick Optics, developed with SENKO using its SEAT detachable optical interface and Metallic PIC Coupler technologies, gives Passage a low-loss, field-detachable fiber connection compatible with mold-and-grind advanced packaging. \# Lightmatter and Flex Bring 204\.8 Tbps Co\-Packaged Optics Into Open Racks

Lightmatter unveiled a 204\.8 Tbps CPO switch tray built with Flex and a 102\.4 Tbps four\-XPU tray at the 2026 OCP Global Summit\, the first systems to carry Passage co\-packaged optics and Guide DR lasers in Open Rack Version 3 and Modular Hardware System designs\. Futurum assesses whether open rack standards can pull co\-packaged optics into volume production\.

\#\# What is Covered in this Article

\- A 204\.8 Tbps CPO switch tray in 1RU developed with Flex as a production validation system
\- A 102\.4 Tbps XPU tray carrying four accelerator ASICs and two CPUs on DC\-MHS chassis infrastructure from a major ODM partner
\- The first ORv3 and MHS\-based systems with Passage CPO\, Guide DR laser modules\, and vClick detachable optics
\- Fiber connectivity from SENKO and expanded beam PRIZM TMT connector technology from Corning
\- The first proof of concept for the Open Silicon Photonics for AI Systems white paper\, with the OCP initiative now above 20 companies
\- Lightmatter’s roadmap through NPO form factors in 2027\-2028 and the Passage M1000 interposer in late 2028

The News\: Lightmatter unveiled Passage co\-packaged optics \(CPO\)\, Guide DR external laser modules\, and vClick Optics integrated into a switch tray and an XPU tray built to Open Compute Project \(OCP\) rack and server specifications at the 2026 OCP Global Summit in San Jose\. Flex collaborated with Lightmatter on the 204\.8 Tbps CPO switch tray\, a 1RU production validation platform that integrates eight Passage CPO bidirectional \(BiDi\) engines powered by Guide DR laser modules in a liquid\-cooled chassis\. Separately\, Lightmatter developed a 102\.4 Tbps CPO XPU tray housing four accelerator ASICs and two CPUs on Data Center Modular Hardware System \(DC\-MHS\) infrastructure provided by another major ODM\, with expanded beam PRIZM TMT optical connector technology from Corning and fiber connectivity from SENKO\. Both designs follow the Open Rack Version 3 \(ORv3\) and Modular Hardware System \(MHS\) specifications\, and the XPU tray is the first proof of concept for the “Architecture Vision\: Open Silicon Photonics for AI Systems” white paper contributed to OCP\.

“In an AI factory\, interconnect bandwidth sets the ceiling on compute\,” said Nick Harris\, Ph\.D\.\, Founder and CEO at Lightmatter\. “Alignment towards a unified rack architecture for silicon photonics will significantly accelerate adoption\.” The companies work together in the Open Silicon Photonics for AI Systems initiative\, announced in August\, which now includes more than 20 companies\.

\#\# Lightmatter and Flex Bring 204\.8 Tbps Co\-Packaged Optics Into Open Racks

Analyst Take\: The Lightmatter CPO systems at OCP Global Summit mark the moment co\-packaged optics stopped being a technology demonstration and started looking like data center infrastructure\. That is the gap the Open Silicon Photonics for AI Systems initiative is built to close\. The white paper incorporates link\-layer work from OIF and the OCI MSA\, which was first to specify BiDi and DWDM for data center optics\, rather than duplicating it\. Lightmatter demonstrated BiDi and DWDM in rack validation systems a year before the OCI MSA was announced and reconfigured its 16\-wavelength demo to replicate the MSA’s Gen 2 spec at OFC\. Standards participation is necessary rather than sufficient\. The initiative must now convert a well\-regarded document into adopted specifications while NVIDIA ships proprietary CPO switches into the same window\.

\#\#\# Flex Turns a Demo Into a Production Validation Exercise

The Flex collaboration is the most commercially meaningful element of the announcement because of what Flex is doing with it\. records.body_text:
Wiwynn, Ayar Labs, and GUC Advance Co-Packaged Optics with Live Demonstration of Integrated Optical Compute System at OCP Global Summit 2026
PR Newswire
SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 13, 2026
Three-way collaboration showcases platform integration, real-time telemetry and system management readiness, accelerating CPO deployment into rack-scale AI infrastructure
SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Wiwynn, an innovative cloud IT infrastructure provider for data centers, Ayar Labs, the leader in co-packaged optics (CPO) solutions for AI scale-up, and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC), the Advanced ASIC Leader, today announced the latest milestone in their strategic collaboration. For the first time, they are presenting a live demonstration at OCP Global Summit 2026, showcasing Wiwynn's compute system integrating GUC's ASIC with Ayar Labs' TeraPHY™ optical engine paired with SuperNova™ light source, streaming real-time health telemetry.
This demonstration marks a significant step forward from the companies' previous rack-level architecture collaboration, advancing to platform integration and functional validation. The system integrates GUC's multi-chip packages (MCPs) with TeraPHY™ optical engines (OEs), powered by the Ayar Labs SuperNova™ light source. In this live demo, telemetry is continuously polled from the OEs within the MCPs and displayed in real time, proving the optical link is up inside the system. As the tuning subsystem tracks thermal and wavelength drift, key signal quality metrics hold steady, validating the system's real-world operational readiness.
"AI infrastructure is rapidly evolving toward an optically connected future," said William Lin, President and CEO of Wiwynn. "This deeper integration with Ayar Labs and GUC, proving that the optical engine and light source can operate reliably within a real system architecture, marks a significant step forward in our collaboration. Together, we are accelerating CPO deployment at scale, helping hyperscalers build high-bandwidth, more power-efficient, and more scalable AI infrastructure."
Live Demonstration Highlights:
- Silicon-to-System Optical Integration: Wiwynn's system architecture integrates GUC's MCP with Ayar Labs' TeraPHY OEs paired with ELSFP-based high-power SuperNova light sources, into an ORV3-ready compute system.
- OE Telemetry and System Health Monitoring: Real-time optical engine telemetry gives data centers visibility into system status, strengthening reliability at scale.
- Stability Metrics Under Live Operation: As the tuning subsystem tracks thermal and wavelength drift (TX heater activity), key eye metrics (eye height, OMA, ER) hold steady alongside OE and ELSFP temperatures.
- Advanced Cooling Solution: Wiwynn's system-level cooling architecture supports stable operation of optical power under real-world conditions.
- Detachable FAU and In-Chassis Fiber Routing: Demonstration of serviceability and manufacturability at the compute system level.
Deepening Collaboration to Accelerate CPO Commercialization
"AI is driving the industry toward an optically-connected future, and the bar is no longer whether it works; it's whether it can be deployed and managed at scale," said Mark Wade, CEO and co-founder of Ayar Labs. "This demonstration with Wiwynn and GUC is about proving integration and operability in a real platform, and giving data center teams the data they'll need to adopt CPO with confidence. We're proud to work with Wiwynn and GUC to make the next generation of AI infrastructure deployable at hyperscale."
"Integrating optical I/O directly into chip design, and proving its functionality through live system-level demonstration, is a significant achievement in our collaboration with Wiwynn and Ayar Labs," said Sean Tai, President of GUC. "This cross-layer collaborative approach allows us to incorporate system requirements earlier in the chip design phase, significantly shortening the development cycle from silicon innovation to system readiness, and providing our customers with a definitive advantage in the global AI race."
Looking Ahead
AI infrastructure is shifting toward optical-electrical convergence. This demonstration shows CPO has progressed from architectural validation to system-level functional proof, laying a solid foundation for hyperscale adoption. The three companies will continue deepening their collaboration, driving CPO from validation toward high-volume deployment.
Visit the Wiwynn booth at OCP Global Summit 2026 to experience the Compute Tray CPO live demonstration firsthand.
About Wiwynn
Wiwynn is an innovative cloud IT infrastructure provider delivering high-quality computing, storage, and rack-level solutions for leading data centers worldwide. Guided by the vision to "unleash the power of digitalization; ignite the innovation of sustainability," Wiwynn actively invests in next-generation technologies to deliver the best TCO, workload- and energy-optimized IT solutions from cloud to edge. Wiwynn's end-to-end capabilities span server design, system integration, and high-volume L10/L11 rack delivery, backed by a manufacturing network spanning Taiwan, the United States, Mexico, Malaysia, and the Czech Republic.
For more information, please visit Wiwynn website, Facebook, and Linkedin.
About Ayar Labs
Ayar Labs is transforming AI infrastructure with the industry's first proven co-packaged optics (CPO) solution manufactured in partnership with the world's leading semiconductor ecosystem. By unlocking performance gains and reducing workload costs in power-constrained environments, Ayar Labs' optical engines are key to enabling next-generation AI scale-up. Founded in 2015, Ayar Labs is funded by domestic and international venture capital firms, as well as strategic investors including AMD, Applied Ventures, MediaTek, NVIDIA, VentureTech Alliance, and Wiwynn. For more information, visit www.ayarlabs.com.
About GUC
GLOBAL UNICHIP CORP. (GUC) is the Advanced ASIC Leader who provides the semiconductor industry with leading IC implementation and SoC manufacturing services, using advanced process and packaging technology. Based in Hsin-Chu, Taiwan, GUC has developed a global reputation with a presence in China, Europe, Japan, Korea, North America, and Vietnam. GUC is publicly traded on the Taiwan Stock Exchange under the symbol 3443.
For more information about GUC's turnkey design services, please visit GUC Official Website

"AI infrastructure is rapidly evolving toward an optically connected future," said William Lin, President and CEO of Wiwynn. "This deeper integration with Ayar Labs and GUC, proving that the optical engine and light source can operate reliably within a real system architecture, marks a significant step forward in our collaboration. Together, we are accelerating CPO deployment at scale, helping hyperscalers build high-bandwidth, more power-efficient, and more scalable AI infrastructure."
Live Demonstration Highlights:
- Silicon-to-System Optical Integration: Wiwynn's system architecture integrates GUC's MCP with Ayar Labs' TeraPHY OEs paired with ELSFP-based high-power SuperNova light sources, into an ORV3-ready compute system.
- OE Telemetry and System Health Monitoring: Real-time optical engine telemetry gives data centers visibility into system status, strengthening reliability at scale.
- Stability Metrics Under Live Operation: As the tuning subsystem tracks thermal and wavelength drift (TX heater activity), key eye metrics (eye height, OMA, ER) hold steady alongside OE and ELSFP temperatures.
- Advanced Cooling Solution: Wiwynn's system-level cooling architecture supports stable operation of optical power under real-world conditions.
- Detachable FAU and In-Chassis Fiber Routing: Demonstration of serviceability and manufacturability at the compute system level.
Deepening Collaboration to Accelerate CPO Commercialization
"AI is driving the industry toward an optically-connected future, and the bar is no longer whether it works; it's whether it can be deployed and managed at scale," said Mark Wade, CEO and co-founder of Ayar Labs. "This demonstration with Wiwynn and GUC is about proving integration and operability in a real platform, and giving data center teams the data they'll need to adopt CPO with confidence. We're proud to work with Wiwynn and GUC to make the next generation of AI infrastructure deployable at hyperscale."
"Integrating optical I/O directly into chip design, and proving its functionality through live system-level demonstration, is a significant achievement in our collaboration with Wiwynn and Ayar Labs," said Sean Tai, President of GUC. "This cross-layer collaborative approach allows us to incorporate system requirements earlier in the chip design phase, significantly shortening the development cycle from silicon innovation to system readiness, and providing our customers with a definitive advantage in the global AI race."
Looking Ahead
AI infrastructure is shifting toward optical-electrical convergence. This demonstration shows CPO has progressed from architectural validation to system-level functional proof, laying a solid foundation for hyperscale adoption. The three companies will continue deepening their collaboration, driving CPO from validation toward high-volume deployment.

records.abstract: Industrial effluents from electroplating and allied surface-finishing operations may contain chromium (Cr) and nickel (Ni) at concentrations that restrict water reuse while representing potentially recoverable metal resources. This study evaluated dispersive liquid–liquid microextraction (DLLME) using 1-butyl-1-methylpyrrolidinium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide ([BMPyrr][TFSI]) for Cr recovery/preconcentration from industrial wastewater and Ni aqueous-phase removal from a separately investigated aqueous feed. Cr and Ni were investigated using independent single-factor experimental designs covering metal concentration, ionic-liquid volume, centrifugation conditions and NaCl addition. Five real industrial wastewaters were screened for total Cr by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS), and the selected metal-plating wastewater contained 10.31 ppm Cr. Post-extraction [BMPyrr][TFSI] and recovered Cr-containing material were evaluated by reuse testing over three cycles, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX). Chromium recovery reached approximately 89% using 400 μL [BMPyrr][TFSI] at pH 6, 2000 rpm centrifugation, 15 min phase separation and 0.4 g NaCl. In the Ni experiments, the highest measured aqueous-phase removal was 98.2% at 40 ppm Ni, pH 10, 5 mL ionic liquid, 2500 rpm and 2.4 g NaCl. Because hydroxo-speciation and Ni(OH) 2 precipitation/co-sedimentation may contribute at pH 10. FTIR retained the principal TFSI-anion and pyrrolidinium signatures after extraction. SEM-EDX showed Cr enrichment in the recovered solid-associated material, with approximately 12.9 wt% Cr and 8.6 wt% Fe, indicating concomitant recovery of competing species. Reuse performance decreased from 96.1% in the first cycle to 81.8% and 65.6% in the second and third cycles, respectively. [BMPyrr][TFSI]-based DLLME provided substantial Cr recovery/preconcentration and high Ni aqueous-phase removal under the investigated conditions.

Front. Chem. Eng., 13 October 2026
Sec. Environmental Chemical Engineering
Near-quantitative nickel recovery and selective chromium preconcentration from complex industrial wastewaters by pyrrolidinium ionic-liquid dispersive liquid–liquid microextraction
1. Department of Chemical Engineering, Kalasalingam Academy of Research and Education, Krishnankoil, Tamil Nadu, India
2. Department of Chemical Engineering, School of Bio Chemical and Processing Engineering, Kalasalingam Academy of Research and Education, Krishnankoil, Tamil Nadu, India
3. Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Karpagam Academy of Higher Education, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, India
4. Centre for AI and Autonomous Aerial Vehicle Systems (CAAAS), Karpagam Academy of Higher Education, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, India
5. Department of Chemical Engineering, Vel Tech High Tech Dr Rangarajan Dr Sakunthala Engineering College, Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

Abstract
Industrial effluents from electroplating and allied surface-finishing operations may contain chromium (Cr) and nickel (Ni) at concentrations that restrict water reuse while representing potentially recoverable metal resources. This study evaluated dispersive liquid–liquid microextraction (DLLME) using 1-butyl-1-methylpyrrolidinium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide ([BMPyrr][TFSI]) for Cr recovery/preconcentration from industrial wastewater and Ni aqueous-phase removal from a separately investigated aqueous feed. Cr and Ni were investigated using independent single-factor experimental designs covering metal concentration, ionic-liquid volume, centrifugation conditions and NaCl addition. Five real industrial wastewaters were screened for total Cr by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS), and the selected metal-plating wastewater contained 10.31 ppm Cr. Post-extraction [BMPyrr][TFSI] and recovered Cr-containing material were evaluated by reuse testing over three cycles, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX). Chromium recovery reached approximately 89% using 400 μL [BMPyrr][TFSI] at pH 6, 2000 rpm centrifugation, 15 min phase separation and 0.4 g NaCl. In the Ni experiments, the highest measured aqueous-phase removal was 98.2% at 40 ppm Ni, pH 10, 5 mL ionic liquid, 2500 rpm and 2.4 g NaCl. Because hydroxo-speciation and Ni(OH)2 precipitation/co-sedimentation may contribute at pH 10. FTIR retained the principal TFSI-anion and pyrrolidinium signatures after extraction. SEM-EDX showed Cr enrichment in the recovered solid-associated material, with approximately 12.9 wt% Cr and 8.6 wt% Fe, indicating concomitant recovery of competing species. Reuse performance decreased from 96.1% in the first cycle to 81.8% and 65.6% in the second and third cycles, respectively. [BMPyrr][TFSI]-based DLLME provided substantial Cr recovery/preconcentration and high Ni aqueous-phase removal under the investigated conditions.
1 Introduction
Water scarcity and pollution from industrial discharges are some of the biggest issues faced by rapidly growing societies. In addition, industrial wastewaters have degraded our freshwaters to the point where they threaten environmental balance, compliance with regulations, and human health (). Metal-contaminated effluents are particularly problematic: conventional physicochemical treatment can be costly, while the metals themselves retain economic value if they can be recovered. Within a circular-economy framework, metal-bearing wastewater is increasingly viewed not only as a disposal burden but also as a resource-recovery opportunity, provided that compact, selective and cost-effective separation methods are available (; ). Metal finishing, electroplating, coatings, leather processing, pharmaceutical manufacturing and mixed industrial drainage can discharge Cr and Ni into wastewater, where these metals may persist, accumulate in sludge and impede water reuse. Established treatment technologies such as precipitation, ion exchange, membrane filtration and adsorption remain useful, but they can generate secondary waste, lose selectivity in high-ionic-strength matrices or become economically prohibitive when target metals occur at trace-to-intermediate concentrations (; ; ). These constraints motivate the search for miniaturized separation methods that reduce the waste burden while enriching potentially recoverable metal fractions.
Cr and Ni are of particular relevance because of their widespread use in surface-treatment and alloy-related industries. Cr is employed in passivation baths for the corrosion protection of steel, in leather tanning, and in coatings and pigment production, while Ni salts are widely used in electroplating baths and specialty surface finishes. Both metals are regulated as environmental priority substances owing to their persistence, bioaccumulation potential and toxicity, and hexavalent chromium is classified as a confirmed human carcinogen. Their removal from industrial wastewater has been documented extensively. Chemical precipitation, adsorption onto activated carbon, biosorption by microbial biomass, electrocoagulation, membrane processes and ion exchange have all proved effective in specific settings (; ; ; ; ). The performance of these methods can nonetheless fall sharply in real effluents, where high suspended solids, dissolved salts, surfactants and competing cations interfere with mass transfer, foul membranes, disrupt coagulation or reduce sorption capacity. An industrially useful separation strategy must therefore operate reliably against chemically challenging backgrounds while still delivering measurable metal enrichment (; ).
Dispersive liquid-liquid microextraction (DLLME), introduced by , is a miniaturized liquid-liquid separation approach in which a water-miscible disperser rapidly distributes an immiscible extraction phase throughout the aqueous sample, creating a large interfacial area for mass transfer. Subsequent centrifugation coalesces the dispersed droplets and permits collection of an analyte-enriched receiving phase. The evolution of DLLME and its extension to inorganic analytes have been described extensively (; ; ), while ionic-liquid DLLME formats have been reviewed by . Relative to conventional liquid-liquid extraction, DLLME can reduce solvent volume and extraction time, although the extent of solvent minimization depends on the specific operating conditions used.
The measured DLLME response is governed by interacting variables including pH, ionic strength, extractant type and volume, disperser composition, complexing chemistry and phase-separation conditions. Chromium microextraction studies have emphasized pH-controlled speciation and ligand selection for differentiating Cr(III) and Cr(VI); an earlier ultrasonic ionic-liquid DLLME method for Cr(VI) was reported by , followed by more recent Cr-speciation and extraction studies (; ; ). For nickel, ionic-liquid DLLME likewise depends strongly on complexation conditions, extractant loading and solution composition (; ). Deep eutectic solvents have also emerged as related alternative extraction media in analytical separations (; ). These variables affect both analyte depletion from the aqueous phase and the composition of the collected phase and therefore require metal-specific experimental screening.
Ionic liquids (ILs) broaden the solvent-design space available for DLLME because their density, viscosity, polarity, hydrophobicity and water solubility can be adjusted through cation-anion selection (; ; ). Hydrophobic ILs can form a discrete receiving phase after dispersion while avoiding the volatility of conventional chlorinated solvents. Water content, chloride and other co-solvents can substantially alter IL density and viscosity, so matrix composition and solvent handling remain important (). Recent reviews also identify solvent recovery, toxicity, aqueous loss and cost as constraints that must be considered together with extraction performance (; ; ).
Recent IL-DLLME investigations have focused predominantly on analytical preconcentration. developed a task-specific IL-DLLME method for sequential Cr(III)/Cr(VI) extraction, while reported an ionic-liquid DLLME procedure for Ni(II) with a preconcentration factor of 100. In both cases, trace determination was the analytical endpoint; recovery of a reusable metal product from high-strength industrial effluent was not evaluated.
Published recovery studies provide quantitative reference values for Cr and Ni separation. reported 99.3% Cr(VI) removal by ion exchange, 96.67% reductive desorption and 98.6% chromium recovery by subsequent precipitation. achieved 99.67% Cr(VI) extraction and 95.40% overall chromium recovery using multistage amide-based solvent extraction, while a later amide-Cyanex 272 system provided more than 99% extraction and more than 98% stripping efficiency (). For nickel, recovered 95.6% of Ni from a concentrated real-electroplating-wastewater eluent by electrodeposition after fixed-bed ion exchange, and reported 94.84% Ni recovery from electroless nickel-plating wastewater using coupled electrocatalytic oxidation and electrodeposition. These values were obtained using different feed compositions, metal species and recovery endpoints. In the present work, AAS quantified total Cr without independent Cr(III)/Cr(VI) speciation; direct mechanistic equivalence with Cr(VI)-specific recovery studies is therefore not established.
The experimental programme evaluated conventional DLLME with [BMPyrr][TFSI] for Cr recovery/preconcentration from an industrial wastewater matrix and for Ni aqueous-phase removal in a separate aqueous feed. It included physicochemical characterization of the source matrices, single-factor screening of operating variables, AAS screening of five real industrial wastewaters for Cr, ionic-liquid reuse over three cycles, FTIR analysis before and after extraction, and SEM-EDX examination of the recovered Cr-containing material. The analysis covered condition-dependent response trends, solvent stability and reuse, aqueous-phase depletion relative to phase-specific extraction, and Cr enrichment in the recovered solid-associated material.
2 Materials and methods
2.1 Wastewater and experimental design
Industrial wastewater was used for the chromium experiments, whereas a separate aqueous feed of comparable volume was used for the nickel experiments. Cr and Ni were evaluated over independent single-factor ranges appropriate to the respective experimental campaigns. For Cr, the 10–60 ppm concentration range included the concentration measured in the selected plating wastewater (10.31 ppm) and extended to higher loadings to examine the concentration response; the 100–600 µL ionic-liquid range corresponded to 1%–6% of the 10 mL aqueous sample volume. For Ni, 40–240 ppm and 1–6 mL ionic liquid were investigated over a broader loading and receiving-phase range. Centrifugation from 500 to 3000 rpm spanned the available laboratory operating window, and graded NaCl additions were used to examine the ionic-strength response. The highest response observed within each single-factor range represents a local experimental maximum; no multivariable statistical optimum was determined. The Ni experiments used ionic-liquid-to-aqueous-feed volume ratios of 0.1–0.6, and these conditions do not represent solvent-minimized operation.
2.2 Wastewater sampling and physicochemical characterization
Wastewater samples were collected from the collection tanks of an industrial effluent treatment facility situated at Malumichampatti, Coimbatore District, Tamil Nadu, India. The facility receives effluent from five industrial sources representative of regional metal-bearing streams: a pharmaceutical manufacturing unit, a municipal/industrial sewage stream, a leather-tanning unit, a paint-and-coating unit and a metal-electroplating unit. Samples of each incoming stream were collected separately at the facility. Grab samples were collected in pre-cleaned high-density polyethylene containers that had been washed with dilute nitric acid and rinsed with deionised water. Samples were transported to the laboratory under cool conditions and stored at 4 °C in the dark before analysis. Aliquots reserved for metal determination were acidified to pH < 2 with concentrated nitric acid, following standard preservation practice for trace-metal samples (). Characterization and extraction experiments were carried out on well-mixed subsamples; coarse settleable solids were allowed to settle only where necessary to obtain clear phase separation.
Baseline water-quality parameters were measured before extraction to establish the chemical context in which the separation experiments were conducted. Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), turbidity, total hardness, chloride concentration, total suspended solids (TSS), total dissolved solids (TDS) and pH for the Cr-bearing industrial wastewater and Ni-bearing aqueous feed are provided in Table 1. These parameters are relevant because particulate load, salinity and solution chemistry can affect DLLME dispersion, sedimentation and apparent aqueous-phase depletion. Standard methods were followed for the reported physicochemical determinations ().
TABLE 1
Parameter | Unit | Chromium-bearing industrial wastewater | Nickel-bearing aqueous feed
---|---|---|---
BOD | mg/L | 19 | 28
COD | mg/L | 389 | 271
Turbidity | NTU | 59 | 49
Total hardness | mg/L as CaCO3 | 568 | 479
Chloride concentration | mg/L | 374.377 | 298.69
TSS | mg/L | 3471.38 | 2987.36
TDS | mg/L | 9742.47 | 7835.98
pH | - | 10.0 | 9.5
Physicochemical characteristics of the chromium-bearing industrial wastewater and nickel-bearing aqueous feed.
2.3 Ionic liquid and DLLME extraction system
The recovery medium used throughout this work was 1-butyl-1-methylpyrrolidinium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide ([BMPyrr][TFSI]), which served as the water-immiscible receiving phase in the DLLME process. The general procedure is summarized schematically in Figure 1. The ionic liquid, pre-dissolved in a water-miscible polar disperser, was rapidly injected into the aqueous sample to generate a fine cloudy dispersion. Centrifugation subsequently coalesced the dispersed droplets and produced a dense ionic-liquid-rich phase that could be collected for analysis. Physicochemical measurements reported for [BMPyrr][TFSI] show a density of approximately 1.40 g cm−3 near room temperature, together with well-characterized viscosity and thermal behaviour, properties that are advantageous for formation and sedimentation of a discrete receiving phase ().
FIGURE 1
[BMPyrr][TFSI] functioned as the hydrophobic, dense and chemically stable receiving phase in the DLLME system. Its water immiscibility limits loss of the receiving phase during dispersion, while a density of approximately 1.40 gcm−3 near room temperature favours formation of a sedimented ionic-liquid-rich phase after centrifugation (). Pyrrolidinium-TFSI systems also exhibit chemical and thermal stability under the mild conditions used here, and the TFSI anion and pyrrolidinium cation provide characteristic FTIR bands for assessment of solvent integrity before and after extraction (; ; ). No comparative screening against alternative ionic liquids was performed; consequently, relative Cr- or Ni-specific affinity among ionic-liquid families was not determined.
TFSI− is a weakly coordinating anion, and metal transfer in ionic-liquid extraction depends on aqueous speciation, complex formation, ion pairing, ionic strength and phase-volume ratio. Under the investigated conditions [BMPyrr][TFSI] formed a separable dense receiving phase after dispersion and centrifugation. Relative extraction performance against imidazolium-, ammonium- or phosphonium-based ionic liquids was not measured in the experimental programme ().
2.4 Chromium-recovery experiments
For chromium recovery, five parameters were screened sequentially. Extractant volume was varied from 100 to 600 μL at an initial chromium concentration of 20 ppm, pH 6.0, 3000 rpm and 10 min. Feed concentration was examined from 10 to 60 ppm at 400 µL extractant, pH 6.0 and 3000 rpm. Centrifugation speed was studied using a 10 ppm feed, 400 µL extractant and pH 6.0, and centrifugation time was varied from 3 to 18 min at 3000 rpm. Finally, NaCl addition (0.1–0.6 g) was tested at pH 6.0, 2000 rpm and 15 min. This sequential single-factor design generated the response profiles used to identify the highest measured response within each operating range (; ).
2.5 Nickel aqueous-phase removal experiments
The nickel aqueous-phase removal experiments covered a wider concentration and ionic-liquid-volume range than the chromium experiments. Initial Ni concentration was varied from 40 to 240 ppm and ionic-liquid volume from 1 to 6 mL, with pH maintained at 10. Centrifugation speed was varied between 500 and 3000 rpm, and NaCl addition between 0.4 and 2.4 g. At pH 10, aqueous Ni depletion can arise from ionic-liquid partitioning together with hydroxo-speciation, complexation and solid formation; the measured response therefore represents the combined decrease in dissolved aqueous Ni under each condition (; ).
2.6 Phase disengagement, salting-out and recovery calculation
Centrifugation was used to promote coalescence of the dispersed ionic-liquid droplets and separation of the ionic-liquid-rich phase from the aqueous phase. Sodium chloride was added in both single-factor studies to examine ionic-strength and salting-out effects. Recovery/removal was calculated directly from the aqueous-phase mass balance (Equation 1) using AAS-measured concentrations before and after treatment:
When the change in aqueous-phase volume is negligible (Vo ≈ Vf), the expression reduces to Equation 2,
R%=CoVo−CfVf/CoVox100(1)
(1)
R%=Co−Cf/Cox100(2)
(2)
Here, C0 and Cf are the initial and final aqueous metal concentrations measured by AAS, and V0 and Vf are the corresponding aqueous-phase volumes. The mass-balance response quantifies the decrease in dissolved aqueous metal and does not distinguish ionic-liquid transfer from precipitation or co-sedimentation. MATLAB served solely as a numerical calculation and plotting environment for the experimentally measured values. No regression equation, response-surface model, machine-learning model, fitted kinetic expression or independently optimized parameter set was used to generate the reported responses. Lines connecting the measured points are visual guides and were not generated by regression. Replicate-level uncertainty estimates were not available for the screening dataset; the figures therefore show the measured responses without error bars, and inferential statistical tests were not performed. R2 and RMSE were not calculated because no predictive model was fitted.
2.7 AAS screening of real industrial samples
Five real industrial wastewaters were screened by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS): pharmaceutical wastewater (S1), industrial sewage (S2), leather-industry wastewater (S3), paint/coating wastewater (S4) and metal-plating wastewater (S5). AAS was used to quantify total chromium in the screened samples; no independent Cr(III)/Cr(VI) speciation measurement was performed. The Cr concentrations determined by AAS were used to select the plating wastewater matrix for the subsequent Cr recovery experiments ().
2.8 Ionic-liquid recycling, FTIR and SEM-EDX characterization
Post-extraction solvent and recovered solids were evaluated by reuse tests, FTIR spectroscopy and SEM-EDX analysis. The reuse experiment tracked extraction performance over three consecutive cycles of [BMPyrr][TFSI] without intermediate regeneration. FTIR spectra recorded before and after extraction were used to assess retention of the principal functional-group signatures of the ionic liquid, providing qualitative evidence of structural stability (; ). SEM-EDX was used for morphological examination and semi-quantitative elemental assessment of the recovered chromium-containing material using an UltraPlus instrument (Carl Zeiss NTS, Germany) fitted with a Flash Quad 5060F EDX detector (Bruker Nano GmbH, Germany), operated at 20 kV with a 50 s live time.
3 Results and discussion
3.1 Physicochemical properties of the source streams
The Cr-bearing industrial wastewater and Ni-bearing aqueous feed were alkaline and contained substantial dissolved and suspended solids. Their measured pH values were 10.0 and 9.5, respectively. These chemically complex matrices can affect DLLME through ionic background, particulate settling and phase-separation behaviour (; ).
The Cr-bearing stream contained TDS = 9742.47 mg/L and TSS = 3471.38 mg/L, while the Ni-bearing feed contained TDS = 7835.98 mg/L and TSS = 2987.36 mg/L. Total hardness values were 568 and 479 mg/L as CaCO3, respectively. These measurements indicate a substantial dissolved and particulate background. In separation terms, particulate material can sediment during centrifugation, and added salt can alter solvation, interfacial transfer and phase disengagement (; ).
3.2 Single-factor screening for chromium and nickel
The operating variables investigated for Cr and Ni included initial metal concentration, ionic-liquid volume, centrifugation conditions and NaCl addition. Because the experimental ranges and fixed conditions differed between the two metals, each response was evaluated within its own single-factor operating window. Table 2 consolidates the experimental ranges, fixed conditions, best observed values, maximum observed response and qualitative response pattern.
TABLE 2
Metal | Variable | Experimental range | Fixed conditions | Best observed value | Maximum response (%) | Response pattern
---|---|---|---|---|---|---
Cr | Extractant volume | 100–600 µL | 20 ppm; pH 6; 3000 rpm; 10 min | 400 µL | 89 | Bell-shaped
Cr | Initial concentration | 10–60 ppm | 400 µL IL; pH 6; 3000 rpm; 10 min | 10 ppm | 86 | Decreases with loading
Cr | Centrifugation speed | 500–3000 rpm | 10 ppm; 400 µL IL; pH 6; 10 min | 2000 rpm | 83 | Bell-shaped
Cr | Centrifugation time | 3–18 min | 10 ppm; 400 µL IL; pH 6; 3000 rpm | 15 min | 93 | Bell-shaped
Cr | NaCl addition | 0.1–0.6 g | 10 ppm; 400 µL IL; pH 6; 2000 rpm; 15 min | 0.4 g | 86 | Bell-shaped
Ni | Initial concentration | 40–240 ppm | 3 mL IL; pH 10; 2000 rpm | 80 ppm | 96.1 | Peak then decline
Ni | Ionic-liquid volume | 1–6 mL | 40 ppm; pH 10; 3000 rpm | 5 mL | 95.4 | Increase to plateau
Ni | Centrifugation speed | 500–3000 rpm | 40 ppm; 5 mL IL; pH 10 | 2500–3000 rpm | 87.6 | Increase to plateau
Ni | NaCl addition | 0.4–2.4 g | 40 ppm; 5 mL IL; pH 10; 2500 rpm | 2.4 g | 98.2 | Monotonic increase
Comparative single-factor experimental ranges, fixed conditions, best observed values, maximum observed responses and response patterns for chromium and nickel.
3.3 Chromium recovery as a function of extraction conditions
The chromium data showed distinct local maxima across the investigated single-factor ranges. Increasing the extractant volume from 100 to 400 µL raised Cr recovery from about 35% to approximately 89% (Figure 2a), whereas further increases to 500 and 600 µL reduced recovery to 73% and 61%, respectively. Thus, 400 µL produced the highest measured recovery within the extractant-volume series under the corresponding fixed conditions (; ).
FIGURE 2
Feed concentration strongly affected the measured Cr response (Figure 2b). Recovery was 86% at a 10 ppm feed, 46% at 20 ppm and 13% at 60 ppm. Under the fixed solvent condition, recovery therefore decreased as the initial Cr loading increased, a trend consistent with finite receiving-phase capacity and changes in the solute-to-solvent ratio (; ).
The highest Cr recovery in the centrifugation-speed series occurred at 2000 rpm (83%; Figure 2c). Recovery was 46% at 500 rpm and decreased to 71% and 53% at 2500 and 3000 rpm, respectively. In the centrifugation-time series (Figure 2d), recovery increased from 49% at 3 min to 93% at 15 min and decreased to 71% at 18 min. The corresponding local maxima were therefore 2000 rpm for centrifugation speed and 15 min for centrifugation time under their respective fixed conditions.
NaCl addition produced a non-monotonic Cr response (Figure 2e). Recovery increased from 47% at 0.1 g to 86% at 0.4 g and then decreased to 68% at 0.5 g and 59% at 0.6 g. Ionic-strength changes can modify aqueous solvation, interfacial transfer, viscosity and phase disengagement; within the tested range, 0.4 g NaCl gave the highest measured Cr recovery (; ).
Application of 400 µL ionic liquid, pH 6, 2000 rpm, 15 min and 0.4 g NaCl in a combined-condition experiment produced approximately 89% Cr recovery. Because the preceding variable screening was conducted one factor at a time, this result represents the measured response at the tested combination and not a statistically derived global optimum.
3.4 Nickel aqueous-phase removal as a function of extraction conditions
Ni aqueous-phase removal was 94.1% at 40 ppm, increased to 96.1% at 80 ppm and then decreased progressively to 56.9% at 240 ppm (Figure 3a). The Ni experiments were conducted in a separate aqueous feed and under a different pH and solvent-volume range from the Cr experiments.
FIGURE 3
At the fixed ionic-liquid dose used in the concentration series, the largest aqueous-phase removal was observed at 80 ppm, followed by a decrease at higher Ni concentrations. In the separate ionic-liquid-volume series, the response increased to 95.4% at 5 mL and remained essentially unchanged at 6 mL (95.1%), indicating a plateau within the investigated range (Figure 3b).
Ni aqueous-phase removal increased from approximately 55.9% at 500 rpm to 87.6% at 2500 rpm and remained essentially unchanged at 3000 rpm (Figure 3c). The centrifugation-speed response therefore approached a plateau at 2500–3000 rpm under the fixed conditions of this series.
NaCl addition produced the largest change in the Ni aqueous-phase response, increasing removal from 70.7% at 0.4 g to 98.2% at 2.4 g (Figure 3d). The monotonic trend establishes an association between NaCl addition and aqueous Ni depletion within the tested alkaline range. Because the response was calculated from residual aqueous Ni, it includes ionic-liquid partitioning together with pH-dependent hydroxo-speciation and precipitation. The 98.2% value therefore quantifies overall aqueous-phase removal rather than an isolated ionic-liquid distribution coefficient ().
The highest Ni responses occurred in separate single-factor series at approximately 80 ppm initial concentration, 5–6 mL ionic liquid, 2500–3000 rpm and 2.0–2.4 g NaCl. These values were obtained under different fixed conditions and therefore represent local maxima within individual experimental series. In the NaCl series, 98.2% aqueous-phase removal was measured at 40 ppm Ni, pH 10, 5 mL ionic liquid, 2500 rpm and 2.4 g NaCl.
3.5 Comparative summary of chromium recovery and nickel aqueous-phase removal
Cr and Ni exhibited different response patterns across the investigated single-factor variables (Table 2). Cr recovery showed non-monotonic maxima with ionic-liquid volume, centrifugation speed, centrifugation time and NaCl addition. Ni aqueous-phase removal increased to a plateau with ionic-liquid volume and centrifugation speed, while the NaCl series increased monotonically over the tested range.
Intrinsic [BMPyrr][TFSI] selectivity cannot be inferred from the numerical difference between the maximum Cr recovery and Ni aqueous-phase removal because the two metals were examined in different matrices and under different pH values, feed concentrations, ionic-liquid volumes and salt loadings. At pH 10, Ni(II) hydroxo-speciation and Ni(OH)2 formation can contribute to the decrease in dissolved Ni together with ionic-liquid partitioning; the 98.2% value consequently represents overall aqueous-phase removal under the stated condition ().
The measured Cr recovery of approximately 89% was lower than the 95.40% overall recovery reported for multistage amide solvent extraction () and the 96.67% reductive desorption/98.6% precipitation recovery reported for an integrated ion-exchange process (). The maximum Ni aqueous-phase removal of 98.2% was numerically higher than the 95.6% electrodeposition recovery reported after fixed-bed ion exchange () and the 94.84% recovery reported for coupled electrocatalytic oxidation-electrodeposition (). These numerical comparisons describe the reported response magnitudes; equivalence of process performance cannot be inferred because the studies differ in feed composition, Cr oxidation-state specificity, recovery endpoint and separation mechanism.
3.6 Real-sample chromium screening by AAS
AAS was used to screen chromium in each of the five industrial wastewaters. As shown in Table 3, chromium concentrations varied widely among sources. The lowest chromium concentration was measured in pharmaceutical wastewater (S1, 0.28 ppm) and the highest in industrial sewage (S2, 21.42 ppm). Plating wastewater (S5) contained 10.31 ppm Cr and was selected for the recovery experiments because the Cr originated from a defined plating process stream. The individual upstream contributors to the S2 industrial-sewage sample were not separately traced; therefore, the measured value characterizes the composite sampled stream without assigning it to a specific upstream operation.

The pharmaceutical, leather and coating samples contained 0.28, 0.41 and 0.53 ppm Cr, respectively, substantially below the concentration measured in the plating wastewater. Chromium is a functional process input to leather tanning, but the measured S3 concentration is specific to the sampled stream and is not representative of untreated tannery effluent. Among the samples screened, plating wastewater (S5, 10.31 ppm) combined a comparatively high Cr concentration with a traceable process origin. Selection of S5 for the recovery experiments was based on these measured characteristics (; ).
3.7 Ionic-liquid recyclability and FTIR evidence of solvent integrity
Reuse of [BMPyrr][TFSI] was evaluated over three consecutive extraction cycles without intermediate regeneration (Figure 4). Recovery decreased from 96.1% in the first cycle to 81.8% and 65.6% in the second and third cycles, respectively. The higher first-cycle value relative to the Cr response in Section 3.3 occurred at a lower metal loading, consistent with the concentration-response trend shown in Figure 2b. The progressive decrease in recovery indicates loss of extraction performance during repeated use without regeneration (; ).
FIGURE 4
FTIR spectra recorded before (Figure 5) and after (Figure 6) extraction were compared to assess retention of the principal ionic-liquid structural signatures. Diagnostic TFSI-anion bands occurred at essentially the same positions in both spectra, including asymmetric SO2 stretching near 1201 cm−1, C-F stretching of the CF3 groups near 1059 cm−1, and S-N-S/SO2 bending near 619 cm−1. Bands associated with the pyrrolidinium cation and ring framework were likewise retained. The band near 3459 cm−1 is assigned to O-H stretching of residual or adsorbed water, while the weak feature near 2075 cm−1 is treated as a non-diagnostic combination/overtone feature. The retained TFSI-anion and pyrrolidinium bands show that major structural decomposition was not detectable by the FTIR comparison after extraction. FTIR alone does not resolve the cause of the progressive recovery decrease during repeated use; solvent loss, water carry-over and matrix fouling require separate phase mass-balance, washing and regeneration measurements (; ).

3.8 SEM-EDX evidence for the chromium-containing recovered material
SEM-EDX analysis of the solid recovered after DLLME showed a collectable Cr-containing solid-associated phase. The SEM micrograph (Figure 7a) shows an irregular, aggregated particulate morphology. The EDX spectrum (Figure 7b) contains Cr Kα and Kβ peaks at approximately 5.41 and 5.95 keV, respectively, and the semi-quantitative EDX estimate (Table 4) gives 12.9 wt% Cr. Carbon, oxygen, sodium and chlorine were also prominent, with smaller amounts of aluminium, sulphur, potassium, calcium, manganese and iron. The simultaneous detection of Cr and other matrix elements indicates Cr enrichment accompanied by co-recovery rather than phase-pure Cr separation.

The elemental composition provides qualitative information on co-recovery under the investigated conditions. Alongside Cr, EDX indicated Fe at 8.6 wt% and smaller amounts of Mn, Ca and K (Table 4). These co-detected elements reduce the compositional purity of the recovered material relative to Cr alone. Quantitative Cr/Fe selectivity coefficients cannot be obtained from the SEM-EDX composition data and require controlled multicomponent extraction with phase-specific mass balances.
The EDX-derived weight fractions are therefore treated as semi-quantitative composition estimates rather than exact bulk-phase assay values. The SEM morphology describes the recovered particulate material, whereas identification of the governing recovery pathways requires direct phase-specific measurements.
3.9 Integrated mechanistic interpretation
Cr and Ni exhibited distinct condition-dependent response profiles under their respective experimental conditions. Cr recovery at pH 6 showed local maxima for extractant volume, phase-separation conditions and salt loading, whereas Ni aqueous-phase removal at pH 10 increased strongly with ionic-liquid dosage and NaCl addition. Under the alkaline Ni condition, hydroxo-speciation and Ni(OH)2 precipitation/co-sedimentation can contribute to the decrease in dissolved Ni. SEM-EDX detected Cr together with Fe and other elements in the recovered solid-associated material. The measured responses thus represent process-level aqueous-phase depletion under defined conditions and do not provide metal-specific distribution coefficients for a single extraction mechanism (; ; ).
4 Conclusion
The present study evaluated [BMPyrr][TFSI]-based DLLME for the recovery and preconcentration of Cr and the aqueous-phase removal of Ni under independently investigated operating conditions. Chromium recovery from the electroplating-type industrial wastewater reached approximately 89% at 400 µL ionic liquid, pH 6, 2000 rpm centrifugation, 15 min phase-separation time and 0.4 g NaCl. The Cr system exhibited distinct condition-dependent maxima with respect to extractant volume, centrifugation conditions and salt addition, indicating that phase ratio and phase-disengagement characteristics strongly influenced the observed recovery. In the Ni experiments, aqueous-phase removal increased with ionic-liquid dosage and NaCl addition, reaching 98.2% at 40 ppm Ni, pH 10, 5 mL [BMPyrr][TFSI], 2500 rpm and 2.4 g NaCl. Under these alkaline conditions, the measured Ni depletion represents the combined effect of aqueous-phase removal mechanisms, including ionic-liquid partitioning and possible hydroxo-speciation and precipitation/co-sedimentation, rather than exclusive extraction into the ionic-liquid phase. Analysis of real industrial wastewater samples by AAS confirmed the occurrence of Cr in all five investigated streams, with the selected plating wastewater containing 10.31 ppm Cr. FTIR spectra obtained before and after extraction retained the characteristic TFSI-anion and pyrrolidinium signatures, indicating preservation of the principal chemical structure of the ionic liquid during the investigated extraction step. Reuse of [BMPyrr][TFSI] without intermediate regeneration resulted in a progressive decrease in recovery from 96.1% in the first cycle to 81.8% and 65.6% in the second and third cycles, respectively, demonstrating the importance of solvent regeneration for repeated operation. SEM-EDX analysis of the recovered Cr-containing material indicated approximately 12.9 wt% Cr together with 8.6 wt% Fe and smaller amounts of other elements, confirming chromium enrichment while also revealing co-recovery of competing species.
Overall, the results establish [BMPyrr][TFSI] as a hydrophobic receiving phase capable of producing substantial Cr enrichment and high Ni aqueous-phase removal under the investigated conditions. The different response patterns of Cr and Ni further demonstrate the importance of metal-specific operating conditions in ionic-liquid-based DLLME. Further development of the process should focus on phase-specific metal mass balances, quantitative selectivity in multicomponent systems, pH-dependent speciation, ionic-liquid regeneration and back-extraction, reduction of the solvent-to-feed ratio for Ni treatment, and validation at larger process scales. Such investigations are necessary to establish the separation mechanism, solvent efficiency and practical applicability of the process for metal recovery from industrial wastewater.

\# Near\-quantitative nickel recovery and selective chromium preconcentration from complex industrial wastewaters by pyrrolidinium ionic\-liquid dispersive liquid–liquid microextraction
