1 Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM) enables the production of metallic components with high geometric complexity and offers greater design freedom than conventional manufacturing methods. Features such as internal cavities, undercuts, or locally adapted material distributions can be realized more easily than with subtractive processes. Among the established metal AM processes, laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is widely used for comparatively small and complex part geometries, whereas laser beam directed energy deposition (DED-LB/M) is particularly attractive for larger structures, repair applications, and the generation of near-net-shape components [1]. In DED-LB/M, metal powder is delivered into a laser beam, which melts both the incoming powder and the underlying substrate or previously deposited material, thereby forming a metallurgical bond between subsequent tracks or layers [2].
The thermal history during metal AM is of central importance because it strongly affects solidification conditions, residual stresses, microstructure formation, and ultimately the mechanical properties of the manufactured component [3, 4]. Consequently, there is considerable interest in measuring and controlling temperature fields during the process [5]. Because of the high temperatures, the moving heat source, and the dynamic nature of the melt pool, contact-based measurements are difficult to apply during DED-LB/M. Thermocouples, for example, provide only point-wise information at fixed positions and cannot capture the spatial temperature field of the process zone. Therefore, in-situ thermal monitoring is commonly performed using contactless radiometric methods, such as pyrometers and infrared cameras [6, 7]. Pyrometers and short-wave infrared (SWIR) cameras are often integrated coaxially to monitor melt pool temperatures, whereas mid-wave infrared (MWIR) cameras are frequently used in off-axis configurations to capture larger fields of view and broader temperature distributions [8, 9].While pyrometers can provide high temporal resolution, they usually deliver only point-like or spatially averaged measurements. Infrared cameras provide spatially resolved temperature fields. However, as with other radiometric methods, their quantitative interpretation depends critically on the assumed emissivity.
A major challenge in quantitative thermography for metal AM is that emissivity is neither constant nor generally known. It can vary substantially between the melt pool, powder, substrate, and previously solidified material, and it depends on the material itself as well as on wavelength, temperature, phase state, oxidation, surface roughness, and viewing angle [10,11,12,13]. Becker et al. showed that the emissivity of 316L and AlSi10Mg surfaces in PBF-LB/M depends strongly on wavelength, material state, oxidation, and observation angle, with clear differences between powder-covered and consolidated surfaces [11]. Although this investigation was carried out for PBF-LB/M, the core conclusions also strongly apply to DED-LB/M, where changing track geometry, powder delivery, melt pool behavior, and off-axis viewing can further amplify spatial and temporal variations in emissivity. Consequently, conventional single-band thermography, in which the user sets a globally constant emissivity, can be insufficient for physically consistent temperature-field interpretation under spatially varying emissivity conditions. This restricts both process monitoring and the validation of thermal process models that rely on reliable temperature-field information.
Different strategies have been proposed to address emissivity-related uncertainties. A simple and widely used approach is to assume a fixed or only weakly varying emissivity [9, 14,15,16]. This is straightforward to implement but is often inadequate for the heterogeneous surface states encountered in metal AM. A related practical approach is single-point calibration, in which one effective emissivity value is selected such that a known reference temperature, for example the solidification plateau of the processed alloy, is reproduced at a selected location [9, 14]. While this can improve the temperature estimate locally, it does not account for spatial emissivity variations across the melt pool, transition region, and surrounding solid material. A more physically motivated approach is region-wise or state-dependent emissivity assignment, in which different emissivity values are associated with regions such as the melt pool, substrate, powder-covered areas, or previously solidified material. Such approaches depend on suitable effective emissivity values as well as reliable identification of the corresponding process regions [8].
Other approaches aim to reduce or separate the emissivity dependence more directly. Ratio pyrometry determines temperature from the intensity ratio at two wavelengths and can reduce the dependence on absolute emissivity under gray-body assumptions. It is widely used for highly dynamic melt pool monitoring in PBF-LB/M and DED-LB/M, often in coaxial configurations [7, 15, 17]. However, its accuracy depends not only on the gray-body assumption, but also on the emissivity ratio at the selected wavelengths. If this ratio varies with material state, oxidation, surface condition, or process region, the resulting temperature can remain biased, which is particularly relevant for metallic AM surfaces with wavelength-dependent emissivity [11]. Multispectral and hyperspectral thermography provide a more rigorous route toward temperature-emissivity separation, but they also require assumptions, models, or prior information about the spectral emissivity behavior over several wavelengths. Since these emissivity ratios or spectral trends can vary between the melt pool, transition region, powder-covered areas, and solidified material, region-dependent emissivity treatment may still be necessary. In addition, such methods typically require sophisticated instrumentation, radiometric calibration, and substantial adaptation to the specific process setup [10, 12, 18, 19]. Breese and Altenburg used hyperspectral SWIR thermography in PBF-LB/M and determined absolute temperatures in the range of approximately 1300–2700 K with an error of less than 6 % relative to the solidification temperature of 316L [18]. Altenburg et al. demonstrated in DED-LB/M that multispectral SWIR thermography can be used for temperature-emissivity separation and can yield more realistic temperature fields than single-point calibration [12]. Dai et al. presented a radiometrically calibrated multispectral CMOS-based approach and reported relative errors of approximately 1.6-−2.0 % after careful calibration [19]. These studies demonstrate the potential of spectral-radiometric methods and their value as reference approaches for simpler emissivity-correction workflows. However, their direct integration into standard process monitoring remains demanding due to instrumentation and calibration requirements.
Recent studies have demonstrated how process models can support the interpretation of in-situ thermal measurements in DED-LB/M. Pereira et al. coupled thermal imaging data with spatio-temporal temperature models and used a simplified emissivity compensation based on infrared melt-pool segmentation [8]. Maximenko et al. combined surface temperature measurements with analytical and finite-element-based modeling to estimate laser absorptivity from temperature data outside the melt pool [20]. These studies show that model-assisted approaches can provide complementary information on effective radiative or energy-related parameters and on the influence of heat-transfer assumptions and process conditions. However, their reliability depends on model assumptions, material data, boundary conditions, heat-source descriptions, and emissivity or absorptivity assumptions used for calibration or validation.
In parallel, visual imaging has become an established and comparatively practical tool for process monitoring in DED-LB/M. Visual cameras are used in coaxial and off-axis configurations for melt pool observation, deposition height measurement, geometric reconstruction, and defect detection [5, 21,22,23,24,25]. Compared with more specialized spectral thermographic systems, visual camera setups are often easier to integrate and can provide high spatial and temporal resolution at comparatively low system complexity. This makes them particularly attractive for segmentation and geometric interpretation of the process zone [26,27,28]. Ansari et al. reviewed visual process monitoring in DED-LB/M and emphasized its relevance for melt pool monitoring, defect detection, and geometric reconstruction [17]. Ning et al. used a machine-vision approach to detect and compensate height deviations in thin-walled DED-LB/M parts and reported an improvement in height consistency of up to 22.8 % [29]. Zhao et al. used high-speed imaging to capture transient melt pool and bead morphologies on inclined substrates and showed that increasing tilt angle and smaller laser spot diameters promote hump formation and morphological instabilities [30]. However, the use of visual imaging has mainly focused on geometric and morphological process monitoring rather than on emissivity-aware correction of infrared temperature fields.
Overall, the literature reveals a trade-off between physical rigor, measurement complexity, and practical integrability. Spectral-radiometric methods can provide more rigorous temperature-emissivity separation, but they require complex instrumentation and calibration. Region-wise emissivity correction is more practical, but depends on reliable segmentation and suitable effective emissivity values. Visual imaging, by contrast, is already widely used in DED-LB/M and provides high-resolution spatial information that can support such segmentation. Nevertheless, the systematic coupling of visual image segmentation with MWIR thermography for region-specific emissivity correction remains comparatively underexplored, especially for DED-LB/M processes with heterogeneous surface states and off-axis observation geometries.
Against this background, this study introduces a hybrid RGB/MWIR workflow for emissivity-aware temperature field correction in DED-LB/M. Simple single-layer AISI 316L structures are manufactured and monitored using a visual RGB camera and an MWIR camera. The RGB images are used to segment process regions such as the melt pool, transition zone, and surrounding material. These regions are then mapped onto the MWIR data to assign effective region-wise emissivity values and compute corrected temperature fields. The aim is not to provide full temperature-emissivity separation, which remains experimentally demanding, but to offer a practically integrable approach that improves the physical consistency of spatially resolved temperature fields compared with common fixed-emissivity thermography approaches.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Sect. 2 presents the DED-LB/M facility, the employed camera systems, and the image processing workflow used to compute emissivity-corrected temperature fields. Section 3 presents the manufactured structures, recorded image data, fused temperature fields, and uncertainty considerations. Finally, Sect. 4 summarizes the main findings and outlines directions for future work.
2 Experimental setup and methods
2.1 Laser beam directed energy deposition system and material
The present study was carried out at the LMD2 facility of the University of Kassel. This research infrastructure features a unique combination of a highly flexible DED-LB/M system (adAM-RD, ODeCon engineering GmbH, Kaiserslautern, Germany) and a high-performance liquid-metal X-ray source (MetalJet E1+ 160 kV, Excillum, Kista, Sweden), complemented by dedicated detectors enabling both radiographic imaging and X-ray diffraction analysis. For the investigations conducted in this study, only the DED-LB/M system of the facility was used. The DED-LB/M system operates with a 4 kW fiber laser (IPG YLS-2000-S2, IPG Photonics GmbH, Burbach, Germany) featuring a top-hat intensity profile and a wavelength of 1070 nm. Furthermore, the system was specifically designed with an open process chamber configuration to facilitate unobstructed X-ray access and to enable the flexible integration of complementary in-situ diagnostic and monitoring systems.
The diameter of the beam can be adjusted in the focal plane between 0.5 and 1.5 mm using a zoom optics system (HD Sonderoptiken für die Lasertechnik GmbH & Co. KG, Übach-Palenberg, Germany). The powder is fed into the process by a four-disk feeder (GTV PF4/4, GTV Verschleißschutz GmbH, Luckenbach, Germany), via a pneumatic powder switch, and delivered through a coaxial 6-jet nozzle (HIGHNO-13-9, HD Sonderoptiken für die Lasertechnik GmbH & Co. KG, Übach-Palenberg, Germany) with a standoff distance of 13 mm.
For the experiments presented in this paper, a constant spot diameter of 1.0 mm was selected. The laser was moved over the component at a constant speed of 10 mm/s. The powder used in this study was AISI 316L, with a particle size distribution ranging from 50 to 150 μm. The powder mass flow was maintained at a constant rate of 12 g/min, the carrier gas flow at 5 l/min, and the shielding gas flow at 9 l/min. High-purity argon (99.999 %) was used as both a carrier and a shielding gas to protect the melt pool from the atmosphere and reduce oxidation.
The experiments were designed using a simple geometry that allowed comprehensive observation with both camera systems. To clearly reveal the differences caused by table inclination, the structure was produced both with and without table inclination. For this purpose, a flat specimen consisting of ten adjacent tracks was manufactured on a stainless steel substrate plate. The process parameters are summarized in Table 1.
In order to provide the cameras with a better perspective of the process, the build plate was tilted for some experiments at an angle of 55° (see Fig. 1) to align the normal surface with the optical axes of the cameras.
2.2 Imaging system
To ensure a comprehensive observation, two cameras were used for the monitoring: one mid-wave infrared (MWIR) camera and one visual (VIS) RGB camera. The technical specifications of the cameras used are listed in Table 2.
Images in the visible spectrum were acquired using an RGB camera (ace 2 R PRO, Basler AG, Ahrensburg, Germany), equipped with a 50-mm lens (C23-5028-5 M-P, Basler AG, Ahrensburg, Germany) and a short-pass filter (900 nm) that protects the camera from laser radiation. The RGB camera was operated at 156 frames per second. Three individual images were captured successively with varying exposure times (19, 500, and 5000 μs), which were then merged into high dynamic range (HDR) images during the post-processing stage.
The MWIR imaging was performed with an infrared camera (ImageIR 8380 hp, InfraTec GmbH, Dresden, Germany), equipped with a 100-mm lens and an additional close-up optic. The image acquisition was carried out at a frame rate of 200 Hz. A fast rotating filter wheel equipped with four neutral-density filters was used during the experiments to enable HDR imaging with different integration times, allowing a temperature measurement range from 300 to 2000 °C black body temperature. The two cameras were used to record the entire build process.
Figure 2 shows the complete experimental setup at the LMD2 facility. The cameras were arranged to maximize the overlap between their fields of view (FOVs). Furthermore, all cameras were inclined by 59° ± 1° relative to the surface normal of the non-inclined build plate, resulting in a measurement distance of 50 cm ± 1 cm.
Two halogen spotlights were used to illuminate the process for visible-spectrum imaging. This was necessary because the intense visible radiation emitted by the melt pool makes it difficult to capture both the entire component and the melt pool in sufficient detail. The halogen spotlights (ELC-3, OSRAM GmbH, München, Germany) were operated at a power of 250 W each. As the radiation from the halogen spotlights is broadband and should not be detectable in the MWIR range, an additional short-pass filter (KG5, SCHOTT AG, Mainz, Germany) was placed in front of each spotlight. Since these filters are highly sensitive to heat and the spotlights generate substantial thermal load, a Plexiglass plate was inserted between each spotlight and filter. This plate absorbs the heat, is relatively inexpensive, and can be easily replaced after several experiments.
2.3 Image processing pipeline
Figure 3 illustrates the image processing pipeline of the proposed method. As illustrated, the DED-LB/M process is initially monitored, and then HDR images are produced and aligned in time. In parallel, a segmentation of the relevant regions is performed in the visual recordings. In the final step, the MWIR-, RGB-data and the \(\varepsilon \)-map are fused together. The specific methods used for each step of the workflow are described in detail in the following subsections.
2.3.1 High dynamic range and time synchronization
HDR imaging extends the dynamic range by combining images acquired with different exposure or integration times. In this work, HDR imaging was employed to cover a wider temperature range using the MWIR camera, and to clearly depict both the entire component and the melt pool in the visual spectrum using the RGB camera.
To generate the visual RGB HDR images, three individual exposures with exposure times of 19, 500, and 5000 μs were acquired in direct succession. These images were subsequently combined into an HDR image using the exposure fusion algorithm by Mertens et al. [31], implemented in Python using the OpenCV library. At the RGB camera frame rate of 156 fps, the available time per individual exposure is approximately 6410 μs. The longest selected exposure time of 5000 μs therefore remained below this limit while leaving a margin for camera readout and image transfer. Since three individual exposures were combined into one HDR image, the resulting RGB HDR image rate was approximately 52 Hz.
The exposure times were selected empirically to cover complementary intensity ranges of the process. The 19 μs exposure corresponds to the minimum exposure time of the camera and was used to avoid saturation in the hottest melt-pool region. The 5000 μs exposure was selected to capture lower-intensity component regions and the overall component geometry, while the melt pool and parts of the transition zone are overexposed. The 500 μs exposure was chosen as an intermediate compromise that provides sufficient contrast between the melt pool and the surrounding high-temperature transition region. The use of the individual exposure images for segmentation is described in Sect. 2.3.2.
For the creation of the MWIR HDR temperature images, four individual recordings were acquired with integration times of 212, 123, 88 and 402 μs. Each of these images was captured using a specific optical filter in combination with a neutral density filter KG3. The assignment of the respective integration times, calibration ranges and filters used, is shown in Table 3.
Conventional algorithms, such as the Mertens algorithm, cannot be used to combine the four images into a single HDR image because they account for varying exposure times but not for different optical filters. Therefore, the four raw images are combined with each other according to the manufacturer’s calibration. The images were not acquired simultaneously but sequentially, which may introduce errors. However, due to the low scan velocity and low process dynamics, only minor errors are expected. These errors are expected to be most significant at the transition from the melt pool to the transition zone or the solid component in the scan direction. Pixels that fall outside the valid calibration range defined by the manufacturer are skipped in the algorithm. If, after this procedure, any pixels in the HDR image remain without a valid value, they are finally assigned with NaN.
For synchronization, the frame in which the melt pool first became visible is identified in the complete recordings of each camera. This frame is designated as the starting frame and serves to temporally align the different imaging sequences. Once this common starting point was established for the cameras, a temporal linear interpolation of the image data was performed for the MWIR camera recordings. Because the MWIR data exhibited lower temporal variability than the RGB recordings, the MWIR images were interpolated to the RGB time points. To achieve this, the timestamps of the MWIR camera images were mapped to the time points of the RGB camera, so that synchronized HDR images were available for each desired moment. This approach enables a precise analysis and a temporally accurate comparison of the image data from both cameras.
2.3.2 Segmentation of RGB images
The raw RGB images were used for an approximate segmentation into three main regions: the melt pool, the transition zone, and the background. The segmentation was performed on the individual exposure images rather than on the fused RGB HDR image to retain direct control over saturation and contrast. The 5000 μs image was used to determine the outer boundary of the combined melt pool/transition zone region relative to the colder surrounding area, but not to segment the melt pool itself because the hottest region is overexposed. The 500 μs image was then used within this mask to separate the melt pool from the transition zone. The 19 μs image served as a short-exposure reference for the hottest melt pool region and was not used as the primary image for defining the final emissivity-mask boundaries.
The images were first converted to a grayscale and normalized to an intensity range of 0 to 1. Initial segmentation of the combined melt pool/transition zone region was performed on the 5000 μs image using a normalized intensity threshold of 0.85. This image provides sufficient signal from the colder component regions and was therefore used to determine the outer boundary of the thermally affected region. Since the hottest regions are overexposed at this exposure time, it was not used to separate the melt pool from the transition zone. Morphological closing with a disk-shaped structuring element of radius 3 pixels was applied to fill small holes, followed by morphological opening with the same radius to remove small isolated objects such as spatters.
Subsequently, the 500 μs image was used within the previously identified outer mask to separate the melt pool from the transition zone by applying a higher normalized intensity threshold of 0.9. The term transition zone is used here in an operational image-processing sense and denotes the visually distinguishable high-temperature region surrounding the melt pool to which an intermediate emissivity value is assigned. It should not be interpreted as an exact thermodynamic liquid–solid boundary. Candidate values for both segmentation thresholds were evaluated from 0.6 to 1.0 in increments of 0.05. This variation was used as a qualitative check of the sensitivity of the segmentation masks and to identify threshold values that yielded stable and visually plausible results for representative images, particularly with respect to the continuity of the melt pool and transition zone masks. The resulting masks were combined, and the largest connected region was retained and further refined using morphological operations. The final thresholds and morphological radii were then selected manually based on visual assessment of representative images from different tracks and process times.
The emissivity values for these regions were selected based on literature values and are interpreted as effective region-wise emissivities. For the experiments with the inclined build plate, \(\varepsilon \_{\text {melt pool}} = 0.22\) was used for the melt pool [32], \(\varepsilon \_{\text {transition}} = 0.26\) for the transition zone, and \(\varepsilon \_{\text {background}} = 0.4\) for the remaining areas, i.e. solidified tracks and the substrate plate [11, 13, 33,34,35]. For the experiments without build plate inclination, the melt pool emissivity was kept at \(\varepsilon \_{\text {melt pool}} = 0.22\) [32], while effective emissivities of \(\varepsilon \_{\text {transition}} = 0.50\) and \(\varepsilon \_{\text {background}} = 0.80\) were used [11, 13, 33,34,35]. These adjusted values were selected empirically based on the apparent RGB transition regions and the consistency of the corrected temperature profile with the expected solidification plateau of AISI 316L. The comparison with the solidification plateau was therefore used as an internal physical-consistency criterion for selecting effective emissivity parameters and should not be interpreted as an independent validation of the absolute temperature accuracy. They should therefore be understood as configuration-specific effective parameters rather than independently measured material emissivities. To avoid sharp discontinuities, sigmoid functions were used to smooth the emissivity transitions. The smoothing widths were 5 pixels and 30 pixels for the inclined configuration and 40 pixels and 60 pixels for the non-inclined configuration for the melt pool/transition and transition/background interfaces, respectively. The sigmoid widths are numerical post-processing parameters used to regularize the emissivity map and to avoid abrupt jumps in the corrected temperature field. While a gradual transition is physically plausible, the selected widths should not be interpreted as directly measured physical transition widths.
2.3.3 Fusion of RGB and MWIR images
Prior to the measurements, specific images of the calibration target were acquired for the fusion of the individual RGB and MWIR images. A detailed description of the target can be found in Schramm et al. [36]. Using these calibration images, the intrinsic distortions of both cameras, such as lens distortion and differences in focal length, were determined. In addition, an initial homography matrix was calculated, enabling a projective transformation between the image planes of the MWIR and RGB cameras. The registration workflow is illustrated in Fig. 4. It is important to note that this homography matrix is valid only for a specific plane in space [37].
Since the actual measurement setup at the LMD2 facility differs from the plane captured during the calibration images, determining an exact homography matrix for the fusion based solely on the calibration images was challenging. Therefore, the calculated matrix was used as an initial estimate and was iteratively refined using the measurement images. For this purpose, RGB and MWIR images were superimposed, and the homography matrix was adjusted until corresponding process features were spatially aligned. In addition to visual assessment, the melt pool center was segmented in both the RGB and MWIR recordings and tracked over time. The remaining registration deviation was quantified as the Euclidean distance between the melt pool center positions in the transformed MWIR image and the corresponding RGB image.
The projective transformation establishes a projective relation between the perspectives of the MWIR and RGB cameras, compensating for differences in angle of view, position, and scale [37]. In the present optical configuration, the depth of field of the MWIR camera is limited to only a few millimeters. Therefore, the image fusion was approximated by a planar homographic transformation, which is currently the most suitable approach for the available image data. This approximation is appropriate for the observed near-planar component region, but local registration errors may occur for height deviations outside the reference plane. Following this transformation, the MWIR image is geometrically mapped onto the RGB image plane so that corresponding features in both modalities are spatially matched. During this process, the spatial resolution of the MWIR image is simultaneously resampled to match that of the RGB images, as bilinear interpolation is inherently part of the transformation operation. This ensures that subsequent region-based analyses are performed on a common pixel grid, allowing for direct comparison and integration of data from both imaging modalities.
The projective transformation enabled not only the superimposition of the RGB and MWIR images, but also the assignment of the region-specific emissivity values to the corresponding segments in the MWIR images.
First, the temperature values were converted into spectral radiance L according to Planck’s law. For this conversion, a lookup table tailored to the specific spectral and temperature range of the MWIR camera was created beforehand. This lookup table was then used to transform the values of the temperature into radiance. Each pixel of the MWIR images was subsequently assigned the corresponding emissivity value. Since the lower calibration limit was set to 573.15 K, ambient radiation was not considered in the calculation of the corrected radiance, as its influence is negligible. In the next step, the corrected radiance \(L\_{i,j}\) was calculated using Eq. (1), in which \(L\_{i,j}^{\text {meas}}\) is the radiance corresponding to the measured temperature (assuming emissivity \(\varepsilon = 1\)) for pixel (i, j), and \(\varepsilon \_{i,j}\) is the emissivity assigned to pixel (i, j). Finally, the result was converted back into a temperature using the lookup table.
$$\begin{aligned} L\_{i,j} = \frac{L\_{i,j}^{\text {meas}}}{\varepsilon \_{i,j}} \end{aligned}$$

3 Results and discussion
3.1 Processed components
Six experimental runs were conducted using identical process parameters to assess repeatability and to investigate the applicability of the workflow for two different build plate configurations. Three components were manufactured with a build plate inclination of 55°, and three were manufactured without inclination (0°). Within each configuration, the components showed a consistent appearance, with no pronounced differences in morphology or surface quality, indicating stable processing conditions for the selected parameter set. All components were processed using the settings described in Sect. 2.
Representative examples of both configurations are shown in Fig. 5.
The side views show flat and uniform structures without pronounced elevations or depressions. The inclined build plate was used to improve the viewing perspective of the cameras, but it also affects the resulting component geometry. Compared with the non-inclined configuration, the inclined setup led to a flatter geometry, consistent with the broader and shallower melt pool expected under inclined processing conditions [38]. A quantitative analysis of the influence of build plate inclination on track height and width was not performed within the scope of this work.
3.2 Metallography
To investigate the influence of the build plate inclination on the geometry and microstructure of the coatings produced by DED-LB/M, cross-sections of two representative samples were compared. The cross-sections of the coatings manufactured at 55° and 0° inclination are shown in Fig. 6, with the 55° sample displayed in Fig. 6a and the 0° sample in Fig. 6b.
The cross-sections reveal significant differences in the resulting coating geometry. The coating produced at 0° exhibits a greater layer height of 1.012 mm and a comparatively lower dilution depth of 0.27 mm. In contrast, the coating manufactured at 55° shows a reduced layer height of 0.537 mm, but a significantly increased dilution depth of 0.58 mm. This behavior is attributed to the altered interaction between the powder stream, laser beam, and melt pool caused by the inclined substrate position. Due to the inclination, not the entire powder stream reaches the melt pool, resulting in a reduced powder feed into the process. Consequently, the deposited material volume and the resulting melt pool volume are reduced. At the same time, the laser beam has a more direct interaction with the substrate surface, leading to increased energy coupling into the base material and promoting the formation of a deeper melt pool. As a result, both the temperature gradients and cooling rates within the melt pool increase. The higher cooling rates and more pronounced temperature gradients are mainly attributed to the enhanced heat dissipation through the substrate. Compared with the 0° configuration, a larger fraction of the melt pool is surrounded by the substrate in the 55° configuration, allowing heat to be transferred more efficiently into the base material.
The metallographic observations qualitatively indicate differences in the resulting microstructures between the two build plate configurations. The coating produced at 0° appears to exhibit a coarser cellular-dendritic microstructure with larger structural spacings, whereas the coating manufactured at 55° shows a finer columnar-dendritic solidification structure. In addition, the microstructure of the 0° sample appears less directionally oriented. These observations are consistent with different thermal conditions during processing. However, no quantitative grain-size or dendrite-arm-spacing analysis was performed. Therefore, the metallographic results are used here as qualitative supporting evidence and not as a quantitative validation of the corrected temperature fields.
3.3 Recorded images
The cameras recorded the entire processing sequence. For clarity, the processing steps are first discussed using one representative measurement with the inclined build plate. A corresponding centerline temperature profile for the non-inclined configuration is added later for comparison. Figure 7a–d shows representative raw images captured by the MWIR camera during the beginning of the first track. All white areas correspond to regions with NaN values, as these are outside the camera’s calibration range. It is evident that, for the analysis of almost the entire cooling process, fusion into an HDR image is essential, as none of the individual images covers the complete dynamic range. In Fig. 7c and d, small circular features can also be observed outside the melt pool. These correspond to hot spatters ejected during processing.
In the MWIR HDR image (Fig. 7e), the increased dynamic range is visible. However, the substrate plate, the nozzle, and similar components are not visible, as their temperatures are below the lower measurement limit of 573.15 K. These temperatures cannot be measured with the configuration used, as the neutral density filters do not permit sufficient radiation in this range. The basic HDR algorithm yields acceptable results, but distinct discontinuities remain, particularly at the boundaries between neighboring calibration ranges. This effect is especially pronounced at higher temperatures. More sophisticated HDR algorithms could improve the quality at these calibration boundaries, but typically require substantially more extensive calibration effort [39].
Figure 8a–c shows representative raw images captured by the RGB camera at the end of the first track. In the image with the shortest exposure time, the melt pool is particularly well depicted. In the medium-exposure image, the transition zone is clearly visible. While spatter can occur during the process, it is not present in this particular frame. In the image with the longest exposure time, the melt pool is overexposed. However, regions such as the substrate plate, weld tracks, and nozzle outside the region of interest (ROI) are well resolved and clearly identifiable. Figure 8d displays the resulting RGB HDR image. Although spatters can occur during the process and are visible in some individual frames, they are not present in the shown HDR image due to the selected recording moment. If spatters are present, they may appear partially doubled and elongated in the HDR image due to the combination of the medium and long exposure times. Nevertheless, the melt pool, transition zone, and weld tracks are clearly depicted. Laser-induced artifacts are also visible, the red spot in the image can be attributed to the laser.
3.4 Image fusion and validation
The regions, i.e. melt pool, transition zone, and background, within the raw images acquired by the RGB camera were segmented using image processing techniques, enabling the assignment of appropriate emissivity values to each region. These segmented images were then used to calculate the corresponding emissivity map for each frame, as described in Sect. 2.3.3. By combining the emissivity map with the HDR temperature field, a corrected temperature field was obtained. To illustrate this process, Fig. 9 presents the results for the first track of a representative component with 55° build plate inclination.
In Fig. 9a, the RGB HDR image is shown, while Fig. 9c shows the calculated smoothed emissivity map. By combining the emissivity map with the HDR temperature field shown in Fig. 9b, the corrected temperature field in Fig. 9d was computed. To assess the spatial registration, the RGB and MWIR images are overlaid in Fig. 9e.
The registration accuracy was additionally evaluated by comparing the melt pool center positions in the RGB and transformed MWIR images over time. The comparison showed for the inclined build plate a mean center-position deviation of approximately 3 pixels, corresponding to approximately 0.1 mm on the RGB image grid. This value characterizes the residual alignment error of the melt pool position after transformation. Its influence on the corrected temperature field is expected to be most relevant near the boundaries between emissivity regions, where small spatial offsets can change the assigned emissivity. In contrast, pixels located well inside one emissivity region are less sensitive to such residual registration errors.
The planar homography assumes that the relevant image features lie approximately in one plane. This is a limitation for DED-LB/M components with pronounced height variations, which can cause local mapping errors between RGB and MWIR images. In the present study, this effect is expected to be limited due to the comparatively flat single-layer geometry. However, small local registration errors may still occur near track edges and emissivity-region boundaries and can locally affect the corrected temperature field.
For comparison, a line through the melt pool center was selected in one frame of the inclined build plate configuration. This is shown in Fig. 10a. The line of interest is indicated in the RGB image, where the melt pool boundaries can be identified. Figure 10b shows the corresponding temperature and emissivity profiles.
It is evident that the temperature curve for \(\varepsilon = 1\) shows a distinct solidification plateau, which slightly decreases behind the laser (scan direction 18.5 - 20.5 mm). This decrease occurs because the emissivity was assumed to be constant (\(\varepsilon = 1\)), which is not fully representative of the local surface state. Compared with the one-point correction using a constant emissivity of \(\varepsilon = 0.26\), the region-specific correction yields higher temperatures in the melt pool region and exhibits a shorter solidification plateau (scan direction 20.0 - 20.5 mm) followed by an exponential temperature decay. The one-point correction shows a longer apparent plateau, indicating that a spatially constant emissivity can influence the apparent width and shape of the solidification plateau. Consequently, local emissivity variations affect the interpretation of the solidification behavior [12]. Methods such as temperature-emissivity separation (TES) could be helpful in this context [12].
To assess the applicability of the correction workflow under a different observation and process geometry, the same centerline evaluation was performed for a representative experiment without build plate inclination. The corresponding profile is shown in Fig. 11. Similar to the inclined configuration, the corrected temperature profile (red curve) exhibits a pronounced solidification plateau in the expected temperature range of AISI 316L and a physically plausible cooling behavior. This comparison should be interpreted as an applicability check for the non-inclined configuration rather than as a full parametric validation, since the material, layer number, and main process parameters were kept constant. In contrast, the one-point correction using a constant emissivity of \(\varepsilon = 0.50\) (green curve) clearly underestimates the melt pool temperature.
Depending on the selected frame and position, local temperatures below the nominal solidification plateau may occur between the melt pool maximum and the plateau region. These deviations may originate from measurement uncertainties, residual registration errors, local emissivity variations, powder interaction, or limitations of the present region-wise emissivity model. Qualitatively similar temperature-profile shapes in uncorrected or single-emissivity thermographic evaluations have also been reported in previous studies [9, 40]. A possible thermophysical explanation is local undercooling, where the liquid phase remains metastable below the equilibrium solidification temperature until nucleation starts. However, distinguishing such thermophysical effects from apparent effects caused by emissivity variations would require further investigation, for example using high-fidelity simulations and complementary spectral approaches such as temperature-emissivity separation. These methods can provide additional insight, but also require careful calibration and are subject to uncertainty. Configuration-specific effective emissivity values and smoothing widths were required, indicating that the present three-zone emissivity model depends on the observation and process geometry. In addition, slightly different temperature profiles may result from different choices of the width and steepness of the sigmoid transition between emissivity regions, particularly near region boundaries.
The differences in the extent of the plateau-like region within the solidification interval in the corrected temperature profiles can also be related to the observed microstructural differences. The plateau-like region may be associated with the formation of initial nuclei after sufficient undercooling, followed by subsequent grain growth. Compared with the non-inclined configuration, the 55° configuration shows a shorter solidification interval along the scan direction. Assuming a constant scan speed, this corresponds to a shorter dwell time within the solidification temperature range. As a result, the undercooling required for nucleation is reached and exceeded more rapidly, causing nucleation to dominate over the further growth of existing nuclei. This promotes the formation of a finer columnar-dendritic microstructure with reduced structural spacings.
In contrast, the plateau-like region is more pronounced for the non-inclined 0° configuration, indicating a longer dwell time within the solidification temperature range. Consequently, more time is available for the growth of already formed nuclei, causing grain growth to dominate over nucleation. As a result, larger grains and a coarser cellular-dendritic microstructure with larger structural spacings are formed, which is consistent with the observations in the corresponding metallographic cross-section.
In addition to the centerline evaluation for the inclined configuration, an edge-oriented line profile was considered to assess the behavior of the emissivity correction in peripheral track regions, where cooling rates, surface roughness, and oxidation conditions may differ from the center of the melt pool. The corresponding profile is shown in Fig. 12.
These regions are more challenging for the present three-zone emissivity model, because small segmentation or registration errors can shift pixels between emissivity regions and therefore locally affect the corrected temperature.
The edge-oriented profile exhibits a lower maximum temperature than the centerline profile, while still showing a pronounced solidification plateau. This indicates that the emissivity correction remains physically plausible in the peripheral track region. However, the edge region is more sensitive to segmentation, smoothing, and registration uncertainties, because the line crosses emissivity-region boundaries over a short spatial distance.
To investigate the influence of position within the inclined configuration, seven different time points were selected for the first track, as shown in Fig. 13. These points are distributed such that edge regions are also included. The maximum temperature remains highly consistent across all points. Furthermore, the cooling after the solidification plateau becomes slower as time progresses, which can be attributed to the overall heating of the component.
In the region of the solidification plateau, various effects become apparent. For points \(t\_{1}\), \(t\_{4}\), and \(t\_{5}\), the selected emissivity in this range appears to be too high. At points \(t\_{2}\), \(t\_{3}\), and \(t\_{7}\), the plateau shows a slightly undulating rather than a strictly horizontal behavior. This can be explained by the assumption of constant emissivity within each region, which does not account for local variations. For example, the formation of oxide islands can locally alter the emissivity and thus affect the corrected temperature values [40]. In addition, local cooling dynamics could also contribute to deviations within the solidification plateau.
To further investigate the influence of the different tracks in the inclined configuration, an analysis was carried out to determine whether differences can be observed between individual tracks for a measurement point along the scan direction (see Fig. 14). The measurement point remains at the same position along the scan direction and is shifted only with respect to the hatching direction from track to track. The exponential temperature decrease becomes progressively slower with an increasing number of printed tracks, as the component heats up continuously due to the ongoing thermal input. Furthermore, differences in the maximum-temperature region are visible between individual tracks, which can be attributed to variations in melt pool dynamics. In the region of the solidification plateau, both flat and undulating plateaus occur, as also observed in Fig. 13.
3.5 Limitations and sensitivity analysis
It should be stressed that the expected solidification interval of AISI 316L was used as an internal physical-consistency criterion for assessing the effective emissivity assignment. Consequently, the agreement with the solidification plateau does not constitute an independent metrological validation of the absolute temperature accuracy. No independent reference temperature measurement with known local emissivity was available during the DED-LB/M process. Therefore, the corrected temperature fields should not be interpreted as fully validated absolute temperature values. Rather, the presented correction approach improves the physical consistency of the thermographic evaluation compared with the assumption of a globally fixed emissivity.
In the following, two aspects are distinguished: first, limitations related to the model assumptions of the emissivity correction, and second, the sensitivity of the corrected temperature field to selected uncertain input parameters. The Monte Carlo-based analysis therefore quantifies parameter-induced variations within the chosen correction framework, but does not represent a full metrological uncertainty budget.
A central model limitation is the simplified three-zone emissivity description. Constant emissivity values were assigned to the melt pool, transition zone, and background, although the actual emissivity in DED-LB/M depends on temperature, phase state, wavelength, surface roughness, oxidation, viewing angle, and temporal process dynamics. In particular, the effective viewing angle can vary spatially due to the off-axis camera configuration and, for the inclined experiments, due to the build plate inclination. The selected emissivity values should therefore be understood as effective region-wise parameters rather than locally exact material properties.
The RGB-based transition zone should also be interpreted as an optically defined emissivity region rather than as an exact thermodynamic liquid–solid boundary. A direct segmentation based on MWIR temperature thresholds was not used because the apparent MWIR temperature field is initially evaluated assuming \(\varepsilon = 1\) and is therefore biased by the unknown local emissivity. Using solidus or liquidus thresholds before emissivity correction would introduce a circular dependency. Instead, the segmented emissivity regions were derived from RGB images acquired with different exposure times. In the present workflow, the 19 μs image served as a short-exposure reference for the hottest melt pool region, the 500 μs image was used to separate the melt pool from the transition zone, and the 5000 μs image was used to determine the outer extent of the combined melt pool/transition zone region. As a consistency check, the apparent melt pool masks obtained from the 19 and 500 μs images were compared quantitatively and showed comparable overlap, with a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.82 and a mean Dice coefficient of 0.89. Alternative exposure settings, for example 50, 1000, and 5000 μs, would mainly affect the intensity distribution and saturation behavior. If the same thresholds were applied, the segmented emissivity regions could change, especially near region boundaries. If the thresholds were re-adjusted and the relevant regions remained unsaturated and sufficiently visible, the main spatial features would be expected to remain qualitatively similar. Nevertheless, local changes in emissivity assignment and therefore in the corrected temperature field cannot be excluded.
The sigmoid smoothing of the emissivity transitions was introduced to avoid discontinuous changes between adjacent emissivity regions. This is physically motivated by the fact that surface state, phase fraction, oxidation, roughness, and apparent optical response do not change discontinuously at a single pixel during solidification and cooling. However, the selected smoothing widths are empirical regularization parameters rather than directly measured physical transition widths. They were chosen to avoid abrupt emissivity-induced temperature jumps and to obtain physically plausible profiles. Their influence was included in the Monte Carlo-based sensitivity analysis by varying the smoothing widths within predefined ranges.
To estimate the influence of selected input parameters within the proposed correction framework, a simplified Monte Carlo-based sensitivity analysis with 500 samples was performed for the first track of each configuration. The analysis should be interpreted as a sensitivity study rather than as a complete metrological uncertainty budget. The region-wise emissivity values, the widths of the smoothed transition regions, and the residual registration offset were varied within predefined uniform perturbation ranges listed in Table 4. These ranges were selected as plausible bounds around the effective baseline parameters and were not derived from statistically identified probability distributions. For each sample, the corrected temperature field was recalculated and compared pixel-wise with the baseline correction obtained using the nominal parameter set. The reported values therefore represent parameter-induced deviations relative to this baseline correction and not errors with respect to an independent reference temperature.
The emissivity ranges were chosen to cover plausible variations around the literature-based and empirically adjusted effective emissivity values used in the baseline correction. The comparatively broad background ranges account for the uncertainty of the effective emissivity of solidified tracks, substrate material, and surrounding solid regions. The sigmoid-width ranges reflect the empirical nature of the smoothing parameters and cover narrower as well as broader transitions between neighboring emissivity regions. The registration shift range of [− 5, 5] pixels was selected as a conservative bound based on the observed residual RGB–MWIR registration deviations. Thus, the analysis quantifies the sensitivity of the corrected temperature field to plausible parameter perturbations, but does not provide a full uncertainty propagation.
The selected parameter ranges were intended to represent plausible bounds for a simplified sensitivity estimate and should not be interpreted as a full metrological uncertainty budget. The deviation metrics were evaluated within a fixed ROI around the process zone, including regions with measurable temperatures above the lower calibration limit of the MWIR camera. The median and 95th percentile values were calculated within each segmented region and averaged over all Monte Carlo samples. The relative deviations refer to the corresponding baseline-corrected temperature values. The resulting parameter-induced deviations are summarized in Table 5.
The Monte Carlo-based sensitivity analysis shows that the parameter-induced deviations of the corrected temperature field depend strongly on the segmented region and on the build plate configuration. The melt pool region shows comparable median deviations for both configurations, whereas the transition zone, i.e. the optically defined region associated with the solidification plateau, exhibits large P95 deviations, especially for the non-inclined configuration. This indicates that the plateau region is particularly sensitive to the selected effective emissivity and to the smoothing of the neighboring emissivity transitions. For the 55° configuration, the largest deviations occur in the background region, which can be attributed to the broad range assigned to the effective background emissivity and to local boundary effects. Overall, the sensitivity of the corrected temperature field is mainly governed by emissivity assumptions and region-boundary definitions rather than being uniformly distributed across the temperature field. Therefore, the reported values should be interpreted as parameter-induced deviations relative to the baseline correction and not as a full metrological uncertainty budget.
Numerical process simulations could provide additional support for interpreting the measured temperature fields and estimating process-dependent effective emissivity or radiative parameters. However, such models introduce their own uncertainties through assumptions on material data, boundary conditions, heat-source description, powder interaction, and calibration strategy. Consequently, model-derived parameters require careful validation before they can be used to support quantitative temperature assessment. Therefore, numerical modeling is considered a valuable complementary tool for future work, but not a substitute for dedicated emissivity-aware measurement or validation.
The utilized setup is a laboratory configuration with open optical access and external illumination. Thus, the direct transferability of the presented results to industrial DED-LB/M systems is limited. However, several methodological elements of the workflow are transferable in principle, including synchronized RGB/MWIR acquisition, geometric image fusion, RGB-based region segmentation, and region-wise emissivity assignment. In contrast, several parameters are setup-specific and would require recalibration for an industrial implementation. These include the camera arrangement and homography, illumination conditions, RGB exposure times, segmentation thresholds, effective emissivity values, and the smoothing widths between emissivity regions. The additional non-inclined data set provides an applicability check under a different observation and process geometry, but it does not constitute a full parametric validation of the method. The material, layer number, laser power, scan speed, and powder feed rate were kept constant. Further studies with varied process parameters, materials, geometries, and more industrially representative optical access are therefore required to assess the robustness of the workflow across a broader process window.
4 Conclusions and outlook
A workflow for deriving emissivity-corrected temperature fields in laser beam directed energy deposition (DED-LB/M) was introduced. The process was monitored using high dynamic range imaging with both an MWIR camera and an RGB camera, enabling an extended temperature range and improved visibility of the component and melt pool region.
By fusing the MWIR and RGB data through a projective transformation, the segmented RGB regions were transferred to the thermal images and used to assign region-specific effective emissivity values. This enabled the calculation of corrected temperature fields that were more physically consistent than those obtained using a globally fixed emissivity assumption. In particular, the region-wise correction better accounts for the spatially varying optical and thermal conditions in the melt pool, transition zone, and background region.
The corrected temperature profiles showed pronounced plateau-like regions close to the expected solidification interval of AISI 316L for both inclined and non-inclined build plate configurations. This supports the physical plausibility of the workflow for the investigated flat single-layer geometries. However, this comparison should be interpreted as a plausibility check rather than as an independent validation of absolute temperature accuracy, since no independent reference temperature measurement with known local emissivity was available. The different extents of the plateau-like regions are qualitatively consistent with the observed microstructural differences. Shorter plateau-like regions were associated with finer columnar-dendritic structures and reduced structural spacings, whereas more pronounced plateau-like regions were observed together with coarser cellular-dendritic structures.
A simplified Monte Carlo-based sensitivity analysis showed that the corrected temperatures are mainly affected by the chosen emissivity values and by the definition of the emissivity regions. The largest effects occurred in different regions depending on the build plate configuration: in the transition zone near the solidification plateau for the 0° configuration and in the background region for the 55° configuration.
The quantitative interpretation and transferability of the corrected temperature fields remain limited by the simplified static emissivity model, the RGB-threshold-based segmentation, empirical smoothing widths, and residual registration uncertainties.
Future work should therefore focus on transferring the approach to more industrially representative DED-LB/M configurations and on replacing the static region-wise emissivity assignment with spatially and temporally resolved emissivity models. In addition, high-fidelity process simulations and temperature-emissivity separation approaches could provide complementary support for further evaluating the corrected temperature fields and distinguishing true thermophysical effects from apparent emissivity-related artifacts. Dedicated validation experiments with independent temperature references would be required to quantify the absolute temperature accuracy of the proposed correction approach. Overall, the presented workflow provides a practical basis for combining visual segmentation and infrared thermography for emissivity-aware thermal process monitoring in metal additive manufacturing.
Data availability
The raw data for the 55º build-plate attachment angle can be found in https://doi.org/10.48662/daks-501. The raw data for the 0º build plate attachment angle and the processed data (e.g. HDR) is available from the authors upon request.
Code availability
The code used is available from the authors upon request.

technical_points: Experimental setup: 4 kW fiber laser (1070 nm, top-hat), 1.0 mm spot, 10 mm/s scan speed, AISI 316L powder (50–150 μm), 12 g/min powder flow, argon carrier (5 l/min) and shielding (9 l/min) gas; ten adjacent tracks on stainless steel substrate, with and without 55° build-plate inclination.

Imaging: RGB camera at 156 fps with three exposures (19, 500 and 5000 μs) fused into HDR images (~52 Hz) using the Mertens exposure-fusion algorithm; MWIR camera at 200 Hz with four integration times (212, 123, 88 and 402 μs) and neutral-density filters, covering a stated black-body range of 300–2000 °C.

Segmentation: normalized intensity thresholds of 0.85 (5000 μs image, outer melt-pool/transition boundary) and 0.9 (500 μs image, melt-pool/transition separation), with morphological closing/opening (radius 3 pixels); a consistency check between 19 μs and 500 μs melt-pool masks gave mean IoU 0.82 and mean Dice 0.89.

Emissivity assignment: for the inclined configuration, ε = 0.22 (melt pool), 0.26 (transition) and 0.4 (background); for the non-inclined configuration, ε = 0.22, 0.50 and 0.80, with sigmoid smoothing widths of 5/30 pixels and 40/60 pixels respectively; values are described as effective, configuration-specific parameters rather than measured material emissivities.

Correction method: measured temperatures are converted to spectral radiance via a Planck-law lookup table, divided by the per-pixel emissivity (L = L_meas/ε), and converted back to temperature; RGB–MWIR registration used a homography refined on measurement images, with a reported mean melt-pool center deviation of about 3 pixels (~0.1 mm).

Sensitivity: a 500-sample Monte Carlo analysis varied emissivities, sigmoid widths and a ±5-pixel registration shift; deviations were region- and configuration-dependent, with large P95 deviations in the transition zone for the 0° configuration and in the background region for the 55° configuration.

Metallography: cross-sections showed 1.012 mm layer height and 0.27 mm dilution at 0°, versus 0.537 mm layer height and 0.58 mm dilution at 55°; microstructural differences (finer columnar-dendritic at 55°, coarser cellular-dendritic at 0°) are reported qualitatively without quantitative grain-size or dendrite-arm-spacing analysis.
limitations: No independent reference temperature measurement with known local emissivity was available; agreement with the AISI 316L solidification plateau is used as an internal consistency criterion, not as validation of absolute temperature accuracy.

The three-zone static emissivity model is a simplification: real emissivity depends on temperature, phase, wavelength, roughness, oxidation and viewing angle, and the segmentation thresholds, effective emissivities and sigmoid widths were selected empirically and are setup-specific.

The planar homography assumes near-planar features, so local registration errors are expected for components with pronounced height variation; the laboratory open-access setup with external illumination limits direct transferability to industrial DED-LB/M systems.

The Monte Carlo analysis quantifies parameter-induced deviations relative to a baseline correction and is explicitly not a full metrological uncertainty budget; only flat single-layer geometries with constant material and main process parameters were tested.

original_evidence.abstract: Abstract Temperature measurement is essential in metal additive manufacturing, as the spatio-thermal profile strongly influences the microstructure and therefore the key mechanical properties of the produced components. Conventional infrared thermography is widely used for in-situ temperature monitoring. However, its quantitative interpretation is often limited by the varying and generally unknown emissivity of the metal surfaces throughout the build process. This paper presents a pipeline that combines visual and infrared imaging to obtain more physically consistent temperature fields under spatially varying emissivity conditions. A high-resolution visual imaging method is used to segment optically distinguishable process regions. These segmented regions are subsequently mapped onto the corresponding infrared images to enable region-specific effective emissivity settings, resulting in emissivity-corrected temperature fields for surfaces above approximately 600 K. The workflow is demonstrated using a laser beam directed energy deposition system and assessed by comparison with the expected solidification behavior of AISI 316L. The results indicate improved physical consistency compared with a globally fixed emissivity assumption, rather than providing an independent metrological validation of absolute temperature accuracy. Although the workflow requires careful system integration and calibration to account for process-specific factors, it provides an approach that can be adapted to other additive manufacturing systems after appropriate modifications. This supports improved process monitoring and may facilitate the development and validation of predictive process models for metal additive manufacturing.
